study.caution: In TIT 2:13 ('the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ') scholars debate whether one person is meant, with Christ called 'great God', or two (God and Christ). Most modern versions favour the first.

study.summary: No one, nothing, not any. A strong negative pronoun or adjective; with 'except' it often makes an exclusive claim, and the neuter can mean 'worthless' or 'not at all'.

senses.label: No one, nobody
senses.definition: Masculine as a noun: not a single person.

senses.label: Nothing
senses.definition: Neuter οὐδέν as a noun: not a single thing.

senses.label: No, not any
senses.definition: As an adjective with a noun: no … at all.

senses.label: None except (exclusive)
senses.definition: With εἰ μή or ἐὰν μή ('no one … except/unless'), stating that something is true of one person or thing only.

senses.label: Of no account
senses.definition: οὐδέν εἰμι / οὐδέν ἐστιν: to be nothing, worthless, meaningless.

senses.label: In no way, not at all
senses.definition: Neuter used adverbially, or in phrases such as ἐν οὐδενί, meaning 'in no respect'.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John often uses οὐδείς with 'except' or 'unless' for exclusive claims about Jesus: no one has seen God, ascended, or comes to the Father except through him.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses 'nothing' in self-assessment and in rejecting false values: without love he is nothing, circumcision is nothing.

study.translationNote: Greek piles up negatives for emphasis instead of cancelling them (e.g. MAR 15:5, 'answered no longer nothing'; LUK 4:2, 'did not eat nothing'). English must reduce these to one strong negative, so versions vary between 'no one', 'not … anyone', 'nothing' and 'not at all'.

background.note: Homer prefers οὔτις and uses οὐδείς mainly in the neuter, apart from the phrase 'yielding to no one'.
Everyday letters show the same piling-up of negatives for emphasis as Mark 15:4–5.
The spelling οὐθείς was dominant in Ptolemaic times and then died out; its survival in some NT manuscripts reflects an early stage of the text.

study.exegesisTip: When οὐδείς is followed by εἰ μή or ἐὰν μή, the sentence makes an exclusive claim; the exception is usually the point.

study.summary: To know, especially to come to know through experience: learn, perceive, understand. With God or Christ it means personal, relational knowledge, and it can be a euphemism for sexual relations.

senses.label: Come to know, learn
senses.definition: To find out or become aware of a fact; in the passive, to become known.
senses.note: 'Know this' (γινώσκετε ὅτι) introduces something the hearers must grasp (MAT 24:43).

senses.label: Perceive, realize
senses.definition: To notice or see what is going on, often suddenly.
senses.note: Esp. aorist forms (ἔγνω, γνούς).

senses.label: Understand
senses.definition: To grasp the meaning of something said or done.

senses.label: Know personally
senses.definition: To have a personal relationship with someone, especially God or Christ; of God, to know someone as his own.
senses.note: Reflects Hebrew yadaʿ, which includes acknowledgement and relationship.

senses.label: Have sexual relations
senses.definition: A euphemism for sexual intercourse.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: For John, knowing God and Christ is eternal life, a mutual knowing like that of shepherd and sheep. 1 John's 'by this we know' tests whether such knowledge is real, through obedience and love.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul gives priority to being known by God over knowing God, and treats knowing Christ as a transforming relationship.

study.translationNote: One Greek verb lies behind 'know', 'understand', 'realize', 'perceive' and 'be aware'. Translators pick by context and tense: the aorist often marks the moment of realizing. In MAT 7:23 ('I never knew you') and MAT 1:25 the Hebrew-style relational or sexual sense is meant, so versions vary ('knew her not' vs 'had no union with her').

background.note: The letter formula 'I want you to know that…' (γινώσκειν σε θέλω ὅτι) is common in papyri, compare PHP 1:12.
Commands like 'know that…' (γίνωσκε ὅτι) appear in ordinary Ptolemaic letters.
The sexual sense is not only a Hebraism; it is found in Greek as early as Menander.

study.exegesisTip: When God or Christ is the object or subject, read γινώσκω as personal, relational knowing rather than mere information; compare 'being known by God' (GAL 4:9).
study.caution: The traditional distinction between γινώσκω (knowledge by experience) and οἶδα (intuitive knowledge) is often overdrawn. In Koine the two overlap heavily, and John can use them side by side (JOH 8:55).

study.summary: The ordinary Greek word for an adult female, which also serves as the normal word for 'wife'; context alone decides which is meant.

senses.label: Woman, adult female
senses.definition: A female person as distinct from a man, whether married or not.
senses.note: 'Born of a woman' (MAT 11:11; GAL 4:4) stresses full, ordinary human birth.

senses.label: Respectful address: 'Woman'
senses.definition: The vocative γύναι, a courteous form of address that carries no rudeness in Greek, though it can mark distance or solemnity.
senses.note: Abbott-Smith: implies 'neither reproof nor severity', often respect and endearment.

senses.label: Wife
senses.definition: A woman as married partner of a particular man, usually marked by a possessive or a man's name.
senses.note: Idioms: γυναῖκα λαμβάνειν/ἔχειν 'take/have a wife' (MAR 12:19; MAR 6:18); γυναῖκα ἀπολύειν 'divorce' (MAR 10:2).

senses.label: 'Husband of one wife'
senses.definition: In the qualifications for church leaders, μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἀνήρ describes marital faithfulness to a single wife.
senses.note: 1TI 5:9 has the reverse phrase ἑνὸς ἀνδρὸς γυνή of widows.

senses.label: Symbolic woman or bride
senses.definition: In Revelation, a woman figure stands for a people or a city: the faithful community, the Lamb's bride, or the harlot Babylon.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John has Jesus address his mother and others as γύναι at key moments, and Revelation develops the woman as a corporate symbol (the woman clothed with the sun, the harlot, the bride).

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke repeatedly names women among Jesus' followers and early converts, often pairing them with men.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses the word heavily in teaching on marriage and worship, where the choice between 'wife' and 'woman' shapes interpretation.

study.translationNote: Greek has no separate everyday word for 'wife', so versions must choose between 'woman' and 'wife' each time. Where a possessive or husband is named the choice is easy; in passages such as 1 Corinthians 11, 1 Corinthians 14:34 and 1 Timothy 2:11–12 translators differ because the decision changes whether the teaching concerns women generally or wives in relation to husbands.

background.note: From Homer onward the word means 'woman' as opposed to man, and also 'wife'.
The oldest extant Greek papyrus, a marriage contract, uses λαμβάνει ... γυναῖκα γνησίαν 'takes as lawful wife', paralleling the idiom of MAR 12:19.

study.exegesisTip: Look for a genitive, possessive or nearby ἀνήρ: these usually signal 'wife'; without them, start from 'woman' and test the context.
study.caution: Interpreters disagree whether γυναῖκας in 1 Timothy 3:11 means women deacons or deacons' wives, and whether 'woman' or 'wife' is meant in 1 Corinthians 11:3–16, 14:34 and 1 Timothy 2:11–12. Moulton–Milligan thinks a married woman is probably in view in Matthew 5:28.

study.summary: A man, an adult male, as distinct from a woman or a child; also the ordinary word for 'husband', and in Luke–Acts the formal word in addresses ('Men of Israel').

senses.label: Man, male (vs. woman)
senses.definition: An adult male person, especially in contrast with women.
senses.note: Feeding-miracle counts number the ἄνδρες 'besides women and children'.

senses.label: Husband
senses.definition: A man as married partner of a particular woman, normally with a possessive or the wife named.
senses.note: Figuratively of Christ as the one husband of the church (2CO 11:2).

senses.label: Grown man (vs. child)
senses.definition: A mature adult as opposed to a child, and so a picture of maturity.

senses.label: A man, someone
senses.definition: An individual, often little more than 'a certain person', frequently with a descriptive word in apposition.
senses.note: E.g. ἀνὴρ ἁμαρτωλός 'a sinful man' (LUK 5:8), ἀνὴρ προφήτης 'a prophet' (LUK 24:19).

senses.label: In formal address
senses.definition: Plural ἄνδρες with a noun or ethnic name in public speeches: 'Brothers', 'Men of Israel', 'Men of Athens'.
senses.note: Mainly Luke–Acts; ἄνδρες ἀδελφοί is idiomatic for 'Brothers'.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: More than half the NT uses are in Luke–Acts, which uses ἀνήρ where others say ἄνθρωπος or τις, and favours speech openings like ἄνδρες ἀδελφοί.

authorNotes.author: James
authorNotes.note: James uses ἀνήρ almost as 'a person' in proverbial descriptions of the believer.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul's uses cluster in household and marriage teaching, where ἀνήρ is 'husband'.

study.translationNote: Versions choose between 'man' and 'husband' by context, since Greek uses one word for both. In addresses like ἄνδρες ἀδελφοί, some versions render 'Men, brothers' or 'Brothers' while gender-inclusive versions use 'Brothers and sisters' or 'Friends'; and James's ἀνήρ is sometimes rendered 'person'.

background.note: In Augustan-era documents a woman acts 'with her guardian, her husband' (μετὰ κυρίου τοῦ ἀνδρός), showing the everyday 'husband' sense.
A marriage contract uses ἀνήρ for the husband in setting out the duties of shared married life.
ἄνδρες in formal address, as in the speeches of Acts.

study.exegesisTip: Unlike ἄνθρωπος (human being), ἀνήρ normally marks a male, so ask whether the maleness matters in the passage or whether the word is simply idiomatic for 'someone'.
study.caution: Whether ἀνήρ means 'man' or 'husband' is debated in 1 Corinthians 11:3–16 and 1 Timothy 2:12, and the meaning of μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἀνήρ (1 Timothy 3:2; Titus 1:6) is disputed (faithful husband, married only once, not polygamous). How far ἀνήρ in James or in addresses is gender-generic is also discussed.

study.summary: To be able, can: having the power, capacity, opportunity or freedom to do something. Most often found with an infinitive, and very often negated ('cannot').

senses.label: Have power or ability
senses.definition: To be able to do something by one's own strength or authority.
senses.note: Doxologies praise God as 'the one who is able' (τῷ δυναμένῳ, JUD 1:24; EPH 3:20).

senses.label: Cannot by nature
senses.definition: Negated, of what is impossible by the nature of things, a logical or natural impossibility.

senses.label: Spiritual or moral inability
senses.definition: Negated, of a human incapacity rooted in one's condition before God: the unregenerate cannot see, come, understand or please God.
senses.note: Esp. John and Paul.

senses.label: Be prevented, have no opportunity
senses.definition: To be able or unable because circumstances allow or hinder, not because of personal strength.

senses.label: May rightly, be permitted
senses.definition: Of what is fitting or morally possible, close to 'may' or 'cannot rightly'.

senses.label: Be capable (absolute or with object)
senses.definition: Without an infinitive, to be capable or strong enough; with an accusative, to be able to do a thing.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John uses the verb most of all, typically negated, to express human inability apart from God's action (being born from above, being drawn by the Father).

authorNotes.author: Mark
authorNotes.note: Mark sets human 'can' and 'cannot' against Jesus' power and against faith, as in the father's 'if you can' and Jesus' limited works in Nazareth.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews contrasts what the old sacrifices could not do with what Christ is able to do for those who approach God.

study.translationNote: English 'can', 'is able' and 'may' divide what δύναμαι covers in one word; versions differ in passages such as 1 John 3:9, where 'cannot sin' and 'cannot keep on sinning' reflect different weight given to the present infinitive.

background.note: A letter-writer says 'I was unable to meet A.', the everyday sense of inability through circumstance.
δύναμαι with a direct object, as in LUK 12:26.
The popular form δύνομαι, read by Codex Vaticanus in some places, is attested in papyri.
A common verb from Homer onward.

study.exegesisTip: When the verb is negated, ask what kind of 'cannot' is meant (natural impossibility, lack of opportunity, moral unfitness or spiritual incapacity), because the theology of the verse often turns on it.

study.summary: To want, wish or will: the common Koine verb for desire and intention, from a passing wish to settled purpose or consent, including God's sovereign will.

senses.label: Want, wish, desire
senses.definition: To have a desire for something or to do something.
senses.note: With ἤ 'rather than', θέλω expresses preference (1CO 14:19).

senses.label: Be willing; (negated) refuse
senses.definition: To consent or be ready to act; with a negative, to be unwilling or refuse.

senses.label: Will, purpose (esp. of God)
senses.definition: To determine or decide; of God, his sovereign purpose and choice.
senses.note: Formula 'if God wills' (ACT 18:21; JAM 4:15).

senses.label: Take pleasure in (OT idiom)
senses.definition: In Old Testament quotations, reflecting Hebrew חפץ: to delight in or desire someone or something.
senses.note: 'I desire mercy, not sacrifice' (MAT 9:13).

senses.label: 'I want you to know'
senses.definition: Fixed letter formula introducing important information, positive or negative ('I do not want you to be ignorant').
senses.note: Common in papyrus letters too.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul sets 'willing' against 'doing': in Romans 7 the self wills the good but cannot perform it, while God works in believers both to will and to act.

study.translationNote: English uses 'want', 'wish', 'desire', 'will' and 'be willing' for θέλω, and the choice can strengthen or soften a verse. The older 'I will that ...' (e.g. John 17:24 KJV) means 'I want', not a future tense.

background.note: Letters use the formula γινώσκειν σε θέλω 'I want you to know', the same epistolary device as Paul's.
θεῶν θελόντων 'if the gods will' parallels τοῦ θεοῦ θέλοντος in ACT 18:21.
θέλω followed by ἤ 'I would rather ... than', as in 1CO 14:19.

study.exegesisTip: Notice whose will is in view and whether the verb is contrasted with doing or with someone else's will; that tension often carries the argument.
study.caution: Older handbooks (e.g. Strong's) sharply distinguish θέλω (active choice) from βούλομαι (deliberate counsel), but in Koine the two overlap heavily and scholars dispute how far any consistent difference holds.

study.summary: To go or come in, enter: used literally of entering places and persons, and figuratively of entering a condition, especially the kingdom of God, eternal life or God's rest.

senses.label: Enter a place
senses.definition: To go or come into a house, town, synagogue, temple or other space.
senses.note: Usually with εἰς; with διά of a gate or door (MAT 7:13; JOH 10:1).

senses.label: Come in to a person
senses.definition: With πρός, to visit or come into someone's presence.

senses.label: Spirits entering someone
senses.definition: Of demons or Satan taking possession of a person or creature.

senses.label: Enter the kingdom, life, rest
senses.definition: To come to share in the blessings of God's reign: the kingdom, life, the master's joy, glory or rest.
senses.note: Reflects Jewish phrases about sharing in God's coming reign.

senses.label: Fall into a condition
senses.definition: To come into a state or experience, especially temptation, or into others' labour.

senses.label: Come into being, arise
senses.definition: Figuratively, of something entering a realm or a mind: sin and deceivers entering the world, a thought arising, cries reaching God.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews builds an argument on 'entering' God's rest (from Psalm 95) and on Christ's once-for-all entry into the heavenly sanctuary.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew frequently speaks of entering the kingdom of heaven, with conditions attached (righteousness, doing the Father's will, becoming like children).

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John uses the image of entering by the door: Jesus is the door, and whoever enters through him will go in and out and find pasture.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: 'Went in and out among us' is a Hebrew-style idiom for living in close company.

background.note: From Homer onward, 'go into, enter', at first with a simple accusative of the place.
'He has not yet come in from the field', a close parallel to LUK 17:7.
Figuratively, 'he shall enter upon the more serious lawsuit'.

study.exegesisTip: Look at the phrase after εἰς: it tells you whether the entry is spatial (a house), relational (to a person) or spiritual (the kingdom, life, rest, temptation).

study.summary: Law: in the NT mostly the law God gave through Moses (the Torah), but also the books containing it, Scripture generally, law as a principle, and a ruling 'law' or force at work in a person.

senses.label: The Mosaic law (Torah)
senses.definition: The body of commandments given by God through Moses, governing Israel's life and worship.
senses.note: 'Works of the law' (GAL 2:16); 'under law' (GAL 4:5; 1CO 9:20).

senses.label: Pentateuch, the Law as book
senses.definition: The books of Moses as a section of Scripture, often in the pair 'the Law and the Prophets'.

senses.label: Scripture generally
senses.definition: The Old Testament as a whole, even when the passage quoted is from the Psalms or Prophets.

senses.label: Law in general
senses.definition: Law as a category or principle of command, of which the Mosaic law is the chief example; often without the article in Paul.
senses.note: 'A law to themselves' (ROM 2:14).

senses.label: Ruling principle or power
senses.definition: A force or controlling principle that operates like a law, such as 'the law of sin' or 'the law of the Spirit of life'.
senses.note: Esp. Paul.

senses.label: Law of Christ, law of liberty
senses.definition: The norm of life for God's new people: the law written on hearts, the law of Christ, the perfect law of liberty.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Nearly two-thirds of NT uses are Paul's: the law is holy yet cannot justify, it brings knowledge of sin, and Christ is its goal or end.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: In John, Jesus speaks to opponents of 'your law' and 'their law', setting it beside the grace and truth that came through him.

authorNotes.author: James
authorNotes.note: James speaks positively of 'the perfect law of liberty' and 'the royal law' of love, to be done and not merely heard.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews treats the law as tied to the Levitical priesthood, a shadow that 'made nothing perfect'.

study.translationNote: English versions always say 'law', so the differences lie in capitalisation and wording: 'the Law' (capital L) signals the Torah or the books of Moses, while 'law' or 'a law' signals law in general or a principle. Some versions render ROM 7:21–23 and 8:2 as 'principle' to show that Paul is not talking about the Mosaic code there.

background.note: Revenue laws cross-refer to their own sections with κατὰ τὸν νόμον, 'according to the law'.
νόμος with a genitive naming a particular statute, like 'the law of the husband' in ROM 7:2.
Inscriptions use the legal phrase ἐν νόμῳ γέγραπται 'it is written in the law' from the 3rd century BC.

study.exegesisTip: Ask in each verse whether νόμος means the commandments of Moses, the Scriptures as a book, or a principle or power, and do not assume one meaning across a whole chapter (see ROM 7:21–8:2).
study.caution: Whether Paul's anarthrous νόμος means 'law in general' or still the Mosaic law (e.g. ROM 2:12–14; 3:20) is debated, as is whether 'the law of faith' (ROM 3:27) and 'the law of the Spirit' (ROM 8:2) refer to the Torah seen in a new light or to a 'principle'.

study.summary: To write: forming letters, composing or recording a text, or writing to someone. The perfect γέγραπται, 'it stands written', introduces Scripture as lasting authority.

senses.label: Form letters, write by hand
senses.definition: The physical act of writing or tracing letters.
senses.note: Paul's own handwriting authenticates his letters (2TH 3:17).

senses.label: Record, compose in writing
senses.definition: To put something into written form: an account, an inscription, a book.

senses.label: Scripture: 'it is written'
senses.definition: The perfect γέγραπται or καθὼς γέγραπται cites Scripture as a fixed, binding authority.
senses.note: The perfect tense stresses that what was written remains valid.

senses.label: Write about someone
senses.definition: Of Scripture or its authors speaking of a person or event, especially prophetically of Christ.
senses.note: With περί, ἐπί or a dative.

senses.label: Write to someone
senses.definition: To send a written message, instruction or letter to a person or group.

senses.label: Prescribe in writing
senses.definition: To lay down a command or legal provision in writing.
senses.note: 'Moses wrote for us that ...'

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John often states why he writes, and Revelation is full of the command 'Write!' and of names written in the book of life.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul quotes Scripture with καθὼς γέγραπται and insists that it 'was written for our sake'.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew's Jesus answers the tempter three times with γέγραπται, treating Scripture as decisive.

background.note: The root sense is 'scratch, graze'; Homer uses it of a spear grazing a bone, before the sense 'draw' and then 'write' developed.
Legal documents use καθότι γέγραπται 'as it stands written' for the binding terms of a contract, the same authoritative ring as the biblical formula.
An inscription cites a Roman law with ὡς καὶ ἐν τῷ Κορνελίωι νόμωι γέγραπται.

study.exegesisTip: When you meet γέγραπται, read it as 'it stands written' and look up the Old Testament passage cited, since the wider context of the quotation often matters to the argument.
study.caution: Whether John 8:6 and 8:8 (in the story of the woman caught in adultery) belong to the original text of John is disputed.

study.summary: Originally 'order' and 'adornment', in the NT usually 'the world': the ordered universe, the inhabited earth, humanity, or human society organized against God, depending on context.

senses.label: Adornment
senses.definition: Ornament or decoration, especially a woman's outward finery.
senses.note: The oldest sense, preserved in English 'cosmetic'.

senses.label: Created universe
senses.definition: The ordered whole of creation that God made.
senses.note: 'Since the foundation of the world' (ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου).

senses.label: Inhabited earth
senses.definition: The earth as the place where people live, often with 'whole'.

senses.label: Humanity, mankind
senses.definition: The people of the world as a whole, especially as objects of God's love, judgment and saving purpose.

senses.label: Society hostile to God
senses.definition: Humanity as organized apart from and against God, with its values, wisdom and desires.
senses.note: Esp. John; often 'this world'.

senses.label: Earthly goods and affairs
senses.definition: The sum of worldly possessions, pleasures and concerns of present life.

senses.label: A world of (totality)
senses.definition: Figuratively, an entire realm or sum of something, as in 'a world of unrighteousness'.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: Over half the NT uses are Johannine. The world is made through the Word and loved by God, yet does not know him, hates the disciples, and lies under the evil one; Jesus is in it but not of it.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul contrasts 'the wisdom of this world' with God's wisdom, speaks of 'the elemental things of the world', and says the world has been crucified to him.

authorNotes.author: James
authorNotes.note: James uses κόσμος in a strongly moral sense: pure religion keeps itself unstained by the world, and friendship with the world is enmity with God.

study.translationNote: Almost every English version says 'world', which hides the very different senses (creation, humanity, hostile society, worldly goods). Only in 1 Peter 3:3 do versions say 'adornment' or 'adorning'.

background.note: In Homer the basic sense is 'order': κατὰ κόσμον 'in good order, duly'.
The LXX uses κόσμος for the 'host' or array of heaven and earth.
The Priene calendar inscription says Augustus' birthday began 'good news to the world', a striking parallel to gospel language.
A bride's trousseau lists 'clothing and adornment' (κόσμος), the sense of 1PE 3:3.

study.exegesisTip: In each verse ask which 'world' is meant (creation, people, rebellious society or worldly goods); John 1:10 and 3:16–19 shift between them within a few lines.
study.caution: James 3:6 ('the tongue is a fire, a world of unrighteousness') is notoriously difficult; some take κόσμος there as 'ornament'. The scope of 'world' in John 3:16 and 1 John 2:2 is debated theologically.

study.summary: A messenger, someone sent with a message; in the NT almost always an angel, a heavenly being who serves God, brings his messages and carries out his purposes.

senses.label: Human messenger
senses.definition: A person sent to carry a message or prepare the way.
senses.note: MAT 11:10 and MAR 1:2 quote Malachi of John the Baptist.

senses.label: Angel sent by God
senses.definition: A heavenly being sent by God to make known his purposes to people or to act for them.
senses.note: 'Angel of the Lord' (ἄγγελος κυρίου) is frequent in the birth and resurrection narratives.

senses.label: Heavenly court and end-time agents
senses.definition: Angels as attendants in God's presence and agents of the final gathering and judgment.

senses.label: Evil or fallen angels
senses.definition: Angels who sinned or serve the devil.
senses.note: 'A messenger of Satan' (2CO 12:7).

senses.label: Angels as spiritual powers
senses.definition: Angels as part of the unseen order of spiritual beings, beside principalities and powers, sometimes wrongly venerated.
senses.note: Esp. Paul.

senses.label: Angels of the churches
senses.definition: The 'angels' of the seven churches addressed in Revelation 2–3.
senses.note: Meaning debated; see caution.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews argues at length that the Son is superior to the angels, who are ministering spirits, and recalls that the law was delivered through angels.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: Most of John's uses are in Revelation, where angels announce, worship, blow trumpets, pour bowls and mediate the vision.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke narrates many angelic interventions, from Gabriel's announcements to Peter's release from prison and Paul's shipwreck.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul mentions angels in connection with the giving of the law, the coming of Christ in judgment and solemn charges.

study.translationNote: English 'angel' comes from this word, but the Greek simply means 'messenger', so versions say 'messenger' where a human is meant (e.g. John the Baptist, Rahab's spies). In Revelation 2–3 most say 'angel', while a few use 'messenger' to reflect the view that human leaders are meant.

background.note: In Homer an ἄγγελος is a messenger, often a messenger of the gods.
An inscription names ἄγγελοι who are human envoys.
δι' ἀγγέλων 'through intermediaries' in an oath, comparable to GAL 3:19.
A Jewish prayer for vengeance calls on the Lord 'and the angels of God', as in 1TI 5:21.

study.exegesisTip: Decide first whether the context points to a human or a heavenly messenger; then note who sends the ἄγγελος and what message or task it carries.
study.caution: The 'angels' of the seven churches (REV 1:20; 2–3) are variously understood as human messengers, church leaders, guardian angels, or the personified spirit of each church. 'Because of the angels' (1CO 11:10) and 'their angels' (MAT 18:10) are also disputed.

study.summary: To find, whether after searching or by chance; also to discover or find out, to obtain or gain, and in the passive 'be found' meaning 'prove to be' or (negated) 'vanish'.

senses.label: Find after seeking
senses.definition: To locate what one has been looking for.
senses.note: Paired with ζητέω 'seek'.

senses.label: Come upon, meet with
senses.definition: To find or encounter someone or something without deliberate search, or to find a situation on arrival.

senses.label: Discover, find out
senses.definition: To learn or recognize by inquiry, examination or experience.
senses.note: Often 'find no fault/cause' (αἰτίαν) in legal settings.

senses.label: Be found = prove to be
senses.definition: Passive: to be shown or discovered to be in a certain state, often before God's judgment.

senses.label: Obtain, gain
senses.definition: To find for oneself, attain or secure: favour, rest, life, redemption.
senses.note: 'Find favour/grace' is a Hebrew idiom (cf. LXX for מצא).

senses.label: Not be found = vanish
senses.definition: Passive with a negative: to disappear or no longer exist.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke accounts for nearly half the NT uses; the lost-and-found parables of Luke 15 turn on this verb.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: In John the first disciples announce 'we have found the Messiah', while opponents 'will seek me and will not find me'; in Revelation, things that are 'not found' are swept away.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses the passive 'be found' for how a person will be found before God or at Christ's coming.

study.translationNote: English versions mostly say 'find', but some contexts need 'obtain' (Hebrews 9:12, 'obtained eternal redemption'), 'discover' (Romans 7:21) or 'prove to be' (1 Corinthians 4:2). In Acts 19:19 εὗρον refers to reckoning a total, so versions say 'came to' or 'found it to be'.

background.note: A common verb from Homer onward.
A clerk writes 'I cannot find the entry in the books', the ordinary sense of finding after search.
The passive 'is not to be found' of a man who has fled the country, comparable to HEB 11:5.
An acrostic has ζητῶι καὶ οὐχ εὑρίσκωι 'I seek and do not find', echoing the seek/find pairing of the Gospels.

study.exegesisTip: Watch the voice: active 'find' is about search and discovery, while passive 'be found' usually describes how someone turns out or is shown to be, often under God's scrutiny.
study.caution: In 2 Peter 3:10 both the text and the sense of εὑρεθήσεται ('will be found', 'laid bare', 'exposed') are debated, and the ancient manuscripts differ.

study.summary: Sin: the NT's main word for wrongdoing against God, used both for individual sinful acts and, especially in Paul, for sin as an enslaving power that rules humanity.

senses.label: Sin as a ruling power
senses.definition: Sin pictured as a master or force that reigns, enslaves, deceives and pays wages of death, rather than as a single act.
senses.note: Esp. Paul (Rom 5–8), usually singular with the article: 'under sin', 'slaves of sin', 'the law of sin'.

senses.label: Guilt; sinful condition
senses.definition: The state of being in the wrong before God, often in the idiom 'to have sin' = to be guilty.
senses.note: Esp. John: ἁμαρτίαν ἔχειν, 'to be guilty of sin'.

senses.label: Sinful acts; sins
senses.definition: Concrete violations of God's will, usually in the plural, as what is confessed, forgiven, borne or atoned for.
senses.note: Frequent in the phrase ἄφεσις ἁμαρτιῶν, 'forgiveness of sins'.

senses.label: A particular sin
senses.definition: A single sinful deed or kind of sin, in the singular without the abstract sense.

senses.label: Sin offering
senses.definition: In the Septuagint idiom περὶ ἁμαρτίας, a sacrifice dealing with sin; this sacrificial sense is used of Christ's death.
senses.note: Reflects the LXX of Leviticus, where ἁμαρτία can render the Hebrew word for 'sin offering'.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul personifies sin as a king and slave-master that entered the world through Adam, uses the law as a base of operations, and is defeated by Christ's death.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John speaks of 'the sin of the world' borne by the Lamb, links sin to unbelief, and defines it as lawlessness.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews frames sin in priestly terms: sacrifices could not remove sins, but Christ's single offering has dealt with them once for all.

study.translationNote: Most versions render 'sin', but where Paul uses the Septuagint sacrificial phrase περὶ ἁμαρτίας (Rom 8:3) some versions translate 'as a sin offering' (NIV, NLT) while others keep 'for sin' (ESV, NASB, KJV). The same question arises in 2 Cor 5:21, 'made him to be sin'.

background.note: In classical Greek the word can mean simply a failure or mistake, e.g. an 'error of judgement', not necessarily moral guilt.
In philosophy and religion it already meant guilt or sin.
The Septuagint uses it chiefly for Hebrew ḥaṭṭāʾt and related words, giving it its strongly ethical and religious colouring.
A 2nd-century AD confession-inscription warns that whoever meddles with the god's affairs 'shall owe a sin' to Men Tyrannus that he cannot expiate.

study.exegesisTip: Notice number and article: the singular 'the sin' in Romans 5–8 usually means sin as a power, while the plural 'sins' means specific wrongdoings that are forgiven.
study.caution: Whether ἁμαρτία means 'sin offering' in Rom 8:3 and 2 Cor 5:21 ('made him sin') is debated; many see the sacrificial sense in Rom 8:3 but fewer in 2 Cor 5:21.

study.summary: The hand — literally, and by a common Hebrew-style figure, the power, control or agency of a person or of God.

senses.label: Physical hand
senses.definition: The literal hand, used in touching, healing, working, washing or being bound.

senses.label: Laying on of hands
senses.definition: Hands placed on someone to bless, heal, impart the Spirit or commission for service.
senses.note: With ἐπιτίθημι (τὰς) χεῖρας; ἐπίθεσις χειρῶν is a recognised practice (Heb 6:2).

senses.label: Seizing; hostile hands
senses.definition: To 'lay hands on' someone means to seize or arrest them.
senses.note: Idiom ἐπιβάλλειν τὰς χεῖρας ἐπί τινα.

senses.label: Power or custody of people
senses.definition: Being 'in' or 'delivered into' someone's hands means being in their power or control.

senses.label: Agency: 'by the hand of'
senses.definition: Prepositional phrases (διὰ χειρός, ἐν χειρί, σὺν χειρί) mean 'through the agency of' someone, often with little thought of a literal hand.
senses.note: A Hebraism reflecting Hebrew bĕyad, 'by the hand of'.

senses.label: The hand of God
senses.definition: God's power and active presence, whether protecting, enabling, creating or judging.
senses.note: Also 1 Pet 5:6, 'the mighty hand of God'.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses χείρ more than any other writer (71×), often in the biblical phrase 'the hand of the Lord' for God's empowering or punishing presence, and for signs done 'through the hands' of the apostles.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul several times notes that he writes the closing greeting 'with my own hand', authenticating letters otherwise written by a scribe.

study.translationNote: Versions agree on 'hand' for the literal sense, but the Hebraic phrases of agency are often smoothed: 'by the hands of lawless men' (ESV, Acts 2:23) vs 'with the help of wicked men' (NIV); 'by the hand of a mediator' vs 'through a mediator' (Gal 3:19).

background.note: A 2nd-century BC official order warns that no one should 'lay hands' violently on certain persons — the same idiom as in the Gospels and Acts.
In legal papyri ἡ χείρ can mean a handwritten bond or document: 'this bond shall be valid as if publicly registered'.
διὰ χειρός, 'from hand to hand', is common in receipts for cash paid directly, illuminating Mark 6:2.

study.exegesisTip: When 'hand' appears in a prepositional phrase or with God as owner, ask whether it means power or agency rather than a literal limb.

study.summary: Glory: honour or reputation, praise given to God, visible splendour, and above all the radiant, manifest presence of God, which believers will share at the end.

senses.label: Honour, reputation, praise
senses.definition: The good opinion or esteem one has from others; the honour that people seek or receive.
senses.note: Opposite of shame (Phil 3:19) and dishonour (2 Cor 6:8); often paired with τιμή.

senses.label: Glory ascribed to God
senses.definition: Praise and acknowledgement of God's worth, as in 'give glory to God' and the doxologies.
senses.note: δοῦναι δόξαν τῷ θεῷ reflects a Hebrew idiom; doxologies use ᾧ ἡ δόξα.

senses.label: Splendour, brightness, magnificence
senses.definition: Visible brilliance of light or heavenly bodies, or the outward magnificence of kings and kingdoms.

senses.label: God's manifest presence
senses.definition: The radiant majesty of God himself (Hebrew kābôd), seen in the Old Testament cloud and tabernacle and now revealed in Christ.

senses.label: Future glorified state
senses.definition: The glory in which Christ will return and the glorious condition into which believers will be brought.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John sees Jesus' glory revealed in his signs and supremely in his 'hour' of death and exaltation, and contrasts seeking glory from people with seeking it from God.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul speaks of humanity falling short of God's glory, of the surpassing glory of the new covenant, and of believers being transformed 'from glory to glory'.

authorNotes.author: Peter
authorNotes.note: 1 Peter repeatedly pairs present suffering with future glory, following the pattern of Christ.

study.translationNote: The genitive 'of glory' often works like a Hebrew adjective, so versions vary between 'the throne of his glory' (KJV, ESV in places) and 'his glorious throne' (NIV, MSB). In John 12:43 KJV renders 'praise of men' where modern versions have 'glory' or 'approval'.

background.note: From Homer on, δόξα meant 'expectation' or 'opinion' (from δοκέω, 'to think, seem'), a sense absent from the NT.
In philosophy it is 'opinion' as opposed to true knowledge.
The Septuagint used δόξα for kābôd, the visible glory of God in the cloud and tabernacle; this transformed the word into the NT sense of divine radiance.
In a public acclamation an official is hailed as 'the glory of the city' — the ordinary sense of renown.

study.exegesisTip: Ask whether the context is human reputation, praise offered to God, or God's own radiant presence; in Paul and John the last often lies behind the others.
study.caution: In James 2:1 the phrase 'our Lord Jesus Christ of glory' is difficult; some (following Hort and Mayor) take 'the Glory' as a title for Christ as God's manifest presence.

study.summary: A city or town: any walled settlement regardless of size, its inhabitants, and especially Jerusalem and the heavenly city God has prepared.

senses.label: City or town
senses.definition: An inhabited settlement, from small towns like Nazareth to great cities; Greek makes no size distinction, though it is set against villages (κῶμαι).
senses.note: κατὰ πόλιν is distributive, 'in every town' (Titus 1:5; Luke 8:1).

senses.label: Inhabitants of a city
senses.definition: By metonymy, the townspeople as a group.

senses.label: Jerusalem, the holy city
senses.definition: Jerusalem as the city of the great King and centre of Israel's worship.

senses.label: The heavenly city
senses.definition: The city built by God, the goal of the faithful, described as the new Jerusalem.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Half of all NT uses are in Luke–Acts, which traces the gospel's spread from town to town and city to city across the Roman world.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews uses 'city' for the lasting homeland that pilgrims of faith seek, contrasted with earthly cities.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: Revelation sets 'the great city' Babylon against the holy city, the new Jerusalem.

study.translationNote: Because Greek has no separate word for a small town, English versions choose 'city' or 'town' by guessing the place's size (MSB: 'city' 99×, 'town' 61×); Nazareth or Bethsaida may be 'town' in one version and 'city' in another.

background.note: Jerusalem as 'the city of the great King' echoes Psalm 48:2 in the Septuagint.
'The city' standing alone often means the chief city of a district, as with Alexandria in Egyptian papyri.
Weavers wish to settle in Philadelphia, 'hearing the fame of the city'.
Stoics spoke of human beings as citizens of 'the highest city' of the universe, of which other cities are like households.

study.exegesisTip: Do not read size or importance into 'city' versus 'town' in English; check the context for whether the place, its people, or the heavenly city is meant.

study.summary: Kingship, royal rule, or a kingdom; in the Gospels chiefly 'the kingdom of God' — God's saving reign, already breaking in through Jesus and awaiting final fulfilment.

senses.label: Royal power, reign
senses.definition: Kingship in the abstract: the authority or rule of a king, or the period of his reign.

senses.label: Kingdom as realm
senses.definition: A territory or people under a king's rule.

senses.label: God's reign present now
senses.definition: God's saving rule breaking into the present through Jesus' ministry and the Spirit.
senses.note: Proclaimed as 'near' (ἤγγικεν, Mat 3:2; Mark 1:15).

senses.label: God's kingdom yet to come
senses.definition: The consummated kingdom which people will enter, inherit or share at the end.
senses.note: With verbs such as 'enter', 'inherit', 'receive'.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew usually writes 'the kingdom of heaven', a reverent Jewish way of saying 'kingdom of God'; the meaning is the same.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: In Acts the kingdom of God summarises the apostolic message, framing the book from beginning to end.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul speaks of the kingdom mostly as a future inheritance that the unrighteous will not inherit, and also as Christ's present rule.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John's Gospel uses the term rarely, linking it to new birth and to a kingship 'not of this world'.

study.translationNote: Nearly all versions say 'kingdom', but because modern English hears a territory, some scholars and versions prefer 'reign' or 'rule' where God's active kingship is meant. Luke 17:21 is rendered both 'within you' (KJV, NIV text) and 'in the midst of you' / 'among you' (ESV, NRSV).

background.note: Jewish writings in Greek already speak of God's kingdom, preparing the Gospels' phrase.
Ptolemaic decrees refer to 'all those under the kingdom', i.e. the king's subjects.
The word also dates documents by a ruler's 'reign'.
An inscription speaks of the 'eternal rule' of the Romans, comparable to 'the eternal kingdom' of 2 Pet 1:11.

study.exegesisTip: Ask whether the context stresses God's present reign (what it does now) or his future kingdom (what people will enter); the NT holds both together.
study.caution: How 'present' and 'future' the kingdom is in Jesus' teaching is a long-standing debate; Mat 11:12 (βιάζεται: 'suffers violence' or 'forcefully advances') and Luke 17:21 ('within' or 'among you') are especially disputed.

study.summary: Other, another: an additional or different one besides those already mentioned; with the article, 'the other(s)' or 'the rest'.

senses.label: Another, an additional one
senses.definition: One more besides those already named, usually of the same kind.

senses.label: Others; the rest
senses.definition: Other people in general, or with the article the remaining members of a group.

senses.label: The other of two
senses.definition: With the article, the second of a pair.

senses.label: One … another (distributive)
senses.definition: Repeated to distribute among individuals: 'one does this, another that'; ἄλλος πρὸς ἄλλον = 'to one another'.

senses.label: Anyone or anything else
senses.definition: With negatives or exceptions, 'no one else', 'nothing other than'.
senses.note: With πλήν, εἰ μή, παρά.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John's Gospel uses ἄλλος often (with Revelation, 50×); Jesus promises 'another Helper', and Revelation repeatedly introduces 'another angel'.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul alternates ἄλλος and ἕτερος in lists and contrasts, most famously 'a different (ἕτερον) gospel, which is not another (ἄλλο)'.

study.translationNote: In Gal 1:6–7 Paul plays ἕτερον against ἄλλο. English versions handle it differently: 'a different gospel — not that there is another one' (ESV) vs 'a different gospel — which is really no gospel at all' (NIV).

background.note: From Homer, ἄλλος … ἄλλος means 'one … another', occasionally even of just two persons.
Ptolemaic lists distinguish people with the same name as 'Thaesis the other', paralleling 'the other Mary' (Mat 27:61).
The idiom ἄλλ' ἐξ ἄλλων seems to mean 'at sixes and sevens', each doing something different.

study.exegesisTip: When ἄλλος stands near ἕτερος, consider whether the author contrasts 'another of the same kind' with 'one of a different kind', but test it in context.
study.caution: The traditional rule that ἄλλος means 'another of the same kind' and ἕτερος 'another of a different kind' is only a tendency in Koine; whether it holds in 1 Cor 12:8–10 or Gal 1:6–7 is debated.

study.summary: The heart as the centre of a person's inner life — where thinking, willing, feeling and moral-religious commitment happen; occasionally the physical centre of life or the middle of something.

senses.label: Seat of thought and understanding
senses.definition: The inner place where a person reasons, ponders and understands, or fails to understand.
senses.note: Often close to what modern English calls the 'mind'.

senses.label: Seat of will and commitment
senses.definition: The source of choices, desires and loyalties; what one loves, believes and intends.

senses.label: Seat of emotions
senses.definition: Where joy, sorrow, anguish and longing are felt.

senses.label: Inner reality vs outward show
senses.definition: The hidden true self contrasted with lips, face or outward ritual.

senses.label: Physical life, appetite
senses.definition: The heart as the seat of bodily life, refreshed by food or indulged.

senses.label: Centre, interior
senses.definition: The innermost part of something.
senses.note: 'The heart of the earth'.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: For Paul the heart is where God acts: he searches hearts, pours his love into them, gives the Spirit there and calls for faith 'with the heart'.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke often shows people pondering or being stirred 'in the heart', and the heart being opened or pierced by God's word.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews warns against the hardened, unbelieving heart (from Psalm 95) and promises the law written on hearts.

study.translationNote: Most versions keep 'heart', but because modern English 'heart' suggests mainly feelings, some versions use 'mind' or 'inmost thoughts' where reasoning is in view (e.g. NIV Luke 1:51 'proud in their inmost thoughts').

background.note: The Septuagint renders Hebrew lēb/lēbāb, whose range (mind, will, inner self) the NT inherits; it can also mean physical vitality.
In Homer the heart pounds in the chest, already the seat of courage and feeling.
A sayings-papyrus laments people who are 'blind in their heart', parallel to 'the eyes of your heart' (Eph 1:18).

study.exegesisTip: Read 'heart' as the whole inner person — mind and will as much as emotion — and ask which aspect the context highlights.

study.summary: Grace: graciousness or charm, favour and goodwill, God's free unearned kindness and the gifts it gives, and the gratitude that answers it ('thanks').

senses.label: Graciousness, attractiveness
senses.definition: The pleasing, winsome quality of speech or manner.

senses.label: Favour, goodwill
senses.definition: Kindly disposition shown by God or by people toward someone.
senses.note: 'Find favour' (εὑρίσκειν χάριν) is a Septuagint idiom.

senses.label: God's saving grace
senses.definition: God's free, unearned kindness toward sinners in Christ, opposed to debt, works and law.
senses.note: Esp. Paul.

senses.label: Grace as sphere and power
senses.definition: The state of grace in which believers stand, and God's enabling strength at work in them.

senses.label: Gift; concrete favour
senses.definition: A particular gift or enablement from God (e.g. apostleship), or a generous act such as the collection for Jerusalem.

senses.label: Thanks, gratitude
senses.definition: The answering response to favour received: 'thanks be to God'; χάριν ἔχειν, 'to be thankful'.

senses.label: Credit, approval
senses.definition: What earns favour or approval, especially before God.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Two-thirds of NT uses are Paul's; grace is the opposite of earning by works or law, and frames every letter in the greeting 'grace and peace' and the closing blessing.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John's Gospel uses χάρις only in the prologue, where the incarnate Word is 'full of grace and truth' and grace is set alongside the law given through Moses.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses χάρις both for favour with God and people and for the grace of God visibly at work in the church and its mission.

study.translationNote: One version may use 'grace' everywhere, but others vary: 'favour' (Luke 1:30; 2:52), 'thanks' (Rom 6:17; 1 Cor 15:57), 'credit' (Luke 6:32 ESV, NIV), 'commendable' or 'gracious thing' (1 Pet 2:19), and 'act of grace' or 'gift' for the collection (2 Cor 8:6). The Greek word is the same; the meaning differs.

background.note: In Homer χάρις is outward grace or beauty poured on a person by a god.
'Thanks to the gods' (χάρις τοῖς θεοῖς) is a stock phrase in private letters.
The notice of Nero's accession urges all to 'give thanks to all the gods'.
Petitioners appeal to 'the grace of the divine emperor', showing χάρις as a ruler's benefaction.

study.exegesisTip: Ask who is giving and who is receiving: favour from a giver, a gift received, or thanks returned — the same word covers the whole circle.
study.caution: John 1:16 χάριν ἀντὶ χάριτος is debated: 'grace upon grace' (one grace following another) or 'grace in place of grace' (the grace of Christ replacing that given through the law).

study.summary: To go, travel or proceed; also to depart, Jesus' 'going' to death and to the Father, and figuratively to conduct one's life or follow someone.

senses.label: Go, travel to a place
senses.definition: To make a journey or proceed toward a destination.
senses.note: Commonly with εἰς, πρός, ἐπί.

senses.label: 'Go and …' (redundant participle)
senses.definition: The participle πορευθείς introduces another action ('go and learn', 'go and tell'), often adding little more than vividness.
senses.note: A Semitic-style construction.

senses.label: Depart, go away
senses.definition: To leave a place or person, including dismissals such as 'go in peace' or 'depart from me'.

senses.label: Jesus' going: death and exaltation
senses.definition: Jesus' journey to his appointed death and his going to the Father or into heaven.
senses.note: 'Go' as a euphemism for dying has Hebrew precedent (Gen 15:2).

senses.label: Live, conduct oneself
senses.definition: Figuratively, to walk in a way of life, whether in God's commandments or in vices.
senses.note: With ἐν, κατά or the dative; reflects Hebrew hālak.

senses.label: Follow after
senses.definition: With ὀπίσω, to go after someone as a disciple or partisan.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Over half the NT uses are in Luke–Acts, where Jesus' resolute journey to Jerusalem shapes the central section of the Gospel.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: In John's farewell discourse the verb describes Jesus 'going to the Father' to prepare a place for his disciples.

authorNotes.author: Jude
authorNotes.note: Jude uses it ethically of false teachers who 'walk' according to their own desires and in the way of Cain.

study.translationNote: Versions differ on the redundant participle: some keep 'go and' (MAT 9:13), others drop it. In Matt 28:19 most render 'Go', though grammatically the command falls on 'make disciples', with 'going' as an accompanying action. Ethical uses may be translated 'walk', 'live' or 'follow'.

background.note: Everyday letters use the verb for ordinary travel: 'know that I have gone to Heracleopolis'.
An official reply: 'Go; the answer will be given through the strategi'.
Sophocles already uses the verb for how one conducts oneself, anticipating the ethical sense in 1 Pet 4:3.
The Hebrew verb hālak, 'go', serves as a euphemism for dying, a background to Luke 22:22.

study.exegesisTip: When the participle πορευθείς precedes a main verb, the weight usually falls on the main verb; when Jesus is the subject, check whether his journey to death is in view.
study.caution: In 1 Pet 3:19 where Christ 'went' and preached to the spirits in prison — whether a descent to the dead, a proclamation at his ascension, or preaching through Noah — is much disputed.

study.summary: Flesh: physical flesh and the body, human beings in their mortality, natural descent, the merely human sphere, and — especially in Paul — fallen human nature opposed to God's Spirit.

senses.label: Physical flesh
senses.definition: The soft substance of a human or animal body, including meat as food.
senses.note: 'Flesh and bones' (Luke 24:39).

senses.label: The body; bodily life
senses.definition: The whole physical body, or present earthly life lived in the body; 'one flesh' of marriage.
senses.note: Often opposite πνεῦμα as body vs spirit (1 Cor 5:5; Col 2:5).

senses.label: Human beings; mortal humanity
senses.definition: People as frail, mortal creatures; 'all flesh' = all humankind, 'flesh and blood' = mere humans.
senses.note: Also human weakness: 'the spirit is willing but the flesh is weak' (MAT 26:41).

senses.label: Natural descent, kinship
senses.definition: Physical ancestry and family or national relationship, especially κατὰ σάρκα 'by human descent'.

senses.label: Outward, merely human sphere
senses.definition: External, human standards or credentials such as circumcision and status, as opposed to what is of God.

senses.label: Fallen nature opposed to Spirit
senses.definition: Human existence under sin's power, the seat of sinful desire that resists God's Spirit.
senses.note: Esp. Paul (Rom 7–8; Gal 5).

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul (92 of about 147 uses) develops the flesh–Spirit contrast: 'flesh' becomes humanity apart from God, under sin, which believers have crucified and must not live by.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John stresses that the Word truly 'became flesh', that confessing Jesus come in the flesh is a test of truth, and that flesh alone cannot give life.

authorNotes.author: Peter
authorNotes.note: 1 Peter speaks of Christ suffering and being put to death 'in the flesh', and calls believers to arm themselves with the same mind.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews uses 'flesh' for Jesus' earthly life and for merely outward, ritual purity.

study.translationNote: The NIV 1984 often rendered Paul's ethical σάρξ as 'sinful nature' (e.g. Rom 8; Gal 5), while the NIV 2011, ESV and NASB keep 'flesh'. 'Sinful nature' makes the moral sense clear but hides the link with the body and with Christ's own 'flesh'; 'flesh' keeps the link but can sound merely physical. Versions also use 'body' (MSB 18×) or 'human' ('by human descent', Rom 1:3 NIV).

background.note: In Homer the word (almost always plural) means the flesh of a body, eaten by dogs and birds.
The Septuagint renders Hebrew bāśār, which can mean one's own kin — the background to 'my flesh' in Rom 11:14.
Inscriptions use σάρξ simply for meat portions from sacrifices; the word seems not to occur in the papyri.
A Jewish prayer for vengeance from Rhenea invokes 'the Lord of the spirits and of all flesh'.

study.exegesisTip: Ask which 'flesh' is meant: body, humanity, ancestry, outward status, or sinful nature opposed to the Spirit; κατὰ σάρκα can be neutral (Rom 1:3) or negative (Rom 8:4).
study.caution: The meaning of 'flesh' in disputed passages such as 1 Cor 5:5 ('destruction of the flesh': physical death or the sinful nature) and the 'I' of Rom 7:14–25 is debated.

study.summary: A prophet: one who speaks for God and makes his will known — the Old Testament prophets (and their writings), John the Baptist, Jesus as the promised Prophet, and prophets in the early church.

senses.label: Old Testament prophets
senses.definition: The spokesmen of God in Israel's history, such as Isaiah, Jeremiah, Elijah and Elisha, often remembered as rejected and persecuted.
senses.note: Often with the prophet's name: 'Isaiah the prophet' (MAT 3:3; ACT 8:30).

senses.label: The Prophets as Scripture
senses.definition: By metonymy, the prophetic books, and in 'the Law and the Prophets' the Hebrew Scriptures as a whole.
senses.note: 'Reading the prophet Isaiah' (ACT 8:28) means reading his book.

senses.label: A prophet in general
senses.definition: Anyone recognised as sent by God to speak his message, the type of figure the crowds take Jesus or others to be.
senses.note: 'A prophet is not without honour except in his own town' (MAR 6:4).

senses.label: John the Baptist
senses.definition: John, regarded by the people as a true prophet and called by Jesus 'more than a prophet'.

senses.label: Jesus, the promised Prophet
senses.definition: Jesus as a prophet, and especially as 'the Prophet' like Moses promised in Deuteronomy 18:15.
senses.note: The article matters: 'the Prophet' (JOH 1:21) is an expected end-time figure, not just any prophet.

senses.label: Christian prophets
senses.definition: Members of the early church gifted to speak revelation from God for the building up of the congregation, ranked after apostles.
senses.note: With apostles as the church's foundation (EPH 2:20; EPH 4:11).

senses.label: A pagan poet as 'prophet'
senses.definition: Loosely, a revered poet or seer of a non-Jewish people, as of the Cretan Epimenides.
senses.note: Reflects the Greek use of the word for an inspired spokesman.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew's fulfilment formula, 'what was spoken by the Lord through the prophet', frames Jesus' life as the goal of prophecy.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke presents Jesus as the rejected prophet who must die in Jerusalem, the Prophet like Moses, and records active Christian prophets in the church.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John reflects popular expectation of 'the Prophet' and debates over whether Jesus fits it.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul treats prophets as a recognised ministry in the church, subject to testing and order, alongside his use of 'the prophets' for Scripture.

study.translationNote: Versions agree on 'prophet', but differ in capitalisation: 'the Prophets' for the Scripture collection (MAT 5:17) and 'the Prophet' for the expected figure (JOH 1:21) are editorial choices that interpret the Greek article.

background.note: In classical Greek a προφήτης is one who speaks for a god and interprets his will, as Tiresias for Zeus.
The term was used of the minister and interpreter of Apollo's oracle at Delphi.
In Egypt 'prophets' were a rank of temple priests, listed with high priests in the Canopic decree.
A papyrus is addressed by Diodorus, 'prophet' of the god Soknopaios.

study.exegesisTip: Ask which prophet is in view — an Old Testament figure, the prophetic books, John, Jesus as the Prophet, or a church prophet — since the setting decides the authority claimed.
study.caution: Whether 'apostles and prophets' in EPH 2:20 and EPH 3:5 are New Testament prophets (the majority view, given the word order) or Old Testament prophets is debated, as is how far Christian prophecy in 1 Corinthians 14 carried the authority of Old Testament prophecy.

study.summary: To let go: to send away or release, to cancel a debt or forgive sins, to leave or abandon, and to let or permit someone to act.

senses.label: Send away, release, give up
senses.definition: To let something or someone go from oneself: dismiss crowds, divorce a wife, give up one's spirit in death, utter a cry.
senses.note: With φωνήν, 'let out a cry' (MAR 15:37).

senses.label: Cancel a debt
senses.definition: To release someone from a financial obligation, the commercial background of the forgiveness language.
senses.note: In the Lord's Prayer sins are pictured as debts (MAT 6:12).

senses.label: Forgive sins or offenders
senses.definition: To release a person from the guilt and penalty of wrongdoing, said of God, of Jesus, and of disciples toward one another.
senses.note: Object in the accusative (sins) and the person in the dative ('forgive them', LUK 23:34).

senses.label: Leave, depart from
senses.definition: To go away from a place or person, or leave something behind; also to leave something to someone as a legacy.
senses.note: Used of a fever leaving a patient (LUK 4:39).

senses.label: Abandon, neglect
senses.definition: To give up or leave undone something one ought to keep, such as a commandment or one's first love.

senses.label: Let, permit, leave alone
senses.definition: To allow someone to do something or let a thing be, often in the imperative 'let', 'leave her alone'.
senses.note: With infinitive, ἵνα or subjunctive; ἄφες ἴδωμεν 'let us see' (MAT 27:49).

authorNotes.author: Mark
authorNotes.note: Mark's healing of the paralytic makes forgiving sins the point of controversy: only God can forgive, yet the Son of Man has authority to do it on earth.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew ties God's forgiveness to forgiving others, from the Lord's Prayer to the parable of the unforgiving servant.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John uses the verb mostly for leaving and letting; forgiveness appears only in the commission of JOH 20:23 (and in 1 John).

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul seldom uses this verb; for forgiving he prefers χαρίζομαι, and ἀφίημι appears in a Psalm quotation, of divorce, and of abandoning natural relations.

study.translationNote: The same verb is 'forgive', 'leave' and 'let' in English, so readers miss the link between releasing a debt and forgiving sin. The KJV's 'suffer' (MAT 19:14) means 'permit', and 'yielded up the ghost' (MAT 27:50) renders 'let go his spirit'.

background.note: Homer uses the verb of Agamemnon roughly sending away the priest Chryses.
The Septuagint uses it of Rachel's soul departing at death, like 'letting go the spirit' in MAT 27:50.
A creditor 'waived' an extra charge, and the Rosetta stone records the full remission of taxes — the commercial sense behind forgiveness.
A notorious letter says of a newborn, 'if it is a boy, let it be', showing the sense 'let alone'.

study.exegesisTip: Let the object decide: sins or debts mean 'forgive', a person or place means 'leave', and an infinitive or subjunctive means 'let'.
study.caution: What JOH 20:23 grants the disciples — authority to declare forgiveness through the gospel, or to effect it — is debated, partly over the perfect tense 'they have been forgiven'.

study.summary: To call: to summon someone, to invite a guest, God's call of people into salvation and service, and to name someone, often meaning 'to be recognised as'.

senses.label: Summon
senses.definition: To call a person to come, as a ruler or master summons servants or officials.
senses.note: Of Israel 'called out of Egypt' (MAT 2:15).

senses.label: Invite to a meal
senses.definition: To invite someone as a guest, especially to a wedding or banquet.
senses.note: οἱ κεκλημένοι 'the invited guests' (MAT 22:8); 'the marriage supper of the Lamb' (REV 19:9).

senses.label: Call to follow, repent
senses.definition: Jesus' summons to individuals to leave all and follow him, and to sinners to repent.

senses.label: God's call to salvation
senses.definition: God's effective summons by which he brings people into fellowship with Christ, his kingdom, holiness and glory.
senses.note: Often with εἰς of the goal; ὁ καλῶν 'the One who calls' is almost a title of God (GAL 5:8; 1TH 5:24). Also God 'calls into being' what does not exist (ROM 4:17).

senses.label: Name, call by a name
senses.definition: To give or use a name; passive 'be named', and the participle 'called' for places and people.
senses.note: ὁ καλούμενος 'the one called', esp. Luke–Acts.

senses.label: Be called = be recognised as
senses.definition: The passive with a title expresses what someone truly is and is acknowledged to be, a Hebrew idiom.
senses.note: 'They will be called sons of God' = they will be God's sons.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: For Paul calling is God's decisive act in the chain of salvation, and believers should live worthily of it in whatever situation they were called.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke has most uses: the naming formula 'called' for people and places, and the banquet invitations of Luke 14.

authorNotes.author: Peter
authorNotes.note: 1 Peter says believers were called out of darkness, to holiness, to suffer as Christ did, and to eternal glory.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew's wedding-feast parable turns ordinary invitations into a picture of God's call to the kingdom and its refusal.

study.translationNote: English uses 'call', 'invite', 'summon' and 'name' for one verb, so the link between a dinner invitation and God's call (MAT 22) is hidden; the KJV 'bidden' keeps it. 'Shall be called sons of God' (MAT 5:9) means 'shall be', which some paraphrases make explicit.

background.note: The Septuagint uses it for naming a child, as 'you shall call his name Ishmael' — the pattern of MAT 1:21.
A fourth-century invitation reads 'Theon invites you to the wedding of his sister tomorrow'.
The participle 'called' is common for places, as 'to the fort called Posideon'.

study.exegesisTip: Check who calls and to what: a host to a meal, Jesus to discipleship, God to salvation, or a name given — the construction (εἰς, passive with a title) usually tells you.
study.caution: How Paul's 'called' (ROM 8:30) relates to the wider invitation of the gospel — an effective call of the elect or an offer that can be refused (cf. Matt 22:14, which uses κλητοί) — is a long-standing theological debate.

study.summary: Body: a corpse or living human body, the person as embodied (esp. Paul), the resurrection body, Christ's body given for us, the church as Christ's body, and other bodies or substance.

senses.label: Dead body, corpse
senses.definition: The body of someone who has died, especially in burial accounts.

senses.label: Living human body
senses.definition: The physical body as distinct from soul or spirit, the sphere of health, clothing and suffering.
senses.note: Paired with ψυχή (MAT 10:28) or πνεῦμα (JAM 2:26).

senses.label: The embodied self
senses.definition: The body as the whole person living in this world, subject to sin and death yet to be offered to God.
senses.note: Esp. Paul; 'body of sin', 'body of this death'.

senses.label: Resurrection body
senses.definition: The transformed body of the age to come, raised and made like Christ's glorious body.
senses.note: σῶμα ψυχικόν vs σῶμα πνευματικόν (1CO 15:44).

senses.label: Christ's body given
senses.definition: Jesus' own body offered in death, and the bread of the Lord's Supper as his body.
senses.note: Also the temple of his body (JOH 2:21).

senses.label: Church as Christ's body
senses.definition: The community of believers as one body with many members, united to Christ its head.
senses.note: Christ as head of the body is developed in Ephesians and Colossians (EPH 5:23).

senses.label: Other bodies; substance
senses.definition: Bodies of animals, seeds and heavenly bodies, and 'body' as solid reality opposed to shadow.
senses.note: Also σώματα = slaves in the merchandise list of REV 18:13.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul (about 90 uses) gives the body moral and theological weight: it belongs to the Lord, is a temple of the Spirit, will be raised, and furnishes his image of the church.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John speaks of the temple of Jesus' body and dwells on the care of his body at burial.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews quotes Psalm 40 ('a body you prepared for me') and finds sanctification in the offering of Jesus' body.

authorNotes.author: James
authorNotes.note: James uses the body for practical religion: bodily needs, the bridled horse, and the tongue that stains the whole body.

study.translationNote: Most versions keep 'body', but some paraphrase where the sense is the person or the community (e.g. 'yourselves' for 'your bodies' in ROM 12:1, 'parts' in 1CO 12:23). In REV 18:13 the KJV's 'bodies' is now rendered 'slaves', the papyri sense.

background.note: In Homer σῶμα always means a dead body; the living body is δέμας.
Letters speak of 'health of body' and routinely wish the recipient bodily well-being.
σώματα alone means slaves in business papers, as in 'wages for the slaves'.
A Christian letter prays for help to 'body, soul and spirit', the triad of 1TH 5:23.

study.exegesisTip: In Paul, 'body' often means you as an embodied person acting in the world, not just your flesh; do not equate σῶμα with σάρξ.
study.caution: Whether 'not discerning the body' (1CO 11:29) refers to the Lord's body in the Supper or to the church as his body is disputed, as is how far σῶμα in Paul simply means 'self'.

study.summary: To love: to hold someone dear and act for their good — love for neighbour and enemy, for God, God's and Christ's love for people — and also to prize or be devoted to things.

senses.label: Love for other people
senses.definition: Goodwill shown in action toward neighbours, fellow believers, spouses and even enemies.
senses.note: Husbands are to love their wives as Christ loved the church (EPH 5:25).

senses.label: Love for God and Christ
senses.definition: Wholehearted devotion and loyalty to God or to Jesus, shown in obedience.
senses.note: 'Those who love God' is a fixed phrase for believers (ROM 8:28).

senses.label: God's and Christ's love for people
senses.definition: The self-giving love of God and Christ toward the world and believers, shown supremely in the cross.
senses.note: Often with παραδίδωμι, 'loved me and gave himself' (GAL 2:20).

senses.label: Love within God
senses.definition: The Father's love for the Son and the Son's love for the Father.

senses.label: Prize, be devoted to things
senses.definition: To value something highly or set one's heart on it, good or bad — praise, the world, darkness, life, or Christ's appearing.
senses.note: Shows the verb itself is not inherently 'divine love'.

senses.label: Beloved (perfect passive)
senses.definition: The participle ἠγαπημένος marks people as the objects of God's love, and Christ as 'the Beloved'.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John (72 uses, half the NT) makes love the bond of Father, Son and disciples and the test of knowing God; it also names 'the disciple whom Jesus loved'.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul grounds love in Christ's self-giving and sees love of neighbour as fulfilling the law.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke stresses love of enemies beyond reciprocity and the love that answers forgiveness.

study.translationNote: Nearly every version says 'love'. In John 21:15–17 English cannot show the alternation of ἀγαπάω and φιλέω, so some versions add a footnote. In MAR 10:21 'loved him' has been taken as 'showed him affection'.

background.note: In Homer it means to greet with affection; in tragedy, to show affection for the dead.
Plato uses it generally of loving, as poets love their poems and fathers their children.
The Rosetta stone calls Ptolemy 'beloved by Ptah', a close parallel to 'beloved by God' in 1TH 1:4.

study.exegesisTip: Note the object and the context rather than the word alone: the same verb describes God's love, love of enemies, and Demas' love of this world (2TI 4:10).
study.caution: Whether ἀγαπάω and φιλέω differ in meaning, especially in John 21:15–17, is debated; John uses both for the Father's love of the Son, and the popular claim that 'agape' always means a unique divine love goes beyond the evidence.

study.summary: To live: to be physically alive, to conduct one's life in a certain way, to live again after death, to share God's own life, and of God as 'the living God'.

senses.label: Be physically alive
senses.definition: To have natural life, be alive rather than dead, or recover from near death; also to sustain life by food.
senses.note: 'Man shall not live on bread alone' (MAT 4:4); ζῆν ἐκ 'make a living from' (1CO 9:14).

senses.label: Conduct one's life
senses.definition: To live in a particular manner or for a particular master, expressed by adverbs, ἐν or κατά, or a dative of the one lived for.
senses.note: 'Live to God' vs 'live to oneself' (ROM 14:7; GAL 2:19).

senses.label: Live again, risen life
senses.definition: To come to life after death, above all of Jesus raised and alive for ever.

senses.label: Live with God's life
senses.definition: To possess the spiritual and eternal life God gives through faith in Christ, now and in the age to come.
senses.note: Habakkuk's 'the righteous shall live by faith' (ROM 1:17; GAL 3:11).

senses.label: The living God
senses.definition: God as the One who truly lives and gives life, in contrast to lifeless idols; also in oaths 'as I live'.
senses.note: 'As I live, says the Lord' (ROM 14:11).

senses.label: Living, life-giving things
senses.definition: Of things that are active, fresh or give life: running water, a living hope, the living word, a living way, living stones.
senses.note: 'Living water' is ordinary Greek for flowing spring water (JOH 4:10).

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul speaks of dying and living with Christ: believers are alive to God, Christ lives in them, and to live is Christ.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John presents Jesus as the source of life — living water, living bread, the resurrection and the life — and Revelation hails God and the Lamb as the One who lives for ever.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews warns of falling away from 'the living God', calls God's word living, and grounds Christ's priesthood in his always living to intercede.

study.translationNote: The KJV's 'quick' means 'living' ('the quick and the dead', ACT 10:42; 2TI 4:1; 'the word of God is quick', HEB 4:12). Modern versions vary between 'live' and 'be alive', and translate the participle as 'living'.

background.note: The oath 'as I live' renders the Hebrew ḥay-ʾānî, which Paul quotes in ROM 14:11.
Epitaphs commonly record how many years someone 'lived'.
A papyrus speaks of someone 'living or departed to the gods', the plain sense of being alive.
ζῆν ἐκ 'make a living from' is everyday Greek, as in 1CO 9:14.

study.exegesisTip: Check what is attached to the verb — an adverb or κατά (manner of life), a dative (whom one lives for), or a context of resurrection or eternal life — before deciding which 'live' is meant.
study.caution: In ROM 1:17 and GAL 3:11 it is debated whether 'by faith' goes with 'the righteous' ('the one righteous by faith will live') or with 'will live' ('will live by faith').

study.summary: People: a crowd or the general populace, a nation, and above all Israel as God's chosen people — a title the New Testament extends to the church of Jews and Gentiles.

senses.label: The people, populace
senses.definition: The ordinary people or a gathered crowd, often distinguished from their rulers and priests.
senses.note: 'All the people' (MAT 27:25; JOH 8:2).

senses.label: A people, nation
senses.definition: A group united by race, language and descent; in the plural, the peoples of the world.
senses.note: Paired with tribe, tongue and nation in Revelation.

senses.label: Israel as God's people
senses.definition: Israel as the nation God chose and owns, 'my people', often set against the Gentiles.
senses.note: 'Elders/chief priests of the people' (MAT 21:23; MAT 26:3).

senses.label: The laity, apart from priests
senses.definition: The worshipping community for whom the priests offer sacrifice.
senses.note: Esp. Hebrews.

senses.label: The church as God's people
senses.definition: Believers, including Gentiles, as the new people God has taken for his name.
senses.note: Israel's titles applied to the church (1PE 2:9; 2CO 6:16).

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke (82 uses) uses 'the people' for Israel as a whole, often favourable to Jesus and the apostles in contrast with the leaders, and then for the Gentile people God gathers.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews uses the word in a cultic sense: the people for whom priests atone, sanctified now by Jesus' blood.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew frames Jesus' mission around 'his people' and records 'all the people' accepting responsibility for his death.

authorNotes.author: Peter
authorNotes.note: 1 Peter applies Exodus 19 and Hosea to believers: once 'not a people', now God's own people.

study.translationNote: English 'people' hides that λαός (God's people, Israel) differs from ὄχλος 'crowd' and ἔθνη 'Gentiles'. In LUK 2:10 the KJV 'to all people' suggests all humanity, while most modern versions read 'all the people', i.e. Israel.

background.note: The Septuagint uses λαός about 1,700 times, mostly for Hebrew ʿam, so it became the word for Israel as God's people.
In Egyptian papyri λαοί is the usual term for the native peasants, as in a salt-tax on 'the people from Kerkeesis'.
The Rosetta stone uses λαός for the common Egyptian populace as distinct from the priests.

study.exegesisTip: Ask whether λαός means the crowd present, the nation of Israel, or the people of God that now includes Gentiles — especially in Luke–Acts.
study.caution: Whether 'his people' in MAT 1:21 means Israel or the church, and how widely 'all the people' in MAT 27:25 should be applied, are debated; the verse has been tragically misused against Jews.

study.summary: Voice or sound: a human or divine voice, the voice of Christ, any sound or noise, a language, and a spoken utterance.

senses.label: Human voice, cry
senses.definition: The sound of a person speaking or crying out, often 'with a loud voice'.
senses.note: φωνῇ μεγάλῃ 'in a loud voice'; φωνὴν αἴρειν 'raise one's voice'.

senses.label: Voice from heaven
senses.definition: The voice of God or of heavenly beings speaking to people.
