senses.note: 'Today, if you hear his voice' (HEB 3:7).

senses.label: The voice of Christ
senses.definition: Jesus' voice, heard and obeyed by his sheep and by the dead at the resurrection.

senses.label: Sound, noise
senses.definition: Any sound from inanimate things: wind, trumpet, instruments, wings, many waters, thunder.
senses.note: Plural φωναί with lightning and thunder in Revelation (REV 4:5).

senses.label: Language, speech
senses.definition: A language or form of speech.

senses.label: Utterance, message
senses.definition: What is spoken: the words or message of a speaker.
senses.note: By metonymy also the speaker: 'I turned to see the voice' (REV 1:12); 'I am the voice' (JOH 1:23).

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John (68 uses, mostly Revelation) has the shepherd's voice in the Gospel and a constant stream of loud heavenly voices in Revelation.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke often marks key moments with a loud voice and recounts the voice at Paul's conversion.

study.translationNote: The KJV's 'voices' with lightning and thunder (REV 4:5) is rendered 'rumblings' or 'sounds' in modern versions. In Paul's conversion accounts ACT 9:7 and ACT 22:9 versions differ between 'heard the voice/sound' and 'did not understand the voice'.

background.note: From Homer on it is the human voice, as in 'an unbroken voice'.
The Septuagint uses it for 'language' in the Babel story ('one speech').
A sixth-century papyrus refers to 'the Egyptian tongue', i.e. Coptic.
Claudius' letter to the Alexandrians speaks of addressing them 'by word of mouth'.

study.exegesisTip: Ask whose sound it is — a person, God, Christ, an instrument or nature — and whether the stress is on the noise or on the message spoken.
study.caution: How to reconcile ACT 9:7 ('hearing the voice') with ACT 22:9 ('did not hear the voice') is debated; appeals to the genitive vs accusative after ἀκούω are not decisive, and 'sound' vs 'understood speech' is a common solution.

study.summary: Life: natural life and lifetime, but above all the life of God given through Christ — eternal life, entered now by faith and fully in the age to come.

senses.label: Natural life, lifetime
senses.definition: Physical life as given by God, and the span of one's earthly existence.
senses.note: 'Breath of life' entering the two witnesses (REV 11:11).

senses.label: Eternal life, the life to come
senses.definition: The life of the age to come, inherited by the righteous; often simply 'life' as the goal one enters.
senses.note: ζωὴ αἰώνιος; 'enter into life' (MAR 9:43).

senses.label: New life now in Christ
senses.definition: God's life already possessed by believers through faith and the Spirit, in contrast to death.
senses.note: 'Has eternal life' in the present tense (JOH 5:24).

senses.label: Christ the life
senses.definition: Christ (and God) as the source and embodiment of life.

senses.label: Life-giving things
senses.definition: In the genitive 'of life', what gives or belongs to that life: bread, light, water, tree, crown, book of life.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John (64 uses) makes life his central theme: eternal life is knowing God, possessed now by the believer, and found in the Son.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul sets life against death: sin pays death but God gives life through Christ and the Spirit.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew's Jesus speaks of 'entering life' and 'inheriting eternal life' as the goal set against judgment.

study.translationNote: English 'life' translates three words: ζωή (life as God's gift), ψυχή (one's own life or self) and βίος (livelihood). JOH 12:25 shows the difference: whoever hates his life (ψυχή) keeps it for eternal life (ζωή). Some recent translations render ζωὴ αἰώνιος 'the life of the age to come'.

background.note: In Homer ζωή can mean one's living, i.e. property or substance.
The Septuagint's 'living soul' (ψυχὴ ζωῆς) of creatures is echoed in Revelation.
Papyri use it for one's lifetime, 'for the period of her life'.
A magical text speaks of the god 'who breathed spirit into men for life'.

study.exegesisTip: When ζωή appears without qualification in the Gospels or Paul, it usually means the life God gives, not mere existence; check whether it is future (inherited) or present (possessed).
study.caution: Whether αἰώνιος in 'eternal life' stresses endless duration or the quality of the coming age is debated; most scholars see both ideas, with John stressing present possession.

study.summary: To send with a commission: to dispatch someone as an envoy or agent, God's sending of Jesus and his messengers, to send things or word, and sometimes to send away or set free.

senses.label: Commission and send people
senses.definition: To send someone on a mission as an authorised representative, especially Jesus' sending of the Twelve.
senses.note: Cognate with ἀπόστολος 'one sent'; often with infinitive of purpose ('sent to preach', MAR 3:14).

senses.label: God sends his Son
senses.definition: God's sending of Jesus into the world as his authorised agent.
senses.note: 'Whoever receives me receives the One who sent me' (MAT 10:40).

senses.label: God sends messengers
senses.definition: God sending prophets, John the Baptist or angels with a task.

senses.label: Send things; send word
senses.definition: To send an object, or, without an object, to send a message or orders.
senses.note: ἀποστείλας + main verb = 'sent and had…' (MAT 2:16).

senses.label: Send away, set free
senses.definition: To dismiss someone, send them away empty, or release the oppressed.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John builds his Christology on Jesus as the One the Father sent, and Jesus sends his disciples as he was sent; he alternates this verb with πέμπω.

authorNotes.author: Mark
authorNotes.note: Mark links the choosing of the Twelve to their being sent to preach and cast out demons.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke presents Jesus as sent to preach and release captives, and the gospel 'word' as sent to Israel and then the nations.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul rarely uses the verb, but grounds preaching in being sent and his own task in Christ's commission.

study.translationNote: Versions vary between 'send', 'send out' and 'send word', but English cannot show that ἀποστέλλω (as against the general πέμπω) often implies an official commission, or its link to 'apostle'. In LUK 4:18 the KJV has 'to set at liberty'.

background.note: In tragedy it means to send away or banish someone from a land.
An official order directs a man to go 'with the officers sent for this purpose', illustrating the commissioning sense.
In letters it can mean 'send word', as 'send me word how many bundles you have received'.

study.exegesisTip: Ask who sends whom and for what: the sender's authority stands behind the one sent, so receiving or rejecting the envoy is receiving or rejecting the sender.
study.caution: Whether ἀποστέλλω carries a stronger sense of authoritative commission than πέμπω, especially in John where both describe the Father's sending of the Son, is debated; many now see them as largely interchangeable in John.

study.summary: To see: to have sight, to look at or notice something, to perceive or understand, and — especially as a command — to watch out, pay attention or beware.

senses.label: Have sight, be able to see
senses.definition: To possess the faculty of sight, as opposed to being blind; often in healing stories.
senses.note: Contrasted with τυφλός; the healed blind man 'now sees' (John 9:19, 25).

senses.label: See, look at
senses.definition: To direct the eyes toward something and perceive it physically: a person, an object, a vision.
senses.note: τὰ βλεπόμενα 'the things that are seen' = the visible world (2 Cor 4:18).

senses.label: Perceive, discern, understand
senses.definition: Mental 'seeing': to grasp, recognise or find something to be the case, often with ὅτι.
senses.note: In Rom 7:23 almost 'I find' (another law at work); cf. the 'seeing but not perceiving' of MAR 4:12.

senses.label: Watch out, beware
senses.definition: As a warning, especially in the imperative: be on guard against a danger or a person.
senses.note: Constructions: βλέπετε ἀπό 'beware of' (Mark 8:15); βλέπετε μή + verb 'see that no one…' (Col 2:8); βλέπετε ἑαυτούς 'watch yourselves' (2 John 8).

senses.label: Consider, pay attention to
senses.definition: To give careful thought to something or to how one acts.
senses.note: Often βλέπετε πῶς 'take care how…' (Luke 8:18; Eph 5:15).

senses.label: Regard someone's face (partiality)
senses.definition: In the idiom βλέπειν εἰς πρόσωπον, to look at a person's status and be swayed by it.
senses.note: Said (with flattery) of Jesus: 'you do not look at the face of men' = you are impartial.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John 9 plays on physical and spiritual sight: the man born blind comes to see, while those who claim 'we see' remain in their sin.

authorNotes.author: Mark
authorNotes.note: Mark repeatedly uses the imperative βλέπετε for Jesus' warnings to his disciples, especially in the end-time discourse of chapter 13.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul contrasts what is seen with what is unseen: hope and faith look beyond visible things to what is eternal.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews uses the word for faith's perception: 'we see Jesus' crowned, and faith concerns 'things not seen'.

study.translationNote: Most versions render 'see' or 'look', but when the word is a warning (Mark 8:15; Col 2:8) the KJV's 'take heed' or 'beware' and modern 'watch out' convey the meaning better than a literal 'see'. In Mark 12:14 the Greek idiom 'look at the face of men' is rendered 'regard the person of men' (KJV) or 'you are impartial / not swayed by appearances' (modern versions).

background.note: A letter of AD 41 warns a friend 'beware of the Jews' with the same construction as Mark 8:15, showing it is ordinary Greek, not a Hebraism.
An Epidaurus healing inscription says a blind man 'went out seeing with both eyes', close to the Gospel healing language.
A man is described as ὀλίγον βλέπων, 'short-sighted', illustrating the word's primary physical sense.
βλέπω can mean 'find' a state of affairs ('however you find the price, buy'), as in Rom 7:23.

study.exegesisTip: When βλέπετε is followed by ἀπό, μή or a reflexive pronoun, read it as a warning ('beware', 'watch out'), not as an invitation to look.
study.caution: Older works distinguished βλέπω (physical sight) sharply from ὁράω (perception), but in Koine the two overlap widely; the distinction should not be pressed in individual verses.

study.summary: The number two; with the article 'the two' (= both), in the legal phrase 'two or three witnesses', and in distributive expressions such as 'two by two'.

senses.label: Two (cardinal number)
senses.definition: The plain number two, counting people, animals or things.
senses.note: Indeclinable except the dative δυσί(ν) (Matt 6:24). Often in contrasted pairs: two masters, two sons, two covenants (GAL 4:22, GAL 4:24).

senses.label: The two, both
senses.definition: With the article, οἱ δύο refers to a pair already in view as a unit, replacing classical ἄμφω 'both'.
senses.note: 'The two shall become one flesh' (Gen 2:24); Eph 2:15 applies 'the two' to Jew and Gentile made one new man.

senses.label: Two or three (legal minimum)
senses.definition: 'Two or three' as the minimum number of witnesses required, or as a small number gathered together.
senses.note: Echoes Deut 19:15; 1 Cor 14:27, 29 limits speakers to 'two or at most three'.

senses.label: Two by two; in two
senses.definition: Distributive and partitive uses: in pairs, two apiece, or (εἰς δύο) into two pieces.
senses.note: δύο δύο 'two by two' (Mark 6:7) has LXX precedent (Gen 6:19) and parallels in the papyri; the temple curtain was torn εἰς δύο 'in two'.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew several times has two persons where the parallel accounts in Mark and Luke mention one: two demoniacs, two blind men.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke likes paired messengers and witnesses: disciples sent in pairs, two men at the tomb and at the ascension.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: Revelation speaks of God's 'two witnesses', drawing on the legal requirement of two witnesses and on the two olive trees of Zechariah.

background.note: The Septuagint already uses the doubled δύο δύο 'two by two' for the animals entering the ark.
A magical papyrus has κατὰ δύο δύο, 'two by two', showing the repeated numeral is ordinary vernacular, not merely a Hebraism.
Documents use οἱ δύο for 'both', as in Mark 10:8, replacing the older ἄμφω.

study.exegesisTip: Where 'two' (or 'two or three') appears, ask whether an Old Testament witness requirement (Deut 19:15) or a pairing pattern is being invoked.
study.caution: Why Matthew reports two demoniacs (Matt 8:28) and two blind men where Mark and Luke have one is debated: separate sources, a focus on the spokesman in Mark, or Matthew's interest in two valid witnesses.

study.summary: Dead: physically lifeless, 'the dead' as a group (especially resurrection 'from the dead'), spiritually dead or lost, and figuratively ineffective, as of 'dead faith' or 'dead works'.

senses.label: Physically dead, lifeless
senses.definition: Of a person or body no longer alive; also 'as though dead'.
senses.note: ὡσεὶ νεκρός 'like a dead man' (Matt 28:4; Rev 1:17). Of the body as mortal, destined for death (ROM 8:10).

senses.label: The dead; resurrection from the dead
senses.definition: As a noun, usually plural, the dead as a class, especially in ἀνάστασις νεκρῶν and ἐγείρω ἐκ νεκρῶν 'raise from among the dead'.
senses.note: 'The living and the dead' = all humanity under judgment (ACT 10:42; 1PE 4:5).

senses.label: Spiritually dead, lost
senses.definition: Alive physically but cut off from God's life, under sin; also of one lost to his family.
senses.note: 'Dead in trespasses and sins' (Eph 2:1); 'this son of mine was dead and is alive again' (Luke 15:24, 32).

senses.label: Dead to sin
senses.definition: Of believers, no longer responsive to sin's claims, having died with Christ, and therefore alive to God.
senses.note: Paul only; ἐκ νεκρῶν ζῶντας 'as those alive from the dead' (Rom 6:13).

senses.label: Ineffective, powerless
senses.definition: Of things without life or force: faith without works, sin apart from the law, works that cannot bring life.
senses.note: 'Dead works' in Hebrews are works that lead to death or lack life, needing cleansing.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul builds his gospel on God 'who raised Jesus from the dead' and argues in 1 Corinthians 15 that the resurrection of the dead stands or falls with Christ's.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: In Acts the resurrection of the dead is the centre of apostolic preaching and the point that provokes opposition.

authorNotes.author: James
authorNotes.note: James argues that faith without works is 'dead', like a body without the spirit.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews speaks of repentance from and cleansing of 'dead works', and of Abraham's faith that God could raise the dead.

background.note: In Homer the noun means a corpse, especially of those slain in battle.
A public physician's report concerns his inspection of the corpse of a man found hanged.
A woman who lived shunned is described as treated 'as dead' while alive, a parallel to the figurative use in Luke 15:24.
An Epicurean epitaph calls the man who hoards without enjoying 'dead while walking about', a pagan counterpart to living death.

study.exegesisTip: ἐκ νεκρῶν is plural: Jesus was raised 'out from among the dead ones', the firstborn of a coming harvest, not merely revived as a corpse.
study.caution: Some see in ἐκ νεκρῶν (e.g. PHP 3:11) a resurrection of the righteous distinct from a general resurrection; others treat it as equivalent to 'resurrection of the dead'. 'Let the dead bury their own dead' (MAT 8:22) is read as spiritual death or as a proverbial idiom.

study.summary: A slave: a person owned by and wholly subject to a master; used of literal slaves, of believers as belonging to God or Christ, of bondage to sin, and of humble service to others.

senses.label: Slave, bondservant
senses.definition: A person legally owned by a master, as opposed to the free; in parables, a household slave answerable to his lord.
senses.note: Opposite ἐλεύθερος (GAL 3:28; 1CO 12:13) and κύριος or δεσπότης (MAT 10:24; TIT 2:9).

senses.label: Servant of God or Christ
senses.definition: One who belongs wholly to God or Christ and serves at his disposal; an honourable title for apostles, prophets and believers.
senses.note: Echoes the OT 'servant of the LORD' (Moses, REV 15:3); used of all believers in 1PE 2:16 and REV 7:3.

senses.label: Enslaved to a power
senses.definition: Under the controlling power of sin, corruption or something other than God.
senses.note: Adjectival in ROM 6:19: members 'enslaved' to impurity or to righteousness.

senses.label: Humble servant of others
senses.definition: One who takes the lowest place to serve others, Jesus' paradoxical standard of greatness.
senses.note: Christ took 'the form of a slave' (Phil 2:7).

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul calls himself a slave of Christ, reminds believers they were 'bought with a price', and declares slave and free one in Christ, while instructing actual slaves and masters.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John contrasts the slave who does not stay in the house with the son who does, and has Jesus call his disciples friends rather than slaves.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew's parables often feature slaves entrusted with their master's goods and called to account at his return.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke stresses the slave's duty ('we are unworthy slaves') and the believers' prayer as God's slaves.

study.translationNote: The KJV and many modern versions usually say 'servant', while the HCSB/CSB and some others prefer 'slave', and the NASB 'bond-servant'. 'Servant' suggests a hired worker who could leave; δοῦλος means someone owned by a master. 'Slave' is more accurate but can evoke modern race-based chattel slavery, so some versions choose 'servant' for believers (Rom 1:1) and 'slave' for the social institution (Eph 6:5).

background.note: Greeks prided themselves on being 'slaves of no man', in contrast to the subjects of the Persian king.
Inscriptions honour officials as 'slave of the lord emperor', a high-status title comparable to Paul's 'slave of Christ'.
The Septuagint increasingly uses δοῦλος for Hebrew 'ebed, emphasising the distance between God and his servants.
The phrase 'worthless slaves' of Matt 25:30 occurs in a papyrus.

study.exegesisTip: Ask whether a social status, a relationship of belonging to God, or a bondage to sin is in view; the image always implies ownership by a master, not just doing tasks.
study.caution: How far first-century slavery (which could include managers and manumission) differs from modern chattel slavery, and therefore whether 'slave' or 'servant' best represents δοῦλος in English, is debated.

study.summary: An age or long period of time: 'this age' versus 'the age to come', ages past, and, with prepositions, 'forever' or 'never'; in a few places the created universe ('the worlds').

senses.label: Age, era of history
senses.definition: A period of world history, especially in the Jewish contrast between 'this age' and 'the age to come'.
senses.note: συντέλεια τοῦ αἰῶνος 'the end of the age' (MAT 13:39; MAT 28:20).

senses.label: This age as hostile to God
senses.definition: The present world order viewed ethically, under evil powers and opposed to God's ways.
senses.note: 'The present evil age' (Gal 1:4); 'the god of this age' (2 Cor 4:4).

senses.label: Forever; never
senses.definition: In εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα, 'for ever', of unending duration; with a negative, 'never'.
senses.note: οὐ μὴ … εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα 'never' (John 4:14; Mark 3:29).

senses.label: Forever and ever (doxologies)
senses.definition: Plural phrases, εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας (τῶν αἰώνων), intensify 'forever', especially in praise.
senses.note: A Hebrew-style intensifying plural ('ages of ages').

senses.label: Ages past, from of old
senses.definition: With ἀπό or ἐκ, time long past, the ages before the present revelation.
senses.note: 'Hidden from the ages' of God's mystery now revealed (Col 1:26).

senses.label: The worlds, the universe
senses.definition: Plural for the created universe viewed as the sum of its ages or world-periods.
senses.note: 1 Tim 1:17 'King of the ages' may mean ruler of the world-periods or 'eternal King'.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew alone among the Gospels uses 'the end of the age' (συντέλεια τοῦ αἰῶνος) for the final judgment and consummation.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John links εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα to the life Jesus gives (never die, never thirst, never perish), and Revelation repeats 'forever and ever' in worship.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses 'this age' for the present order under sin from which Christ rescues, set against conformity to God's will.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews speaks of the Son through whom God made 'the ages', and of Christ as priest 'forever' after Melchizedek.

study.translationNote: English renderings vary widely because the word combines time and world. The KJV often has 'world' (Matt 13:39; 28:20 'end of the world'; 2 Cor 4:4 'god of this world'), where modern versions read 'age'. The prepositional phrases are rendered idiomatically ('forever', 'never', 'forever and ever'), and plural αἰῶνες in Heb 1:2 appears as 'worlds' (KJV) or 'universe' (NIV, ESV).

background.note: Crowds acclaim the emperors with 'Lords Augusti forever!' (εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα), showing the phrase is ordinary Greek.
An athlete claims to be the only one 'since time began' (ἀπ᾽ αἰῶνος) to win at Olympia, a hyperbolic 'ever'.
εἰς αἰῶνα can mean simply 'for the rest of your life' in a private letter.
The Septuagint renders Hebrew 'ôlām with αἰών; 'ages of ages' reflects Hebrew intensifying phrases.

study.exegesisTip: Let the construction decide: with οὗτος, νῦν or μέλλων it means an era; inside a prepositional phrase (εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα, ἀπ᾽ αἰῶνος) it expresses duration, 'forever' or 'from of old'.
study.caution: Whether αἰών (and αἰώνιος) in itself means unending eternity or a long but limited 'age' is debated, notably in discussions of final punishment (e.g. REV 14:11); context and the intensified plurals carry much of the weight.

study.summary: To throw or cast, with or without force: to hurl, throw into judgment or prison, cast nets or lots, and often simply to put, place or pour.

senses.label: Throw, hurl
senses.definition: To throw an object or person with force, such as a stone, millstone or oneself.
senses.note: Intransitive once: a wind 'rushed down' (ACT 27:14).

senses.label: Cast into judgment
senses.definition: To be thrown into fire, hell or the lake of fire as divine punishment.
senses.note: Often passive ('be thrown'), with God as implied agent.

senses.label: Cast nets; cast lots
senses.definition: Technical uses: to let down a fishing net, or to throw lots to decide something.
senses.note: κλῆρον βάλλειν 'cast lots' (Ps 22:18).

senses.label: Put, place, pour
senses.definition: To put something somewhere without violence: coins into the treasury, a bit into a mouth, wine into wineskins, a hand into a wound.
senses.note: Of liquids, 'pour' (Matt 9:17; John 13:5).

senses.label: Put in prison
senses.definition: To commit someone to prison or custody.

senses.label: Lie ill (passive)
senses.definition: Perfect passive 'having been laid down': lying sick or helpless.

senses.label: Bring, introduce (figurative)
senses.definition: To bring about or put something into a situation: peace or a sword on earth, a thought into the heart, fear cast out.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: Revelation repeatedly uses the passive 'was thrown' for judgment on the dragon, the beast and the wicked; John 15:6 uses ἐβλήθη 'is thrown out' as a timeless aorist.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew often speaks of being 'thrown' into fire, hell or the furnace as the end of the unfruitful and wicked.

authorNotes.author: Mark
authorNotes.note: Mark's account of the widow's offering uses βάλλω repeatedly for 'putting' money into the treasury.

study.translationNote: The KJV renders 'cast' very often, which can suggest violence where none is meant. Modern versions vary between 'throw', 'put', 'pour' and 'lay' according to context (e.g. 'put your hand into my side', John 20:27; 'put bits into horses' mouths', Jas 3:3).

background.note: A calf is 'put' before the sheep with no hint of violence, showing the weakened sense 'put, place' in everyday Greek.
A farmer writes βάλλω of 'manuring' (putting manure on) six arourae of land.
'He will be thrown into prison' (εἰς δεσμευτήριον βληθήσεται) parallels Matt 5:25.
Cuttings are to be 'put' in water at once so they do not wither, another unemphatic use.

study.exegesisTip: Do not assume force: decide from context whether βάλλω means 'hurl' (Rev 20:10) or simply 'put' (Jas 3:3).

study.summary: High priest: in the singular, the Jewish high priest (or Christ as the true High Priest in Hebrews); in the plural, the 'chief priests', the priestly aristocracy in Jerusalem.

senses.label: The Jewish high priest
senses.definition: The head of the Jerusalem priesthood and president of the Sanhedrin, such as Caiaphas or Ananias.
senses.note: Former high priests kept the title: Annas is called high priest alongside Caiaphas (LUK 3:2; ACT 4:6).

senses.label: Chief priests (plural)
senses.definition: The leading priests, including former high priests and members of high-priestly families, who with scribes and elders formed the ruling council.
senses.note: Frequently paired with 'scribes' and 'elders' in the passion narratives.

senses.label: OT high priest (Levitical office)
senses.definition: The high priest of the Mosaic law, who offered gifts and sacrifices and entered the Most Holy Place on the Day of Atonement.

senses.label: Christ the High Priest
senses.definition: Jesus as the merciful, faithful and eternal High Priest who offered himself and intercedes for his people.
senses.note: 'After the order of Melchizedek' (Heb 5:10; 6:20).

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews is the only NT book to call Jesus ἀρχιερεύς: a 'great high priest' after the order of Melchizedek, superior to the Levitical high priests.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John notes Caiaphas was high priest 'that year' and that his words unwittingly prophesied Jesus' death for the nation; Jesus is first taken to Annas.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Acts shows the high priest and chief priests as the main opponents of the apostles, and records Paul's clash with the high priest Ananias.

study.translationNote: The same Greek word is rendered 'high priest' (singular) and 'chief priests' (plural). The plural refers to a group of senior priests, not to several simultaneous high priests; the KJV's 'Annas and Caiaphas being the high priests' (Luke 3:2) reflects the Greek singular ἐπὶ ἀρχιερέως applied to both.

background.note: Herodotus uses the Ionic form for the chief priest of Egyptian cults.
Rare in the canonical Septuagint (usually 'the great priest'), but used for the anointed priest of Lev 4:3, and common in Maccabees.
In the eastern provinces ἀρχιερεὺς μέγιστος translated the emperor's title pontifex maximus.
An inscription calls a priest-king Ἀρχιερεὺς μέγας, 'great high priest', the phrase of Heb 4:14.

study.exegesisTip: Check the number: a singular normally means the reigning (or a former) high priest, while the plural 'chief priests' is the priestly ruling class.
study.caution: Mark 2:26 places David's eating of the bread 'in the time of Abiathar the high priest', while 1 Samuel 21 names Ahimelech; explanations (ἐπί 'in the passage about Abiathar', Abiathar's later prominence, or a slip) are debated. Whether Sceva in ACT 19:14 was a genuine 'Jewish chief priest' or claimed the title is also uncertain.

study.summary: To remain: to stay in a place, continue in a state, endure or last, stay alive, and — especially in John — to abide in a lasting, personal relationship with God and Christ.

senses.label: Stay, lodge, dwell
senses.definition: To stay in a place or with someone for a time, often as a guest.
senses.note: 'Teacher, where are you staying?' (John 1:38).

senses.label: Last, endure, remain in force
senses.definition: Of things and persons: to continue to exist, persist or be permanent, as opposed to passing away.
senses.note: Also negatively: God's wrath or sin 'remains' on someone (John 3:36; 9:41).

senses.label: Remain alive
senses.definition: To stay alive, survive, rather than die.

senses.label: Remain in a state
senses.definition: To continue in a condition or status: unmarried, faithful, a priest.

senses.label: Abide in (relational)
senses.definition: To remain in a close, continuing personal union, as believers in Christ and Christ, the Father, the Spirit or the word in believers.
senses.note: Reciprocal formula: 'remains in me, and I in him' (John 6:56).

senses.label: Continue in, hold fast to
senses.definition: To persevere in teaching, faith or love, keeping to it rather than abandoning it.

senses.label: Wait for, await
senses.definition: Transitively, to wait for someone, or of something that awaits a person.
senses.note: 'Imprisonment and afflictions await me' (Acts 20:23).

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: Over half of all uses are Johannine. John develops 'abiding' into a theology of mutual indwelling: the Spirit remains on Jesus, believers remain in Christ and his love, and God remains in them.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses the word for remaining in one's calling or marital state, and for what endures: faith, hope and love, and the permanent new covenant.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews contrasts what remains with what passes: Christ's permanent priesthood, a lasting possession, and the unshakable things.

study.translationNote: In John's writings the KJV and ESV often use 'abide', while the NIV and many others prefer 'remain'. 'Abide' is old-fashioned but keeps the sense of dwelling in a lasting relationship; 'remain' is clearer but can sound merely static. The same word is also rendered 'stay', 'continue', 'endure' and 'dwell' by context.

background.note: In Homer the verb often means to stand one's ground in battle rather than flee.
A man writes 'I am staying in Alexandria', the ordinary local sense.
Lease contracts say an agreement 'remains valid' in all its terms, the sense of lasting in force.
An epitaph says 'death awaits me too', the transitive sense of Acts 20:23.

study.exegesisTip: In John, μένω ἐν + a person describes an ongoing relationship, not a single act; watch for the reciprocal pattern 'you in me and I in you'.
study.caution: Whether Johannine warnings about failing to remain (e.g. JOH 15:6; 1JO 2:19) imply that true believers can be lost, or show that those who leave never truly belonged, is debated theologically.

study.summary: Power: ability or capacity, God's power at work (often linked with the Spirit), miracles as 'mighty works', and spiritual or cosmic 'powers'; once also the 'Power' as a reverent name for God.

senses.label: Ability, capacity, means
senses.definition: What a person is able to do or afford; the capacity to perform.
senses.note: κατὰ / ὑπὲρ δύναμιν 'according to / beyond means' (2 Cor 8:3). Once of the 'force' or meaning of a word (1CO 14:11).

senses.label: Power, might (esp. God's)
senses.definition: Power in action, above all God's power displayed in creation, salvation, resurrection and the Spirit's work.
senses.note: Contrasted with weakness (1CO 15:43) and with mere outward form (2TI 3:5).

senses.label: Miracle, mighty work
senses.definition: A deed displaying supernatural power; usually plural, 'miracles'.
senses.note: Often with σημεῖα and τέρατα, 'signs and wonders' (2CO 12:12; HEB 2:4).

senses.label: Spiritual or cosmic powers
senses.definition: Supernatural beings or forces (angelic or hostile), and 'the powers of the heavens', the heavenly bodies.
senses.note: Listed with 'rulers' and 'authorities' (Eph 1:21).

senses.label: 'The Power' (name for God)
senses.definition: A reverent Jewish way of referring to God, avoiding the divine name; also claimed by Simon Magus ('the Great Power').
senses.note: 'At the right hand of the Power' (Mark 14:62).

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: For Paul the gospel and the message of the cross are themselves God's power, and that power is shown in human weakness.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke closely links power with the Holy Spirit, from Jesus' conception and ministry to the promise to the disciples.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: The Synoptic Gospels, Matthew especially, call Jesus' miracles δυνάμεις, 'mighty works', which should lead to repentance.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: The Gospel of John never uses the word (preferring 'signs'); the Johannine uses are in Revelation, mostly in hymns ascribing power to God and the Lamb.

study.translationNote: Most versions translate 'power', but the plural is rendered 'miracles' (NIV), 'mighty works' (ESV, RSV) or 'wonderful works' (KJV, Matt 7:22). Because 'powers' in English can mean either abilities, miracles or spiritual beings, versions differ in passages like Matt 24:29 ('powers of the heavens' vs 'heavenly bodies').

background.note: In Homer the word denotes bodily strength or ability.
Marriage contracts promise to support a wife κατὰ δύναμιν, 'according to one's means', as in 2 Cor 8:3.
A Lydian inscription honours a god as 'the great power of the immortal God', illuminating the claim about Simon in Acts 8:10.
In the plural the word also means military forces, the background of 'hosts' (LXX for צָבָא).

study.exegesisTip: Singular δύναμις is usually 'power'; the plural can mean 'miracles' or 'powers' (beings) — let the verb (ποιεῖν 'perform') or a list of rulers decide.
study.caution: The popular claim that δύναμις means 'dynamite' is anachronistic: the English word derives from the Greek, not the reverse, and Paul's 'power of God' (ROM 1:16) should not be read through explosive imagery.

study.summary: To go away, depart; also simply to go somewhere, to go after (follow), and of conditions or things, to pass away or leave.

senses.label: Go away, depart, leave
senses.definition: To leave a place or person, with the emphasis on departure.
senses.note: Of disciples turning away from Jesus (JOH 6:66) or the rich man going away sad (MAT 19:22).

senses.label: Go to a destination
senses.definition: To go to a place or person, the thought moving on to the goal (sometimes 'arrive').
senses.note: Also of final destiny: 'these will go away into eternal punishment' (MAT 25:46).

senses.label: 'Went and …' (with another verb)
senses.definition: The participle ἀπελθών often simply introduces the main action, 'went and did'.
senses.note: Partly reflects a Semitic narrative style.

senses.label: Go after, follow
senses.definition: With ὀπίσω, to follow someone as a disciple, or (negatively) to pursue something.
senses.note: Septuagint idiom from Hebrew 'go after'.

senses.label: Pass away, leave (of things)
senses.definition: Of diseases, troubles or the old creation: to depart, cease, be gone.
senses.note: 'The leprosy left him' (Luke 5:13); 'the former things have passed away' (Rev 21:4).

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John uses the verb for Jesus' necessary 'going away' to the Father, and for disciples who turn back; Revelation uses it of woes and of the old creation passing away.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew frequently uses the participle ἀπελθών as a narrative link, and ends the judgment scene with 'these will go away into eternal punishment'.

background.note: Homer uses it of departing from one's homeland.
A son writes to his father of the time when he will have 'departed to the gods', a euphemism for death.
A Christian epitaph says a young woman 'departed to the bright land'.
In later Greek the verb can look to the goal, 'arrive at' or 'come near' a person.

study.exegesisTip: Do not over-translate ἀπελθών before another verb; often it simply means 'went and…'.

study.summary: Death: the end of bodily life, death as a judicial penalty, Christ's saving death, death as a hostile power, spiritual and final separation from God, and (in Revelation) deadly pestilence.

senses.label: Physical death
senses.definition: The end of bodily life, whether natural or violent; also mortal danger that threatens it.
senses.note: Idioms: 'see death' (LUK 2:26), 'taste death' (MAR 9:1), 'sorrowful to the point of death' (MAT 26:38); plural 'deaths' = deadly perils (2CO 11:23).

senses.label: Death as legal penalty
senses.definition: Execution as the sentence of a court or of the Law; a crime 'worthy of death'.
senses.note: ἄξιος / ἔνοχος θανάτου 'deserving death'; θανάτῳ τελευτάτω 'let him surely die' reproduces the Hebrew idiom of EXO 21:17.

senses.label: Christ's death
senses.definition: Jesus' death on the cross as the saving event believers share in and proclaim.

senses.label: Death as a ruling power
senses.definition: Death personified as an enemy that reigns over humanity since Adam and is finally destroyed.
senses.note: Paired with Hades in Revelation (REV 6:8; REV 20:14).

senses.label: Spiritual and eternal death
senses.definition: Separation from God's life as the fruit of sin, now and finally; 'the second death' is final judgment.
senses.note: 'The second death' is a Revelation phrase (REV 2:11; REV 20:6; REV 20:14).

senses.label: Pestilence, deadly plague
senses.definition: A deadly epidemic, reflecting Septuagint use of θάνατος for Hebrew deber 'plague'.
senses.note: In REV 6:8 the word appears twice: the rider named Death, then 'killing with … pestilence'.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul treats death as a power that entered through Adam's sin, is the wages of sin and draws its sting from sin and the Law, and is defeated in Christ's death and resurrection.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John speaks of believers already having 'passed from death to life' and never 'seeing' death; the narrator notes 'by what kind of death' Jesus and Peter would glorify God. Revelation adds the 'second death'.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews presents Jesus tasting death for everyone in order to destroy the devil who held the power of death and free those enslaved by fear of it.

study.translationNote: Almost always 'death'. In Revelation some versions render it 'pestilence' or 'plague' (e.g. ESV, NRSV at Rev 6:8; 18:8) where the Septuagint sense of deber is in view, while KJV keeps 'death'. 'The shadow of death' (MAT 4:16; LUK 1:79) follows the Septuagint reading of Hebrew ṣalmāwet, which some modern OT versions take as 'deep darkness'.

background.note: From Homer on the ordinary word for death, natural or violent; θάνατόνδε 'to death'.
θανάτῳ τελευτάτω 'let him die the death' renders the Hebrew infinitive-plus-verb idiom môt yûmāt, quoted by Jesus in Mark 7:10.
The Jerusalem temple warning inscription threatens death to any non-Jew entering the inner court — background to the riot of Acts 21.
A papyrus speaks of many who 'preferred death to life', showing the everyday life–death antithesis.

study.exegesisTip: Ask whether 'death' is the physical event, a court sentence, a personified power, spiritual separation from God, or (in Revelation) plague; Paul can move between these within a few verses (ROM 5:12–21; ROM 6:23).
study.caution: Whether 'death' that came through Adam's sin (ROM 5:12) is physical, spiritual or both is debated, as is the meaning of 'sin leading to death' in 1JO 5:16.

study.summary: To hand over: give or entrust something to someone, deliver a person into custody or to death, betray, give people up to a power, give oneself up, and pass on tradition.

senses.label: Hand over, entrust, commend
senses.definition: To give something into another's keeping or control, or commit someone to God's care.
senses.note: Commit to God's grace (ACT 15:40); Jesus 'entrusted himself' to the just Judge (1PE 2:23); 'risked/devoted their lives' (ACT 15:26). In MAR 4:29 the crop 'permits' (is ripe).

senses.label: Deliver into custody, judgment
senses.definition: To hand a person over to authorities for arrest, trial, imprisonment or execution.
senses.note: Also of disciples handed over to councils (MAT 10:17) and prisoners transferred (ACT 28:16).

senses.label: Betray
senses.definition: To hand someone over treacherously to enemies, especially Judas handing Jesus over.
senses.note: ὁ παραδιδούς 'the one handing him over' = 'the betrayer' (MAR 14:42; JOH 13:11). Treachery comes from context; the verb itself means 'hand over'.

senses.label: Give people up to a power
senses.definition: God's judicial act of abandoning people to the consequences they chose; also handing someone over to Satan for discipline.
senses.note: Reflexive in EPH 4:19 (they gave themselves up to sensuality); church discipline in 1CO 5:5 and 1TI 1:20.

senses.label: Christ given up for us
senses.definition: Christ handed over to death by God for our sins, or giving himself up out of love.
senses.note: JOH 19:30 'he gave up his spirit'. The passion predictions' passive 'will be handed over' (MAR 9:31) may imply God as agent.

senses.label: Hand down tradition
senses.definition: To pass on teaching, practices or a body of faith received from others.
senses.note: Correlative with παραλαμβάνω 'receive' (1CO 11:23; 1CO 15:3), the language of formal transmission; cf. ROM 6:17 'the pattern of teaching to which you were handed over'.

authorNotes.author: Mark
authorNotes.note: Mark builds a chain of 'handings over': John is handed over, then Jesus (by Judas, the Sanhedrin and Pilate), and the disciples will be too.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses the verb for God's giving people up to their desires, for Christ's self-giving love, and for the apostolic handing on of tradition.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John stresses Jesus' foreknowledge of who would hand him over and closes with Jesus himself 'handing over' his spirit.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses the verb of eyewitness tradition handed down and of decrees delivered to the churches.

study.translationNote: Versions choose between 'betray' and the more neutral 'hand over/deliver up'. KJV and most modern versions say Judas 'betrayed' Jesus, but some (e.g. NABRE at 1 Cor 11:23, 'the night he was handed over') keep the neutral sense, since the same verb is used of God and of Christ himself (ROM 8:32; GAL 2:20). Elsewhere renderings vary with context: 'commend', 'commit', 'pass on', 'give up'.

background.note: Plato speaks of handing on life to the next generation 'like a torch' — the verb of transmission.
Leases pair 'I will hand over' with 'as I received', the same correlation as Paul's tradition language.
A prisoner 'was handed over to Paos the gaoler' — the custodial sense.
A magical curse says 'I hand you over to black chaos', comparable in form to handing someone over to Satan (1 Cor 5:5).

study.exegesisTip: Identify who hands over whom to whom: Judas, the leaders, Pilate, God or Christ himself can all be the subject of the same verb in the passion story.
study.caution: What 'handing over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh' (1CO 5:5) involves — excommunication, physical affliction, or both — is debated; and some scholars argue Judas's act should be read as 'handing over' rather than 'betrayal', though the Gospels' context clearly portrays treachery.

study.summary: To seek: look for someone or something, try to do something, plot against a life, strive after a goal, seek God, or require and demand.

senses.label: Look for, search
senses.definition: To try to find a person or thing that is missing or wanted; also to inquire or discuss.
senses.note: Of inquiry or discussion: JOH 16:19.

senses.label: Seek to kill, plot
senses.definition: To seek someone's life; to look for a way to destroy or arrest them.
senses.note: ζητεῖν τὴν ψυχήν 'seek the life' is a Septuagint idiom (EXO 4:19).

senses.label: Try, attempt
senses.definition: With an infinitive: to try or endeavour to do something.
senses.note: Often imperfect ἐζήτει/ἐζήτουν 'kept trying'.

senses.label: Strive after, aim at
senses.definition: To set one's heart on a goal or value and pursue it.
senses.note: Negative: seeking one's own interests or human glory (PHP 2:21; 1TH 2:6).

senses.label: Seek God; God seeks people
senses.definition: To turn to God in search and prayer; also God or Christ seeking out people.
senses.note: 'Seek and you will find' (MAT 7:7); the Son of Man came 'to seek and to save the lost' (LUK 19:10).

senses.label: Require, demand
senses.definition: To ask for something as a requirement or proof; passive 'it is required'.
senses.note: Demanding a sign (MAR 8:11–12; LUK 11:29).

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John repeatedly notes that the authorities 'were seeking to kill' Jesus, contrasts seeking one's own glory with seeking God's, and frames discipleship with the question 'What/whom are you seeking?'.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke often uses the conative imperfect for people 'trying' to see, touch or reach Jesus, and states his mission as seeking the lost.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul makes not seeking one's own advantage a mark of love and of genuine ministry.

study.translationNote: English versions vary between 'seek', 'look for', 'search for' and 'try', depending on whether the object is a person, a goal or an infinitive. In 1CO 1:22 the verb is often rendered 'seek' or 'look for' wisdom, while in 1CO 4:2 and LUK 12:48 it means 'required'.

background.note: The verb occurs only once in Homer, of Zeus searching for Sleep.
The idiom 'seek someone's life' comes from the Septuagint rendering of Hebrew biqqēš nep̄eš.
A schoolroom acrostic reads 'I seek and do not find', a common pairing with εὑρίσκω.
An Oxyrhynchus logion says the seeker should not stop until he finds, recalling Matt 7:7.

study.exegesisTip: With an imperfect plus infinitive (ἐζήτουν ἀποκτεῖναι, JOH 5:18) read 'were trying to' — an attempt not yet carried out.
study.caution: Strong's gloss 'to worship God' (by Hebraism) overstates the case: 'seeking God' (ACT 17:27) means turning to him, not a technical term for worship.

study.summary: Love: the self-giving goodwill and devotion that God shows to people and to Christ, that believers show to God and one another, and (in the plural) the church's 'love feasts'.

senses.label: Love for others
senses.definition: Active goodwill and care toward fellow believers and neighbours; the defining Christian virtue.
senses.note: Supreme over knowledge and spiritual gifts (1CO 8:1; 1CO 13:1–13); the 'kiss of love' (1PE 5:14).

senses.label: Love for God (or truth)
senses.definition: Human devotion directed toward God, shown in obedience; also love for the truth.
senses.note: 'The love of God' can mean love for God or God's love; context decides.

senses.label: God's love
senses.definition: God's love for humanity and for his Son, shown supremely in sending Christ to die.
senses.note: 'God is love' (1JO 4:8; 1JO 4:16).

senses.label: Christ's love
senses.definition: Christ's love for his people, expressed in laying down his life and in which they are to remain.

senses.label: Love feast
senses.definition: In the plural, the common meals of early Christian fellowship.
senses.note: Also a variant reading at 2 Pet 2:13, where most texts read 'deceptions'.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul (75 uses) makes love the greatest of faith, hope and love, the fulfilment of the Law, the first fruit of the Spirit and the bond that holds the virtues together.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John's letters ground love in God's nature ('God is love'), make abiding in love and keeping commandments inseparable, and say perfect love drives out fear; Revelation rebukes Ephesus for leaving its first love.

authorNotes.author: Jude
authorNotes.note: Jude urges readers to keep themselves in God's love and warns of intruders at the love feasts.

study.translationNote: The KJV often has 'charity' (from Latin caritas), famously in 1 Cor 13; modern versions use 'love'. Versions also differ on genitive phrases: 'the love of Christ controls us' (ESV, 2CO 5:14) keeps the ambiguity, while 'Christ's love compels us' (NIV) decides for Christ's love toward us.

background.note: In the Septuagint the noun is rare and mostly used of human, even sexual, love, as in the Song of Songs and Jeremiah's image of Israel's bridal love.
Ecclesiastes sets 'love and hatred' side by side, showing the word's ordinary range.
Before the Bible the noun is barely attested: one doubtful instance in the Herculaneum papyri of Philodemus; Aristeas uses it of a higher love.
In late Christian papyri the word narrows to 'charity, alms'.

study.exegesisTip: In 'the love of God/Christ' ask whether God's love for us or our love for God is meant; ROM 5:5 is best read in light of ROM 5:8 (God's love for us).
study.caution: Avoid overstating the contrast between ἀγάπη and φιλία/φιλέω: the Septuagint uses ἀγάπη of Amnon's lust (2SA 13:15), and the alternation of verbs in John 21:15–17 is widely read as stylistic. The word's meaning comes from how the NT describes God's love in Christ, not from its etymology.

study.summary: King: an earthly monarch or ruler (including the Roman emperor), Jesus as the Messianic King of Israel, God as eternal King, and the King of kings.

senses.label: Earthly king, ruler
senses.definition: A human monarch or client ruler, including Herodian rulers and foreign kings.
senses.note: Used loosely of Herod Antipas, strictly a tetrarch (MAR 6:14; MAT 14:9); 'kings of the earth' (MAT 17:25).

senses.label: Roman emperor
senses.definition: The Caesar as supreme ruler, called βασιλεύς as in common Greek usage.

senses.label: Messianic King of Israel
senses.definition: Jesus as the promised Davidic King: 'King of the Jews' or 'King of Israel'.
senses.note: The charge on the cross (JOH 19:19).

senses.label: God as King
senses.definition: God as the eternal, universal sovereign.
senses.note: 'The great King' (MAT 5:35, from Ps 48:2).

senses.label: King in parables
senses.definition: A king figure in Jesus' parables standing for God or the Son of Man as judge.

senses.label: King of kings
senses.definition: Title of supreme sovereignty over all earthly kings, given to the Lamb.
senses.note: Cf. 'ruler of the kings of the earth' (REV 1:5).

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John's trial before Pilate turns on Jesus' kingship ('You are a king, then?'), ending with the leaders' 'We have no king but Caesar'. Revelation sets 'the kings of the earth' against the Lamb, King of kings.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew contrasts the newborn 'King of the Jews' with King Herod, and portrays the Son of Man as the King who judges the nations.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke adds 'the King' to the Psalm acclamation at the entry to Jerusalem, and records the charge that Christians proclaim 'another king, Jesus'.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews interprets Melchizedek as 'king of righteousness' and 'king of peace'.

study.translationNote: Usually 'king'. Where the Roman emperor is meant, many modern versions (NIV, ESV, NRSV) translate 'emperor' (1 Pet 2:13, 17), while KJV keeps 'king'.

background.note: In Homer kings are 'nurtured by Zeus'; the title often carries the sense of judge or leader.
Alexander the Great adopted the title, and it became the standard style of the Hellenistic monarchs.
Inscriptions call Roman emperors βασιλεύς, as in 1 Pet 2:13.
A magical papyrus invokes a deity as 'king of kings', a title also used of great Eastern monarchs.

study.exegesisTip: Notice who calls Jesus king: outsiders (Magi, Pilate, soldiers) say 'King of the Jews', while Israelites say 'King of Israel' (JOH 1:49; MAR 15:32).

study.summary: To judge: form an opinion, decide, evaluate others, try a case in court, pronounce God's judgment, condemn, or (Hebraic) rule.

senses.label: Consider, regard, esteem
senses.definition: To form an opinion or value judgement about something.
senses.note: ROM 14:5: one 'esteems' one day above another.

senses.label: Decide, resolve
senses.definition: To make up one's mind or reach a formal decision.
senses.note: Usually with an infinitive, as in papyri.

senses.label: Pass judgment on others
senses.definition: To evaluate and criticise others, often with a censorious, condemning attitude.
senses.note: JOH 7:24 commends 'right judgment' rather than judging by appearances.

senses.label: Try in court; go to law
senses.definition: To hear a case and give a verdict; middle/passive: to be on trial or to sue.
senses.note: MAT 5:40 'sue'; 1CO 6:1–6 believers going to law.

senses.label: God's judgment
senses.definition: God's or Christ's act of judging the world and each person, especially at the last day.

senses.label: Condemn
senses.definition: To judge adversely and pronounce guilty, equivalent to κατακρίνω.
senses.note: Context, not the verb alone, shows when judgment means condemnation.

senses.label: Rule, govern
senses.definition: As Hebrew šāp̄aṭ, to exercise leadership and authority over a people.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John holds together that the Son did not come to judge (condemn) the world, yet the Father has given all judgment to him; the unbeliever is 'already judged' and Jesus' word will judge on the last day.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul warns against judging fellow believers over disputed matters, yet requires the church to judge those inside it, not outsiders.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Acts uses the verb for church decisions and travel plans and for Paul's repeated trials 'concerning the hope of the resurrection'.

authorNotes.author: James
authorNotes.note: James forbids speaking against and judging a brother, since there is one Lawgiver and Judge, and reminds readers they will be judged by the law of liberty.

study.translationNote: Versions vary between 'judge' and 'condemn' (e.g. JOH 3:17–18; KJV's 'damned' at 2TH 2:12), and between 'judge' and 'rule' (MAT 19:28). Neutral uses become 'consider', 'esteem', 'decide' or 'sue' (ROM 14:5; ACT 15:19; MAT 5:40).

background.note: κρίνω with an infinitive, 'we have decided not to record', parallels Acts 20:16 and 1 Cor 2:2.
The forensic sense is common: proceedings follow 'what was judged by our lord the prefect'.
A lead curse-tablet from Amorgos prays the goddess to 'judge what is right', illuminating Luke 12:57.
Translating šāp̄aṭ, the verb can mean 'rule, govern', as of the earth's judges in Psalm 2.

study.exegesisTip: Ask whether κρίνω is neutral (assess, decide), forensic (try a case), or adverse (condemn); compare MAT 7:1 with JOH 7:24.
study.caution: The scope of 'Do not judge' (MAT 7:1) is debated — it targets hypocritical, condemning judgment rather than all discernment (cf. JOH 7:24; 1CO 5:12). Whether the apostles 'judging' the twelve tribes (MAT 19:28) means passing sentence or ruling is also disputed.

study.summary: House: a dwelling or home, God's house (tabernacle or temple), a household or family, a royal or national line ('house of David/Israel'), and God's people as his house.

senses.label: House, home
senses.definition: A dwelling place, or one's home.
senses.note: ἐν οἴκῳ 'at home' (MAR 2:1; 1CO 11:34); κατ' οἶκον 'in homes' (ACT 2:46); κατ' οἴκους 'house to house' (ACT 20:20); 'the church in their house' (ROM 16:5). Figuratively of a person possessed by a demon (MAT 12:44).

senses.label: House of God, sanctuary
senses.definition: The tabernacle or temple as God's dwelling.
senses.note: 'Your house is left desolate' (MAT 23:38; LUK 13:35) may refer to the temple or Jerusalem.

senses.label: Household, family
senses.definition: The people living under one head, including family members and servants.
senses.note: Managing one's household is a qualification for church leaders (1TI 3:4–5, 12).

senses.label: Lineage, nation
senses.definition: Descendants of an ancestor: a dynasty or a whole people.
senses.note: 'House of Israel/Jacob/David', following Hebrew bayit.

senses.label: God's people as his house
senses.definition: The church or people of God as God's household or spiritual temple.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke (58 uses) highlights whole households hearing the message, believing and being baptized, and the church meeting 'in homes'.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul greets churches meeting in the homes of believers and calls the church 'the household of God'.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews contrasts Moses, faithful as a servant in God's house, with Christ, faithful as Son over it — 'whose house we are'.

authorNotes.author: Peter
authorNotes.note: 1 Peter calls believers living stones built into a spiritual house, where judgment begins.

study.translationNote: Rendered 'house', 'home' or 'household' depending on whether the building or its people are meant; versions differ in places such as HEB 3:2–6 ('house' vs 'household') and ACT 16:31 ('household' vs 'house').

background.note: From Homer, any dwelling — even the Cyclops' cave — could be an οἶκος.
The Septuagint uses οἶκος even of a tent, reflecting the broad Hebrew bayit.
Everyday papyri use the word for an inhabited house: 'my house has been searched'.
Inscriptions speak of a 'sacred house' of a deity, a parallel to 'house of God'.

study.exegesisTip: Decide whether a building, the people in it, or a family line is meant; 'house of David' (LUK 1:69) is a dynasty, not a building.
study.caution: Whether 'household' baptisms (ACT 16:15; 1CO 1:16) included infants is debated; the word itself does not settle it. The classical distinction between οἶκος (estate) and οἰκία (dwelling) is not consistently kept in the NT.

study.summary: To raise or to rise: transitively, raise someone up (from death) or bring someone onto the scene; intransitively, stand up, set out, rise from the dead, or arise.

senses.label: Raise up, raise from death
senses.definition: Transitive: to make someone stand up, especially God raising the dead.
senses.note: ACT 9:41: Peter raised Tabitha up by the hand.

senses.label: Raise up, bring forward
senses.definition: Transitive: to cause someone to appear or be born, such as a prophet or offspring.
senses.note: 'Raise up offspring' for a dead brother (MAT 22:24).

senses.label: Stand up, get up
senses.definition: Intransitive: to rise from lying or sitting, often to speak or act.

senses.label: Set out (pleonastic)
senses.definition: The participle ἀναστάς before a verb of going marks the start of an action: 'set out, got ready'.
senses.note: A Semitic idiom reflecting Hebrew qûm.

senses.label: Rise from the dead
senses.definition: Intransitive: to come back to life, of Jesus or of the dead at the end.
senses.note: Often ἐκ νεκρῶν 'from the dead'.

senses.label: Arise, appear; rise against
senses.definition: To come on the scene, or to rise up in hostility or as a witness.
senses.note: MAT 12:41: the men of Nineveh 'will rise up' at the judgment.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke (73 uses) loves the participle ἀναστάς to open an action or a speech, and the apostolic preaching formula 'God raised him up'.

authorNotes.author: Mark
authorNotes.note: Mark's passion predictions say the Son of Man 'will rise after three days'.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: In John, Jesus himself 'will raise up' believers at the last day, and Martha confesses the resurrection.

study.translationNote: Versions differ on whether 'raised up' in Acts means resurrection or bringing Jesus onto the scene (ACT 3:26; ACT 13:33). The pleonastic ἀναστάς is variously rendered 'got up', 'set out', 'got ready' or left untranslated (LUK 1:39).

background.note: Homer uses the transitive sense: Achilles 'raised the old man up by his hand'.
A Christian letter writer says she is unable 'to rise from my bed' — the plain intransitive sense.
Rising to confer with assessors is compared with Acts 26:30.
In Phrygian and Lycaonian epitaphs ἀνέστησα, 'I set up (a gravestone)', became formulaic.

study.exegesisTip: Check whether the verb is transitive (God raises someone) or intransitive (someone rises); in Luke, ἀναστάς often simply marks the beginning of a new action.
study.caution: Whether 'raising Jesus' in ACT 13:33 refers to the resurrection or to God bringing him onto the stage of history (cf. ACT 3:22) is debated. ἀνίστημι and ἐγείρω are near-synonyms for resurrection; no theological distinction should be pressed.

study.summary: To die: of natural or violent death, Christ's death for others, believers' dying to sin and the Law, spiritual and eternal death, and of seeds and plants.

senses.label: Die (natural death)
senses.definition: To cease living through illness, age or accident; present/imperfect 'be dying'.
senses.note: LUK 8:42 'was dying'.

senses.label: Be killed; face death
senses.definition: To die violently or by execution; to be constantly exposed to death.
senses.note: Functions as the passive of ἀποκτείνω; 'I die daily' (1CO 15:31; 2CO 6:9).

senses.label: Christ's death for others
senses.definition: Jesus' death on behalf of others, usually with ὑπέρ 'for'.

senses.label: Die to sin, Law, world
senses.definition: With a dative: to have one's relationship to a power ended by union with Christ's death.
senses.note: Esp. Paul.

senses.label: Spiritual, eternal death
senses.definition: To perish under sin and judgment, cut off from God's life.

senses.label: Seeds and trees die
senses.definition: Of plants: a seed 'dies' in the ground before new life, or trees are dead and fruitless.
senses.note: Used as images of Jesus' death and of resurrection.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul (42 uses) centres on Christ who 'died for us/our sins' and on believers who 'died with Christ' to sin and the Law, so that 'to die is gain'.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John contrasts physical death with never dying for those who believe, and records Caiaphas' unwitting prophecy that one man should die for the people.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews notes that people die once and then face judgment, and that the faithful 'died in faith' without receiving the promises.

study.translationNote: Usually 'die'. Versions differ mainly on tense: imperfect or present can mean 'was dying' (LUK 8:42) or describe repeated dying ('mortal men', HEB 7:8; 'those who die in the Lord', REV 14:13). In 2CO 5:14 'all died' (ESV, NIV) vs 'all have died' (NRSV).

background.note: The usual prose and comic word for 'die', even with cause, e.g. 'from wounds'.
A desperate letter complains 'we may die' in a great forest, cast there by false gods.
A slave writes to her master 'we are dying because we do not see you daily' — a figurative use like 1 Cor 15:31.
A judge says even beasts spare 'those who die', a frequentative present like Heb 7:8 and Rev 14:13.

study.exegesisTip: A dative after the verb ('died to sin', ROM 6:2) marks a broken relationship, not the end of temptation or existence.
study.caution: The force of 'one died for all, therefore all died' (2CO 5:14) — representative or participatory death — is debated, as is the sense of 'will never die' in JOH 11:26 (spiritual or eternal death rather than physical).

study.summary: To be about to, intend, or be destined to; the participle means 'coming, future' ('the age to come'); occasionally 'to delay'.

senses.label: Be about to
senses.definition: With an infinitive: something is on the point of happening.

senses.label: Intend, plan
senses.definition: To mean or plan to do something of one's own will.

senses.label: Be destined; will surely
senses.definition: Of what must or will certainly happen, often under God's plan; a periphrastic future.
senses.note: Esp. of Jesus' coming passion (MAT 17:22; JOH 12:33).

senses.label: Coming, future (participle)
senses.definition: ὁ μέλλων: what is to come — the coming age, wrath, judgment or good things.
senses.note: τὰ μέλλοντα 'things to come' (ROM 8:38; 1CO 3:22); εἰς τὸ μέλλον 'next year' (LUK 13:9).

senses.label: Delay
senses.definition: To hesitate or put off acting.
senses.note: 'Why do you delay?'

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses the verb for the 'departure' Jesus was about to fulfil and for the future resurrection and judgment in Paul's speeches.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John's narrator uses it to show Jesus' foreknowledge — what he would do, who would betray him, what death he would die.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews speaks of 'the world to come', 'the age to come', 'the good things to come' and 'the city to come'.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul sets the present against what is coming: the age to come, the glory about to be revealed, the shadow of things to come.

study.translationNote: Versions choose between 'about to' (imminence), 'going to', 'will' and 'to come', so the same phrase may sound near or simply future. REV 1:19 is 'what will take place' (ESV) or 'what is about to take place'; ROM 8:18 'the glory that is to be revealed' or 'about to be revealed'.

background.note: Rare in the translated books of the Septuagint, more frequent in Wisdom and 2 and 4 Maccabees.
As in the NT, the verb is usually followed by a present infinitive: 'I intend to bring in'.
'Come if you are coming' — everyday use of μέλλω with an aorist infinitive.
εἰς τὸ μέλλον means 'for next year', supporting that rendering in Luke 13:9.

study.exegesisTip: Decide from context whether μέλλω stresses imminence ('about to'), intention, or divine certainty ('was destined to').
study.caution: Whether μέλλω implies nearness in time or only futurity is debated in texts such as REV 1:19 and ROM 8:18; both meanings are lexically possible. In 2 Pet 1:12 some scholars read μελήσω 'I will take care' instead of μελλήσω.

study.summary: Truth: what is real and genuine as opposed to falsehood or mere appearance; in the NT especially God's revealed reality, the gospel message, and the truthfulness and integrity that should mark believers.

senses.label: Truth as opposed to falsehood
senses.definition: What corresponds to the facts; telling the truth rather than lying or concealing.
senses.note: Common phrase ἀλήθειαν λέγειν 'tell the truth'; Mark 5:33 'the whole truth'.

senses.label: In truth, truly (idiom)
senses.definition: In the phrase ἐπ' ἀληθείας: 'in accordance with the facts', 'really, truly'.
senses.note: Thoroughly idiomatic Koine, found in the papyri, not translation Greek.

senses.label: The reality of God
senses.definition: God's own reality and faithfulness as revealed to humanity, which people may acknowledge or suppress and exchange for a lie.
senses.note: In ROM 15:8 'the truth of God' is close to the Hebrew sense of faithfulness to promises.

senses.label: The gospel as 'the truth'
senses.definition: The Christian message as the true account of God's saving work, to be believed, obeyed, known and not departed from.
senses.note: Phrases: 'the word of truth', 'knowledge of the truth' (Pastorals), 'wander from the truth' (JAM 5:19).

senses.label: Truth revealed in Christ and Spirit
senses.definition: Divine reality made known and embodied in Jesus and communicated by the Spirit, which frees and sanctifies.
senses.note: Esp. John: 'full of grace and truth', 'the Spirit of truth'.

senses.label: Truthfulness, sincerity, integrity
senses.definition: A quality of character and conduct: genuineness, honesty, faithfulness in word and deed; 'practising' or 'walking in' the truth.
senses.note: ἐν ἀληθείᾳ can mean 'sincerely, truly' (2JO 1:1; 3JO 1:1).

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John (45 uses) makes truth a revealed reality bound up with Jesus himself: he is the truth, the Spirit is the Spirit of truth, believers are 'of the truth', 'do' it and 'walk in' it.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul often uses 'the truth' as shorthand for the gospel; the Pastorals speak repeatedly of 'the knowledge of the truth' over against false teaching.

study.translationNote: Almost every version uses 'truth', but phrases differ: ἐπ' ἀληθείας is 'truly', 'in truth' or 'in accordance with the truth' (MAR 12:14), and ἐν ἀληθείᾳ in 2JO 1:1 is 'in truth' (KJV, ESV) or 'truly' (NIV). The English hides the Hebrew background of 'truth' as faithfulness (Hebrew 'emet).

background.note: In Homer ἀλήθεια is simply the opposite of a lie: to tell the whole truth.
Sworn declarations are made ἐπ' ἀληθείας 'truthfully', showing that Mark's phrase is ordinary idiom.
Letters greet those 'who love you in truth', a close parallel to 2 and 3 John.
A Christian oracle-prayer asks God to 'reveal to me the truth that is with you'.

study.exegesisTip: Ask whether ἀλήθεια means factual accuracy, the gospel message, God's revealed reality, or personal integrity; in John 1:14, 17 'grace and truth' likely echoes God's 'steadfast love and faithfulness' (Exod 34:6).
study.caution: Scholars debate how far John's 'truth' reflects the Hebrew sense of faithfulness ('emet) versus the Greek sense of unveiled reality; most see both at work.

study.summary: To call someone to one's side: to summon or invite, to beg or plead, to urge or exhort, and to encourage or comfort. Context decides which.

senses.label: Summon, invite
senses.definition: To call someone to come, or to invite or press someone to do something, such as stay or sit with one.
senses.note: The root idea is 'call alongside'.

senses.label: Beg, plead, entreat
senses.definition: To make an earnest request, especially of a superior; often of people or demons begging Jesus, or of prayer to God.
senses.note: Usually with infinitive or ἵνα; of prayer to the Father in MAT 26:53.

senses.label: Urge, exhort, appeal
senses.definition: To call on people earnestly to adopt a course of action; an appeal that carries authority yet speaks as to family.
senses.note: Paul's formula 'I urge you (therefore)' often opens the ethical part of a letter (ROM 12:1; EPH 4:1).

senses.label: Encourage, strengthen
senses.definition: To put heart into someone, bracing them to persevere in faith and duty.
senses.note: Often paired with 'strengthen' (στηρίζω).

senses.label: Comfort, console
senses.definition: To bring consolation to those who grieve or suffer; in the passive, 'be comforted'.
senses.note: This is the main LXX sense (Hebrew nāḥam); Rachel 'refused to be comforted' (MAT 2:18).

senses.label: Conciliate, speak kindly
senses.definition: To speak to someone in a soothing, placating way, or to apologise to them.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul (54 uses) uses the verb for apostolic appeal and for the comfort God gives in affliction, which believers pass on to others; the verb and its noun παράκλησις come ten times in 2 Cor 1:3–7.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses the whole range: begging Jesus in the Gospel, and in Acts preaching exhortation and the strengthening of churches.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews calls believers to exhort one another daily and describes itself as a 'word of exhortation'.

study.translationNote: One verb covers pleading, exhorting and comforting, so versions vary widely: KJV 'beseech', 'exhort', 'comfort'; modern versions 'urge', 'appeal', 'encourage', 'beg'. In passages such as 1TH 4:18 or 2CO 1:4 the choice between 'comfort' and 'encourage' changes the tone, and the Greek may hold both.

background.note: Classical writers use it for calling in or summoning allies and advisers.
In the LXX it mostly renders nāḥam 'comfort', as in 'comfort, comfort my people' and Isaiah's call to strengthen weak hands.
'I ask and urge you' (ἐρωτῶ σε καὶ παρακαλῶ) is a stock formula in private letters.
A man healed at Epidaurus says 'concerning this I besought the god', a parallel to Paul's prayer in 2 Cor 12:8.

study.exegesisTip: Decide by who speaks to whom: a suppliant to a superior begs, an apostle to a church urges, and anyone to the grieving comforts; related words are παράκλησις and παράκλητος.

study.summary: To save: rescue from danger or death, preserve life, heal from illness, and above all deliver from sin and God's judgment into eternal life.

senses.label: Rescue from physical danger
senses.definition: To bring someone safely out of a life-threatening situation such as a storm, shipwreck or catastrophe.
senses.note: The mockers at the cross: 'save yourself' (MAT 27:40; LUK 23:35).

senses.label: Preserve one's life
senses.definition: To keep a life (ψυχή) safe; in Jesus' sayings, with a play between saving earthly life and losing true life.

senses.label: Heal, make well
senses.definition: To restore someone to health from illness, disability or demon possession.
senses.note: 'Your faith has saved you' (MAR 10:52) is regularly 'made you well'; the wider sense may also be heard.

senses.label: Save from sin and its consequences
senses.definition: God's act through Christ of delivering people from sin, lostness and death and bringing them into eternal life.
senses.note: With ἀπό/ἐκ: from sins (MAT 1:21), from wrath (ROM 5:9), from death (JAM 5:20).

senses.label: Final, end-time salvation
senses.definition: Being kept safe through the last judgment and brought into God's kingdom.
senses.note: σώζειν εἰς 'bring safely into' the heavenly kingdom (2TI 4:18).

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul speaks of salvation as past (you have been saved), present (we are being saved) and future (we shall be saved from wrath).

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses 'your faith has saved you' both for healing and for the forgiven woman who was not ill, and in Acts 'be saved' summarises the gospel offer.

authorNotes.author: James
authorNotes.note: James asks whether faith without works can save, and uses the verb of the sick restored through the prayer of faith and of the sinner's soul rescued from death.

study.translationNote: Versions divide between 'save' and 'heal' / 'make well' (KJV 'make whole') in the healing stories, so English readers miss that the same verb is used for spiritual salvation (e.g. MAR 5:34, LUK 8:48). JAM 5:15 ('the prayer of faith will save/restore the sick') is translated both ways.

background.note: A soldier writes that when he was in danger at sea the god 'saved me immediately' (cf. Matt 14:30).
A worshipper's life is 'saved in sickness' by the god Socnopaeus, the same healing sense as in the Gospels.
An official is asked 'to save many lives' (σῶσαι ψυχὰς πολλάς) during famine.
Thank-offering inscriptions are set up by one 'saved from great dangers' at sea.

study.exegesisTip: Ask 'saved from what?': look for an ἀπό or ἐκ phrase or the context (storm, illness, death, sins, wrath), and note the tense (past, present, future).
study.caution: The sense of σωθήσεται in 1TI 2:15 ('saved through childbearing') and whether the healing stories' 'your faith has saved you' implies more than physical cure are debated.

study.summary: Life, soul, self: the life-breath that animates a living being, a person's life, the inner self with its feelings and will, the person as a whole, and the self God saves.

senses.label: Physical life
senses.definition: Bodily life that can be sought, risked, lost or laid down.
senses.note: 'Lay down one's life' (JOH 10:11; 1JO 3:16); 'give his life a ransom' (MAR 10:45).

senses.label: True life, the self at stake
senses.definition: In Jesus' sayings, the life one may try to keep and lose, or give up and find: one's whole self and destiny.

senses.label: Inner self: feelings, desires, will
senses.definition: The seat of emotions, desires and devotion; the inner person who is troubled, rejoices, loves or longs.
senses.note: 'With all your soul' (MAR 12:30); ἐκ ψυχῆς 'from the heart' (EPH 6:6; COL 3:23).

senses.label: Person, individual
senses.definition: A person counted as an individual; 'every soul' = everyone.
senses.note: Reflects Hebrew nepeš, 'person'.

senses.label: Living being
senses.definition: A living creature, a being that has life.
senses.note: 'Living soul' (Gen 2:7) quoted in 1CO 15:45 and contrasted with 'life-giving spirit'.

senses.label: Soul as object of salvation
senses.definition: The person's inner, lasting life that God cares for and saves, and which survives bodily death.

authorNotes.author: Peter
authorNotes.note: 1 Peter speaks of the salvation of souls, purifying souls, desires that war against the soul, and Christ as the Shepherd of souls.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews uses ψυχή for the inner life: the word divides soul and spirit, hope is an anchor of the soul, leaders keep watch over souls.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John repeatedly speaks of laying down one's life: the good shepherd's death and the love it calls for.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses ψυχή relatively rarely (13 times), mostly for life or person, and prefers πνεῦμα for the inner life; the related ψυχικός means merely natural.

study.translationNote: Versions shift between 'soul', 'life', 'self' and 'person'. In MAT 16:25–26 many versions use 'life' in verse 25 and 'soul' in verse 26, hiding that the same word runs through the saying; ACT 2:41 is 'souls' (KJV, ESV) or 'people' (NIV). 'Soul' can also bring in a Greek idea of an immaterial part that the Hebrew-shaped NT usage does not always mean.

background.note: In Homer ψυχή is the life that leaves a man when he dies; Achilles and Hector run 'for the life of Hector'.
Papyri use it for life itself: 'to save many lives' in famine.
A love poem speaks of 'the great fire burning in my soul', the soul as seat of feeling.
The word is common in memorial inscriptions addressing the dead, e.g. 'may you be remembered, good soul'.

study.exegesisTip: Before reading 'soul' as an immaterial part, test whether 'life', 'self' or 'person' fits; behind most uses stands Hebrew nepeš, the whole living person.
study.caution: Whether 1TH 5:23 and HEB 4:12 teach distinct parts of human nature (soul vs spirit) is debated, as is what MAT 10:28 implies about the soul's existence apart from the body.

study.summary: Impersonal verb 'it is necessary, one must': necessity arising from God's plan and Scripture, from moral obligation, or from circumstances; past ἔδει often means 'ought to have'.

senses.label: Necessity of God's plan
senses.definition: What must happen because God has willed it and Scripture foretells it, especially Jesus' suffering, death and resurrection.
senses.note: The 'divine δεῖ' of the passion predictions; esp. Luke.

senses.label: End-time events that must occur
senses.definition: Events that must come before the end, according to God's purpose.
senses.note: Revelation's recurring 'what must soon take place' echoes Dan 2:28.

senses.label: Requirement for salvation
