senses.note: Formula ἵνα πληρωθῇ τὸ ῥηθέν 'so that what was spoken might be fulfilled'.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew's fulfilment formula presents events in Jesus' life as completing what the prophets said.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John uses the word both for Scripture fulfilled in the passion and for joy brought to completion.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke often uses it of time running its course and of a mission carried to completion.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul speaks of the law fulfilled through love and of believers being filled with God's fullness in Christ.

study.translationNote: English needs several words for one Greek verb: 'fill', 'complete', 'fulfil', 'accomplish'. Versions differ in borderline cases: Php 4:18 'I am amply supplied' (ESV) or 'I have been paid in full' (Moffatt, Goodspeed, following the papyrus sense 'pay'); Rom 15:19 'fully preached' versus 'fulfilled the gospel'. Seeing the shared idea of fullness links 'fill' and 'fulfil'.

background.note: The basic sense is to fill something full, e.g. chests filled with stones.
Very common for paying a debt in full, which may illuminate Paul's 'I have been paid in full' (Php 4:18).
Used of carrying out an official duty, such as completing the regular order of the census.
The Priene calendar inscription says Providence 'filled' Augustus with virtue — a parallel to Jesus 'filled with wisdom' (Luke 2:40).

study.exegesisTip: Ask what is being filled or completed — a space, a person, a time, a task, a command or a prophecy — and what the 'full measure' is in that context.
study.caution: What Jesus means by 'fulfilling' the law (MAT 5:17) — obeying it, completing it, bringing out its true intent, or bringing it to its goal — is debated; so is whether πληρουμένου in EPH 1:23 is middle ('who fills all') or passive ('who is being filled').

study.summary: To pray: to speak to God in petition, intercession or worship, whether privately or in the gathered church.

senses.label: Pray, address God
senses.definition: To speak to God in prayer, used absolutely of the act or habit of praying.
senses.note: Always of prayer to God (or, outside the NT, to gods); often of Jesus withdrawing to pray.

senses.label: Pray for others; intercede
senses.definition: To pray on behalf of someone, including enemies and fellow believers.
senses.note: With ὑπέρ or περί + genitive.

senses.label: Pray for something; ask that
senses.definition: To pray with a specific request in view, naming what is asked.
senses.note: With ἵνα, an infinitive, or τοῦ + infinitive (JAM 5:17).

senses.label: Pray in or with the Spirit
senses.definition: Prayer enabled by or carried on in the Spirit, including Spirit-given speech that bypasses the mind.
senses.note: Paul contrasts praying 'with the spirit' and 'with the mind' (1 Cor 14:15).

senses.label: Prayer in worship and commissioning
senses.definition: Public prayer in the assembly, and prayer that goes with laying on hands or appointing leaders.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke (35 uses) repeatedly shows Jesus praying at turning points — baptism, choosing the Twelve, transfiguration — and the church praying at key moments.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew gathers Jesus' teaching on how not to pray (for show, with empty words) and the Gethsemane prayers.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul reports constant prayer for his churches and asks them to pray for him.

authorNotes.author: James
authorNotes.note: James links prayer to suffering, sickness and the elders, with Elijah as model.

study.translationNote: Renderings are uniform ('pray'), but προσευχῇ προσηύξατο (JAM 5:17), literally 'prayed with prayer', is a Hebraism for intensity, hence 'prayed earnestly' (ESV, NIV) rather than a literal rendering.

background.note: Used of offering prayers or worship to the gods.
Socrates is described as praying to the sun at dawn.
A man struck with illness prays to Sarapis, promising to build his temple, and is healed.
An inscription records a man praying to the gods of Abydos for someone's health.

study.exegesisTip: Note the construction: ὑπέρ/περί shows for whom one prays, ἵνα or an infinitive shows what is asked.
study.caution: In 1 Cor 14:14–15 interpreters disagree whether 'my spirit prays' means the human spirit or the Holy Spirit working through it, and how this prayer relates to tongues.

study.summary: Time viewed as a definite point or period: the appointed or right time, a season, an opportunity, or an age — especially God's decisive time.

senses.label: Appointed, decisive time
senses.definition: A definite moment fixed for something to happen, often God's appointed time.
senses.note: πρὸ καιροῦ 'before the time' (MAT 8:29; 1 Cor 4:5).

senses.label: Season of the year
senses.definition: A recurring season, especially harvest or fruit season, and festival seasons.
senses.note: GAL 4:10 refers to observing sacred seasons.

senses.label: Opportunity, right moment
senses.definition: A favourable or suitable occasion to be seized or used.
senses.note: 'Redeeming/making the most of the time' (EPH 5:16; COL 4:5).

senses.label: Period, era, present time
senses.definition: A span of time characterised by its events, including 'this present time' as an era in God's plan.
senses.note: ἐν ἐκείνῳ τῷ καιρῷ 'at that time' is a narrative link in Matthew.

senses.label: End-time times and seasons
senses.definition: The periods leading to and marking the end, known only to God.
senses.note: Paired with χρόνοι 'times and seasons' (ACT 1:7; 1 Thess 5:1).

senses.label: Adverbial phrases
senses.definition: Fixed phrases: 'for a while' (πρὸς καιρόν), 'in due time' (ἐν καιρῷ), 'at the right time' (κατὰ καιρόν).

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul speaks of 'the now time' as the moment of God's saving action, and urges believers to live alert to it.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: In John Jesus speaks of 'my time' not yet having come, his own God-given hour of action.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew uses 'at that time' as a narrative connective.

study.translationNote: Most versions render 'time', but choose 'season', 'opportunity', 'proper time' or 'while' by context. The KJV's 'redeeming the time' (Eph 5:16) is rendered 'making the most of every opportunity' (NIV) or 'of the time' (ESV), reflecting the sense 'opportunity'.

background.note: The earliest sense is 'due measure, fitness'; 'due measure is best in all things' became proverbial.
An advocate says a woman 'seized a favourable opportunity' to carry off a foundling.
A wife writes of steering herself and her child through such a 'crisis'.
Used for 'at the due time' in contracts.

study.exegesisTip: Ask whether the context stresses a fixed moment, a season, an opportunity to be used, or an era in God's plan.
study.caution: The popular contrast of καιρός as 'qualitative, decisive time' versus χρόνος as 'clock time' has been criticised (notably by James Barr) as overdrawn; the two overlap (ACT 1:7), and context, not the word alone, must decide.

study.summary: Mother: a woman in relation to her child, and by extension one who acts as a mother, spiritual kin, or a city or power pictured as a mother.

senses.label: Biological mother
senses.definition: A woman who has borne a child, especially Mary the mother of Jesus.
senses.note: 'From the mother's womb' = from birth (LUK 1:15; ACT 3:2; GAL 1:15).

senses.label: Parent in family duty
senses.definition: Mother with father as the parents owed honour, love and care, whose claims may be outranked by loyalty to Christ.

senses.label: One who acts as a mother
senses.definition: A woman treated as a mother, or members of Jesus' new family who do God's will.

senses.label: Figurative: city or source
senses.definition: A city or power pictured as the mother of its people or of evils.
senses.note: The heavenly Jerusalem as 'our mother'; Babylon 'mother of prostitutes'.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew's infancy story repeats 'the child and his mother', keeping Jesus at the centre.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John never names Mary but calls her 'the mother of Jesus', present at Cana and at the cross.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke highlights Mary's role and her place among the first believers.

background.note: Standard word for mother from Homer on.
Also used of animals, a dam.
Used loosely as an affectionate title, even of an old servant — compare Paul's 'his mother and mine' (Rom 16:13).

study.exegesisTip: When Jesus redefines 'mother' (MAT 12:50) or entrusts his mother to the beloved disciple (JOH 19:27), read it against the strong family duty of the commandment to honour one's mother (MAT 15:4).

study.summary: To begin: to start doing something, or to begin from a starting point; in the Gospels often a near-auxiliary 'began to'.

senses.label: Begin to do
senses.definition: To start an action, with an infinitive naming what is begun.
senses.note: Marks the start of a new phase, e.g. Jesus' public preaching (MAT 4:17).

senses.label: Begin from a starting point
senses.definition: To start from a place, person or event, often with ἀπό, marking a sequence or range.
senses.note: Participle ἀρξάμενος ἀπό 'beginning from' functions almost adverbially.

senses.label: Near-auxiliary 'began to'
senses.definition: With an infinitive where the stress falls on the action itself, so 'began to' adds little beyond 'proceeded to'.
senses.note: Very frequent in Mark; widely linked to Semitic idiom.

authorNotes.author: Mark
authorNotes.note: Mark uses the verb very often (26×) as a vivid near-auxiliary.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses it to frame beginnings: Jesus 'beginning' his ministry, and Acts as what Jesus 'began' to do and teach, preached 'beginning from Jerusalem'.

study.translationNote: Versions differ on how often to keep 'began to': formal versions keep it, while others drop it in Mark, treating it as an idiom. The active ἄρχω 'rule' is a separate entry.

background.note: Land surveys use ἀρξάμενοι ἀπό 'beginning from' a corner, like the stereotyped participle of Luke 24:47.
Also with a genitive: 'let us begin the work'.

study.exegesisTip: Ask whether 'began' marks a real new start (ACT 1:1; MAT 4:17) or is simply Mark's vivid narrative style.
study.caution: Scholars debate how far the 'began to' construction is a Semitic pleonasm with little force, and whether Luke uses it with more meaning than Mark; whether ACT 1:1 implies Acts continues what Jesus 'began' is also discussed.

study.summary: One sent with a commission: a messenger or envoy, and in the NT especially the authorised witnesses of Christ — the Twelve, Paul and some others.

senses.label: Messenger, envoy
senses.definition: Anyone sent on a mission to represent the sender.
senses.note: Christ himself is 'the apostle' sent from God (HEB 3:1).

senses.label: The Twelve
senses.definition: The twelve men chosen by Jesus as his authorised representatives and foundational witnesses.
senses.note: Matthias replaces Judas (ACT 1:26).

senses.label: Paul's apostleship
senses.definition: Paul's commission from the risen Christ, which he claims as equal in authority to the Twelve.

senses.label: Wider circle of apostles
senses.definition: Other commissioned missionaries or church founders called apostles.
senses.note: Barnabas (ACT 14:14); probably Silvanus and Timothy (1 Thess 2:6).

senses.label: False apostles
senses.definition: People who claim apostolic authority without true commission.
senses.note: 'Super-apostles' (2 Cor 11:5).

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke mostly reserves the title for the Twelve as witnesses of the resurrection, but calls Paul and Barnabas apostles in ACT 14.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul opens letters by naming himself apostle 'by the will of God' and defends his apostleship with signs and the converts he has made.

study.translationNote: Most versions transliterate as 'apostle', but render 'messengers' or 'representatives' where the sense is non-technical (2 Cor 8:23; Php 2:25). In Rom 16:7 versions differ between 'outstanding among the apostles' and 'well known to the apostles', and between Junia (a woman) and Junias.

background.note: Herodotus uses it of a messenger or envoy sent on a mission.
In Attic it usually meant a naval expedition or fleet.
The one Septuagint use describes the prophet Ahijah as a messenger sent from God with a hard message.
In papyri it can denote a cargo ship or a bill of lading.

study.exegesisTip: Ask whether 'apostle' refers to the Twelve, to Paul, to a wider group of missionaries, or simply to an envoy of a church.
study.caution: Whether Rom 16:7 names a woman apostle (Junia) 'outstanding among the apostles' or someone 'well known to the apostles' is debated, as is how broad the circle of 'apostles' was and whether the office continued after the first generation.

study.summary: Righteous, just: conforming to God's standard of what is right — of upright people, of God and Christ, of fair judgment, and of what is right or due.

senses.label: Upright, devout person
senses.definition: A person who lives in conformity with God's will and law, faithful in duty to God and others.
senses.note: Paired with 'devout', 'holy', 'good', 'God-fearing'.

senses.label: God or Christ, the Righteous One
senses.definition: God as perfectly righteous, and Jesus as 'the Righteous One' who is innocent and faithful.

senses.label: Just, fair in judging
senses.definition: Rendering to each what is due, especially of God's judgments and of Christ as judge.
senses.note: ROM 3:26: God 'just and the justifier'.

senses.label: Right, proper, due
senses.definition: Neuter: what is right or fitting, what one owes.
senses.note: δίκαιόν ἐστιν 'it is right'.

senses.label: The righteous as a group
senses.definition: Those counted righteous, contrasted with sinners or the wicked, sometimes with irony toward the self-righteous.

senses.label: Righteous through faith
senses.definition: In Paul and Hebrews, the one who stands right with God by faith.
senses.note: Quoting Habakkuk 2:4.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew contrasts the righteous and the wicked at the final judgment.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke presents Jesus as 'the Righteous One' and has the centurion declare him δίκαιος at the cross.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul shows God as both just and the one who justifies, and the righteous living by faith.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: 1 John grounds believers' righteousness in Christ the righteous one.

study.translationNote: English uses 'righteous' (moral and religious uprightness) and 'just' (fairness in judging) for one Greek word, so versions alternate by context (e.g. 1 John 1:9 'faithful and just'). In LUK 23:47 the centurion's words are rendered 'righteous' (ESV, NASB) or 'innocent' (NRSV, NIV); in Matthew 1:19 'righteous' or 'just man'.

background.note: In Homer it describes people who observe custom and social order, i.e. civilised.
Applied to a just or accurate measure.
The neuter plural is used for the duties of marriage — 'the rights' each owes the other.
A petitioner asks the king that she may 'obtain justice' (τοῦ δικαίου τύχω).

study.exegesisTip: Ask whose standard is in view — God's law, human fairness, or Paul's righteousness by faith — and whether the word describes character, a verdict or what is owed.
study.caution: In ROM 1:17 and GAL 3:11 it is debated whether 'by faith' goes with 'the righteous' ('the one righteous by faith will live') or with 'will live' ('the righteous will live by faith').

study.summary: To go up, climb or ascend — of people, things rising, pilgrims going up to Jerusalem, and Christ ascending to heaven; also of thoughts or prayers rising.

senses.label: Go up, climb
senses.definition: To move upward to a higher place: a mountain, a tree, a boat, an upper room.

senses.label: Go up to Jerusalem or temple
senses.definition: The customary verb for travelling to Jerusalem or the temple, set on high ground, often as pilgrimage.
senses.note: Used whatever the compass direction.

senses.label: Come up out of water
senses.definition: To come up from the water after baptism.

senses.label: Ascend to heaven
senses.definition: To rise to heaven, of Christ's ascension, of angels, or of anyone reaching God's presence.

senses.label: Rise, come up (things)
senses.definition: Of things coming up: plants growing, a fish surfacing, smoke rising, a beast emerging.

senses.label: Rise in the mind; reach
senses.definition: Figuratively, thoughts arising in the heart, prayers rising before God, or reports reaching an authority.
senses.note: 'Come up into the heart' is a Hebrew idiom.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John pairs ascending and descending to express the Son of Man's heavenly origin and return.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke structures journeys as 'going up' to Jerusalem and the temple.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses it of his Jerusalem visits and of Christ's ascension 'on high'.

background.note: Used of going up to heaven or to an upper room.
Used for going up to the temple of Sarapis to worship, a parallel to going up to the temple (Luke 18:10).
A labour account notes a worker 'gone up to the city', like the NT phrase for Jerusalem.

study.exegesisTip: Watch for paired 'up/down' language (ἀναβαίνω/καταβαίνω), which often carries theological weight, especially in John.
study.caution: Which of Paul's 'going up' visits in GAL 2:1 corresponds to the Jerusalem visits in Acts (Acts 11 or 15) is debated.

study.summary: To dip, wash or immerse, used in the NT chiefly of the religious rite of baptism (John's and Christian), and figuratively of being overwhelmed by suffering or the Spirit.

senses.label: Ritual washing
senses.definition: To wash oneself or perform ceremonial washing, as in Jewish purity customs.
senses.note: KJV renders 'wash' here.

senses.label: John's baptism
senses.definition: The baptism of repentance administered by John in the Jordan, in preparation for the coming one.
senses.note: ὁ βαπτίζων 'the baptizer' = John (MAR 6:14).

senses.label: Christian baptism
senses.definition: The rite of initiation into the church, administered in or into the name of Jesus or the triune God.
senses.note: With ἐν, ἐπί or εἰς τὸ ὄνομα.

senses.label: Baptized into Christ
senses.definition: Baptism as union with Christ, his death, and his body.
senses.note: Esp. Paul; εἰς marks incorporation.

senses.label: Baptize with the Spirit
senses.definition: The coming one's act of immersing people in the Holy Spirit (and fire), contrasted with John's water baptism.

senses.label: Overwhelmed by suffering
senses.definition: Figuratively, to be engulfed by an ordeal, of Jesus' coming passion.
senses.note: With the cognate 'baptism'.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Acts links baptism with repentance, the name of Jesus and receiving the Spirit, in varying order.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul treats baptism as union with Christ but subordinates the act of baptizing to preaching.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John reports Jesus' disciples baptizing alongside John, with the note that Jesus himself did not baptize.

study.translationNote: Nearly all versions transliterate as 'baptize', which leaves the rite's meaning to be read from context; some translations render 'immerse' or 'dip'. At Mark 7:4 and Luke 11:38 most render 'wash'.

background.note: Polybius uses it of ships being sunk.
Naaman 'dipped himself' seven times in the Jordan.
An early letter seems to use it metaphorically of being 'overwhelmed' by calamities — compare Jesus' passion as a baptism.
A magic papyrus pairs it with bathing: 'having washed and dipped oneself'.

study.exegesisTip: Notice the preposition: ἐν/dative marks the element (water, Spirit), εἰς marks the person or purpose one is baptized into.
study.caution: Christians differ on the mode (immersion versus pouring or sprinkling) and on whether the word itself requires immersion, citing both its basic sense 'dip' and uses like 'wash' (MAR 7:4). They also differ on how baptism relates to salvation (ACT 2:38), on 'baptism for the dead' (1CO 15:29), and on Spirit-baptism; MAR 16:16 lies in the textually disputed longer ending.

study.summary: To go or come down, descend — from mountains or cities, from heaven (God's Spirit, angels, Christ, gifts), and of things falling, such as rain or hail.

senses.label: Go down (geography)
senses.definition: To travel down from a higher place, from a mountain, or from Jerusalem to lower towns.
senses.note: The opposite of 'going up' to Jerusalem.

senses.label: Get down from a place
senses.definition: To step down from a roof, tree, boat or cross.

senses.label: Come down from heaven
senses.definition: Of the Spirit, angels, Christ, or the returning Lord descending from heaven.

senses.label: Things falling or coming down
senses.definition: Of rain, storm, fire, hail, a vision-sheet, the new Jerusalem, or good gifts from God.

senses.label: Descend to the depths
senses.definition: Descent to the abyss or the lower regions, of Christ's humiliation and death.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John repeats that Jesus is the bread that 'came down from heaven', stressing his heavenly origin.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses it for journeys down from Jerusalem and for the Spirit descending on Jesus.

background.note: Used from Homer on for going or coming down.
A letter asks to be told about tax-collecting 'until you come down'.
Used of a coin's value that 'has come down', i.e. depreciated.
Used of malefactors who might 'come down' out of a temple asylum.

study.exegesisTip: Read 'came down' and 'went up' together, especially in John and Ephesians 4, where descent and ascent frame Christ's whole mission.
study.caution: Whether 'descended to the lower parts of the earth' (EPH 4:9) refers to the incarnation, burial, a descent to Hades, or the Spirit's coming at Pentecost is debated.

study.summary: To send: dispatch a person on an errand or mission, or send a thing; in John above all God the Father 'who sent' Jesus, the ground of his authority.

senses.label: Send someone on an errand
senses.definition: To dispatch a person, usually as messenger or agent, to a place or to someone.
senses.note: Often with εἰς (place or purpose) or πρός (person); with an infinitive of purpose (1CO 16:3).

senses.label: Act through agents
senses.definition: A participle πέμψας before a main verb means a person acted through others: 'sent and had John beheaded'.
senses.note: Often followed by λέγων, reflecting a Hebrew idiom ('sent, saying').

senses.label: Sent by God
senses.definition: God commissioning his messengers, above all the Father sending the Son, who therefore speaks and acts with the Father's authority.
senses.note: ὁ πέμψας με, 'the One who sent me', is almost a title for God in John.

senses.label: Send things or gifts
senses.definition: To send objects, letters or material help to someone.

senses.label: Send forth an action
senses.definition: To put forth or send upon: the harvest sickle 'thrust in', or God sending a deluding power on those who refuse the truth.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: Nearly half of all NT uses are in John, mostly in the phrase 'the One (or the Father) who sent me': Jesus' words, works and will derive from the sender, so honouring or receiving him is honouring the Father.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses the verb chiefly for sending co-workers such as Timothy, Tychicus and Epaphroditus as his representatives to the churches.

background.note: An everyday verb in letters: 'get the kid from Aristion and send it to me'.
The colourless verb could cover official banishment: a woman 'sent to the Oasis' by the authorities.
The Hebrew idiom 'send by the hand of' someone lies behind πέμψας διά in MAT 11:2.

study.exegesisTip: In John, read 'sent' as a statement of agency: the one sent represents the sender, so the response to Jesus is a response to the Father (JOH 13:20).
study.caution: Whether John means anything different by πέμπω and ἀποστέλλω is debated: some (following Westcott and Rengstorf) see πέμπω stressing the sender's authority and ἀποστέλλω the commission, but most recent scholars treat them as stylistic variants, since John uses both of the Father sending the Son.

study.summary: Mouth: the bodily mouth of people and animals, above all as the organ of speech; by extension a person's words or testimony, God's word through prophets, and the 'edge' of a sword.

senses.label: Physical mouth
senses.definition: The mouth of a person or animal, through which food enters and things are taken in.
senses.note: 'Mouth of the lion' is used figuratively of mortal danger (2TI 4:17).

senses.label: Organ of speech
senses.definition: The mouth as what speaks, revealing what fills the heart; hence a person's words and speech.
senses.note: Often paired with or opposed to καρδία (ROM 10:8; ROM 10:10). 'I will give you a mouth and wisdom' = eloquence (LUK 21:15).

senses.label: Channel of another's word
senses.definition: The mouth through which God, the Spirit or a witness speaks: 'through the mouth of the prophets', 'from his own lips', 'on the testimony of two witnesses'.
senses.note: 'On the mouth of two or three witnesses' (Deut 19:15) = on their testimony (2CO 13:1).

senses.label: Speech idioms
senses.definition: 'Open the mouth' introduces solemn or deliberate speech or restored speech; 'mouth to mouth' means face to face.
senses.note: 2CO 6:11 'our mouth is open to you' = we have spoken frankly.

senses.label: Mouth of judgment
senses.definition: In apocalyptic imagery, the mouth from which the Lord's sword or breath goes out to judge and destroy.

senses.label: Edge or opening
senses.definition: The 'mouth' of things: the edge of a sword (a Hebrew idiom) or the earth opening its mouth.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew stresses that what comes out of the mouth flows from the heart and defiles, unlike food entering it, and that lip-service is not worship.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke often speaks of God speaking 'through the mouth' of David, the prophets or Peter, framing Scripture and preaching as God's own speech.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul links confession with the mouth to faith in the heart, and calls for speech that builds up rather than corrupts.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: In Revelation the mouth is a seat of power: a sword from Christ's mouth, fire from the witnesses' mouths, blasphemy and unclean spirits from the beast's.

study.translationNote: Most versions keep 'mouth', but idioms are often rendered by sense: 'lips' (LUK 22:71), 'began to speak' for 'opened his mouth' (ACT 10:34), 'testimony' for 'mouth of two witnesses', 'face to face' for 'mouth to mouth' (2JO 1:12), and 'edge of the sword' for 'mouth of the sword' (LUK 21:24).

background.note: Homer speaks of 'the mouth of war', the jaws of battle as of a devouring monster.
'Mouth to mouth' (Num 12:8) describes God speaking directly with Moses, the background to 2JO 1:12.
The Rosetta stone uses the plural for the mouths of rivers or canals.
Witnesses speak 'from one mouth' (in agreement), comparable to 'from his mouth' in ACT 22:14.

study.exegesisTip: When στόμα is paired with καρδία, the mouth is what expresses or confesses what the heart holds (MAT 12:34; ROM 10:10).

study.summary: To open: doors, tombs, seals, books, eyes and mouths; figuratively to open a door of opportunity or access, and 'to open the mouth' for beginning to speak.

senses.label: Open a physical object
senses.definition: To open doors, gates, treasure boxes, tombs or a pit.
senses.note: Prison doors opened by divine intervention are a pattern in Acts.

senses.label: Door of opportunity
senses.definition: Metaphorically, God opening a 'door' for faith or for effective preaching.

senses.label: Grant entry or welcome
senses.definition: Opening to one who knocks: access granted in answer to prayer, to the kingdom, or fellowship with Christ.

senses.label: Heaven opened
senses.definition: Heaven opened as a sign of divine revelation or intervention.
senses.note: Often the perfect participle: heaven 'standing open'.

senses.label: Open seals and scrolls
senses.definition: To unseal and open a sealed scroll or book, so that its contents are revealed and set in motion.

senses.label: Open eyes
senses.definition: To restore sight to the blind, or figuratively to give spiritual understanding.

senses.label: Open the mouth
senses.definition: A Hebrew idiom for beginning solemn speech; also recovering speech, or a mouth (or throat) gaping open.
senses.note: Perfect ἀνέῳγεν, 'stands open', = speaking freely (2CO 6:11); cf. ROM 3:13 'an open grave'.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John 9 repeats 'opened eyes' as the leading question of the healing of the man born blind; Revelation uses opening for heaven, doors, seals and books as stages of revelation.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Acts tells of prison doors opened by God and of God 'opening a door of faith' to the Gentiles.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul speaks of 'a door opened' for his mission and asks prayer that God would open one.

study.translationNote: Literal versions keep 'he opened his mouth and taught' (MAT 5:2) or 'Philip opened his mouth' (ACT 8:35); idiomatic ones render 'began to teach/speak', which is the sense but loses the note of solemn, deliberate utterance. Likewise 2CO 6:11 is 'our mouth is open to you' (literal) or 'we have spoken freely' (dynamic).

background.note: Inscriptions use the same phrase as MAT 2:11 for officials opening a temple treasury.
'Let him open the seals', as in Revelation's opening of sealed documents.
A Neoplatonist epitaph speaks of seeing 'heaven opened to men', echoing the biblical phrase.
'I will open my mouth in parables' (Ps 78:2) is quoted in MAT 13:35.

study.exegesisTip: Passive forms are often divine passives: heaven 'was opened', eyes 'were opened', a door 'has been opened' all imply that God did it.

study.summary: Evil: bad or worthless, painful or harmful, and above all morally wicked; used of people, deeds, thoughts and spirits, and with the article as a title for Satan, 'the evil one'.

senses.label: Painful, harmful
senses.definition: Causing distress or harm: 'evil days', a malignant sore.
senses.note: The older sense 'toilsome, grievous' (from πονέω 'to toil').

senses.label: Bad, worthless
senses.definition: Of poor quality or useless, as diseased fruit from a bad tree.

senses.label: Evil eye: envy, stinginess
senses.definition: ὀφθαλμὸς πονηρός, a Semitic idiom for a grudging, envious or ungenerous disposition.
senses.note: In MAT 6:23 also read as an 'unhealthy' eye; the stinginess idiom fits the context on money.

senses.label: Wicked people
senses.definition: Morally bad people, often as a substantive 'the wicked', opposed to the good or righteous.
senses.note: 'Evil generation' (MAT 12:39; LUK 11:29).

senses.label: Evil deeds, words, thoughts
senses.definition: Things morally evil: acts, speech, thoughts or a heart turned from God.
senses.note: Neuter τὸ πονηρόν 'evil' opposite τὸ ἀγαθόν (ROM 12:9).

senses.label: Evil spirits
senses.definition: Demonic spirits described as evil.

senses.label: The evil one (Satan)
senses.definition: With the article, a personal title for the devil.
senses.note: Possibly also MAT 5:37 and MAT 6:13, where the genitive could be neuter ('evil').

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew has a third of all NT uses: the 'evil generation', evil and good people side by side until judgment, and 'the evil one' who snatches the word.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: 1 John uses ὁ πονηρός as the name of the adversary whom believers have overcome and in whose power the world lies; Jesus prays that his own be kept from him.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul applies the word to the present age and 'evil days', and to the evil one whose arrows faith quenches.

study.translationNote: The genitive τοῦ πονηροῦ can be neuter ('evil') or masculine ('the evil one'). So in the Lord's Prayer KJV and NASB have 'deliver us from evil', while ESV, NIV and others have 'from the evil one' (MAT 6:13); similar splits occur at MAT 5:37 and JOH 17:15. In MAT 5:39 'do not resist the evil person' (most versions) vs 'evil' (KJV) changes the application.

background.note: The root sense 'toilworn': Heracles is called 'most toil-laden and best'.
Sirach speaks of a 'time of evil', a season of trouble, like the 'evil day' of EPH 6:13.
A deed of divorce blames the break-up on 'some evil deity'.
A will uses 'evil fraud' (δόλος πονηρός), the Greek of the Latin legal formula dolus malus.

study.exegesisTip: Decide whether the word means harm or distress, worthlessness, moral wickedness, or a personal agent; an articular masculine singular (ὁ πονηρός) usually signals Satan.
study.caution: Two debates: whether ambiguous genitives (MAT 5:37; MAT 6:13) mean 'evil' or 'the evil one' (scholars and early interpreters divide; the Greek allows both), and whether πονηρός differs from κακός, as Trench and Strong's claim (active, harmful malice vs inner badness). Most lexicographers now see the two as largely overlapping.

study.summary: Face: the human face, and through Hebrew idiom a person's presence ('before', 'from the presence of'), outward appearance or status (as in 'showing partiality'), and the surface of things.

senses.label: Face, countenance
senses.definition: The front of the head, its look and expression.

senses.label: Falling on one's face
senses.definition: πίπτειν ἐπὶ πρόσωπον: prostration in worship, fear, supplication or thanksgiving.

senses.label: In person, face to face
senses.definition: Personal presence: 'to see someone's face' = to meet them; κατὰ πρόσωπον = to one's face.

senses.label: Presence (Hebrew idiom)
senses.definition: In prepositional phrases the face stands for presence: 'before' (πρὸ προσώπου), 'from the presence of' (ἀπὸ προσώπου), 'in the presence of' (ἐν προσώπῳ).
senses.note: God's 'face' = his favour or opposition (1PE 3:12) and his presence seen (MAT 18:10; REV 22:4).

senses.label: Outward appearance; partiality
senses.definition: External status or appearance; λαμβάνειν πρόσωπον ('to receive a face') and βλέπειν εἰς πρόσωπον mean to show favouritism.
senses.note: Contrasted with the heart (2CO 5:12; 1TH 2:17).

senses.label: Surface or look of things
senses.definition: The face of earth or sky: its appearance or its whole surface.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke has the most Hebrew-style phrases: Jesus 'set his face' toward Jerusalem, and many uses of 'before the face of' and 'from the presence of'.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: In 2 Corinthians Paul contrasts Moses' fading, veiled face with believers who with unveiled face behold the Lord's glory, the glory of God 'in the face of Christ'; he also hopes to see God 'face to face'.

study.translationNote: English often drops 'face' where the Greek uses it idiomatically: 'facedown', 'before', 'from the presence of', 'in person', 'show partiality' (lit. 'receive a face'). 2CO 2:10 ἐν προσώπῳ Χριστοῦ is 'in the person of Christ' in KJV but 'in the presence of Christ' in most modern versions.

background.note: In Homer the word is almost always plural, even of one person's face.
'Man looks on the outward appearance (face), but the Lord on the heart' (1 Sam 16:7) underlies Paul's contrast in 2CO 5:12.
In everyday Koine the word could simply mean 'person', as in 'to strangers' (lit. 'to strange faces').
A wife complains her husband used abuse 'to my face' (εἰς πρόσωπόν μου).

study.exegesisTip: Many 'face' phrases are Hebrew idioms for presence or partiality; translate the idiom, not the anatomy, but notice when the author is playing on a literal face (2CO 3:18).

study.summary: Good news: in the NT the message of God's saving reign and of salvation through Jesus Christ, the activity of proclaiming it, and the cause for which believers labour and suffer.

senses.label: Message of salvation
senses.definition: The good news about what God has done in Jesus Christ, to be believed and obeyed.
senses.note: Genitives name the source ('of God', ROM 15:16), content ('of Christ', ROM 15:19) or preacher ('my gospel', ROM 2:16).

senses.label: Gospel of the kingdom
senses.definition: Jesus' announcement that God's reign is arriving, with healing as its sign.
senses.note: Esp. Matthew.

senses.label: The gospel as norm
senses.definition: The apostolic gospel as a fixed standard by which other teaching and conduct are measured.
senses.note: 'Another gospel' (GAL 1:6) is no gospel at all.

senses.label: Proclaiming the gospel
senses.definition: The work or activity of spreading the message; gospel ministry and partnership in it.

senses.label: Cause worth sacrifice
senses.definition: The gospel as the cause for which one gives up life, home and comfort, and for which one suffers.
senses.note: 'For my sake and the gospel's' (Mark).

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: About four-fifths of all uses are Paul's. He calls it 'the gospel of God', 'of Christ' and 'my gospel', sees himself set apart and called to priestly service for it, and defends its truth against alternatives.

authorNotes.author: Mark
authorNotes.note: Mark opens with 'the beginning of the gospel', places it beside Jesus himself ('for my sake and the gospel's') and stresses its proclamation to all nations.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew's characteristic phrase is 'the gospel of the kingdom'.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses the noun only twice (both in Acts), preferring the verb εὐαγγελίζομαι.

study.translationNote: Traditional versions use 'gospel', a technical term from Old English 'good spell'; NRSV, CEB, GNT and others often prefer 'good news', which makes the plain meaning visible but loses the sense of a fixed, recognised message. Neither should be read as 'a book about Jesus', a later meaning.

background.note: In Homer the singular is the reward given to a messenger for good news.
In Attic Greek the plural is used for sacrifices offered in thanks for good news.
In the Septuagint the word still means a reward for good news (2 Sam 4:10).
The Priene calendar inscription (c. 9 BC) says the birthday of the god Augustus was for the world 'the beginning of good tidings'.

study.exegesisTip: Watch the genitive: 'of God' (the giver), 'of Christ' or 'of his Son' (the content), 'my/our gospel' (the preacher), 'of the circumcision' (the hearers).
study.caution: How far NT 'gospel' language deliberately challenges imperial 'good news' (Priene inscription) is debated; its main roots are probably in Isaiah's herald of good tidings (verb forms), with the imperial echo heard by Gentile readers. Whether MAR 1:1 is a title for the whole book or the opening of the story is also disputed.

study.summary: Sign: an identifying mark or token, a portent of things to come, and especially a miracle understood as a sign pointing to God's power and authority, or a counterfeit one meant to deceive.

senses.label: Identifying mark, token
senses.definition: A mark or signal by which a person or thing is recognised or authenticated.
senses.note: Circumcision as 'sign' and 'seal' (ROM 4:11); Paul's own signature (2TH 3:17).

senses.label: Sign as pointer or warning
senses.definition: A person or event that points to God's dealings and calls for response, often unwelcome.

senses.label: Portent of the future
senses.definition: An unusual event, often cosmic, indicating that something (especially the end) is coming.
senses.note: 'Signs of the times' (MAT 16:3).

senses.label: Demanded proof
senses.definition: A miracle demanded as credentials, which Jesus refuses except for 'the sign of Jonah'.

senses.label: Miracle as attesting sign
senses.definition: A miraculous deed regarded as a sign of divine authority, revealing who Jesus is or confirming the apostles' message.
senses.note: Often in the pair 'signs and wonders' (ACT 2:43; ROM 15:19).

senses.label: Counterfeit signs
senses.definition: Deceptive wonders worked by false prophets, the lawless one or demonic powers.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John calls Jesus' miracles 'signs' (never δυνάμεις), counts them, and writes so that readers may believe; yet faith resting only on signs is shown to be shallow.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Acts repeatedly reports 'signs and wonders' done through the apostles, echoing Moses and confirming the word.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul cites 'the signs of an apostle' as credentials, yet sets the crucified Christ against Jewish demands for signs.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew twice records Jesus refusing a sign to an 'evil and adulterous generation' except the sign of Jonah.

study.translationNote: KJV often has 'miracle' in John ('this beginning of miracles', JOH 2:11); NIV 1984 has 'miraculous sign'; ESV, NASB and NIV 2011 simply 'sign'. 'Miracle' names the event but hides John's point that it points beyond itself; bare 'sign' keeps that point but may not tell the reader a miracle is meant.

background.note: From Herodotus on, a mark by which a thing is known.
Sale documents describe a camel by its identifying brand or mark.
An inscription speaks of a god foretelling events 'through the signs that occurred in the temple'.

study.exegesisTip: Ask what a sign points to; in John, follow each sign into the discourse that interprets it (e.g. the feeding, JOH 6:14, and the bread of life).
study.caution: How tongues are 'a sign for unbelievers' (1CO 14:22) is much debated: a sign of judgment on unbelief (following Isa 28:11), or a sign that leaves outsiders unconvinced, in contrast to prophecy.

study.summary: To lead or bring: take people or animals somewhere, bring someone before a court, guide inwardly (by the Spirit or by desires); also 'spend a day' and, intransitively, 'let us go'.

senses.label: Lead, bring
senses.definition: To lead or bring a person or animal to a place or person.
senses.note: With πρός, εἰς, ἐπί, ἕως or a simple dative.

senses.label: Lead away; arraign
senses.definition: To take someone into custody or bring them before a court or ruler.
senses.note: Regularly with ἐπί + a ruler or tribunal.

senses.label: Guide, impel
senses.definition: To lead inwardly: the Spirit guiding, God's kindness leading to repentance, or desires driving people.
senses.note: Usually passive: 'be led'.

senses.label: Bring to salvation
senses.definition: God bringing his people into his fold, to glory, or with Jesus at his coming.

senses.label: Spend, keep a day
senses.definition: To pass or observe time; courts 'are in session'.
senses.note: LUK 24:21: 'this is the third day'.

senses.label: Let us go; come now
senses.definition: Intransitive ἄγωμεν 'let us go'; imperative ἄγε as an interjection 'come now'.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Over half of all uses are in Luke–Acts, often in legal scenes: Jesus and the apostles are 'brought' before councils, governors and the Areopagus.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul contrasts being 'led' by the Spirit, the mark of God's children, with former pagan life 'led astray' to idols.

study.translationNote: Idiomatic uses are rendered by sense: ἄγωμεν 'let us go' or 'let us be going' (MAT 26:46), ἄγε 'come now' (JAM 4:13), and LUK 24:21 'it is the third day' (lit. 'he is spending this third day').

background.note: Petitions ask that accused persons 'be brought before' the official, the same legal construction with ἐπί as MAT 10:18.
Used for fetching or carrying goods: bundles of reeds to be brought at the rising of the Nile.

study.exegesisTip: Notice the passive 'be led' in ROM 8:14 and GAL 5:18: the Spirit is the active guide, and believers follow.
study.caution: Whether 'led by the Spirit' (ROM 8:14; GAL 5:18) concerns guidance in decisions or, as most commentators hold from the context, the Spirit's moral leading against the flesh is debated in popular use; the contexts favour the moral sense.

study.summary: To kill: put to death, whether by murder, execution or violence; also of God's judgments, and figuratively of sin, the letter of the law, or hostility being 'killed'.

senses.label: Kill, put to death
senses.definition: To take a person's life, by murder, execution or persecution.
senses.note: Often of the killing of prophets, apostles and Jesus himself.

senses.label: Kill the body only
senses.definition: Bodily killing contrasted with the soul, which human killers cannot touch.

senses.label: Destroy life
senses.definition: To take life as the opposite of saving it.

senses.label: Judgment and slaughter
senses.definition: In Revelation, mass killing as judgment or by beasts and enemies of God's people.

senses.label: Figurative killing
senses.definition: To bring spiritual death or to abolish: sin 'killed me', 'the letter kills', Christ 'killed the hostility'.
senses.note: Esp. Paul.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John repeatedly says the authorities 'sought to kill' Jesus, building tension toward the cross.

authorNotes.author: Mark
authorNotes.note: Mark's passion predictions say the Son of Man will be killed and after three days rise.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke frames Jesus' death as part of Israel's pattern of killing prophets, and in Acts confronts hearers: 'you killed the Author of life'.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses the verb figuratively for sin and the written code bringing death, and for Christ abolishing enmity.

background.note: Complaints use the verb hyperbolically: 'half killed them with blows'.
A complainant says a man would have killed him had he not fled; Moulton–Milligan note the verb is surprisingly rare in popular papyri.

study.exegesisTip: In ROM 7:11 and 2CO 3:6 the verb is figurative for condemnation and spiritual death; read it alongside its opposite, 'gives life' (2CO 3:6).
study.caution: 'The letter kills' (2CO 3:6) is read either as the Mosaic law as written code without the Spirit, which condemns, or (traditionally) as a literalistic way of reading Scripture; most modern commentators favour the first.

study.summary: Head: the literal head of a person or animal, in gestures and idioms; the 'head of the corner'; and metaphorically Christ as head of the church and of all powers, and the husband as head of the wife.

senses.label: Literal head
senses.definition: The head of a human or animal body, including John the Baptist's severed head.
senses.note: Anointing the head (MAT 26:7; LUK 7:46).

senses.label: Gestures and idioms
senses.definition: The head in symbolic acts and phrases: shaking the head in mockery, blood on one's head (responsibility), coals on the head, lifting up the head.

senses.label: Head covering in worship
senses.definition: In 1 Corinthians 11, the literal head covered or uncovered, with a play on 'head' in the metaphorical sense.

senses.label: Head of the corner
senses.definition: From Psalm 118, the rejected stone that becomes the chief stone of the building.

senses.label: Christ as head
senses.definition: Christ as head over all things and of his body, the church: ruling it and supplying its growth.
senses.note: Esp. Paul (Ephesians, Colossians).

senses.label: Headship in relationships
senses.definition: The man (or husband) as 'head' of the woman, Christ of every man, God of Christ.
senses.note: See caution.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul alone uses 'head' metaphorically for relationships: Christ to the church and the cosmic powers, and husband to wife, combined with the image of the body that grows from the head.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: Revelation describes the Son of Man's white head and the many heads and crowns of the dragon and beasts, which it interprets as mountains and kings.

study.translationNote: Versions keep 'head' in 1CO 11:3 and EPH 5:23, leaving readers to interpret the metaphor. They differ on κεφαλὴ γωνίας (MAT 21:42): 'cornerstone' (ESV, NIV 2011), 'capstone' (NIV 1984), 'head of the corner' (KJV).

background.note: Homer measures stature 'by a head' (taller by the head).
A land survey uses κεφαλή for the far end or extremity of a plot, supporting 'extremity of the corner' in MAT 21:42.
In business documents κεφαλή can mean the whole amount or total.

study.exegesisTip: Let each context define the metaphor: in Ephesians and Colossians the head both rules the body and nourishes its growth (EPH 4:15; COL 2:19).
study.caution: The metaphorical sense in 1CO 11:3 and EPH 5:23 is much debated: many (e.g. Grudem, Fitzmyer) argue for 'authority over', citing Septuagint usage for leaders; others (e.g. Bedale, Kroeger) argue for 'source' or 'origin' (woman made from man, later in 1 Corinthians 11), and some for 'preeminent, prominent'. Each side cites the surrounding context: the call to submit, and Christ nourishing and cherishing the church, both later in Ephesians 5.

study.summary: To bear witness: to testify to what one has seen or knows, to affirm solemnly, and (often passive) to speak well of someone or be well attested — a key word for John's theme of witness to Jesus.

senses.label: Testify as an eyewitness
senses.definition: To declare what one has personally seen or heard, as a witness whose report others should believe.
senses.note: Often paired with 'seeing' and 'hearing' (JOH 3:11, 3:32).

senses.label: Bear witness to a person
senses.definition: To give testimony about someone's identity or claims, especially witness that points to Jesus as the Christ and Son of God.
senses.note: Usually μαρτυρέω περί τινος, 'testify concerning'.

senses.label: Scripture or God attests
senses.definition: Of Scripture, the prophets or the Spirit as a witness that confirms a truth.
senses.note: Impersonal 'it is testified' introduces a scriptural quotation (HEB 7:17).

senses.label: Affirm, solemnly declare
senses.definition: To vouch personally for a fact about others, as a guarantor of its truth: 'I can testify that…'.
senses.note: Paul's μαρτυρῶ γάρ + dative + ὅτι; parenthetical in 2CO 8:3.

senses.label: Testify in a judicial setting
senses.definition: To give evidence for or against someone, as in a trial: to testify about wrongdoing, against oneself, or to the truth before judges.
senses.note: κατά + genitive 'testify against' (1CO 15:15).

senses.label: Speak well of; be well attested
senses.definition: To give a favourable report of someone; in the passive, to have a good reputation or be approved, especially by God.
senses.note: A late-Greek sense, common in the passive (ἐμαρτυρήθησαν, 'were commended').

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: Nearly two-thirds of the uses are Johannine. Witness is a structuring theme: John the Baptist, the Father, Jesus' works, the Scriptures, the Spirit and the disciples all 'testify' about Jesus, as in a trial of the world.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews uses the passive for God's approval of the faithful ('were commended') and the impersonal form for Scripture's testimony.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Acts often uses the passive for a person's good standing in the community, a qualification for service.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses μαρτυρῶ as a personal guarantee of others' zeal or generosity, much like a witness's signature on a document.

study.translationNote: Most versions use 'testify' or 'bear witness'; the KJV also has 'bear record'. For the passive sense of approval the KJV says 'obtained a good report' (Heb 11:2), while modern versions say 'were commended' (NIV, ESV) or 'gained approval' (NASB) — the same verb, not a different word for praise.

background.note: In classical Greek it is the ordinary verb for giving evidence in court, e.g. trusting a witness who testifies.
The Septuagint uses it chiefly for Hebrew ʿēd, as of the heap of stones that 'witnesses' between Jacob and Laban.
Witnesses sign wills and contracts with a simple μαρτυρῶ, 'I witness' — a parallel to Paul's 'I testify' in 2 Cor 8:3.
A mother writes that her son's former teacher 'spoke very well' of his tutor — the favourable sense of Luke 4:22.

study.exegesisTip: Note who testifies and to what: in John the piling up of witnesses is a deliberate legal case for Jesus, while a passive form often means 'was approved', not 'was told about'.
study.caution: The later Christian sense 'to die as a martyr' developed after the NT (it is debated already in 1 Clement 5); NT uses mean 'bear witness', though Revelation links witness with suffering. Whether 1TI 6:13 refers to Jesus' testimony before Pilate or under his governorship is also debated.

study.summary: Fire: literal fire for burning and warmth, and in Scripture above all a symbol of God's judgment, of testing and purification, and of his holy presence; also a figure for destructive forces such as the tongue.

senses.label: Literal fire
senses.definition: Ordinary fire that burns, warms or destroys.
senses.note: 'Fire and sulphur' on Sodom (LUK 17:29).

senses.label: Fire of judgment
senses.definition: Fire as God's instrument of punishment on the unfruitful and the wicked, whether in history or at the end of the age.
senses.note: Images of burning trees, chaff and weeds.

senses.label: Eternal fire, hell-fire
senses.definition: The final punishment pictured as unquenchable, eternal fire: Gehenna, the furnace, the lake of fire.
senses.note: γέεννα τοῦ πυρός; πῦρ αἰώνιον; πῦρ ἄσβεστον; ἡ λίμνη τοῦ πυρός.

senses.label: Testing, refining fire
senses.definition: Fire that proves or purifies, revealing the true quality of work or faith as metal is assayed.
senses.note: δοκιμάζειν διὰ πυρός; 'saved, but as through fire' (1CO 3:15).

senses.label: Sign of God's presence
senses.definition: Fire or flame as the visible manifestation of God's holy presence and power, or of heavenly beings.
senses.note: 'Our God is a consuming fire' (HEB 12:29).

senses.label: Figurative destructive force
senses.definition: A picture of something that spreads and destroys, or of division and conflict.
senses.note: 'Coals of fire' (ROM 12:20) is a proverb about provoking shame or remorse.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: Almost all John's uses are in Revelation: eyes 'like a flame of fire', fire hurled from the altar, and the lake of fire as final judgment.

authorNotes.author: Mark
authorNotes.note: Mark's sayings on cutting off a hand or foot pile up images of Gehenna's unquenchable fire, ending with the enigmatic 'salted with fire'.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews uses fire for the terror of Sinai and the judgment awaiting apostates, and calls God himself a consuming fire.

authorNotes.author: James
authorNotes.note: James makes fire the image of the tongue's destructive power, set on fire by Gehenna.

study.translationNote: πῦρ is almost always 'fire'. Phrases differ: γέεννα τοῦ πυρός is 'hell fire' (KJV), 'fire of hell' (NIV) or 'hell of fire' (ESV), all for the same genitive phrase.

background.note: From Homer on it is the everyday word for fire, e.g. kindling fire in camp.
The Septuagint uses it chiefly for Hebrew ʾēš; Jewish martyr literature already speaks of the tyrant's 'eternal fire'.
A report of a sudden fire breaking out in heaps of hay shows the ordinary use.
A magical papyrus calls a powerful spirit 'the deathless fire', a pagan phrase comparable to 'eternal fire'.

study.exegesisTip: Ask what the fire does in each passage — destroys, tests, purifies or reveals God's presence; in 1CO 3:13–15 it tests the builders' work rather than punishing the person.
study.caution: Several uses are debated: 'baptize with the Holy Spirit and fire' (LUK 3:16) may mean judgment, purification or the Pentecost flames; 'salted with fire' (MAR 9:49) is obscure; and whether eternal fire implies everlasting conscious punishment or final destruction is a long-standing theological dispute.

study.summary: To keep: to guard or hold in custody, to keep something safe or reserved for a set time, to protect, and — very often in John — to keep God's word or commandments by obeying them.

senses.label: Guard, hold in custody
senses.definition: To watch over a person or place as a guard, especially a prisoner.

senses.label: Reserve for a future time
senses.definition: To keep something or someone set aside for a purpose or appointed day, whether blessing or judgment.
senses.note: τηρέω εἰς, 'keep for'.

senses.label: Protect, preserve
senses.definition: Of God or Christ keeping believers safe from evil and preserved until the end.
senses.note: τηρέω ἐκ, 'keep from' (JOH 17:15; REV 3:10).

senses.label: Keep oneself; maintain
senses.definition: To keep oneself or a quality intact — pure, unstained, in God's love — or to hold on to the faith and unity.
senses.note: With reflexive ἑαυτόν.

senses.label: Observe, obey
senses.definition: To keep a commandment, word, law, tradition or day by doing what it requires.
senses.note: With ἐντολή, λόγος, νόμος, παράδοσις, σάββατον.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John's characteristic phrase is 'keep my word' or 'keep my commandments', the mark and proof of love for Jesus; the Father in turn 'keeps' the disciples.

authorNotes.author: Jude
authorNotes.note: Jude plays on the word: angels who did not keep their position are kept in chains for judgment, while believers are kept for Jesus Christ and must keep themselves in God's love.

authorNotes.author: Peter
authorNotes.note: 2 Peter uses it for God reserving the wicked, fallen angels and the present heavens for judgment; 1 Peter for the inheritance kept in heaven.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: In Acts it is mainly the custody of apostles in prison.

study.translationNote: With commands or words, versions vary between 'keep' (KJV, ESV), 'obey' (NIV, e.g. John 14:15) and 'observe' (Matt 28:20). 'Obey' is clearer in modern English; 'keep' preserves the link with God 'keeping' his people and with guarding something precious.

background.note: Classical writers use it for guarding a place, e.g. a city wall 'constantly guarded'.
A letter asks the recipient to take two vessels 'and keep them for me until I come up' — the sense 'reserve'.
An inscription says of the deceased 'I kept the faith', the same phrase as 2 Tim 4:7.
background.citation: Brit. Mus. Inscrr . Part III. No. 587

background.note: A writer says he 'kept himself blameless' in friendship, comparable to 1 Thess 5:23.

study.exegesisTip: Check the object and preposition: a word or command means 'obey', a person with εἰς means 'reserve for', and ἐκ means 'protect from'.
study.caution: REV 3:10 ('I will keep you from the hour of trial') is debated: preservation through the trial (as in JOH 17:15) or removal from it, a key text in rapture debates.

study.summary: Twelve: the ordinary numeral, but especially 'the Twelve', Jesus' chosen circle of apostles, and a symbolic number for the twelve tribes and the restored people of God.

senses.label: The number twelve
senses.definition: The plain numeral, counting years, baskets, legions and the like.

senses.label: The Twelve (apostles)
senses.definition: With the article and no noun, a fixed title for the inner group of disciples Jesus appointed.
senses.note: Also 'one of the Twelve', especially of Judas (MAT 26:14, 26:47).

senses.label: Twelve tribes; renewed Israel
senses.definition: Twelve as the number of Israel's tribes, and so a symbol of the whole people of God, restored and completed.
senses.note: In Revelation twelve (and its multiples) shapes the new Jerusalem.

authorNotes.author: Mark
authorNotes.note: Mark establishes 'the Twelve' as a title from their appointment onward.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: The Gospel uses 'the Twelve' sparingly but pointedly (Peter's confession, Judas, Thomas); Revelation builds the new Jerusalem on twelves — gates, foundations, apostles, fruits.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul's only use is in the early creed of 1 Cor 15, where 'the Twelve' is already a fixed title even though Judas was gone.

study.exegesisTip: When the article stands alone (οἱ δώδεκα), read it as a title for the apostolic group; the number's link with the twelve tribes signals that Jesus is reconstituting Israel.
study.caution: In 1CO 15:5 some manuscripts read 'the eleven', a scribal correction; 'the Twelve' is the better-attested reading and shows the term functioned as a title.

study.summary: To drink: literally to take in liquid, and figuratively to share table fellowship, to undergo a 'cup' of suffering or judgment, and to receive spiritual life from Christ.

senses.label: Drink liquid
senses.definition: To drink water, wine or other liquid, including habitual drinking or abstaining.
senses.note: δοῦναι πιεῖν, 'give to drink' (JOH 4:7).

senses.label: Eat and drink: ordinary life
senses.definition: Paired with 'eat', of daily needs, table fellowship, or carefree and self-indulgent living.
senses.note: Context decides whether it is neutral, fellowship or revelry (MAT 24:49).

senses.label: Drink the cup: suffering
senses.definition: To undergo a destiny of suffering or divine wrath, pictured as drinking a cup.
senses.note: An OT image of the cup of God's wrath.

senses.label: Drink at the Lord's table
senses.definition: Drinking the cup at the Last Supper and the Lord's Supper, as participation in Christ's covenant.
senses.note: By metonymy 'drink the cup' (1CO 10:21).

senses.label: Drink spiritually
senses.definition: To receive life from Christ or the Spirit by faith, pictured as drinking living water or his blood.

senses.label: Absorb (of the earth)
senses.definition: Of ground soaking up rain.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John uses drinking as a picture of believing in Jesus and receiving the life he gives: living water and drinking his blood.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul's uses cluster around the Lord's Supper and Christian freedom over food and drink.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke highlights eating and drinking as table fellowship, criticised by opponents and promised in the kingdom.

background.note: The ordinary verb for drinking from Homer on.
A sulking schoolboy tells his father, 'I won't eat, I won't drink!'
A grave epigram urges the passer-by, 'Drink, you see the end' — the attitude Paul quotes in 1 Cor 15:32.
Poetry speaks of 'the black earth drinks', as of the ground drinking rain in Heb 6:7.

study.exegesisTip: When 'cup' is the object, ask whether the cup is the Supper, suffering, or God's wrath; the image carries OT associations.
study.caution: Whether 'drinking his blood' in JOH 6:53–56 refers primarily to the Lord's Supper or to believing in Christ's death is debated.

study.summary: To rejoice or be glad; in the imperative and infinitive also the standard greeting, 'Hail!' or 'Greetings', at meetings and at the head of letters.

senses.label: Rejoice, be glad
senses.definition: To feel and express joy at good news or events.
senses.note: With cognate χαρὰν μεγάλην (MAT 2:10); ἐπί + dative, 'over'.

senses.label: Rejoice amid suffering
senses.definition: Joy that persists in, or even because of, persecution and suffering for Christ.

senses.label: Rejoice in the Lord
senses.definition: Joy commanded as a settled Christian disposition, grounded in the Lord and shared with others.
senses.note: Opposite of weeping (ROM 12:15).

senses.label: Take pleasure in (wrongly)
senses.definition: To be glad about something evil, or the world's gloating joy.

senses.label: Greeting: hail, farewell
senses.definition: Imperative χαῖρε/χαίρετε as a spoken greeting on meeting, sometimes mocking, or as a farewell.

senses.label: Letter opening 'Greetings'
senses.definition: Infinitive χαίρειν (understood 'says') as the standard epistolary greeting.
senses.note: Paul replaces it with χάρις 'grace'.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul is the chief user; Philippians, written from prison, repeatedly commands and models joy.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke links rejoicing with God's saving acts — births, finding the lost, receiving the gospel.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John ties joy to Jesus' departure and return: sorrow now, joy at seeing him again.

study.translationNote: Greetings vary: 'Hail' (KJV), 'Greetings' (NIV, ESV), and some render LUK 1:28 'Rejoice!' to echo prophetic calls to Zion. In PHP 3:1 and 4:4 nearly all versions say 'rejoice', but the RV margin has 'farewell', since the same imperative was used for goodbye.

background.note: Common from Homer on for gladness.
The infinitive greeting already stands in the Septuagint, as at the head of letters in 2 Maccabees.
Letters routinely say 'I rejoiced on reading your letter', the natural personal sense.

study.exegesisTip: Distinguish greeting formula from exhortation: χαίρειν in a letter opening is 'Greetings', while the repeated imperative in Philippians is a real command to rejoice.
study.caution: PHP 3:1 and 4:4 are debated: 'rejoice' or 'farewell'? Lightfoot combined both, but most commentators prefer 'rejoice', especially with 'always' in PHP 4:4.

study.summary: To ask for something: to request from people or from God in prayer, and sometimes to demand or call for insistently.

senses.label: Ask for, request
senses.definition: To ask someone for something one wants or needs.
senses.note: Double accusative 'ask someone something' (MAR 6:22).

senses.label: Ask God in prayer
senses.definition: To petition God, with promises that he gives to those who ask.
senses.note: In John, 'ask in my name'.

senses.label: Demand, call for
senses.definition: To ask insistently, especially of a crowd demanding a release, an execution or a king.
senses.note: Usually middle voice.

senses.label: Require, ask an account
senses.definition: To ask for or require something as due — signs, an explanation, or what is owed.
senses.note: αἰτεῖν λόγον, 'ask for a reason' (1PE 3:15).

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John links asking with abiding in Jesus and asking 'in my name', with the promise that the Father gives.

authorNotes.author: James
authorNotes.note: James urges asking God for wisdom in faith, and diagnoses unanswered prayer: 'you do not have because you do not ask; you ask and do not receive because you ask wrongly'.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke stresses the crowd's demand for Jesus' death and a murderer's release.

study.translationNote: Usually 'ask'; the KJV also has 'desire', 'require', 'crave' and 'beg'. English 'ask' also covers ἐρωτάω, so a contrast may vanish: in JOH 16:23 'you will ask (ἐρωτάω) me nothing… whatever you ask (αἰτέω) the Father', though by NT times the two words overlap.

background.note: From Homer on: 'ask a person for a thing'.
An everyday letter instructs, 'ask Saras for the twelve drachmae'.

study.exegesisTip: Note who is asked (God or people) and whether a nearby ἐρωτάω or the middle voice (αἰτοῦμαι) adds nuance.
study.caution: Whether the middle voice differs from the active (as in JAM 4:2–3 or MAR 6:22–25) is debated; Moulton saw the middle as more formal or earnest, others see little difference. EPH 3:13 may be a request to the readers or a prayer to God.

study.summary: Eternal: belonging to the age to come and lasting without end; used for God, his covenant and salvation, eternal life, and eternal judgment, and occasionally for time stretching back before creation.

senses.label: Eternal life
senses.definition: The life of the age to come, given by God, which in John believers already possess.
senses.note: Most common with ζωή.

senses.label: Unending, everlasting
senses.definition: Lasting forever, of God's abiding gifts and realities as opposed to temporary ones.
senses.note: Contrast with πρόσκαιρος 'temporary' (2CO 4:18).

senses.label: Eternal judgment
senses.definition: Punishment or judgment that is final and lasting.

senses.label: From ages past
senses.definition: Without beginning: of time reaching back before creation.
senses.note: χρόνοις αἰωνίοις / πρὸ χρόνων αἰωνίων.

senses.label: Of God himself
senses.definition: Without beginning or end: describing God's Spirit and his everlasting dominion.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John uses it almost only with 'life', which believers have now through faith and which consists in knowing God.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew sets eternal punishment and eternal life side by side in the same sentence.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews uses it for the permanent results of Christ's work: eternal salvation, redemption, inheritance and covenant.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul contrasts the eternal with the temporary and speaks of grace given 'before eternal times'.

study.translationNote: Most versions use 'eternal'; the KJV alternates with 'everlasting' (e.g. MAT 25:46, 'everlasting punishment… life eternal' for the same word). A few versions render 'age-long' or 'of the age' to bring out the link with αἰών ('age'), which can imply a limit some readers then press; standard lexicons give 'eternal'.

background.note: Plato already uses it for the eternal, unchanging realm compared with time.
The Septuagint uses it chiefly for Hebrew ʿôlām, e.g. God's 'everlasting covenant' with Noah.
A deed gives property 'by perpetual and irrevocable grant', showing the everyday sense 'perpetual'.
It became a standing epithet of imperial power, the 'eternal' rule of the emperor.

study.exegesisTip: Read αἰώνιος against the Jewish contrast of 'this age' and 'the age to come' (MAR 10:30): eternal life is the life of the coming age, which in John begins now.
study.caution: Scholars debate how much αἰώνιος means endless duration versus quality (belonging to God's age); and some argue 'age-long' punishment need not be endless. MM note that outside the NT it never loses the sense 'perpetual', and MAT 25:46 uses the one word for both life and punishment.

study.summary: Light: physical light and its sources, heavenly radiance, and above all a metaphor for God's holiness, Christ as the revealer, saving truth, and the new life of believers in contrast with darkness.

senses.label: Physical light; light source
senses.definition: Daylight, sunlight or lamplight; by extension a fire or torches giving light.
senses.note: 'At the fire' (MAR 14:54; LUK 22:56).

senses.label: Heavenly radiance; God's light
senses.definition: Supernatural light from heaven or the unapproachable splendour of God himself, who is light.
senses.note: 'Father of lights' (JAM 1:17) = maker of the heavenly bodies.

senses.label: Christ the light
senses.definition: Jesus as the one who brings God's revelation and life to the world.

senses.label: Spiritual light, salvation
senses.definition: God's truth and salvation, and the realm of those who belong to him, in contrast with the darkness of sin and ignorance.
senses.note: 'Sons/children of light' (LUK 16:8; 1TH 5:5).

senses.label: Believers as light
senses.definition: Disciples who reflect God's light to others by their lives and witness.

senses.label: Inner light; openly
senses.definition: The light within, i.e. one's moral perception; and 'in the light', meaning publicly.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John builds a light–darkness contrast: Jesus is the light of the world, people love darkness or come to the light, and God is light with no darkness.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul speaks of believers as children of light who put on the armour of light, with God's creative light shining in their hearts.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke echoes Isaiah's 'light to the nations' and narrates the blinding light of Paul's conversion three times.

study.translationNote: Almost always 'light'. In MAR 14:54 the KJV says Peter 'warmed himself at the fire', which fits papyri where φῶς stands for fire, while others keep 'by the light'. Some versions capitalise 'Light' in John 1 as a title for Christ.

background.note: In the plural it is used of window-lights.
A Christian epitaph invokes Christ, who gave the blind to see the light of the sun.
An inscription calls a wife 'the light of the household', a metaphor for one who brightens others.

study.exegesisTip: Light usually stands opposite darkness: ask which darkness is in view (ignorance, sin, hostility to God) to see what the light brings.
study.caution: In JOH 1:9 it is debated whether 'coming into the world' describes the light (Christ's coming) or 'every person' coming into the world.

study.summary: That which is spoken: a word, saying or message, especially God's spoken word or the proclaimed gospel; and, like Hebrew dāḇār, a 'thing' or event that is talked about.

senses.label: Word, utterance
senses.definition: A spoken word or words; in the plural, someone's speech or discourse.

senses.label: A saying or statement
senses.definition: A particular saying, prediction or instruction, often one the hearers fail to grasp or later remember.

senses.label: God's spoken word
senses.definition: What God says — his creative command, promise or prophetic word.
senses.note: ῥῆμα θεοῦ / κυρίου.

senses.label: The proclaimed message
senses.definition: The gospel as a spoken message that creates faith and life.

senses.label: Thing, matter, event
senses.definition: A matter or event that is talked about, after Hebrew dāḇār; also a matter or charge in a legal case.
senses.note: Mostly in Luke's more Hebraic chapters.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses half the NT occurrences, including the Hebraic sense 'thing, event' in the infancy narratives.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: In John, Jesus speaks the very words of God, and his words are 'spirit and life'.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul speaks of 'the word of faith' and 'the word of Christ' that is preached and believed.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews stresses the power of God's spoken word in creation and sustaining all things.

study.translationNote: Renderings range from 'word' and 'saying' to 'thing' or 'matter'. LUK 1:37 is the clearest case: 'no word from God will ever fail' (ESV, MSB) treats ῥῆμα as 'word', while 'nothing will be impossible with God' (KJV, NIV) treats it as 'thing'.

background.note: Classical Greek often contrasts mere 'words' with deeds.
The Septuagint uses it chiefly for Hebrew dāḇār, so it can mean 'matter' or 'event' ('after these things').
Papyri speak of 'improper words', the ordinary sense of spoken words.

study.exegesisTip: In Luke 1–2, test whether ῥῆμα means 'saying' or 'event'; the shepherds go to see 'this thing that has happened' (LUK 2:15).
study.caution: The popular distinction between ῥῆμα as a personal, present word from God and λόγος as the written word lacks lexical support; the two largely overlap (compare 1 Pet 1:23 with 1:25).

study.summary: To loose or let go: release a prisoner or debtor, dismiss or send people away, divorce a wife (or husband); middle 'depart'. Context decides which.

senses.label: Release, set free
senses.definition: To free someone from custody, restraint or affliction, especially a prisoner set at liberty by an authority.
senses.note: Pilate's repeated wish to 'release' Jesus (LUK 23:16; LUK 23:22). LUK 13:12 uses it of a woman freed from her infirmity.

senses.label: Release from debt; pardon
senses.definition: To let someone off an obligation or penalty, and so, figuratively, to forgive.
senses.note: In LUK 6:37 'release, and you will be released' stands parallel to 'do not judge … do not condemn'.

senses.label: Dismiss, send away
senses.definition: To let people go or send them off: a crowd sent home, a healed person sent on his way, delegates or missionaries sent off.
senses.note: Of envoys and missionaries 'sent off' (ACT 13:3; ACT 15:30).

senses.label: Let depart in death
senses.definition: To dismiss a servant from his post, used by Simeon as a gentle image for being allowed to die.
senses.note: The 'Nunc dimittis'; compare the papyri term for a soldier honourably discharged.

senses.label: Divorce
senses.definition: To send away a wife (or, in Greco-Roman practice, a husband), i.e. to dissolve a marriage.
senses.note: Usually τὴν γυναῖκα ἀπολύειν; of a wife divorcing her husband only MAR 10:12.

senses.label: Depart (middle)
senses.definition: In the middle voice, to take one's leave, go away.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses the word more than anyone (31×): Pilate's threefold intention to release Jesus, the healed woman 'released' from infirmity, Simeon's departure in peace, and in Acts the release of apostles and the sending off of missionaries and delegates.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew applies it to Joseph's planned quiet divorce of Mary and to Jesus' divorce teaching, where the exception for πορνεία is included.

study.translationNote: One Greek verb covers what English splits into 'release', 'let go', 'dismiss', 'send away' and 'divorce'. The KJV's 'put away' in the divorce texts (MAT 5:31-32; MAR 10:2-12) has led some readers to distinguish 'putting away' from a legal divorce, whereas modern versions render 'divorce'. In LUK 6:37 versions vary between 'forgive' and 'release'.

background.note: In Homer the verb is concrete: loosing a strap or undoing a fastening.
Plato speaks of the philosopher 'releasing' the soul from its partnership with the body.
A Ptolemaic letter uses it of simply dismissing someone, telling him to come back earlier next time.
A tombstone of a veteran 'honourably discharged' uses the perfect participle, illustrating the military image behind Simeon's 'now you dismiss your servant'.

study.exegesisTip: Identify the object: a prisoner or debtor (release), a crowd or envoy (dismiss), a wife (divorce), or oneself in the middle voice (depart).
study.caution: Whether ἀπολύω in the divorce sayings means full legal divorce (the majority view) or mere separation without the certificate of MAT 5:31 is debated. In HEB 13:23 Timothy 'released' may mean freed from prison or sent off on a mission.

study.summary: The Sabbath, Israel's weekly seventh-day rest and its law; by extension, the week, especially in the phrase 'the first day of the week'.

senses.label: The Sabbath day
senses.definition: The seventh day of the week, kept as Israel's day of rest and synagogue worship.
senses.note: Often plural for a single Sabbath (τοῖς σάββασιν, ἡ ἡμέρα τῶν σαββάτων), reflecting Aramaic šabbetā. 'A Sabbath day's journey' (ACT 1:12) was a fixed short distance.

senses.label: The Sabbath as institution and law
senses.definition: The Sabbath as a divine ordinance with its regulations, the subject of controversy between Jesus and his opponents.
senses.note: 'The Sabbath was made for man' (MAR 2:27); 'Lord of the Sabbath' (MAT 12:8).

senses.label: Week
senses.definition: The seven-day period running from one Sabbath to the next.
senses.note: ἡ μία τῶν σαββάτων 'the first day of the week' (Sunday); δὶς τοῦ σαββάτου 'twice a week' (LUK 18:12).

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
