authorNotes.note: Luke shows Jesus teaching and healing on the Sabbath in synagogue settings, and in Acts Paul regularly uses Sabbath synagogue gatherings to preach.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: In John, Sabbath healings (the lame man, the man born blind) provoke the claim that Jesus 'breaks the Sabbath' and works as the Father works.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses the word only twice: 'first day of the week' for the collection, and Sabbaths as part of the 'shadow' of things to come.

study.translationNote: Versions agree on 'Sabbath' for the day but differ where the meaning is 'week': μία τῶν σαββάτων is 'the first day of the week', not 'one of the Sabbaths'. MAT 28:1 ὀψὲ σαββάτων is 'in the end of the sabbath' (KJV) or 'after the Sabbath' (most modern). In COL 2:16 the KJV's 'sabbath days' reflects the plural form, which modern versions take as 'a Sabbath'.

background.note: The word first appears in Greek in the Septuagint, which introduces the Sabbath in the manna story.
The NT dative plural σάββασι already appears in 1 Maccabees, in the account of Jews attacked on the Sabbath.
A Zenon papyrus of the 3rd century BC already uses the plural for a single Sabbath day.

study.exegesisTip: Check whether σάββατον/σάββατα means the day of rest or 'week'; with a numeral like μία or πρώτη it almost always means 'week'.
study.caution: Whether σαββάτων in COL 2:16 means the weekly Sabbath (the majority view, given the series feast–new moon–sabbath) or only special ceremonial sabbaths is debated, as is the exact time meant by ὀψὲ σαββάτων in MAT 28:1.

study.summary: A professional writer or secretary; in the Gospels and Acts a Jewish scribe, expert interpreter and teacher of the Law of Moses; once the town clerk of Ephesus.

senses.label: Scribe, expert in the Law
senses.definition: A Jewish scholar trained in the Scriptures and their interpretation, who taught and ruled on the Law.
senses.note: Often paired with the Pharisees; Luke also calls them νομικοί ('lawyers') and νομοδιδάσκαλοι.

senses.label: Scribes in the ruling council
senses.definition: Scribes as one of the three groups, with chief priests and elders, making up the Jerusalem leadership and Sanhedrin.
senses.note: The formula 'chief priests, scribes and elders' marks official action against Jesus and the apostles.

senses.label: Learned teacher (positive)
senses.definition: A person learned in Scripture, used positively of disciples trained for the kingdom, or generally of the learned man of this age.
senses.note: 1CO 1:20 'Where is the scribe?' echoes Isaiah's question to worldly wisdom.

senses.label: Town clerk, secretary
senses.definition: A civic official who kept records and presided over public business, as in Ephesus.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew pronounces the sharpest woes on the 'scribes and Pharisees', yet also speaks of Christian scribes 'trained for the kingdom'.

authorNotes.author: Mark
authorNotes.note: Mark contrasts Jesus' authority with the scribes', but also portrays one scribe as 'not far from the kingdom'.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: In Acts scribes join the opposition to the apostles, but scribes of the Pharisees' party defend Paul; Luke alone has the town clerk of Ephesus.

study.translationNote: Most versions keep 'scribe', but the NIV and some others use 'teacher(s) of the law', because 'scribe' suggests a mere copyist, whereas these men were authoritative interpreters. In ACT 19:35 the same word is rendered 'town clerk' or 'city clerk'.

background.note: In Athens the 'clerk of the city' was a public officer who read official correspondence to the assembly.
The Septuagint uses the word for the Israelite officers (Hebrew šōṭēr) set over the people under the Egyptian taskmasters.
Egyptian papyri use it of military registrars, the background to the Septuagint's use for army officials.
Ephesian inscriptions confirm the 'clerk of the people' as a leading civic office, as in Acts 19.

study.exegesisTip: Notice who the scribes are grouped with: with Pharisees they represent legal piety; with chief priests and elders they represent the governing council.
study.caution: How far scribes formed a distinct group is debated: many were Pharisees ('scribes of the Pharisees', MAR 2:16), but some served priestly circles. JOH 8:3 belongs to the textually disputed account of the adulterous woman.

study.summary: Trustworthy, faithful, reliable (of God, people and sayings); also, actively, believing, so 'a believer'. Context decides which side is meant.

senses.label: Faithful, trustworthy (people)
senses.definition: Reliable in carrying out a trust, especially of servants and stewards who can be counted on.
senses.note: With ἐν 'faithful in' (LUK 16:10) or ἐπί 'over' (MAT 25:23); 'faithful unto death' (REV 2:10).

senses.label: Faithful (of God and Christ)
senses.definition: God or Christ as utterly dependable, keeping his promises and covenant.
senses.note: The formula 'God is faithful' (πιστὸς ὁ θεός) recalls the Hebrew ʾāman, firm and reliable.

senses.label: Reliable, sure (of words, things)
senses.definition: Of sayings, promises or blessings that can be relied on as true and certain.
senses.note: πιστὸς ὁ λόγος 'the saying is trustworthy', a formula of the Pastoral Letters.

senses.label: Believing; a believer
senses.definition: Actively, one who trusts in God or Christ; as a noun, a Christian believer.
senses.note: Opposite of ἄπιστος (JOH 20:27; 2CO 6:15); a usage apparently new with the NT.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul anchors assurance in the formula 'God is faithful'; the Pastoral Letters add 'the saying is trustworthy' and use πιστός as a noun for 'believers'.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: Revelation names Christ 'the faithful witness' and 'Faithful and True'; Jesus tells Thomas to be not unbelieving but believing.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews presents Jesus as a 'faithful high priest', faithful like Moses over God's house, and grounds hope in the faithfulness of God who promised.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke's parables praise the faithful steward in small things, while Acts uses the word for believers, including Gentile and Jewish converts.

study.translationNote: English must choose between 'faithful' (trustworthy) and 'believing' (trusting). In EPH 1:1 and COL 1:2 versions vary between 'the faithful' and 'believers'; in TIT 1:6 between 'faithful children' (KJV) and 'children who are believers' (ESV); in ACT 16:15 'faithful to the Lord' versus 'a believer in the Lord'.

background.note: A Christian letter entrusts a woman's body to 'the good and faithful' among the grave-diggers, recalling 'good and faithful servant'.
A document speaks of 'true and trustworthy advocates', the ordinary passive sense.

study.exegesisTip: Ask whether the context stresses reliability (passive: trustworthy) or faith (active: believing); of God it always means reliable.
study.caution: In several verses (EPH 1:1; COL 1:2; 1CO 7:25; 1TI 3:11; TIT 1:6) scholars disagree whether 'faithful' or 'believing/Christian' is meant; Lightfoot noted the difficulty of choosing.

study.summary: Older, an older person; the ancestors; and an 'elder', a leader in Jewish communities, in the early church, or among the twenty-four elders of Revelation.

senses.label: Older (in age)
senses.definition: Comparatively older, or as a noun an older person, contrasted with the young.
senses.note: 'His older son' (LUK 15:25); 'your old men will dream dreams' (ACT 2:17).

senses.label: Ancestors, men of old
senses.definition: Earlier generations whose teaching or example is authoritative.
senses.note: 'The tradition of the elders' = ancestral oral law.

senses.label: Jewish elders, leaders
senses.definition: Senior lay leaders of the Jewish people, in local communities or as members of the Jerusalem Sanhedrin.
senses.note: Commonly listed with chief priests and scribes; 'elders of the people' (MAT 21:23).

senses.label: Church elders
senses.definition: Leaders appointed to oversee, shepherd and teach a Christian congregation.
senses.note: Plural in every congregation mentioned; 1 Peter calls them shepherds of the flock (1PE 5:1).

senses.label: Heavenly elders
senses.definition: The twenty-four elders enthroned around God's throne in John's visions, who worship and explain the visions.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Acts traces church elders from Jerusalem, where they act with the apostles at the council, to the elders Paul appoints in each church and the Ephesian elders he addresses.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: The writer of 2 and 3 John calls himself simply 'the elder'; Revelation has the twenty-four elders in heavenly worship.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: In the Pastoral Letters elders are appointed in every town, honoured for leading and teaching, and protected from unsupported accusation; 1 Timothy also uses the word for older men and women.

authorNotes.author: Peter
authorNotes.note: Peter appeals to the elders as a 'fellow elder' to shepherd God's flock; the following call to 'younger' people uses the word of age or office.

study.translationNote: Most versions use 'elder(s)', but where age is in view the word becomes 'older man/woman' (1TI 5:1-2) or 'his older son' (LUK 15:25), and 'tradition of the elders' may be read as 'of the ancestors'. Some church traditions render the office 'presbyter' or 'priest'; English 'priest' derives from presbyter.

background.note: Village 'elders' in Ptolemaic Egypt collected corn and handled local affairs, showing the word as an official title.
Inscriptions from Asia Minor use πρεσβύτεροι for members of a corporation or association.
An inscription praises a man who honoured older people as parents and contemporaries as brothers, like 1 Tim 5:1–2.

study.exegesisTip: Decide first whether age, ancestry or office is meant; the comparative form can still mean simply 'older', especially opposite νεώτερος ('younger').
study.caution: The relation of 'elder' to 'overseer' (ἐπίσκοπος) is debated: in ACT 20:17 and TIT 1:5 the terms seem interchangeable (Lightfoot), while later usage distinguished them. Whether 1PE 5:5 refers to age or office, and who the twenty-four elders of Revelation are (angels or representatives of God's people), are also disputed.

study.summary: A vessel for sailing: in the Gospels a fishing boat on the Sea of Galilee; in Acts, James and Revelation a seagoing ship.

senses.label: Fishing boat on the lake
senses.definition: A small working boat used by Galilean fishermen for fishing and mending nets.

senses.label: Boat for crossing the lake
senses.definition: A lake boat in which Jesus and his disciples cross the Sea of Galilee, teach the crowds, and face storms.
senses.note: Mark also uses the diminutive πλοιάριον for a small boat kept ready (Mark 3:9).

senses.label: Seagoing ship
senses.definition: A merchant or passenger ship sailing the Mediterranean, such as those on Paul's voyages.
senses.note: ACT 27:37 numbers those on board at 276.

senses.label: Ships as image or commerce
senses.definition: Ships as an illustration of control by a small rudder, or as the shipping trade affected by God's judgments.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses the word for Peter's fishing boat in his call and for the ships of Paul's voyages, culminating in the detailed shipwreck narrative.

authorNotes.author: Mark
authorNotes.note: In Mark the boat is a recurring setting: a teaching platform, the place of the storm, and the vehicle of repeated crossings in which the disciples misunderstand.

study.translationNote: The KJV uses 'ship' throughout, even for Galilean fishing boats; modern versions say 'boat' on the lake and 'ship' on the open sea, following the size of the vessel in context.

background.note: Classical writers qualify the general word to specify a fishing boat, warships or merchantmen.
A writer asks for supplies to be sent quickly because he is 'on board a boat'.
A papyrus mentions a tax-collector requiring a ship's cargo to be unloaded, recalling ACT 21:3.

study.exegesisTip: Let context set the size: the same word covers a lake fishing boat and an ocean grain freighter carrying 276 people (ACT 27:37).

study.summary: The number three, used for counting and periods of time, in the resurrection formula 'three days', and in 'two or three' as a small or legally sufficient number.

senses.label: Three (counting)
senses.definition: The cardinal number three, counting people or things.
senses.note: 'These three' (faith, hope, love) in 1CO 13:13; place name 'Three Taverns' (ACT 28:15).

senses.label: Periods of time
senses.definition: A span of three days, months, hours or years.
senses.note: 'Three years and six months' (LUK 4:25; JAM 5:17).

senses.label: Three days to resurrection
senses.definition: The interval between Jesus' death and resurrection, in the sign of Jonah and the temple saying.
senses.note: μετὰ τρεῖς ἡμέρας is equivalent to 'on the third day' by inclusive reckoning (MAR 10:34).

senses.label: 'Two or three': a few, witnesses
senses.definition: A small number, especially the minimum of witnesses required by the Law.
senses.note: From Deuteronomy's rule of two or three witnesses.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: Revelation is full of triads (three angels and woes, three plagues, three unclean spirits, three gates on each side), and 1 John speaks of three witnesses that agree.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses the witness rule for church discipline, limits tongue-speakers and prophets to 'two or three', and names the abiding three: faith, hope and love.

study.translationNote: Renderings rarely differ, but in 1JO 5:7-8 the KJV (following the late Textus Receptus) includes 'three that bear record in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost' (the Comma Johanneum); modern versions omit it as absent from the early Greek manuscripts.

background.note: A papyrus instructs that branches be tied together 'three by three' (τρία τρία), showing the distributive idiom of Mark 6 in everyday Greek.
A letter's parenthetic nominative of time ('many days we have been waiting') parallels ἡμέραι τρεῖς in Mark 8:2.

study.exegesisTip: Read 'after three days' and 'in three days' as the idiom for 'on the third day', not as a precise count of seventy-two hours.
study.caution: How 'three days and three nights' (MAT 12:40) fits a Friday burial and Sunday resurrection is debated; most take it as Jewish inclusive reckoning, while some propose a Wednesday or Thursday crucifixion.

study.summary: Fruit or crop: the produce of trees, vines and fields; offspring; and figuratively the deeds that reveal character, the qualities the Spirit produces, or the result and profit of something.

senses.label: Fruit of trees and vines
senses.definition: The edible produce of a tree or vine.
senses.note: Idioms: ποιεῖν, φέρειν, διδόναι καρπόν 'bear fruit'.

senses.label: Crop, harvest, produce
senses.definition: The yield of a field or vineyard, the harvest a farmer gathers and shares.
senses.note: A tenant's 'share of the fruit' (MAT 21:34).

senses.label: Offspring
senses.definition: Children or descendants as the 'fruit' of the womb or loins.
senses.note: A Hebrew idiom (peri beten).

senses.label: Deeds that reveal character
senses.definition: A person's conduct as the outward product showing what they truly are.
senses.note: 'Fruit worthy of repentance' (MAT 3:8).

senses.label: Spiritual fruit, godly qualities
senses.definition: The qualities and righteousness God produces in his people, especially through the Spirit.
senses.note: 'The fruit of lips' = praise (HEB 13:15).

senses.label: Result, gain, profit
senses.definition: The outcome, benefit or reward that follows from an activity or way of life.
senses.note: Also of a financial gift (ROM 15:28).

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew presses the tree-and-fruit test: a tree is known by its fruit, and the kingdom is given to a people producing its fruits.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: In John's vine discourse fruit-bearing is the outcome of abiding in Christ and glorifies the Father; the dying grain bears much fruit.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul speaks of the singular 'fruit of the Spirit' against the 'works of the flesh', and also uses fruit for the results of a life and for a financial gift.

authorNotes.author: James
authorNotes.note: James uses the farmer awaiting the crop as a picture of patience and speaks of the 'fruit of righteousness' sown in peace.

study.translationNote: Versions vary between 'fruit', 'crop', 'harvest' or 'grain' in farming contexts, and between 'fruit' and plainer words like 'results', 'profit' or 'gift' in Paul (PHP 1:22 'fruitful labor'; PHP 4:17 'fruit that increases to your credit' or 'profit'; ROM 15:28 'this fruit' or 'what has been collected').

background.note: In Homer καρπός is usually the produce of the earth, especially grain.
The 'fruit of lips' (praise) of HEB 13:15 comes from the Septuagint of Hosea.
Papyri commonly use it for the produce of a vineyard or estate.
An inscription says virtue alone yields the greatest 'fruits', a metaphor like JAM 3:17–18.

study.exegesisTip: Note number and source: the singular 'fruit of the Spirit' (GAL 5:22) is set against plural 'works of the flesh', and fruit language usually implies a visible test of what is within.
study.caution: The exact sense of 'sealed to them this fruit' (ROM 15:28) and whether PHP 4:17 uses a commercial metaphor of interest are debated.

study.summary: Night, the hours of darkness; a particular night; 'night and day' for unceasing activity; and figuratively the present dark age or the end of opportunity.

senses.label: Night-time
senses.definition: The period of darkness between evening and morning, often as the time when something happens.
senses.note: Genitive νυκτός 'by night'; 'the fourth watch of the night' (MAT 14:25); διὰ νυκτός 'during the night'.

senses.label: 'Night and day': continually
senses.definition: In pairs with 'day', unceasing activity such as prayer, work or worship.
senses.note: Paul usually says 'night and day', Luke and Revelation often 'day and night'.

senses.label: A particular, decisive night
senses.definition: A specific night on which a momentous event occurs.
senses.note: Dative 'this night' (ταύτῃ τῇ νυκτί).

senses.label: Setting of visions and rescue
senses.definition: Night as the time of divine visions and angelic deliverance.

senses.label: Figurative darkness
senses.definition: The time when work is no longer possible, or the present evil age and moral darkness before the day of the Lord.
senses.note: 'There will be no night there' (REV 21:25).

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John gives night symbolic weight: Nicodemus comes by night, Judas goes out 'and it was night', and the night comes when no one can work; Revelation's new city has no night.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul speaks of labouring and praying 'night and day', and contrasts the night of this age with the coming day.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: In Acts night is repeatedly the setting of divine intervention: prison doors opened, visions given and assurance in danger.

background.note: A letter-writer says 'night and day I make intercession to God for you', a close parallel to 1 Thess 3:10.
Papyri date night events by the following day ('the night leading to the 25th'), reflecting a reckoning of the day from sunrise to sunset.
An epitaph uses night as a metaphor for death.

study.exegesisTip: Watch the case: genitive νυκτός 'during the night', accusative 'throughout the night', dative 'on that night'; and ask whether John or Paul intends a symbolic sense.
study.caution: How days and nights were reckoned (Jewish sunset-to-sunset or other) affects debates on the passion chronology and 'three days and three nights' (MAT 12:40); how far JOH 13:30 is symbolic is a matter of interpretation.

study.summary: Will: what someone wills or desires. Mostly God's will, as his saving purpose, his commands to be done, or his ordering of events; also human wishes and desires.

senses.label: God's saving purpose
senses.definition: God's sovereign plan and good pleasure, which he accomplishes.
senses.note: With εὐδοκία or βουλή in Ephesians 1.

senses.label: What God requires
senses.definition: God's will as the conduct he commands and approves, to be known and done.
senses.note: ποιεῖν τὸ θέλημα 'do the will'; 1TH 4:3 and 1TH 5:18 define it.

senses.label: God's ordering of events
senses.definition: God's will as permitting or directing circumstances, including callings, journeys and suffering.
senses.note: διὰ θελήματος θεοῦ 'by the will of God' in Paul's greetings; 'the Lord's will be done' (ACT 21:14).

senses.label: Jesus' obedience to the Father
senses.definition: The Father's will as the goal Jesus came to fulfil, even to the cross.

senses.label: Human will, desire
senses.definition: A person's own wish, choice or desires, sometimes in contrast with God's.
senses.note: Plural in EPH 2:3 'the desires of the flesh'; 2TI 2:26 of the devil's will.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John frames Jesus' whole mission as doing the will of the one who sent him, and his letter links abiding and prayer to God's will.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul grounds his apostleship 'through the will of God' and, in Ephesians, unfolds God's will as his eternal purpose in Christ.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews applies Psalm 40, 'I have come to do your will', to Christ's self-offering, by which believers are sanctified.

authorNotes.author: Peter
authorNotes.note: 1 Peter relates God's will to doing good and to suffering 'according to the will of God'.

study.translationNote: Usually 'will', but versions vary: REV 4:11 'for thy pleasure they are and were created' (KJV) versus 'by your will' (modern); EPH 2:3 plural 'desires'; and in 1CO 16:12 'it was not his will' (Apollos) versus 'it was not God's will' (NIV mg) reflects an ambiguity in the Greek.

background.note: The word is rare outside biblical and church writing; an early instance occurs in the sophist Antiphon.
In the Septuagint of Esther each guest drinks 'according to his will' at the king's feast.
A 4th-century Christian charm asks God to act 'according to your will first and her faith'.

study.exegesisTip: Ask whether 'God's will' is his purpose that will surely happen, his command to be obeyed, or his permission over circumstances.
study.caution: In 1CO 16:12 it is debated whether the unexpressed subject is Apollos's will or God's; some also distinguish θέλημα from βουλή, though the two overlap in EPH 1:11.

study.summary: To carry or bring: to bear a load, bring people or things somewhere, bring forward charges or teaching, bear fruit, endure hardship, or (passive) be carried along by a force.

senses.label: Carry, bear a load
senses.definition: To carry something or someone physically from place to place.
senses.note: In Heb 1:3 the Son 'upholds' or 'sustains' all things by his word, a cosmic use of the same idea of bearing.

senses.label: Bring, fetch, lead
senses.definition: To bring people or objects to someone, or to lead a person somewhere; also of a road or gate that 'leads' into a city.
senses.note: Of persons it can mean 'lead' against their will (John 21:18; Mark 15:22).

senses.label: Bring forward, present
senses.definition: To put forward a charge, a message or a teaching; passive of grace or a voice 'brought' to someone.

senses.label: Bear fruit, produce
senses.definition: Of plants, and figuratively of disciples, to yield a crop or result.

senses.label: Bear patiently, endure
senses.definition: To put up with something hard or someone troublesome.
senses.note: Rom 9:22: God 'endured with much patience' the vessels of wrath.

senses.label: Be carried along, be driven
senses.definition: Passive: to be swept along by wind or another force, or moved by God's Spirit.
senses.note: The sailing image of Acts 27 lies behind 2 Pet 1:21: prophets were 'carried along' by the Holy Spirit.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John uses the verb most (20×), above all for 'bearing fruit' in the vine discourse: fruit-bearing is the mark of remaining in Christ and glorifies the Father.

authorNotes.author: Peter
authorNotes.note: 2 Peter uses the passive three times in close succession: the Father's voice was 'borne' from heaven, and prophecy was not 'borne' by human will, but prophets were 'borne along' by the Holy Spirit.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews applies the verb to the Son who 'upholds all things', to believers being 'carried on' to maturity, and to bearing Christ's reproach outside the camp.

study.translationNote: Because φέρω is so general, versions choose many English verbs. In 2 Pet 1:21 the KJV's 'moved by the Holy Ghost' becomes 'carried along' (ESV, NIV), which keeps the image of a ship driven by wind. In Heb 6:1 the passive 'let us be carried on' is often smoothed to 'let us go on' or 'move beyond'. In Heb 9:16 the death of the testator must be 'established' or 'proved' (ESV, NIV) rather than literally 'brought'.

background.note: Everyday letters use the verb for bringing people and goods: a man asks his brother to come up and bring his wife with him.
A question to an oracle ends 'bring me this truly', i.e. 'tell me': the verb could mean 'announce, make known'.
A door is described as 'leading into the public street', the same idiom as the iron gate 'leading into the city' (Acts 12:10).

study.exegesisTip: Watch the passive forms: being 'carried along' (Acts 27:15; 2 Pet 1:21; Heb 6:1) stresses a power acting on the subject rather than the subject's own effort.
study.caution: In Heb 9:16 θάνατον ... φέρεσθαι is disputed: 'the death must be brought in/proved', or, following papyrus usage, 'be made publicly known'; it also depends on whether διαθήκη means 'will' or 'covenant' there.

study.summary: Beloved, dearly loved: used of Jesus as God's beloved Son, of believers as loved by God, and very often as an affectionate address among Christians ('dear friends').

senses.label: God's beloved Son
senses.definition: Title for Jesus in the heavenly voice at his baptism and transfiguration, marking him as the uniquely loved Son.
senses.note: Matthew applies it to the Servant of Isa 42:1 (Matt 12:18).

senses.label: Only, cherished child
senses.definition: An only son or daughter, especially precious because there is no other; the classical and Septuagint background of the title.
senses.note: The LXX renders Hebrew yāḥîd 'only' with this word in the story of Isaac (Gen 22:2).

senses.label: Loved by God
senses.definition: Of God's people, who are the objects of his love, including Israel 'beloved for the sake of the fathers'.

senses.label: Dear (named fellow believer)
senses.definition: Describing a particular Christian brother, sister or co-worker as dear to the writer and to the church.

senses.label: Form of address: 'dear friends'
senses.definition: Vocative plural used to address a congregation warmly, typically before an exhortation.
senses.note: Often combined with 'my brothers' (1 Cor 15:58; Jas 1:16).

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses the word 28 times, both to address churches before an appeal and to commend named co-workers such as Timothy, Tychicus, Epaphras and Luke.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: In 1–3 John 'beloved' is the standard address, tied directly to the call to love one another because God first loved us.

authorNotes.author: Peter
authorNotes.note: 1 and 2 Peter open new sections with 'beloved', and 2 Peter calls Paul 'our beloved brother'.

study.translationNote: Traditional versions keep 'beloved' throughout, linking the Son, Israel and the church. The NIV and others often use 'dear friends' for the address in the letters, which sounds natural but hides that it is the same word God uses of his Son. A few scholars and versions suggest 'only' for the Father's words at the baptism, because of the Septuagint usage.

background.note: In Homer the word describes an only child, as in the only son who must be cherished.
Jephthah's daughter is called his 'only, beloved' child, showing how 'beloved' could imply 'only'.
A late third-century Christian letter is addressed 'to Apollo the presbyter, beloved brother in the Lord', exactly the New Testament idiom.

study.exegesisTip: When the letters address readers as 'beloved', read the following command in light of God's love for them: the address grounds the exhortation (e.g. Rom 12:19; 2 Cor 7:1).
study.caution: Scholars debate whether ὁ ἀγαπητός in the baptism and transfiguration voice should be heard as 'beloved' or, via the Septuagint of Gen 22, as 'only' Son with an echo of Isaac; the two readings overlap rather than exclude each other.

study.summary: To glorify: to praise or honour someone, especially God, and in biblical usage also God's act of clothing someone with glory, above all Jesus' glorification through death and exaltation.

senses.label: Praise God in response
senses.definition: To praise and acknowledge God aloud, especially as people's response to a healing or saving act.

senses.label: Honour God by one's life
senses.definition: To bring honour to God through conduct, obedience, suffering or fruitfulness, so that others see his worth.

senses.label: Honour, esteem a person
senses.definition: To speak well of or give honour to a human being, or to claim honour for oneself.
senses.note: Rom 11:13: Paul 'magnifies' his ministry.

senses.label: Clothe with glory
senses.definition: God's action of making someone or something glorious, sharing his own splendour with it.
senses.note: A biblical development from the Septuagint, where Moses' face was 'glorified' (Exod 34:29).

senses.label: Jesus' glorification
senses.definition: In John, the 'hour' when the Son is glorified through his death, resurrection and return to the Father, and the Father glorified in him.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John (25×) uses the verb for the mutual glorifying of Father and Son, centred on the cross as the hour of glory; even Peter's death will 'glorify God'.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke repeatedly closes a miracle or saving event with people 'glorifying God', making praise the fitting response to God's visitation.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul sets the failure to glorify God at the root of human sin and places 'glorified' as the final link of God's saving purpose.

study.translationNote: Most versions use 'glorify', but some vary with 'praise' (crowds after miracles), 'honour' (1 Cor 12:26), 'magnify' (Rom 11:13 KJV), or 'take glory' (Heb 5:5). The variety hides that one verb covers both human praise of God and God's act of glorifying.

background.note: In classical Greek the verb usually means 'think, suppose, imagine', from δόξα 'opinion' — a meaning absent from the New Testament.
The Septuagint uses the verb for Moses' face being made radiant, the basis of the biblical sense 'make glorious'.
A third-century epitaph speaks of a man 'glorified for his piety even after oblivion'.
A magical papyrus prays to Isis, 'glorify me, as I have glorified the name of your son Horus', close in form to John 12:28.

study.exegesisTip: Ask who glorifies whom: when people glorify God it means praise or honour; when God glorifies someone it means he invests them with his own glory.
study.caution: The aorist 'he also glorified' in Rom 8:30 is read by most as describing a future certainty as already done, but some see present participation in glory; John's 'now is the Son of Man glorified' (13:31) likewise blends the cross and exaltation.

study.summary: Throne: the seat of a king or judge, and so royal power itself; above all God's heavenly throne, Christ's throne, and the thrones of those who share his rule.

senses.label: God's heavenly throne
senses.definition: The seat of God's sovereign rule in heaven, often standing for God himself and his presence.

senses.label: Royal throne; kingship
senses.definition: The throne of an earthly king, especially David's, standing for the kingship itself.

senses.label: Christ's throne of glory
senses.definition: The throne from which the exalted Son of Man reigns and judges.

senses.label: Thrones of those who reign with him
senses.definition: Seats of authority given to the apostles, the elders and the faithful who share Christ's rule and judgment.

senses.label: Angelic powers
senses.definition: By extension, a rank of spiritual rulers called 'thrones'.
senses.note: Listed with dominions, rulers and authorities, all created through Christ.

senses.label: Throne of rival powers
senses.definition: The seat of Satan or the beast, a counterfeit of God's rule.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: Revelation uses the word about 47 times: the throne and 'the One seated on the throne' are the fixed centre of the vision, around which all heaven worships and from which judgment and new creation come.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews pictures the exalted Christ seated at the right hand of the throne, and invites believers to approach 'the throne of grace' with confidence.

study.translationNote: The KJV sometimes renders the word 'seat', e.g. 'Satan's seat' (Rev 2:13) and the elders' 'seats' (Rev 4:4), which hides that the elders and Satan occupy 'thrones' that echo or rival God's throne. Modern versions use 'throne' throughout.

background.note: In Homer the word means simply a seat or chair, before it became the 'throne' of kings.
An account lists a chair for 20 drachmae, showing the plain everyday sense survived.
A royal inscription of Commagene speaks of a kingdom subject to the king's thrones and of the heavenly thrones of Zeus.
The Septuagint normally renders Hebrew kissēʾ, as of Pharaoh 'who sits on his throne'.

study.exegesisTip: In Revelation, track where each scene stands in relation to the throne: nearness to it, worship before it, or rival thrones opposed to it shape the meaning of the vision.
study.caution: 'Satan's throne' at Pergamum (Rev 2:13) is variously identified with the great altar of Zeus, the imperial cult, or Roman judicial power seated there; the text does not settle it.

study.summary: Demon: in the New Testament an evil spirit that oppresses people and stands behind idolatry and false teaching; in wider Greek also a 'divine being' or deity.

senses.label: Evil spirit afflicting people
senses.definition: A hostile spirit that enters and controls a person, causing affliction; equivalent to 'unclean spirit'.

senses.label: Demons cast out
senses.definition: Demons as a realm under their ruler Beelzebul, whose expulsion shows the arrival of God's kingdom.

senses.label: 'Have a demon' = be mad
senses.definition: Charge levelled at John and Jesus, meaning to be possessed and so deranged or deluded.

senses.label: Powers behind idols and error
senses.definition: Spiritual beings who receive pagan worship and inspire false teaching; they know God's oneness but fear him.
senses.note: Paul echoes Deut 32:17: idols are nothing, but sacrifices to them reach demons.

senses.label: Foreign deity (pagan sense)
senses.definition: A god or divine being in the neutral Greek sense.
senses.note: The Athenians think Paul proclaims 'foreign divinities' — the charge once brought against Socrates.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses the word most (23×) and alone writes 'spirit of an unclean demon'; in Acts 17:18 he reports the classical neutral sense on pagan lips.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John records no exorcisms; the word appears only in the charge that Jesus 'has a demon', which Jesus and others refute.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul names demons as the real recipients of idol sacrifices and as the source of ascetic false teaching.

study.translationNote: The KJV renders δαιμόνιον 'devil(s)', the same word it uses for διάβολος, so English readers lose the distinction between the one devil (Satan) and the many demons. Modern versions use 'demon(s)'. In Acts 17:18 versions vary between 'gods', 'deities' and 'divinities' because the sense there is pagan and neutral.

background.note: In classical Greek τὸ δαιμόνιον means 'the divine power' or 'Divinity', without any evil connotation.
Socrates was accused of introducing new divine beings (καινὰ δαιμόνια), the same charge brought against Paul at Athens.
The Septuagint applies the word to the false gods of the nations, to whom Israel sacrificed.
A magical papyrus asks a power to 'turn away this demon', showing the hostile sense in popular religion.

study.exegesisTip: Notice who uses the word: on Jesus' opponents' lips 'demon' is an accusation, on pagan lips a neutral deity, and in apostolic teaching the reality behind idolatry.
study.caution: The New Testament says little about the origin of demons; their identification with fallen angels or with spirits of the dead is drawn from Jewish tradition and is debated.

study.summary: To think or suppose, often wrongly; to seem or be reputed; and impersonally 'it seems good', used for opinions, reputations and formal decisions.

senses.label: Think, suppose
senses.definition: To hold an opinion or assume something, frequently a mistaken impression.

senses.label: 'What do you think?'
senses.definition: Impersonal τί σοι δοκεῖ, inviting a listener's judgment, often before a parable or a test question.

senses.label: Think oneself to be
senses.definition: To consider oneself something (wise, religious, a prophet), usually exposing self-deception.

senses.label: Seem, appear
senses.definition: To give an impression to others, whether true or not.

senses.label: Be reputed, recognised
senses.definition: Οἱ δοκοῦντες: those regarded as leaders or as having standing.

senses.label: Seem good, decide
senses.definition: Impersonal ἔδοξε, 'it seemed good', the standard formula for a considered decision.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul often uses 'if anyone thinks he is...' to puncture self-estimation, and refers with some irony to the Jerusalem leaders as 'those who seemed to be something'.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses the formal 'it seemed good' for his own decision to write and for the Jerusalem council's ruling.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew's Jesus repeatedly opens a challenge with 'What do you think?'.

study.translationNote: Gal 2:6 is rendered 'those who seemed to be somewhat' (KJV), 'those who were held in high esteem' (NIV), or 'those who seemed to be influential' (ESV); translators must decide how much irony to convey. In Acts 15:28 'it seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us' (ESV, KJV) uses the same formula as an official decree; renderings such as 'we decided' or 'it was resolved' bring out that it records a binding decision rather than a mere impression.

background.note: Already in Homer the verb means 'think, expect': Ajax says he expects to win.
Civic decrees open with ἔδοξε τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ, 'it was resolved by the assembly', the formula behind Acts 15.
A letter uses δοκῶ absolutely, 'my mother went, I think, to Antinoöpolis', as in 1 Cor 4:9.

study.exegesisTip: Ask whether the verb reports what is true or only what people supposed: in many narratives δοκέω flags a misunderstanding the story then corrects (Mark 6:49; John 20:15).
study.caution: Whether Paul's 'I think I too have the Spirit of God' (1 Cor 7:40) is modest uncertainty or ironic understatement is debated, as is the tone of 'those who seemed to be pillars' in Gal 2:9.

study.summary: To proclaim publicly as a herald; in the New Testament mainly to announce the kingdom of God, repentance and the gospel of Christ with authority.

senses.label: Announce publicly, make known
senses.definition: To spread news or a message openly, as a herald does.

senses.label: John's call to repentance
senses.definition: John the Baptist's proclamation of a baptism of repentance and of the one coming after him.

senses.label: Proclaim the kingdom, the gospel
senses.definition: Jesus' and his disciples' announcement that God's reign has come near, and the worldwide proclamation of the good news.

senses.label: Preach Christ
senses.definition: The apostolic announcement of Jesus as Christ, crucified and risen.

senses.label: Advocate a demand or practice
senses.definition: To publicly urge a requirement, such as keeping the Law or circumcision.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: For Paul preaching is a commissioned act: no one can believe without hearing a preacher who is sent; its content is 'Christ crucified'.

authorNotes.author: Mark
authorNotes.note: Mark frames Jesus' ministry as preaching and stresses that the gospel must first be proclaimed to all nations.

authorNotes.author: Peter
authorNotes.note: 1 Peter's single use, Christ 'preached to the spirits in prison', is one of the most debated verses in the New Testament.

study.translationNote: Versions alternate between 'preach' and 'proclaim' for the same verb. 'Preach' now suggests a sermon to a congregation, while the Greek describes a herald's public announcement of news, often to outsiders; 'proclaim' keeps that sense. In 1 Pet 3:19 some render 'made proclamation' to avoid implying an evangelistic sermon.

background.note: In Homer the verb means to act as a herald, the official who announced the king's commands aloud.

study.exegesisTip: Note what is proclaimed (kingdom, repentance, Christ) and on whose authority: a herald announces another's message rather than his own opinions.
study.caution: The meaning of 1 Pet 3:19 is disputed: Christ announcing victory to imprisoned fallen angels, offering the gospel to the dead, or preaching through Noah to his generation.

study.summary: To gather or bring together: harvesting and storing goods, convening or assembling people, God's final gathering, and in a special sense taking in a stranger as a guest.

senses.label: Gather things, store up
senses.definition: To collect crops, goods or leftovers into one place.
senses.note: In Luke 15:13 συναγαγὼν πάντα probably means 'turned everything into cash'.

senses.label: Convene, call together
senses.definition: To summon people to an official or deliberative meeting.

senses.label: Gather, come together
senses.definition: Passive: to come together as a crowd or for a meeting.

senses.label: Assemble as the church
senses.definition: Believers coming together for worship, prayer, report or discipline in Jesus' name.

senses.label: Gather for judgment or salvation
senses.definition: God's or his agents' final gathering of people or nations, for salvation or for judgment.

senses.label: Welcome as a guest
senses.definition: To take a stranger into one's home and show hospitality.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew (24×) links the verb to the end-time harvest and judgment, to discipleship ('whoever does not gather with me scatters'), and to welcoming the least of Christ's brothers.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John uses the verb for Jesus' death gathering God's scattered children into one, and for the harvest gathered for eternal life.

study.translationNote: In Matt 25:35 versions render 'took me in' (KJV), 'welcomed me' (ESV) or 'invited me in' (NIV) for the hospitality sense. In Luke 15:13 'gathered all together' (KJV, ESV) contrasts with 'got together all he had' (NIV) or 'sold all he had' (some modern versions), reflecting the commercial sense 'convert into cash'.

background.note: The Septuagint uses the verb for bringing a lost animal or a person into one's house, the background of the hospitality sense.
Accounts use the passive for the total sum realised, supporting 'turned it all into money' in Luke 15:13.
An inscription mentions those who 'gather' as a festive club, a social use of the verb.

study.exegesisTip: Watch for the opposite verb 'scatter' nearby (Matt 12:30; John 11:52): gathering is often the work of the Messiah restoring God's people.
study.caution: In Acts 11:26 συναχθῆναι ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ is usually 'they met with the church', but some (following Hort) take it as 'they were hospitably received'; Luke 15:13 'gathered' versus 'sold off' is also debated.

study.summary: To greet: to welcome someone on meeting, to send or pass on greetings in a letter, to take leave, or to pay respects; once of hailing God's promises from afar.

senses.label: Greet on meeting
senses.definition: To welcome someone in person with words of greeting, often with an embrace.

senses.label: Send or pass on greetings
senses.definition: Letter-closing formula: third person 'X greets you' or imperative 'greet X'.

senses.label: Greet with a holy kiss
senses.definition: The church's greeting expressed by a kiss among fellow believers.

senses.label: Say farewell, take leave
senses.definition: To greet someone on parting.

senses.label: Pay respects to
senses.definition: A formal courtesy visit to an official.
senses.note: Agrippa and Bernice come to pay their respects to Festus.

senses.label: Hail, welcome from afar
senses.definition: Figuratively, to greet promised realities while still at a distance.
senses.note: The patriarchs saw and 'greeted' the promises like travellers sighting home.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul accounts for two-thirds of the uses, mostly in closing greetings; Romans 16 names some twenty-six people, and the scribe Tertius adds his own greeting.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke records Jesus forbidding the seventy-two to greet anyone on the road (urgency of the mission), and uses the verb for Paul's visits to churches and for a formal courtesy call.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews uses the verb both in its closing greetings and for the patriarchs' welcoming of promises from afar.

study.translationNote: The KJV's 'salute' sounds military today; modern versions use 'greet'. For the third-person formula 'X greets you', many translate 'sends greetings'. In Heb 11:13 the KJV 'embraced them' contrasts with 'greeted' or 'welcomed' (ESV, NIV), and in Acts 20:1 the word is rendered 'embraced' or 'said goodbye'.

background.note: Homer describes people greeting with the right hand and gentle words.
Private letters regularly end 'greet Diodorus...', proving this was the standard closing formula.
A father adds his own greeting to his daughter's letter written by the same hand, a parallel to Tertius in Rom 16:22.
A report says someone 'paid his respects to the most illustrious prefect', as in Acts 25:13.

study.exegesisTip: Do not skip the greeting lists: who greets whom (e.g. Jews and Gentiles in Rom 16) reveals the relationships and unity Paul wants the church to embody.

study.summary: To cry out or shout: a scream of fear or pain, an urgent plea for help, a crowd's shout, a loud solemn proclamation, and the believer's Spirit-given cry 'Abba, Father'.

senses.label: Scream, shriek
senses.definition: An inarticulate cry of fear, pain or torment, including the shrieks of the possessed.

senses.label: Cry for help or justice
senses.definition: An urgent appeal for mercy or for vindication.
senses.note: In Jas 5:4 withheld wages 'cry out', like Abel's blood calling for justice.

senses.label: Shout (crowd)
senses.definition: A crowd shouting acclamation or demands.

senses.label: Demons' outcry
senses.definition: Demons or the possessed crying out who Jesus is.

senses.label: Solemn loud proclamation
senses.definition: A public, authoritative declaration made with a loud voice, by Jesus, John, a prophet or an angel.

senses.label: Cry 'Abba, Father'
senses.definition: The believer's prayer of address to God, prompted by the Spirit of adoption.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: In the Gospel John uses the verb for solemn public announcements by the Baptist and by Jesus in the temple; in Revelation for loud angelic and heavenly cries.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses the verb for Isaiah's urgent prophecy and for the cry of adoption, attributed in one place to believers and in the other to the Spirit himself.

authorNotes.author: Mark
authorNotes.note: Mark repeatedly reports the shrieks of unclean spirits and the cries of those seeking mercy, as well as the crowd's 'Crucify him!'.

study.translationNote: Versions vary between 'cry', 'cry out', 'shout' and 'shriek' according to the speaker, so readers may not notice that the same verb covers a demon's scream, Bartimaeus's plea and Jesus' public proclamation. In John 1:15 the perfect κέκραγεν has present force, 'cries out' rather than 'cried'.

background.note: Classical comedy uses the verb for a shouting match between rival demagogues.
The Septuagint uses it for importunate prayer: 'I cried to the Lord with my voice'.
A first-century petitioner complains that he was 'shouting and crying out' in protest.
A farm letter reports that Pasis 'is crying out' that the manure must not be ruined by the water.

study.exegesisTip: Ask what kind of cry it is — terror, plea, mob demand or authoritative proclamation — since the same verb carries all of these.
study.caution: Whether the cry 'Abba, Father' in Rom 8:15 and Gal 4:6 refers to ecstatic, charismatic prayer or to a liturgical acclamation in worship is debated.

study.summary: A stone: a loose stone or rock, a building stone, a tomb's sealing stone, a millstone or a precious gem; figuratively Christ as the rejected cornerstone and stumbling stone, and believers as living stones.

senses.label: Loose stone, rock
senses.definition: An ordinary stone lying on the ground, picked up, thrown or contrasted with bread.
senses.note: 'A stone's throw' (Luke 22:41) is a measure of distance.

senses.label: Stones thrown to kill
senses.definition: Stones taken up for stoning, the legal or mob penalty for blasphemy and adultery.

senses.label: Stone sealing a tomb
senses.definition: The large disc or block rolled across the entrance of a rock-cut tomb.
senses.note: The stone 'rolled away' is a fixed feature of all four resurrection accounts (cf. John 20:1).

senses.label: Building stone; temple masonry
senses.definition: Dressed stone used in construction, especially the great stones of Herod's temple whose total destruction Jesus foretold.
senses.note: 'Not one stone left upon another' = complete demolition.

senses.label: Millstone
senses.definition: A heavy grinding stone, used as an image of drowning and of sudden, total destruction.

senses.label: Christ the cornerstone
senses.definition: Christ as the stone rejected by the builders but set by God as cornerstone, on which some stumble; believers are 'living stones' built on him.
senses.note: Built on Ps 118:22, Isa 28:16 and Isa 8:14.

senses.label: Precious stone, gem
senses.definition: A costly stone such as jasper, used for adornment, trade or the walls of the new Jerusalem; figuratively, durable work built on Christ.
senses.note: Always masculine in the NT even of gems, where Attic preferred the feminine.

senses.label: Stone as material
senses.definition: Stone as the substance of the Sinai tablets or of carved idols, often implying something lifeless.

authorNotes.author: Peter
authorNotes.note: 1 Peter chains the OT 'stone' texts: Christ is the living stone, chosen and precious to God but a stumbling stone to unbelievers, and believers become living stones of a spiritual house.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul fuses Isa 28:16 and Isa 8:14 to explain Israel's stumbling over Christ, the stone laid in Zion.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: In the Gospel stones are taken up against Jesus and lie on Lazarus' and Jesus' tombs; in Revelation precious stones adorn the throne, Babylon and the new Jerusalem.

background.note: From Homer on, of stones hurled by warriors in battle.
Common for squared building stones, here blocks transportable by camel.
Used of a gemstone set in a necklace, matching the NT 'precious stone'.
An early collection of sayings ascribed to Jesus has 'Raise the stone and there you will find me; cleave the wood and I am there.'

study.exegesisTip: When λίθος is used of Christ, read it against the OT stone texts (Ps 118:22; Isa 8:14; Isa 28:16), which the NT combines to explain both his rejection and his exaltation.
study.caution: Matthew 21:44 is missing from some early manuscripts, and in Revelation 15:6 manuscripts divide between λίθον ('stone') and λίνον ('linen'), so the angels' clothing is uncertain.

study.summary: Middle: as an adjective 'in the middle'; far more often in phrases with the neuter (ἐν μέσῳ, εἰς τὸ μέσον, ἐκ μέσου, ἀνὰ μέσον) meaning 'among', 'into the centre', 'out of the way' or 'between'.

senses.label: Middle (adjective)
senses.definition: Situated at the middle point of something in space or time, e.g. the middle cross, midnight, midday.
senses.note: 'Burst in the middle' (Acts 1:18); 'middle of the night' (Matt 25:6).

senses.label: Among, in the midst of
senses.definition: With ἐν μέσῳ (or μέσος + genitive), present among a group of people or things.
senses.note: Mirrors Hebrew בְּתוֹךְ 'in the midst of'.

senses.label: In the middle of a place
senses.definition: In the central part of a place or area, such as the sea, a courtyard or a street.

senses.label: Into the centre, before all
senses.definition: εἰς (τὸ) μέσον: brought or standing out in the open, in full view of everyone present.

senses.label: Out from among; out of the way
senses.definition: ἐκ (τοῦ) μέσου: removed or separated from a group, or taken away altogether.
senses.note: In Col 2:14 the record of debt is 'taken out of the way', i.e. removed entirely.

senses.label: Between, through
senses.definition: ἀνὰ μέσον or διὰ μέσου: between two parties or areas, or passing through the midst of a crowd or region.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses the word most (24×), especially for public scenes in which someone is set or stands 'in the middle' before all.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: The risen Jesus 'came and stood in the midst' of the disciples; in Revelation Christ walks among the lampstands and the Lamb stands in the midst of the throne.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses ἐκ μέσου for decisive removal: of the offender from the church, of believers from pagan defilement, of the debt-record, and of 'the one who restrains'.

study.translationNote: Because μέσος mostly appears in set phrases, English versions vary: ἐν μέσῳ may be 'in the midst of' (KJV) or simply 'among'; ἐκ μέσου 'out of the way' (KJV, ESV) or 'set aside' (NIV in Col 2:14). In Luke 17:11 διὰ μέσον Σαμαρείας καὶ Γαλιλαίας is rendered 'through the midst of' (KJV) or 'along the border between' (NIV, ESV), depending on how the route is understood.

background.note: From Homer on of the middle point of an object, such as the centre of a shield.
Common in personal descriptions, e.g. a scar 'on the middle of the forehead'.
'Take these things out of the way' (ἐκ τοῦ μέσου), the same idiom as Col 2:14.
ἀνὰ μέσον 'between' is very frequent in the Septuagint, e.g. God separating between light and darkness.

study.exegesisTip: Look at the preposition before μέσον: ἐν = 'among', εἰς = 'into public view', ἐκ = 'removed', ἀνά/διά = 'between, through'; the phrase, not the word alone, carries the meaning.
study.caution: In 2 Thess 2:7 'until he is taken out of the way' (ἐκ μέσου γένηται) the identity of the restrainer, and whether he is removed or simply departs, is much debated.

study.summary: To bow down before someone in reverence: to worship God (or false gods), and also to pay humble homage, often kneeling or prostrate, to a person of higher rank.

senses.label: Worship God
senses.definition: To reverence and adore God, often with bodily prostration, as the act owed to him alone.
senses.note: 'Worship the Lord your God and serve him only' (Matt 4:10).

senses.label: Go up to worship
senses.definition: Used without object of travelling to a sanctuary, especially Jerusalem, to worship at a feast.

senses.label: Homage given to Jesus
senses.definition: People falling before Jesus in reverence; in some scenes supplication or respect, in others recognition of his divine status.
senses.note: Heb 1:6 commands God's angels to worship the Son.

senses.label: Obeisance to a superior
senses.definition: Kneeling or prostrating before a human master, king or holy person to show deference or to plead.
senses.note: The soldiers' kneeling in Mark 15:19 is mock homage.

senses.label: Worship false gods, beast
senses.definition: Rendering worship to idols, demons, Satan, the beast or its image, the rival allegiance Scripture condemns.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John has the most uses: in John 4 true worship is 'in spirit and truth', not tied to a mountain; in Revelation heaven's worship of God and the Lamb is set against the world's worship of the beast, and John is twice forbidden to worship an angel.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew repeatedly shows people falling before Jesus — magi, a leper, a ruler, disciples in the boat and at the resurrection — so the reader sees the response Jesus' identity calls for.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke reserves the word for God and the risen Christ: Peter refuses Cornelius' prostration, and the disciples worship Jesus at the ascension.

study.translationNote: The word describes a physical act (bowing, prostration) as well as an inward attitude, so versions differ: 'worship' (KJV, ESV) or 'bow down', 'kneel before', 'pay homage' (NIV, NRSV, NASB in places). The choice is interpretive in scenes such as Matt 8:2 or Mark 5:6, where 'knelt before him' may say less than 'worshipped him'.

background.note: Classically of making obeisance to the gods or their images, falling down in worship.
Inscriptions use it with the accusative of homage to a deity, e.g. 'I have worshipped the great goddess Isis'.
Used of respect to a human: a writer regrets not being present 'to do obeisance to you'.
'If I go up to worship' — a close parallel to Paul's going up to Jerusalem to worship (Acts 24:11).

study.exegesisTip: Ask who receives the act and how the narrative frames it: homage to a king, a plea for help, or worship due to God alone (compare Peter and the angel refusing it with Jesus accepting it).
study.caution: Scholars debate how much divine worship προσκυνέω implies in the Gospels' scenes with Jesus (homage to a teacher or king versus worship of God), and whether the NT's shift between dative and accusative constructions carries any difference in meaning.

study.summary: To say or declare: mostly introducing quoted speech ('he said, replied'), sometimes stating a solemn point ('this I mean'), or reporting what someone or Scripture says.

senses.label: Said, replied (narrative)
senses.definition: Introducing someone's direct words in a narrative, often as a reply in dialogue.
senses.note: Usually the aorist/imperfect ἔφη.

senses.label: Inserted 'he says'
senses.definition: φησίν placed inside or just after the quoted words, a lively Greek storytelling idiom.

senses.label: Assert, mean (Paul)
senses.definition: To state a point emphatically or explain what one means, as in 'this I declare'.

senses.label: It says; they claim
senses.definition: Indefinite or impersonal use, reporting what Scripture says or what opponents allege.
senses.note: Rom 3:8: 'as some claim that we say'.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses φημί most (32×), especially in the formal exchanges of Acts between Paul and Roman officials, giving the scenes a polished literary tone.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses τοῦτο δέ φημι or ὅ φημι to flag a key statement that his readers must weigh.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew often prefers ἔφη where Mark has λέγει or εἶπεν to introduce replies.

study.translationNote: Versions vary the verb ('said', 'replied', 'declared', 'answered') according to context; the Greek word itself is neutral. In 1 Cor 6:16 and Heb 8:5 φησίν may be 'he (God) says' or 'it (Scripture) says'; in 2 Cor 10:10 some manuscripts read φασίν 'they say', so English has 'they say' or 'some say'.

background.note: One of the oldest Greek verbs of saying, used from Homer onward.
Common in reports: a man 'stated he had bought' a property by contract.
Frequent in document subscriptions: the writer signs for parties 'saying that they do not know letters', i.e. professing to be illiterate.

study.exegesisTip: Do not over-read the choice of φημί over λέγω; the force lies in what is said, though in Paul 'this I declare' marks a statement he wants emphasised.

study.summary: Joy or gladness: the emotion of delight, joy as a gift of God's Spirit that can coexist with suffering, and by extension the person or thing that brings joy.

senses.label: Joy, gladness (emotion)
senses.definition: The feeling of delight at good news or a happy event.
senses.note: Often intensified: 'great joy' (χαρὰ μεγάλη).

senses.label: Joy of salvation, Spirit-given
senses.definition: Joy as a mark of God's kingdom and a fruit of the Holy Spirit in believers.

senses.label: Joy in suffering
senses.definition: Joy held together with trial, loss or grief, grounded in hope beyond the suffering.
senses.note: Grief 'turned to joy' (John 16:20).

senses.label: Shared, completed joy
senses.definition: Joy that belongs to Christ or the apostle and is made full when shared with others in fellowship.

senses.label: Source of joy
senses.definition: By metonymy, the person or thing that causes joy, such as good news or one's converts.
senses.note: 'You are our glory and joy' (1 Thess 2:20).

senses.label: The master's joy
senses.definition: The joyful fellowship of the master into which the faithful servant is welcomed.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke ties joy to the arrival of salvation: the angel's 'good news of great joy', heaven's joy over a repentant sinner, and joy wherever the gospel spreads.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John speaks of Christ's own joy given to the disciples and 'made complete' (πεπληρωμένη); it survives sorrow and no one can take it away.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul (20×) links joy with the Spirit and with his churches, calling his converts his joy and crown; Philippians, written in prison, is especially full of it.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews presents joy as the outlook of endurance: believers accepted loss joyfully, and Jesus endured the cross 'for the joy set before him'.

study.translationNote: Almost always 'joy'. Where Greek pairs the noun with its own verb, a Semitic-style intensive (χαρᾷ χαίρει, John 3:29; ἐχάρησαν χαρὰν μεγάλην, Matt 2:10), versions often render idiomatically ('rejoices greatly', 'overjoyed'), so the noun disappears in English. 'Enter into the joy of your master' (Matt 25:21) is paraphrased by some as 'share your master's happiness'.

background.note: First attested in Sappho, then in tragedy and prose for joy or delight.
Joy can mingle with tears, as when women weep for joy at a homecoming.
'That we may receive you with joy' — the same phrase μετὰ χαρᾶς as in the Gospels.
A Christian presbyter's letter greets brothers with χαρᾷ χαίρειν, the cognate idiom of John 3:29.

study.exegesisTip: Notice what the joy is 'in' or 'because of' (the Lord, the Spirit, converts, a coming reward): NT joy is defined by its object, which is why it can coexist with grief.
study.caution: Some scholars suggest that in Matt 25:21, 23 χαρά carries the sense 'festive banquet' (the master's celebration), but most take it as the master's joy or blessedness generally.

study.summary: To receive or accept: to take what is handed over, to welcome a guest, and to accept a message, God's kingdom or grace; receiving Christ's messengers means receiving Christ himself.

senses.label: Take what is handed over
senses.definition: To take hold of or receive an object, letter, cup or gift offered by another.
senses.note: Simeon 'took him into his arms' (Luke 2:28).

senses.label: Welcome a guest
senses.definition: To receive a person hospitably, giving them a place and a hearing.

senses.label: Receive Christ through his envoys
senses.definition: Welcoming a disciple, a child or a messenger in Christ's name counts as welcoming Christ and the Father who sent him.

senses.label: Accept a message, teaching
senses.definition: To accept God's word or teaching inwardly, believing and embracing it.
senses.note: Contrasted with rejecting 'the love of the truth' (2 Thess 2:10).

senses.label: Receive the kingdom, grace
senses.definition: To accept God's offered kingdom or grace as a gift, with the humility of a child.

senses.label: Receive into a dwelling
senses.definition: To take someone into a house or abode; used of heaven receiving Christ and of Stephen's prayer for his spirit.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: In Acts 'receiving the word' is shorthand for conversion as the gospel reaches Samaria, the Gentiles and Berea.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul stresses how the gospel was received — as God's word, with joy amid affliction — and warns against receiving grace in vain or a different gospel.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: The Fourth Gospel uses the verb only once, of the Galileans welcoming Jesus; elsewhere John prefers λαμβάνω for receiving him.

study.translationNote: Modern versions often say 'welcome' when the object is a person and 'receive' or 'accept' when it is a thing or message, whereas the KJV uses 'receive' throughout. 'Welcome' brings out the hospitality the word often implies; 'receive' keeps visible the link between receiving a person and receiving a message.

background.note: Standard in receipts: 'I have received from you the sum in full without arrears'.
Often of receiving letters: 'as soon as you receive my letter, let me know'.
A Christian letter asks the recipient to 'deign to receive' a small gift sent through a brother.

study.exegesisTip: Check the object: a person (hospitality), a message (belief) or a gift (acceptance); in the mission sayings, welcoming the messenger is the test of welcoming Christ.
study.caution: Some distinguish δέχομαι ('welcome, accept willingly') sharply from λαμβάνω ('take, get'), but the overlap is large — John 13:20 gives the 'whoever receives' saying of Matt 10:40 with λαμβάνω — so the distinction should not be pressed.

study.summary: A teacher: anyone who instructs; especially a Jewish teacher of the Law, the title by which Jesus was addressed (Greek for 'Rabbi'), and a recognised teaching ministry in the church.

senses.label: Teacher, instructor (general)
senses.definition: One who teaches others, often contrasted with the pupil or disciple who learns from him.
senses.note: 'A disciple is not above his teacher.'

senses.label: Jewish teacher of the Law
senses.definition: A recognised expert who taught Israel the Scriptures and traditions.
senses.note: Nicodemus is 'the teacher of Israel'.

senses.label: Jesus addressed as Teacher
senses.definition: The respectful address διδάσκαλε, the Greek equivalent of 'Rabbi', used to Jesus by disciples, inquirers and opponents.
senses.note: John 1:38 and 20:16 translate Rabbi / Rabbouni explicitly.

senses.label: Jesus as 'the Teacher'
senses.definition: A title used of Jesus in the third person and accepted by him, implying unique authority.

senses.label: Teachers in the church
senses.definition: Believers gifted and recognised to instruct the church in the faith, ranked with apostles and prophets.
senses.note: James warns that teachers face stricter judgment.

senses.label: False teachers
senses.definition: Teachers chosen by people to suit their own desires rather than sound doctrine.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: In Matthew 'Teacher' is mostly on the lips of outsiders and opponents (scribes, Pharisees, Herodians), while disciples usually address Jesus as 'Lord'.

authorNotes.author: Mark
authorNotes.note: Mark has Jesus' own disciples address him as 'Teacher', reflecting the rabbi–disciple setting of his ministry.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John glosses 'Rabbi' with διδάσκαλε and has Jesus affirm the title while washing feet, redefining the teacher's authority as service.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul ranks teachers third among God's gifts to the church and calls himself a teacher of the Gentiles.

study.translationNote: The KJV usually renders the vocative 'Master' and calls the temple teachers 'doctors' (Luke 2:46); modern versions use 'Teacher'. 'Master' suggests authority or ownership rather than instruction, so 'Teacher' is closer to the Greek and to the Rabbi title it translates.

background.note: Classically any teacher or master of a skill; Aeschylus calls fire 'teacher of every art' for mortals.
Used of the schoolmaster: 'to go to school' is literally 'to go to the teacher's'.
In apprenticeship contracts the διδάσκαλος is the master craftsman who trains the apprentice.
Very rare in the Septuagint, appearing in Esther and 2 Maccabees only.

study.exegesisTip: Note who calls Jesus 'Teacher' and in what tone — sincere inquiry, flattery before a trap, or a disciple's devotion — since the same word carries different weight in each scene.
study.caution: In Eph 4:11 scholars debate whether 'pastors and teachers' are one combined ministry (a single article governs both) or two distinct, overlapping groups.

study.summary: Third: the ordinal number, used for the third in a series, the third day or hour, 'a third time', and in Revelation 'a third (part)' of creation struck by judgment.

senses.label: Third in a series
senses.definition: The third of several persons, things or places in order.
senses.note: 'The third heaven' (2 Cor 12:2) = the highest heaven, God's presence.

senses.label: On the third day
senses.definition: The day after tomorrow by inclusive reckoning, above all in the formula of Jesus' resurrection.
senses.note: Also of ordinary days, e.g. Cana (John 2:1); Luke 13:32 uses it for a short, set time.

senses.label: Third hour or watch
senses.definition: A point in the day or night: the third hour (about 9 a.m.) or the third night watch.

senses.label: A third time, thirdly
senses.definition: Neuter used adverbially: for the third time; or 'third' in a ranked list.
senses.note: ἐκ τρίτου = 'a third time' (Matt 26:44).

senses.label: A third part
senses.definition: τὸ τρίτον + genitive: one third of something, in Revelation's partial judgments.
senses.note: The judgments are severe but limited, leaving room to repent.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: Most of John's uses are in Revelation's trumpet visions, where 'a third' marks partial, warning judgment; the Gospel notes the 'third' appearance of the risen Jesus and Peter's 'third' questioning.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke repeats 'on the third day' in the passion predictions and resurrection accounts, presenting it as the fulfilment of Scripture.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul passes on the early creed 'raised on the third day according to the Scriptures' and speaks of his third visit to Corinth and the 'third heaven'.

study.translationNote: 'The third hour' is kept literally (KJV, ESV) or converted to clock time, 'nine in the morning' (NIV) (Mark 15:25; Acts 2:15). Matthew and Luke's 'on the third day' and Mark's 'after three days' (a different expression) describe the same interval by inclusive reckoning, which some versions harmonise.

background.note: Used from Homer for the third person to arrive or act in a sequence.
τρίτος ὤν 'being one of three', i.e. with two others, in a report of stealing sheaves.
A letter lists 'first… second… third(ly)', the same enumerating use as 1 Cor 12:28.
Time of day: 'about the third hour'.

study.exegesisTip: Remember inclusive counting: 'the third day' after Friday is Sunday, so it need not mean seventy-two hours.
study.caution: How 'on the third day' relates to 'three days and three nights' (Matt 12:40) and to OT background such as Hos 6:2 or Jonah is debated, though most see inclusive Jewish reckoning rather than a contradiction.

study.summary: Beginning or origin, and by extension first principle or source; also rule, office and those who hold it — human rulers and especially spiritual 'principalities' — and, physically, the corner of a sheet.

senses.label: The absolute beginning
senses.definition: The starting point of creation and history, or what existed before all else ('in the beginning', 'from the beginning').
senses.note: John 1:1 echoes Gen 1:1 (Ἐν ἀρχῇ).

senses.label: Start of something specific
senses.definition: The first point of a particular event, period or activity, such as the gospel, birth pains, or Jesus' signs.

senses.label: Origin, first cause
senses.definition: The source or originating principle from which something comes, applied to God and to Christ.
senses.note: 'The Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end.'

senses.label: First principles, rudiments
senses.definition: The elementary teachings or basic principles of the faith.

senses.label: Corner, end
senses.definition: The extremity or corner of an object, such as the four corners of the sheet in Peter's vision.

senses.label: Rule, office, domain
senses.definition: Authority or jurisdiction held by someone, or the assigned sphere of a being.
senses.note: Jude 6: angels who did not keep their own position of authority.

senses.label: Rulers, authorities
senses.definition: Those who exercise rule: human magistrates, and especially spiritual powers in the unseen realm, often paired with 'authorities'.
senses.note: KJV 'principalities'.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John's 'in/from the beginning' reaches back to before creation (the Word) and, in 1 John, to the beginning of the gospel message the readers first heard.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul pairs ἀρχαί with ἐξουσίαι for cosmic powers created through Christ, disarmed at the cross and finally subjected to him.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews speaks of the 'beginning' of confidence and of salvation's first announcement, and calls the elementary teachings 'the first principles'.

study.translationNote: The double meaning 'beginning' / 'rule' creates real differences: in Rev 3:14 Christ is 'the beginning of the creation of God' (KJV, ESV), 'the origin' (NRSV) or 'the ruler' (NIV); in Col 1:18 he is 'the beginning'. Plural ἀρχαί is 'principalities' (KJV) or 'rulers' (most modern versions). In Heb 6:1 'the beginning of Christ' becomes 'elementary teachings about Christ'.

background.note: From Homer on 'beginning, origin', e.g. the beginning of a quarrel.
An inscription honours Aion (Eternity) as 'having no beginning, middle or end', a striking parallel to divine titles in Revelation.
μηδ᾽ ἀρχήν 'not at all', relevant to the difficult τὴν ἀρχήν of John 8:25.
Of public office: 'having held the same offices (ἀρχάς)'.

study.exegesisTip: Decide first whether the context is about time (beginning), source (origin) or power (rule); then ask, for 'from the beginning', which beginning is meant — creation, Jesus' ministry, or the readers' conversion.
study.caution: Disputed are Rev 3:14 (Christ as first created being, source, or ruler of creation — most reject 'first created'), Col 1:18, and John 8:25, where τὴν ἀρχήν may mean 'from the beginning' or adverbially 'at all' ('Why do I speak to you at all?').

study.summary: To look at, watch or observe attentively; in common usage simply 'see' or 'perceive'; in John it also describes seeing Jesus with faith, and in idiom experiencing death or glory.

senses.label: Watch as a spectator
senses.definition: To look on attentively at an event or spectacle, often over a period of time.
senses.note: Of the women and crowd watching the crucifixion.

senses.label: See, catch sight of
senses.definition: To see a person or thing, with little difference from ὁράω.

senses.label: Perceive, realize
senses.definition: To notice and conclude that something is so, often with ὅτι 'that'.
senses.note: 'I perceive that you are a prophet' (John 4:19).

senses.label: Behold Jesus in faith
senses.definition: Seeing Jesus in a way that leads to or expresses faith and knowledge of the Father, which the world cannot do.

senses.label: Experience (death, glory)
senses.definition: Hebrew-style idiom: to undergo or share in something, as 'see death' or 'behold my glory'.

senses.label: Consider, reflect
senses.definition: To observe mentally and weigh the significance of something.
senses.note: 'Consider how great this man was.'

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John uses θεωρέω for a seeing that may or may not lead to faith: crowds see the signs, believers 'behold' the Son and the Father, and in John 16:16–19 'you will not see me' alternates with another verb for seeing him again.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses the word for crowds viewing the crucifixion as a spectacle and, in Acts, for perception that prompts speech or action.

authorNotes.author: Mark
authorNotes.note: Mark repeats it for the women who watched the cross and burial and then saw the stone rolled away, making them the eyewitness link of the passion.

study.translationNote: Versions render it 'see', 'behold', 'watch', 'look on' or 'perceive' according to context. Older versions' 'behold' suggests prolonged gazing, which suits the spectator scenes but can over-translate where Koine θεωρέω means simply 'see'.

background.note: Originally to be a θεωρός, a spectator at games and festivals, or an envoy sent to them.
Used lightly for seeing or noticing: 'seeing me in daily attendance, he lost heart'.
Of mental perception: 'seeing that you have repented of your former errors'.
'Behold one led off to death', in a dramatic account of a trial.

study.exegesisTip: Ask whether the context stresses looking on (spectacle), noticing a fact, or perceiving Jesus' identity; in John the same verb can describe sight without faith and sight that leads to life.
study.caution: Whether θεωρέω keeps a distinct nuance of attentive watching in John, as against ὁράω and βλέπω, or is simply a synonym in Koine usage, is debated.

study.summary: A gathering or assembly: in the NT chiefly the Jewish synagogue, both the local congregation with its leaders and discipline and the building where it met; once of a Christian meeting.

senses.label: Jewish congregation, assembled community
senses.definition: The local body of Jews gathered for worship, reading and teaching of Scripture, with its own officers and membership.
senses.note: ACT 6:9 names a particular congregation of Freedmen and others from the Diaspora.

senses.label: Synagogue building
senses.definition: By extension, the meeting-house where the congregation gathered, typically on the Sabbath.
senses.note: LUK 7:5: a Gentile centurion 'built us our synagogue'.

senses.label: Local court and discipline
senses.definition: The synagogue as a community authority that could try, punish and flog offenders.
senses.note: Paired with councils and governors as places where disciples will be tried.

senses.label: Christian meeting
senses.definition: A gathering of believers in Christ for worship or for settling matters.
senses.note: The only NT use for a Christian assembly; ἐκκλησία is the usual word.

senses.label: Hostile gathering ('of Satan')
