senses.definition: A group claiming to be God's people whose conduct shows it serves Satan instead.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses the word most (35×). Jesus begins his ministry in the Nazareth synagogue, and in Acts Paul regularly starts his mission in each city's synagogue before turning to Gentiles.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew often says 'their synagogues' and, in Jesus' words to opponents, 'your synagogues', reflecting distance between Jesus' followers and synagogue authorities.

authorNotes.author: James
authorNotes.note: James alone uses the word of a Christian gathering, a sign of the letter's Jewish-Christian setting.

study.translationNote: In James 2:2 most versions render 'assembly' (KJV, ESV) or 'meeting' (NIV), while a few keep 'synagogue'. The Greek is the ordinary word for a Jewish synagogue; translators avoid that rendering because the gathering is plainly Christian.

background.note: In classical Greek the word means simply 'a bringing together', e.g. of a man and a woman in match-making.
The Septuagint uses it for the 'congregation' of Israel (Hebrew ʿēdâ), e.g. at the first Passover.
A papyrus records the Jewish synagogue of Oxyrhynchus acting in the release of Jewish slaves.
Pagan clubs also called their meetings συναγωγαί, as in a meeting of an association devoted to the emperor cult.

study.exegesisTip: Ask whether the word means the people, their building, or their authority: 'they will flog you in their synagogues' (Matt 10:17) refers to community discipline, not to a room.
study.caution: In James 2:2 scholars debate whether the 'assembly' is a worship service or a church court hearing a case, which affects how the rich and poor visitors are understood.

study.summary: To announce good news; in the NT usually to proclaim the gospel of Jesus Christ and the kingdom of God, naming either the message or the people who hear it.

senses.label: Bring good news (general)
senses.definition: To report welcome news of any kind, without a technical Christian sense.
senses.note: 1 Thess 3:6: Timothy brought good news of the Thessalonians' faith and love.

senses.label: Proclaim the gospel
senses.definition: To announce the Christian message of salvation in Christ, often used absolutely: 'preach the gospel'.

senses.label: Proclaim a specific content
senses.definition: To announce a named message as good news: Jesus, peace, the kingdom of God, or the fulfilled promise.
senses.note: The content can be a person: 'he proclaimed Jesus to him' (Acts 8:35).

senses.label: Evangelize people or places
senses.definition: With a direct object of persons or towns: to bring the gospel to them.
senses.note: This construction is not classical but common in the NT.

senses.label: Passive: receive or be proclaimed
senses.definition: Of people, to have good news proclaimed to them; of the message, to be announced as good news.
senses.note: MAT 11:5 echoes Isaiah 61:1: the poor are evangelized.

senses.label: God's announcement (active)
senses.definition: In Revelation, God or an angel announcing his saving purpose.
senses.note: The rare active form, as in late Greek.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke prefers the verb (25×) where Mark and Matthew use the noun εὐαγγέλιον; it frames Jesus' mission from Nazareth on and the spread of the church in Acts.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul pairs verb and noun ('the gospel I gospelled to you') and stresses that the message he preached came from God, not from men.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews says the wilderness generation also had good news proclaimed to them but did not enter God's rest through unbelief.

authorNotes.author: Peter
authorNotes.note: 1 Peter links the preached word with the enduring word of the Lord and the Spirit-empowered messengers.

study.translationNote: Versions vary between 'preach the gospel', 'proclaim the good news', 'bring good news' and 'evangelize'. The Greek stresses that the message is good news; English 'preach' can suggest a formal sermon, which the verb does not require (e.g. Philip and the Ethiopian, Acts 8:35).

background.note: The Septuagint uses it for Hebrew bāśar, from ordinary reports of battle to the herald of God's coming salvation in Isaiah.
It can mean news welcome to the hearers but not to all, as when the Philistines announce Saul's death.
A papyrus uses the active form of a slave arriving to announce his master's victory.
Menander uses the middle for announcing welcome news to someone.

study.exegesisTip: Check the object: is it the message (Jesus, peace, the kingdom) or the hearers (towns, the poor)? The passive can make the hearers the subject: 'the poor are evangelized' (Matt 11:5).
study.caution: In 1 Peter 4:6 'the gospel was preached even to the dead' is debated: those now dead who heard it in life, the spiritually dead, or a proclamation to the dead after Christ's death.

study.summary: Remaining, the rest: 'the others' of a group, the remaining things, and, as adverbial τὸ λοιπόν, 'finally', 'for the rest' or 'from now on'.

senses.label: The rest of a group
senses.definition: The remaining members of a group already mentioned in part.
senses.note: Often with a noun: 'the other virgins', 'the other apostles'.

senses.label: Outsiders, everyone else
senses.definition: All other people, often those outside the circle of disciples or believers, sometimes with a negative tone.
senses.note: 'The rest, who have no hope' (1 Thess 4:13).

senses.label: The remaining things
senses.definition: Neuter plural: other matters or things not yet mentioned.
senses.note: 2 Pet 3:16 sets Paul's letters alongside 'the other Scriptures'.

senses.label: Finally, for the rest
senses.definition: Adverbial τὸ λοιπόν introducing a further or concluding point: 'as for the rest', 'furthermore', 'finally'.
senses.note: Marks a transition, not necessarily the end of a letter.

senses.label: Henceforth, from now on
senses.definition: Adverbial: for the time that remains, from this point on.
senses.note: τοῦ λοιποῦ (Gal 6:17) means 'from now on'.

senses.label: Besides, moreover
senses.definition: Adverbial: beyond that, in addition.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses τὸ λοιπόν as a transition marker in letters, sometimes well before the close (Phil 3:1), and οἱ λοιποί for those outside Christ.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: Revelation speaks of 'the rest' who survive or escape God's judgments, stressing their response: some repent, some do not.

study.translationNote: τὸ λοιπόν is usually 'finally', but in Phil 3:1 and 1 Thess 4:1 it introduces a substantial new section; versions such as the ESV in places use 'finally', others 'furthermore' or 'as for other matters'. English 'finally' can wrongly suggest the letter is about to end.

background.note: Deissmann showed from papyrus letters that λοιπόν without the article was a colloquial 'well then', 'henceforth' in everyday correspondence.

study.exegesisTip: Decide whether τὸ λοιπόν looks forward in time ('from now on') or marks a transition in the argument ('for the rest'); the context, not the English 'finally', settles it.
study.caution: Because 'finally' in Phil 3:1 is followed by two more chapters, some scholars take it as evidence that Philippians combines several letters; others read it simply as 'furthermore'.

study.summary: Right, as opposed to left: the right side or right hand, and figuratively the place of honour and authority, above all Christ seated 'at the right hand of God'.

senses.label: Right (not left)
senses.definition: The right-hand member or side of a body or object.
senses.note: 'Cast the net on the right side of the boat' (John 21:6).

senses.label: The right hand
senses.definition: ἡ δεξιά (χείρ), the right hand as the hand that acts, holds, gives, or pledges.
senses.note: Giving 'the right hand of fellowship' (Gal 2:9) seals agreement and partnership.

senses.label: On the right side
senses.definition: ἐκ δεξιῶν, a position to someone's right, at times with the idea of favour.
senses.note: The sheep on the right receive the blessing (Matt 25:33–34).

senses.label: Seat of honour beside a king
senses.definition: The place nearest a ruler, implying honour and a share in his rule.

senses.label: Christ at God's right hand
senses.definition: Christ's exaltation to share God's throne and authority, from Psalm 110:1.
senses.note: Royal-court language for supreme authority and intercession, not a physical location.

senses.label: God's right hand as power
senses.definition: God's right hand as the instrument of his saving might.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews repeatedly says Christ 'sat down' at God's right hand, marking his once-for-all priestly work as finished.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke grounds the apostles' preaching in Psalm 110, and Stephen sees the Son of Man 'standing' at God's right hand.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: In Revelation the risen Christ holds the seven stars in his right hand and the scroll is held in God's right hand.

study.translationNote: In Acts 2:33 and 5:31 the dative τῇ δεξιᾷ can mean 'exalted to the right hand of God' (most modern versions) or 'exalted by the right hand of God', i.e. by his power (KJV; noted in margins). Both readings are grammatically possible.

background.note: Homer uses it of the right breast or shoulder, the plain physical sense.
Solomon seats his mother at his right hand, the Old Testament picture of the place of honour.
A papyrus letter uses 'right hand' for a pledge: it is madness 'not to keep your pledge'.
Personal descriptions in documents note a scar 'on the right', the same phrase as 'at the right'.

study.exegesisTip: 'At the right hand' of God comes from Psalm 110:1 and speaks of shared royal authority; trace how each writer uses that psalm.
study.caution: 'Weapons of righteousness for the right hand and the left' (2 Cor 6:7) is read either as offensive and defensive weapons (sword and shield) or simply as being fully equipped on every side.

study.summary: To persuade; in the passive to be persuaded, believe or obey; in the perfect to be convinced, or (πέποιθα) to trust and be confident in someone or something.

senses.label: Persuade, win over
senses.definition: To bring someone to a belief or action by argument or appeal; the present can mean 'try to persuade'.

senses.label: Conciliate, seek favour, reassure
senses.definition: To win someone's goodwill, placate them, or set a mind at rest.
senses.note: 'We will satisfy him' (Matt 28:14); 'we will reassure our hearts' (1 John 3:19).

senses.label: Be persuaded, believe
senses.definition: Passive: to be won over and come to believe what is said.

senses.label: Be convinced, be sure
senses.definition: Perfect passive πέπεισμαι: to hold a settled conviction.
senses.note: 'I am convinced that neither death nor life…' (Rom 8:38).

senses.label: Obey, follow
senses.definition: Passive with dative: to heed, comply with, or follow a person or the truth.

senses.label: Trust, be confident
senses.definition: Second perfect πέποιθα: to rely on someone or something, or be confident that something is so.
senses.note: Objects range from God to riches, armour, oneself, or 'the flesh'.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul often speaks of confidence 'in the Lord' about churches and colleagues, set against misplaced confidence 'in the flesh'.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Acts portrays Paul's mission as reasoned persuasion in synagogues and before rulers, with mixed results.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews uses the passive for obeying church leaders and the perfect for the author's confidence in the readers.

study.translationNote: Agrippa's words in Acts 26:28 are rendered 'Almost you persuade me' (KJV), 'In a short time would you persuade me to be a Christian?' (ESV), or 'Do you think that in such a short time you can persuade me?' (NIV). Modern versions read ἐν ὀλίγῳ as 'in a short time' and the present as an attempt.

background.note: Homer already uses the word for persuading by speech.
A letter uses the rare perfect with a dative, 'I trust myself', like Paul's usage.
A writer says 'I am sure' (πέπεισμαι) he will easily be introduced to the king.
The middle passes into 'obey', as in 'being obedient to my native city'.

study.exegesisTip: Watch tense and voice: active 'persuade', passive 'be persuaded' or 'obey', πέπεισμαι 'be convinced', πέποιθα 'trust'; the meaning shifts with the form.
study.caution: In Gal 1:10 'Am I now persuading men or God?' is read either as 'seeking to win human approval' or as answering a charge that Paul's persuasion was manipulative; interpreters differ.

study.summary: To sow seed; used literally of farming and figuratively for spreading God's word, for deeds that bring a harvest, for generosity, and for the burial of the body awaiting resurrection.

senses.label: Sow seed (farming)
senses.definition: To scatter seed on ground so that it will grow.

senses.label: Sow the word
senses.definition: In parable interpretations, to spread God's message; hearers are described as 'what is sown'.
senses.note: The passive identifies people with the seed: 'this is the one sown on rocky ground'.

senses.label: Labour and its reward (proverb)
senses.definition: In the saying 'one sows, another reaps': work whose fruit someone else may gather.

senses.label: Actions bearing consequences
senses.definition: To do deeds, give, or minister in ways that produce a corresponding harvest.
senses.note: Used both for moral consequence (Gal 6:7) and generous giving (2 Cor 9:6).

senses.label: Body sown in death
senses.definition: Of the mortal body placed in the ground like seed, to be raised transformed.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses sowing for the resurrection body, for moral harvest (flesh or Spirit), and for generous giving.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew has the most uses (18), including the parables of the weeds and the mustard seed and their explanation.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John applies the sower–reaper proverb to mission: the disciples reap where others have sown.

study.translationNote: In the explanation of the sower (Matt 13:19–23; Mark 4:15–20) the passive participle literally says 'this is the one sown'. The KJV has 'he which received seed', the ESV 'this is what was sown', the NIV 'the seed sown'; versions differ in whether the hearer is the seed or the soil.

background.note: Farm leases use it routinely of sowing land with wheat.
Tenants write that they hope 'with God' to have the field sown.
The Septuagint uses 'sown' for offspring: no more of a name will be sown.
Plato uses it figuratively of the creator sowing the seed of souls.

study.exegesisTip: In parables, ask both what is sown (the word) and who is described as 'sown'; in Paul, ask what harvest the sowing image points to.
study.caution: In 1 Cor 15:42–44 some take 'it is sown' as burial of the corpse, others as the whole of earthly life in a mortal body; the analogy works either way, but emphasis differs.

study.summary: Time, especially a span or duration of time, short or long; also a particular time or period, time granted or delayed, and in the plural 'times' or ages.

senses.label: A span of time
senses.definition: An interval or duration, often qualified as long, short, or 'some'.
senses.note: 'For a long time' is χρόνῳ ἱκανῷ or πολὺν χρόνον.

senses.label: As long as (legal term)
senses.definition: In ἐφ' ὅσον χρόνον or ὅσον χρόνον, the period during which a state or obligation lasts.

senses.label: A particular time
senses.definition: A point or period at which something happens or is due.
senses.note: 'The fullness of time' (Gal 4:4) is the appointed moment of God's plan.

senses.label: Time granted, delay
senses.definition: Time allowed for something, or the delay before an event.
senses.note: 'There will be no more delay' (Rev 10:6).

senses.label: Times, eras
senses.definition: Plural: periods of history, especially those of God's plan and the last times.
senses.note: Often paired with καιροί, 'times and seasons'.

senses.label: Ages of eternity
senses.definition: In πρὸ χρόνων αἰωνίων, 'before eternal times': before time or the ages began.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses the word most (23×), often for lengths of stay or ministry, giving Acts its sense of time passing.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul places God's purpose 'before eternal times', Christ's coming at 'the fullness of time', and declines to write about 'the times and seasons'.

study.translationNote: Revelation 10:6 was rendered 'there should be time no longer' (KJV), suggesting the end of time itself; modern versions read 'there will be no more delay', which fits the context. 2 Tim 1:9 is variously 'before the world began' (KJV), 'before the ages began' (ESV) or 'before the beginning of time' (NIV).

background.note: Classical writers could distinguish χρόνος, time, from καιρός, the right moment.
Contracts use it for a fixed term, 'the time assigned to him'.
Letters close with a wish for health 'for many times', where χρόνος approaches 'years'.

study.exegesisTip: Note the grammar: the accusative gives duration (Mark 2:19), the dative extension over a period (Luke 8:29), and phrases with prepositions set limits.
study.caution: The popular contrast of χρόνος as clock time with καιρός as the decisive moment is often overstated; in 'times and seasons' (Acts 1:7; 1 Thess 5:1) the two are near synonyms.

study.summary: Blind: physically unable to see, frequently of those Jesus heals; and figuratively lacking spiritual or moral insight, especially of self-confident guides and those unaware of their own condition.

senses.label: Physically blind
senses.definition: Unable to see, whether from birth, illness, or a divine act.

senses.label: The blind as a class
senses.definition: Blind people among the poor and disabled, for whom Jesus' healing signals the age of salvation.
senses.note: Echoes Isaiah 35:5 and 61:1.

senses.label: Blind guides
senses.definition: Leaders who lack spiritual discernment yet presume to guide others.

senses.label: Blind to one's own state
senses.definition: Spiritually unable to perceive the truth or one's real condition, often while claiming to see.
senses.note: 'Because you say "We see", your guilt remains' (John 9:41).

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew's woes call the scribes and Pharisees 'blind guides' and 'blind fools' five times.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John 9 moves from a man born blind who comes to see to leaders who claim sight but are blind, an extended irony.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke has the blind invited to the banquet, and in Acts blindness falls on Elymas as judgment.

background.note: Homer uses it once, of Lycurgus struck blind by Zeus.
Sophocles has the seer foretell Oedipus will be 'blind instead of seeing', mixing literal and figurative blindness.
An inscription from a healing shrine records the lame and blind cured after a dream.
Documents use 'a blind street' for a dead-end alley.

study.exegesisTip: In John 9 and Matthew 23 the word shifts between physical and spiritual blindness; trace who actually sees by the end of the passage.

study.summary: Bad, evil: morally wicked persons, thoughts and deeds; as a noun, evil or wrongdoing, including harm done to others; and in a non-moral sense, harmful, painful, or misfortune.

senses.label: Morally bad, wicked
senses.definition: Of persons, thoughts, desires, or company: base and evil in character.
senses.note: 'Bad company corrupts good character' (1 Cor 15:33) quotes Menander.

senses.label: Evil, wrongdoing
senses.definition: Neuter τὸ κακόν: what is wrong, especially as done or practised, opposite to the good.
senses.note: 'What evil has he done?' (Matt 27:23) asks for a crime.

senses.label: Harm done to others
senses.definition: Wrongs inflicted on a neighbour, enemy, or the church.
senses.note: 'Repay no one evil for evil' (Rom 12:17).

senses.label: Harmful, painful, misfortune
senses.definition: Non-moral: bad things suffered, or things that are injurious.
senses.note: Lazarus received 'bad things' (Luke 16:25): hardship, not sin.

senses.label: Evil as moral category
senses.definition: Good and evil as categories to be discerned, avoided, or judged.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses the word most (28×), often in the antithesis of good and evil and in the call not to repay evil but overcome it with good.

authorNotes.author: Peter
authorNotes.note: 1 Peter, drawing on Psalm 34, forbids returning evil for evil and calls believers to turn from evil.

study.translationNote: 1 Tim 6:10 reads 'the root of all evil' (KJV) or 'a root of all kinds of evil' (ESV, NIV); the Greek plural πάντων τῶν κακῶν supports 'all kinds of evils'. Elsewhere versions vary between 'evil', 'wrong', 'bad' and 'harm' according to context.

background.note: Homer uses it of a coward, showing its early range beyond morality.
The Septuagint renders Hebrew raʿ, as in the 'evil desires' of the wicked.
A letter speaks of someone held back by 'an evil conscience'.
It also means trouble: a man 'is going to get into trouble'.

study.exegesisTip: Ask whether 'evil' is wickedness done, harm inflicted, or misfortune suffered; Luke 16:25 and Rom 12:17 use the same word in different senses.
study.caution: The distinction often drawn between κακός (bad in itself) and πονηρός (actively malicious) is easily overpressed; in NT usage the two overlap heavily.

study.summary: A child, from newborn infant to young boy or girl; also used as a model of how to receive God's kingdom, figuratively of immature thinking, and as an affectionate address to adults.

senses.label: Infant, newborn
senses.definition: A baby from birth through early infancy.

senses.label: Young child
senses.definition: A boy or girl not yet grown, often still in the parents' care.
senses.note: Jairus's daughter is twelve years old (Mark 5:42).

senses.label: Model for disciples
senses.definition: A child as the pattern of humble, dependent reception of God's kingdom.

senses.label: Childish thinking
senses.definition: Figuratively: immature in understanding.
senses.note: 'Do not be children in your thinking; be infants in evil.'

senses.label: Children given to Christ
senses.definition: God's people as the children who share flesh and blood with Christ.

senses.label: Affectionate address
senses.definition: A familiar address to adults, like English 'lads' or 'my children'.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew 2 repeatedly speaks of 'the child and his mother', keeping Jesus at the centre of the infancy story.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke's infancy narratives use the word for both John and Jesus and their growth.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: The risen Jesus calls the disciples παιδία, and 1 John addresses readers the same way.

study.translationNote: In John 21:5 versions render παιδία 'Children' (KJV, ESV), 'Friends' (NIV), or 'Lads'. It is a colloquial address to grown men and does not imply they were young.

background.note: Papyri use it from birth onward, e.g. 'her child at the breast'.
A husband writes to his wife asking her to take care of the child.
It could also mean a young slave, like English 'boy' for a servant.

study.exegesisTip: παιδίον is a diminutive of παῖς; context, not the form alone, shows the child's age, from newborn (Luke 2) to twelve (Mark 5).
study.caution: What 'becoming like children' (Matt 18:3) means is debated: humility, trustful dependence, or accepting the low status children had in that society.

study.summary: Wisdom: skill and learning, practical insight for right living, the clever 'wisdom of this world' that cannot know God, and God's own wise purpose — revealed supremely in Christ crucified.

senses.label: Human skill, learning and insight
senses.definition: Accumulated knowledge or practical ability as people recognise it, such as Egyptian learning or Solomon's renowned wisdom.
senses.note: Neutral in itself; Joseph's wisdom before Pharaoh is God-given (Acts 7:10).

senses.label: Worldly wisdom opposed to God
senses.definition: Merely human cleverness, philosophy or rhetorical brilliance that sets itself up as the measure of truth and so finds the cross foolish.
senses.note: James likewise speaks of a wisdom that is 'earthly, unspiritual, demonic' (Jas 3:15).

senses.label: God-given wisdom for living
senses.definition: Spiritual insight and sound judgment given by God, shown in godly conduct, wise speech and the right handling of practical matters.
senses.note: Includes the 'message of wisdom' among the Spirit's gifts (1 Cor 12:8) and the insight needed to decode Revelation's symbols (Rev 13:18; 17:9).

senses.label: God's own wise purpose
senses.definition: The wisdom of God himself, seen in his saving plan, once hidden and now made known, and worthy of praise.
senses.note: Eph 3:10 calls it 'manifold' (πολυποίκιλος).

senses.label: Christ's wisdom; Christ as wisdom
senses.definition: The wisdom Jesus displayed in his growth and teaching, and Paul's claim that Christ himself is God's wisdom, in whom all its treasures are hidden.
senses.note: See also Col 2:3.

senses.label: Wisdom personified
senses.definition: Wisdom pictured as a person who sends messengers and is proved right by her 'children', drawing on Jewish wisdom tradition.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: In 1 Corinthians 1–3 Paul sets the 'wisdom of the world' against God's 'foolish' message of the cross, yet speaks a hidden wisdom among the mature; in Colossians and Ephesians wisdom is a gift prayed for and a treasure found in Christ.

authorNotes.author: James
authorNotes.note: James treats wisdom as practical godliness, asked of God in trials and shown in meek conduct, and contrasts 'wisdom from above' with jealous, earthly wisdom.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke notes the child Jesus 'filled with' and growing in wisdom, and pairs wisdom with the Spirit in the church's leaders, notably Stephen.

study.translationNote: Nearly all versions say 'wisdom'. They differ on σοφία λόγου in 1 Cor 1:17: 'wisdom of words' (KJV), 'words of eloquent wisdom' (ESV), 'cleverness of speech' (NASB) or 'eloquence' (NIV paraphrase), because the phrase refers to persuasive rhetorical skill rather than to wisdom in general.

background.note: In Homer the word means craftsmanship — the skill of a master carpenter — long before it meant philosophical wisdom.
Aristotle lists wisdom with intelligence (σύνεσις) and prudence (φρόνησις) as the intellectual virtues; σοφία is the broadest of the three.
In later Christian letters 'your wisdom' became a polite form of address.

study.exegesisTip: Ask whose wisdom is meant — the world's, God's, or wisdom God gives — since Paul can condemn σοφία in one sentence and commend it in the next (1 Cor 2:5–6).
study.caution: How far the personified Wisdom of the Gospels (Matt 11:19; Luke 11:49) and Paul's 'Christ the wisdom of God' draw on Jewish Wisdom speculation (Proverbs 8, Wisdom of Solomon) to express Christ's pre-existence is debated; some see a developed 'Wisdom Christology', others mainly a rhetorical contrast with Corinthian pride.

study.summary: Tongue: the bodily organ, the tongue as the instrument of speech and moral conduct, a language or language group, and the Spirit-given speech called 'tongues'.

senses.label: The bodily organ
senses.definition: The physical tongue in the mouth.

senses.label: Tongue as speech
senses.definition: The tongue as the organ of speech, standing for what a person says and so for their moral character.
senses.note: Also of joyful praise, 'my tongue rejoiced' (Acts 2:26), and mere talk opposed to deeds (1 John 3:18).

senses.label: 'Every tongue': all people
senses.definition: By metonymy, every speaking person; 'every tongue confess' means universal acknowledgement.
senses.note: From Isa 45:23.

senses.label: Tongue-shaped flame
senses.definition: Something shaped like a tongue, the flames seen at Pentecost.

senses.label: Language; people by language
senses.definition: A human language, and by extension a people distinguished by its speech, often with tribe, people and nation.

senses.label: Spirit-given 'tongues'
senses.definition: Speech prompted by the Holy Spirit in a language the speaker has not learned, a sign in Acts and a gift needing interpretation in the church at Corinth.
senses.note: In Acts 2 the hearers recognise their own languages (Acts 2:8–11); in 1 Cor 14 'no one understands' without an interpreter.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: In 1 Corinthians 12–14 Paul ranks tongues below prophecy in church because uninterpreted speech does not build others up, values it for private prayer, and insists on order and interpretation.

authorNotes.author: James
authorNotes.note: James makes the tongue the test of true religion: small like a bit or rudder, set on fire by hell, and untamed by any human.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: Revelation repeats a fourfold formula — every tribe, tongue, people and nation — to describe the worldwide church and the worldwide reach of evil.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: In Acts speaking in tongues marks the Spirit's coming to new groups: Jews at Pentecost, Gentiles at Cornelius's house, and John's disciples at Ephesus.

study.translationNote: Most versions keep 'tongue(s)' throughout, which preserves the link between organ and gift; some (e.g. NLT, CEB) say 'languages' in Acts 2 and elsewhere to make clear real speech is meant. The KJV added 'unknown' (in italics) in 1 Cor 14 ('an unknown tongue'), which is not in the Greek. In Revelation 'tongue' means a language group.

background.note: From Homer on the word means the tongue of the mouth, and is also used of the tongues of sacrificial victims.
Curse tablets 'bind' the tongue of an enemy to make him dumb; Deissmann read the loosing of the deaf man's tongue in Mark 7:35 against this background.
A hymn sung 'in a foreign tongue' shows γλῶσσα of an actual foreign language.
A prayer asks protection from 'evil tongues', the tongue of slander.

study.exegesisTip: Decide first whether γλῶσσα is the organ, speech, a people, or the spiritual gift; in 1 Cor 14 note that γλώσσῃ λαλεῖν is set against speaking 'with the mind' (1 Cor 14:14–19).
study.caution: Whether the tongues of 1 Corinthians are the same as the recognised foreign languages of Acts 2 (xenolalia), or non-human speech such as 'tongues of angels' (1 Cor 13:1), is debated, as is whether 'tongues will cease' (1 Cor 13:8) refers to the end of the apostolic age or to Christ's return. Each view has serious defenders.

study.summary: Writing; in the New Testament always the sacred writings — 'the Scriptures' as a whole (usually plural) or a particular passage (usually singular) — treated as God's authoritative, fulfilled word.

senses.label: The Scriptures as a whole
senses.definition: The sacred writings of Israel (our Old Testament) taken together as God's word, usually in the plural.
senses.note: 'Holy Scriptures' (Rom 1:2), 'prophetic Scriptures' (Rom 16:26).

senses.label: A particular passage
senses.definition: A specific text of Scripture, often introduced as 'this Scripture' or 'another Scripture'.
senses.note: Abbott-Smith notes the singular usually means a particular passage, the plural the whole.

senses.label: Scripture that must be fulfilled
senses.definition: Scripture as prophecy that comes true in the events of Jesus' life, death and resurrection.

senses.label: Scripture speaking as God
senses.definition: Scripture personified as speaking, foreseeing or confining, because what it says is what God says.
senses.note: In Rom 9:17 'the Scripture says to Pharaoh' quotes words God spoke.

senses.label: Scripture extended to apostolic writings
senses.definition: The term applied, by implication, to Christian writings set alongside the older Scriptures.
senses.note: 2 Pet 3:16 counts Paul's letters with 'the other Scriptures'; 1 Tim 5:18 cites a saying of Jesus (Luke 10:7) next to Deuteronomy.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John repeatedly says events happened 'so that the Scripture might be fulfilled', especially in the passion, and insists 'the Scripture cannot be broken'.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke stresses that the risen Jesus 'opened' the Scriptures, and that the apostles and Apollos argued from them that the Messiah had to suffer.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul personifies Scripture as foreseeing and preaching the gospel in advance, and grounds the gospel's core in what happened 'according to the Scriptures'.

study.translationNote: Versions differ over capitalising 'Scripture(s)', and especially over 2 Tim 3:16: 'All Scripture is breathed out by God and profitable' (ESV, NIV, most) or 'Every Scripture inspired of God is also profitable' (ASV, RV margin). The Greek has no verb, so translators must supply 'is' and decide where it goes.

background.note: The basic classical sense is drawing or painting, a representation in lines.
In the papyri γραφή is a document, list or register — for example a list of property that had belonged to Jews.
'According to the writings' (κατὰ γραφάς) is used of legal texts, a parallel to 1 Cor 15:3–4.
The Letter of Aristeas already uses γραφή of the Jewish holy writings.

study.exegesisTip: Notice singular versus plural: 'the Scripture' usually points to one identifiable passage, worth finding before interpreting the New Testament use of it.
study.caution: In 2 Tim 3:16 πᾶσα γραφή may mean 'all Scripture' (the whole) or 'every Scripture' (each passage), and θεόπνευστος may be predicate ('is inspired') or attributive ('inspired Scripture is also profitable'); most scholars prefer the predicate reading, but both are grammatically possible.

study.summary: Blessed, fortunate, happy: chiefly in declarations ('Blessed are…') that someone is truly well off because of God's favour; also of God's own blessedness and of ordinary good fortune.

senses.label: Declared blessed by God
senses.definition: A pronouncement that a person is truly well off in God's sight, often despite present appearances, because of God's favour now or to come.
senses.note: Usually without a verb: 'Blessed the poor…' — a formula going back to Hebrew ʾašrê ('O the happiness of…').

senses.label: Blessed at the Lord's coming
senses.definition: The happiness of those found faithful and ready when Christ returns, or who share the final banquet.

senses.label: Fortunate, enviable
senses.definition: Fortunate or better off in an everyday sense, as people judge circumstances.
senses.note: Comparative μακαριωτέρα 'happier' (1 Cor 7:40).

senses.label: God's own blessedness
senses.definition: Applied to God as perfectly blessed in himself, and to the hope of Christ's glorious appearing.
senses.note: A Hellenistic Jewish usage (cf. Philo's 'alone blessed').

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew's nine Beatitudes speak in the third person and include spiritual qualities ('poor in spirit', 'hunger and thirst for righteousness').

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke has more uses than any other writer: his Beatitudes address 'you' directly, concern literal poverty and hunger, and are paired with woes; he also records Elizabeth's 'blessed is she who believed'.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: Revelation contains seven beatitudes, from reading the prophecy to entering the city; John's Gospel blesses those who believe without seeing and who do what they know.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul quotes Psalm 32 to show blessedness consists in sins forgiven apart from works, and in the Pastorals calls God 'the blessed God'.

study.translationNote: Most versions say 'Blessed', while some (Good News, Jerusalem Bible, Phillips) say 'Happy', and others 'Fortunate'. 'Blessed' signals that God is the source and judge of this well-being; 'happy' gets the congratulatory tone but can sound like a passing feeling. μακάριος should also be kept distinct from εὐλογητός, 'blessed' in the sense of 'praised' (Luke 1:68).

background.note: In classical prose μακάριος is used of people as 'blessed, happy'; Aristotle distinguishes it from εὐδαίμων ('prosperous, happy').
In polite address ὦ μακάριε meant 'my good sir'.
Later documents use 'the blessed' of the departed, as 'the late' in English.
A Christian epitaph says 'the blessed Semeuga died'.

study.exegesisTip: Read a beatitude as a declaration about someone's real standing before God, explained by its 'for' (ὅτι) clause, rather than as a description of how they feel.
study.caution: Whether the Beatitudes are mainly ethical conditions for entering the kingdom ('be like this') or announcements of grace to the needy ('God favours such people') is debated; many scholars see Luke's form as more announcement and Matthew's as including both.

study.summary: Comparison: an illustration or figure that sets one thing beside another — especially Jesus' parables — and also a proverb, and in Hebrews a symbol or type.

senses.label: Parable of Jesus
senses.definition: A short story or picture from nature or daily life that Jesus used to teach about God's kingdom.
senses.note: Found only in the Synoptic Gospels; John uses παροιμία instead.

senses.label: Speaking in veiled figures
senses.definition: Teaching in parables as an indirect mode that reveals to disciples and conceals from outsiders.

senses.label: Comparison, illustration
senses.definition: A comparison or analogy used in argument, not necessarily a story.
senses.note: 'Learn the parable (lesson) from the fig tree' (Matt 24:32).

senses.label: Proverb, byword
senses.definition: Like Hebrew māšāl, a popular saying or proverb.
senses.note: 'Physician, heal yourself' (Luke 4:23).

senses.label: Symbol, type
senses.definition: A figure that points beyond itself: the earthly tabernacle as a symbol for the present age, Isaac's return as a figure of resurrection.

authorNotes.author: Mark
authorNotes.note: Mark stresses that parables reveal 'the mystery of the kingdom' to insiders while outsiders hear without understanding, and that Jesus explained everything privately to his disciples.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew gathers parables into a discourse (ch. 13) and sees Jesus' parabolic speech as fulfilling Psalm 78:2.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke often states a parable's purpose before telling it and uses the word broadly for proverbs and illustrations.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews uses the word for a symbolic figure: the tabernacle and Isaac's restoration point to greater realities.

study.translationNote: Gospels: 'parable' almost everywhere, but 'proverb' in Luke 4:23 (KJV, ESV). In Hebrews versions vary widely — 'figure' (KJV), 'symbolic' (ESV), 'illustration' (NIV) in Heb 9:9; 'in a figure' or 'figuratively speaking' in Heb 11:19 — because there it means a type or symbol, not a story.

background.note: Aristotle uses παραβολή for an illustrative comparison in argument, such as those of Socrates, distinct from a fable.
Aelian uses the dative παραβολῇ, 'by way of comparison', a parallel to Heb 11:19.
The Septuagint uses it for Hebrew māšāl, including Balaam's oracles and proverbial sayings.

study.exegesisTip: Look for the setting and audience Jesus addresses, and ask what single comparison the parable draws before pressing every detail for meaning.
study.caution: Two debates affect reading: whether the ἵνα of Mark 4:12 (cf. Luke 8:10) expresses purpose (parables meant to conceal) or result (so that, as Isaiah said, they do not see); and how far parables are allegorical, with older interpreters finding meaning in many details and Jülicher-influenced scholarship stressing one main point.

study.summary: To take or receive: take someone along or into one's care, lead someone off, and above all receive what is handed on — tradition, teaching, a ministry or a kingdom.

senses.label: Take along, take aside
senses.definition: To take a person with oneself as companion, or privately apart from others.
senses.note: Often a participle before the main verb: 'taking… he went'.

senses.label: Take control of, lead off
senses.definition: To take charge of someone and lead them away, of the devil with Jesus, soldiers with a prisoner, or a spirit bringing others.

senses.label: Taken at the coming
senses.definition: Passive: to be taken away when the Son of Man comes, while another is left.

senses.label: Take to oneself, welcome
senses.definition: To receive someone into one's home or company as one's own: Joseph taking Mary as wife, Jesus taking his disciples to himself, his own people refusing him.

senses.label: Receive handed-down teaching
senses.definition: To receive tradition, teaching or the gospel passed on by another, the counterpart of παραδίδωμι 'hand over'.
senses.note: Also traditions the Pharisees 'received' to keep (Mark 7:4), and receiving 'Christ Jesus the Lord' (Col 2:6).

senses.label: Receive a trust or kingdom
senses.definition: To receive something entrusted, such as a ministry, or to inherit a kingdom.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses the verb as a technical term for receiving authoritative tradition, paired with 'handed on', yet insists his gospel was received by revelation, not from a human source.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew uses it frequently in narrative: Joseph taking Mary and the child, the devil taking Jesus, Jesus taking chosen disciples, and one 'taken' and one left.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John uses it of the world's refusal to receive the Word and of Jesus' promise to take his disciples to himself.

study.translationNote: English must switch between 'take' and 'receive' depending on the object, which hides that 'took Peter, James and John' (Matt 17:1) and 'what I received I passed on' (1 Cor 15:3) are the same verb. In John 1:11–12 versions use 'receive' for both παρέλαβον and ἔλαβον, though the first suggests welcoming him as one's own.

background.note: Classical writers use it of succeeding to an office or kingdom received from a predecessor (compare Heb 12:28).
The Rosetta inscription speaks of receiving the kingdom from one's father.
A temple inventory begins 'we received these from the temple officials… and handed them over to our successors', showing the pair receive/hand on.
In everyday letters it is the normal word for receiving goods (not money): 'receive the reeds from Pothus'.

study.exegesisTip: When the object is teaching or tradition, look for the matching 'hand on' (παραδίδωμι) nearby; the pair marks a chain of authoritative transmission (1 Cor 11:23; 15:3).
study.caution: In Matt 24:40–41 and Luke 17:34–35 it is debated whether those 'taken' are gathered to salvation (the more common view, matching the gathering of the elect) or taken away in judgment like those swept away by the flood; the parallel in Matt 24:39 uses a different verb. Also debated is whether 'I received from the Lord' (1 Cor 11:23) means direct revelation or tradition that originated with Jesus.

study.summary: To make visible or known: reveal what was hidden (God's plan, people's hearts), display openly, and of Christ, to appear — in his incarnation, after his resurrection, and at his return.

senses.label: Reveal God's hidden plan
senses.definition: To make known what God had kept hidden and now discloses, such as his righteousness, the mystery, or his word.

senses.label: Bring to light, expose
senses.definition: To bring hidden things, deeds or motives into the open, often at judgment.
senses.note: Passive in 2 Cor 5:10: all must 'appear', that is, be laid bare, before Christ's judgment seat.

senses.label: Display, show openly
senses.definition: To show something plainly so it can be seen, such as God's works, glory or name, or the life of Jesus in his servants.

senses.label: Christ's appearing in the flesh
senses.definition: Of Christ's coming into the world, made visible as man at the end of the ages to take away sin.

senses.label: Resurrection appearances
senses.definition: Of the risen Jesus showing himself to his disciples.

senses.label: Christ's appearing at his return
senses.definition: Of Christ's future appearing, when believers will appear with him in glory.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John uses the verb for Jesus revealing his glory and the Father's name, for his appearing after the resurrection, and in 1 John for the 'life' that was manifested and for his future appearing.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul pairs 'hidden then, revealed now' to describe the gospel as God's long-concealed mystery now disclosed, and speaks of the apostle's suffering life as manifesting Jesus.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews uses it of the way into the holy place not yet revealed, and of Christ appearing once for all to put away sin.

authorNotes.author: Peter
authorNotes.note: 1 Peter contrasts Christ foreknown before creation but revealed in the last times, and promises the crown when the chief Shepherd appears.

study.translationNote: Versions vary between 'reveal', 'make known', 'appear' and 'manifest' as the context requires; older versions keep 'manifest' throughout. In 1 Tim 3:16 the KJV reads 'God was manifest in the flesh', while most modern versions read 'He was manifested/appeared', following earlier manuscripts that have ὅς ('who') instead of θεός.

background.note: Herodotus uses the passive of becoming conspicuous or famous among the Greeks through lavish spending.
The Septuagint uses the verb only once, for Hebrew gālâ ('reveal').
A Christian prayer asks, 'O God, reveal to me your truth' about whether to make a journey.

study.exegesisTip: Note whether Christ is the subject: his 'appearing' can mean his first coming, a resurrection appearance or his return, and the tense and context usually decide which.
study.caution: In 1 John 3:2 'when he/it appears' may refer to Christ's appearing or to 'what we shall be' being revealed; both readings are defended, though the parallel in 1 John 2:28 favours Christ.

study.summary: To sit or sit down — to rest, teach, judge or reign — and transitively to seat or appoint someone; also to stay in a place.

senses.label: Sit down
senses.definition: To take a seat in ordinary life, including sitting on an animal.
senses.note: The participle καθίσας 'sitting down' often just introduces an action (Luke 14:28; 16:6).

senses.label: Sit to teach
senses.definition: To sit in the posture of a teacher addressing listeners.
senses.note: Jewish teachers normally sat to teach.

senses.label: Sit in judgment
senses.definition: To sit on a judicial seat or throne to hear cases or rule.

senses.label: Sit enthroned at God's right
senses.definition: Of Christ taking his seat at God's right hand after his work is complete, sharing God's rule.
senses.note: From Psalm 110:1.

senses.label: Seat, set, appoint
senses.definition: Transitive: to cause to sit, set someone in place or appoint to a role.

senses.label: Stay, settle
senses.definition: To remain or settle in a place for a time.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews uses 'sat down' at God's right hand as a sign that Christ's sacrifice is finished, in contrast to priests who stand daily.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew uses the word for sitting on thrones: the Son of Man on his glorious throne, the Twelve judging Israel, and the request to sit at his right and left.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses it of rulers taking the judgment seat and of the disciples 'staying' in Jerusalem until clothed with power.

study.translationNote: Versions differ between 'sit', 'sat down' and, where the sense is staying, 'tarry' (KJV) or 'stay' (modern) in Luke 24:49. In John 19:13 nearly all have Pilate 'sat down' on the judgment seat, but the verb could be transitive ('seated him', i.e. Jesus).

background.note: Homer uses the aorist transitively: Charis 'seated' Thetis on a chair.
A transitive use: an overseer 'set us', the local inhabitants, to work on the dykes.
Intransitive use of judges 'sitting' to hear a case, as perhaps in John 19:13.

study.exegesisTip: Watch whether the verb is transitive (God 'seated' Christ, Eph 1:20) or intransitive (Christ 'sat down', Heb 10:12); the posture often carries authority — to teach, judge or reign.
study.caution: In John 19:13 scholars debate whether Pilate himself sat on the judgment seat or, ironically, seated Jesus there as 'your King' (John 19:14); the grammar allows both, though most translations prefer the intransitive.

study.summary: Judgment: the act or verdict of judging, especially God's judgment (often condemning) and the final Day of Judgment; also justice as a standard, a local court, and an accusation.

senses.label: Judging, verdict
senses.definition: The act of judging or the decision reached, whether by humans or by Jesus.

senses.label: God's judgment, often condemning
senses.definition: God's act of judging, frequently with the result of condemnation and punishment.
senses.note: Plural 'judgments' of God's acts of justice (Rev 16:7; 19:2).

senses.label: The Last Judgment
senses.definition: The final judgment at the end of the age, often 'the day of judgment'.
senses.note: Also 'the judgment of Gehenna' (Matt 23:33).

senses.label: Justice, what is right
senses.definition: Like Hebrew mišpāṭ, justice as a standard or cause that God upholds.
senses.note: Quoting Isa 42:1–3 in Matt 12:18–20.

senses.label: Local court
senses.definition: A tribunal, probably the local Jewish court.

senses.label: Accusation, condemning charge
senses.definition: A charge or condemnation pronounced against someone.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John presents judgment as already taking place in response to Jesus: believers 'do not come into judgment', the world is judged now, and the Spirit convicts concerning judgment.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew repeats 'the day of judgment' in warnings to unrepentant towns and also uses κρίσις for justice as a weighty matter of the law.

authorNotes.author: Jude
authorNotes.note: Jude speaks of angels kept for 'the judgment of the great day' and of Michael not daring to bring a slanderous judgment against the devil.

authorNotes.author: Peter
authorNotes.note: 2 Peter stresses that the Lord knows how to keep the unrighteous for the day of judgment.

study.translationNote: Modern versions mostly say 'judgment', but the KJV often used 'damnation' or 'condemnation' (Mark 3:29; John 5:29) where the context implies an adverse verdict, and 'judgment' in Matt 23:23 where modern versions say 'justice'. The word itself is neutral; context shows whether it means condemnation.

background.note: The root sense is separating or distinguishing, from which come decision and judgment.
The Septuagint uses κρίσις for Hebrew mišpāṭ, 'justice', which explains the Gospels' sense 'justice'.
Petitioners ask that no action be taken 'until the trial' (μέχρι κρίσεως).
A legal decision: 'judgment against him being entered in my favour'.

study.exegesisTip: Decide whether κρίσις is the process of judging, its (often negative) outcome, or justice itself; John's 'does not come into judgment' (John 5:24) means escaping condemnation, not escaping assessment.
study.caution: In Matt 5:21–22 it is debated whether 'the judgment' is a local human court (with the Sanhedrin and Gehenna forming an escalating series) or already God's judgment; Abbott-Smith and many take it as a local court, others see Jesus deliberately blurring human and divine courts.

study.summary: To bring to: bring people or things to someone, present a gift, offer a sacrifice or prayer to God — above all in Hebrews of Christ's once-for-all offering of himself — and to deal with someone.

senses.label: Bring people to someone
senses.definition: To bring the sick, children or others to Jesus, or a person before a ruler.

senses.label: Bring or hold out an object
senses.definition: To bring or hold something out to a person, such as a coin or sour wine.

senses.label: Present a gift
senses.definition: To present gifts or money to someone.

senses.label: Offer to God
senses.definition: To offer sacrifices, gifts or service to God, the regular term for presenting offerings in worship.
senses.note: Also of prayers (Heb 5:7) and of Abraham offering Isaac (Heb 11:17); 'offering service to God' by killing believers (John 16:2).

senses.label: Christ's offering of himself
senses.definition: Of Christ presenting himself as the once-for-all sacrifice for sins.

senses.label: Deal with, treat
senses.definition: Passive: to behave toward or treat someone in a certain way.
senses.note: 'God is treating you as sons.'

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews uses the verb about twenty times to contrast the repeated offerings of the Levitical priests with Christ's single offering of himself, which perfects and ends sacrifice.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew uses the verb often in both senses: crowds bringing the sick to Jesus, and worshippers offering gifts at the altar.

study.translationNote: English uses 'bring', 'offer' and 'present' for one verb, so readers miss that bringing the sick to Jesus and offering a gift at the altar are expressed alike. In Heb 11:17 the imperfect is rendered 'was ready to offer' or 'was offering up' (Abraham began but did not complete it), and in Heb 12:7 'deals with you' (ESV, KJV) or 'treats you' (NIV).

background.note: Classical writers use it of bringing something to or against something, such as scaling ladders to towers.
In the oldest dated Greek papyrus, a marriage contract, the bride 'brings' clothing and jewellery as her dowry.
The passive 'deal with' someone, as in Heb 12:7, appears in a letter asking a brother to treat an opponent severely.

study.exegesisTip: In Hebrews track the tenses: present tenses describe the priests' constant offering, while aorists describe Christ's single offering (Heb 10:11–12).
study.caution: Scholars debate when and where Christ 'offered' himself in Hebrews: on the cross alone, or (also) in presenting himself in the heavenly sanctuary after his resurrection, as on the Day of Atonement (Heb 9:24–25). Most see the cross as central, but the heavenly-sanctuary reading has recent support.

study.summary: Need: the state of lacking something, the thing lacked (often material needs), and occasionally a task or duty. Most often in the idiom χρείαν ἔχω, 'to have need (of)'.

senses.label: Need of something or someone
senses.definition: Lack of a thing or person that is required, usually in the idiom χρείαν ἔχω with a genitive: 'to need'.
senses.note: 'Those who are well have no need of a physician' (Mark 2:17). In Rev 3:17 the thing lacked stands in the accusative, a Koine usage also found in the papyri.

senses.label: Need to do something
senses.definition: χρείαν ἔχω with an infinitive or ἵνα clause: it is necessary, or (with a negative) unnecessary, for someone to act.
senses.note: Often negative: 'you have no need that anyone write to you' (1 Thess 4:9).

senses.label: Material needs, want
senses.definition: Want of the necessities of life, or (plural) the needs themselves, which believers meet by sharing and giving.
senses.note: 'As anyone had need' (Acts 2:45; 4:35) describes the Jerusalem church's sharing.

senses.label: Necessity; what the occasion requires
senses.definition: That which is necessary or urgent, or the need of a particular moment or situation.
senses.note: 'One thing is needful' (Luke 10:42). In Eph 4:29 speech should build up 'as the need may be' or 'as fits the occasion'.

senses.label: Task, duty, office
senses.definition: A matter of business or an assigned responsibility, a sense common in later Greek.
senses.note: The Seven are appointed 'over this business' (KJV) or 'duty' (ESV), i.e. the daily distribution.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses the word for the concrete needs that believers meet for one another and that God supplies, including his own needs met by the Philippians' gifts.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John often states what is not needed: Jesus needs no one's testimony about people, anointed believers need no teacher, and the New Jerusalem needs no sun.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews uses 'need' in its argument: readers who need milk again, the 'need' for another priest, and the need for endurance.

study.translationNote: In Eph 4:29 KJV 'good to the use of edifying' renders τῆς χρείας loosely; RSV/ESV 'as fits the occasion' take it as the occasion, NIV 'according to their needs' as the hearers' need. In Acts 6:3 KJV 'business' and modern 'duty' or 'task' reflect the less common sense 'office, matter in hand'.

background.note: Tragedy uses the word for distress or the pressure of need.
A husband writes that his wife should be given whatever she needs until he returns, 'let her want for nothing'.
χρείαν ἔχω followed by an accusative, as in Rev 3:17, occurs in everyday letters.
The sense 'matter, business' appears in the Maccabean books, as in Acts 6:3.

study.exegesisTip: Check whether χρεία names a lack (need of something), a necessity (need to do something), or concrete material needs, which in Acts and Paul usually call for practical sharing.
study.caution: Two phrases are disputed: ὁ κύριος αὐτοῦ χρείαν ἔχει (Mark 11:3; Luke 19:31) may mean 'the Lord needs it' or, as some argue from word order, 'its owner needs it'; and πρὸς οἰκοδομὴν τῆς χρείας (Eph 4:29) is rendered in several ways.

study.summary: To give back or give what is due: return something, pay a debt or obligation, render an account, recompense good or evil; in the middle, to sell.

senses.label: Give back, return, hand over
senses.definition: To return something to its owner or hand it over to the proper person.
senses.note: Jesus hands the scroll back to the attendant (Luke 4:20) and restores the healed boy to his father (Luke 9:42).

senses.label: Pay what is owed
senses.definition: To pay a debt, wages, taxes or any obligation; to render to someone what is rightfully theirs.
senses.note: Also of vows (Matt 5:33) and marital duty (1 Cor 7:3); children 'repay' their parents (1 Tim 5:4).

senses.label: Render account or testimony
senses.definition: To give, as a matter of duty, an account of one's conduct or testimony to what one has seen; also of a vine or tree yielding its due fruit.
senses.note: λόγον ἀποδίδωμι is a fixed phrase for accountability, often before God's judgment.

senses.label: Recompense, reward by God
senses.definition: God's repaying of people according to their deeds, whether with reward or with punishment.
senses.note: 'Your Father who sees in secret will reward you' (Matt 6:4, 6, 18).

senses.label: Repay evil for evil
senses.definition: To retaliate, paying back harm with harm, which believers are forbidden to do.
senses.note: In Rev 18:6 the command to 'pay her back' belongs to God's judgment on Babylon, not to personal revenge.

senses.label: Sell (middle voice)
senses.definition: In the middle voice, to give up what is one's own for a price; to sell.
senses.note: Joseph's brothers sold him (Acts 7:9); Esau sold his birthright (Heb 12:16).

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew (18 uses) builds a theology of repayment: debts that must be paid to the last penny, the Father who rewards secret piety, and the Son of Man who repays each according to his deeds.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul forbids believers to repay evil for evil while affirming that God will repay each according to his works.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews and 1 Peter use 'render an account' for leaders and for all people before God.

study.translationNote: In 'Render to Caesar' (Matt 22:21) KJV 'render' and ESV 'render' keep the idea of paying what is due; NIV 'give back to Caesar' brings out the prefix ἀπο- (the coin bears Caesar's image and is owed to him). Elsewhere English varies between 'give', 'pay', 'repay', 'reward' and 'render' for the same verb, all expressing what is owed.

background.note: Homer already uses the verb of children repaying parents for their upbringing, the idea behind 1 Tim 5:4.
The Septuagint uses it for making restitution for a wrong done.
ἀπόδος, 'deliver to', is the standard address on the back of a letter.
It is the ordinary verb for paying back what is owed, such as wages received for services not fully rendered.

study.exegesisTip: The prefix ἀπο- usually signals something owed or returned; ask what is due, to whom, and who will do the repaying.

study.summary: To take hold of and keep hold: seize or arrest someone, grasp a hand, hold something firmly, hold fast to teaching or hope, or restrain and retain.

senses.label: Seize, arrest
senses.definition: To lay hold of a person by force, especially to arrest them.
senses.note: In Mark 3:21 Jesus' family set out 'to take charge of him'.

senses.label: Take by the hand
senses.definition: To grasp someone's hand or body, especially in Jesus' healing touch; also to lay hold of an animal.
senses.note: κρατήσας τῆς χειρός recurs in raising and healing stories.

senses.label: Hold, cling to
senses.definition: To hold something in one's grasp or cling to a person.
senses.note: The risen Christ 'holds the seven stars in his right hand' (Rev 2:1).

senses.label: Hold fast teaching, faith
senses.definition: To keep firmly to a tradition, teaching, confession, name or hope and not let it go.
senses.note: Used both of human tradition (Mark 7:8) and of apostolic tradition (2 Thess 2:15).

senses.label: Restrain, retain
senses.definition: To hold back or keep in a state: eyes kept from recognizing, death unable to hold Jesus, winds held back, sins retained.

senses.label: Attain, take hold of
senses.definition: To gain or lay hold of something sought.
senses.note: 'To take hold of the hope set before us' (Heb 6:18).

authorNotes.author: Mark
authorNotes.note: Mark (15 uses) uses the verb for both Jesus' life-giving grip on the sick and the hostile 'seizing' of Jesus at his arrest.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: In Revelation the churches are urged to 'hold fast' what they have, while some 'hold' false teaching.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews uses it with the genitive for holding fast the confession and seizing the hope offered.

study.translationNote: Versions differ in John 20:23: KJV/ESV 'retain' or 'withhold forgiveness', NIV 'do not forgive'. In Mark 3:21 KJV 'lay hold on him' becomes 'take charge of him' (NIV) or 'seize him' (ESV). The same verb is rendered 'arrest', 'take', 'hold' and 'keep' depending on context.

background.note: Its basic classical sense is to be strong and so to rule or hold sway.
A papyrus recalls how Caesar 'conquered' Cleopatra's kingdom, the sense 'become master of'.
A land survey allows tenants 'to keep' the land, the sense 'retain'.
A Delos dedication honours Zeus 'who rules over all', comparable to παντοκράτωρ.

study.exegesisTip: Notice whether the grip is hostile (arrest), compassionate (healing touch) or faithful (holding fast), since the same verb carries all three.
study.caution: What it means for the disciples to 'retain' sins in John 20:23, and how far the authority extends, is debated between church traditions.

study.summary: Fear: fright and terror, the awe people feel at God's acts, the reverent fear of God that shapes life, and the respect owed to others.

senses.label: Fright, terror, alarm
senses.definition: The emotion of being afraid in the face of danger, the uncanny, or people who can do harm.
senses.note: 'For fear of the Jews' (John 7:13; 19:38; 20:19) uses an objective genitive.

senses.label: Awe at divine action
senses.definition: Awe or holy dread that falls on people who witness God's power in miracles, judgment or revelation.
senses.note: Often joined with glorifying God (Luke 5:26; 7:16).

senses.label: Reverent fear of God
senses.definition: A settled reverence toward God or Christ that governs conduct, rooted in the Old Testament 'fear of the LORD'.

senses.label: Respect toward people
senses.definition: Deference or respect owed to those in authority, masters or husbands.
senses.note: In 1 Peter this respect is usually grounded in reverence for God.

senses.label: 'Fear and trembling'
senses.definition: A fixed pairing expressing anxious humility and earnest concern to do one's duty, not panic.

senses.label: A cause of fear
senses.definition: By extension, that which inspires fear.
senses.note: 'Rulers are not a terror to good conduct' (Rom 13:3).

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke repeatedly reports 'fear' falling on people at God's acts, usually as awe that leads to praising God and the growth of the church.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: The Gospel stresses 'fear of the Jews' that silences disciples; 1 John declares that perfect love casts out fear of punishment.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul makes the fear of the Lord or of Christ a motive for holiness, mission and mutual submission, and uses 'fear and trembling' for humble earnestness.

authorNotes.author: Peter
authorNotes.note: 1 Peter calls believers to live 'in fear' during their exile and to show respectful conduct, yet not to fear their persecutors.

study.translationNote: Versions choose between 'fear', 'awe', 'reverence' and 'respect'. In Eph 5:21 KJV 'in the fear of God' becomes 'out of reverence for Christ' (NIV, ESV); in 1 Pet 2:18 'with all fear' (KJV) becomes 'with all respect' (ESV); in 2 Cor 5:11 KJV has 'the terror of the Lord'. The choice decides whether readers hear dread or reverence.

background.note: In Homer φόβος usually means panic flight in battle, not simply the feeling of fear.
After the prefect's amnesty, a letter writer reports 'there is no longer any fear at all'.
A fourth-century Christian letter speaks of 'having the fear of God in the heart', as in Acts 9:31.

study.exegesisTip: Ask what or whom is feared and what the fear produces: flight and silence, praise of God, or careful obedience.
study.caution: In 1 Pet 3:14 (quoting Isa 8:12) τὸν φόβον αὐτῶν may mean 'do not fear them' or 'do not fear what they fear'; in 2 Cor 5:11 some prefer 'terror' of the Lord's judgment to 'reverence'.

study.summary: Guard or watch: the act of guarding, the guards themselves, a prison or imprisonment, and one of the watches into which the night was divided.

senses.label: Guard, watch kept
senses.definition: The act of keeping watch, or the soldiers posted as a guard.
senses.note: Shepherds 'keeping watch' (φυλάσσοντες φυλακάς, Luke 2:8); Peter passed 'the first and second guard' (Acts 12:10).

senses.label: Prison
senses.definition: The place where people are held under guard.

senses.label: Imprisonment
senses.definition: The condition of being held in custody, often listed among sufferings for faith.

senses.label: Watch of the night
senses.definition: One of the periods into which the night was divided for sentry duty (four in Roman reckoning).
senses.note: The 'fourth watch' is roughly 3–6 a.m.

senses.label: Confinement of spirits
senses.definition: A place where evil spirits or Satan are held, or a haunt of unclean spirits.
senses.note: Babylon becomes 'a haunt' or 'prison' of every unclean spirit (Rev 18:2).

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: More than half the uses are in Luke–Acts, where apostles are repeatedly jailed and miraculously released, showing that prison cannot stop the word.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew uses the word both for night watches in calls to vigilance and for prison, where visiting 'the least' is visiting Christ.

authorNotes.author: Peter
authorNotes.note: 1 Peter speaks of Christ preaching to 'the spirits in prison'.

study.translationNote: In time expressions versions may keep 'the fourth watch of the night' (ESV) or convert it to clock time, 'shortly before dawn' (NIV, Mark 6:48). In Rev 18:2 KJV 'hold' and 'cage' become 'haunt' (ESV) or 'prison' (NASB), since the same Greek word is used.

background.note: A surety declares to 'the governor of the prison of Zeus' that he will return a debtor he bailed out of the public prison.
A report marks time 'at the beginning of the first watch', as in the Gospels.
A sister begs her brother not to face danger 'without a guard', the sense of guard as persons.

study.exegesisTip: Decide whether φυλακή names an action, the guards, a place, a condition or a time of night; Luke 12:38 is about time, Luke 22:33 about imprisonment.
study.caution: Who 'the spirits in prison' are in 1 Pet 3:19 (fallen angels, the dead of Noah's day, or Noah's contemporaries preached to through Noah) and when Christ preached to them are long debated.

study.summary: Sinner or sinful: anyone who sins against God, those publicly regarded as notorious law-breakers, Gentiles from a Jewish standpoint, and the ungodly facing judgment.

senses.label: Every person as sinner
senses.definition: A human being who has sinned and stands in need of God's mercy; in Paul all people are included.
senses.note: 'God, be merciful to me, the sinner' (Luke 18:13).

senses.label: Notorious, disreputable people
senses.definition: People publicly known for breaking the law or living immorally, and so shunned by the religious, as in 'tax collectors and sinners'.
senses.note: Also used as an accusation against Jesus for breaking the Sabbath (John 9:16, 24).

senses.label: Gentiles as 'sinners'
senses.definition: Non-Jews, regarded as sinners because they lived outside the law of Moses.
senses.note: Luke 6:32 'even sinners' parallels 'even the Gentiles' in Matt 5:47.

senses.label: The ungodly, the wicked
senses.definition: The impious who reject God and face his judgment, as in the Septuagint's use for the wicked.

senses.label: Sinful (adjective)
senses.definition: Characterised by sin, said of people, a generation, or even sin itself.
senses.note: Through the commandment sin became 'exceedingly sinful' (Rom 7:13).

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke has the most uses and highlights Jesus' welcome of sinners, his eating with them, and heaven's joy over one sinner who repents.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul turns the label against all: Jews who called Gentiles 'sinners' are themselves found sinners, and Christ died for sinners.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: In John 9 the authorities brand Jesus a 'sinner' for healing on the Sabbath, while the healed man reasons that God does not hear sinners.

study.translationNote: Versions differ on how much social meaning to show. In Luke 7:37 KJV 'a woman in the city, which was a sinner' becomes 'a woman who had lived a sinful life' (NIV); in Gal 2:15 NIV puts 'Gentile sinners' in quotation marks to show Paul is quoting a Jewish label.

background.note: Classical writers use the adjective rarely, meaning 'erring' or 'faulty'.
The Septuagint makes 'sinner' a standard term for the wicked, starting with the men of Sodom.
An inscription declares that officials who neglect a sacrifice shall be 'sinners against all the gods'.
Tomb inscriptions in Asia Minor threaten anyone who disturbs the grave: 'let him be a sinner before the gods below'.

study.exegesisTip: Ask who is using the label and why: Pharisees excluding others, Jesus calling them, or Paul including everyone; the word often carries a social judgment as well as a moral one.
study.caution: Scholars debate who 'the sinners' in the Gospels were: ordinary people who did not keep Pharisaic purity rules, or the flagrantly wicked who had abandoned the covenant.

study.summary: To marvel or be amazed: wonder at the extraordinary, surprise at the unexpected, and admiration of a person; passive, to be marvelled at.

senses.label: Marvel at the extraordinary
senses.definition: To be filled with wonder at an unusual deed or word, especially Jesus' miracles and teaching.
senses.note: Jesus himself marvels at a Gentile's faith (Matt 8:10) and at his hometown's unbelief (Mark 6:6).

senses.label: Be surprised, wonder why
senses.definition: To be surprised or puzzled by something unexpected or improper, often with ὅτι or εἰ.
senses.note: 'Do not be surprised' (John 3:7; 1 John 3:13) corrects misplaced astonishment.

senses.label: Admire, be impressed by
senses.definition: To regard a person or thing with admiration, sometimes leading to following them.
senses.note: Jude 16 θαυμάζοντες πρόσωπα, a Septuagint idiom for flattering or showing favouritism.

senses.label: Be marvelled at (passive)
senses.definition: To be the object of wonder and praise.
senses.note: At his coming Christ will be 'marvelled at' among all who have believed.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke records wonder as a frequent crowd response to Jesus and the apostles, a reaction that does not necessarily amount to faith.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John's Jesus often says 'do not marvel', redirecting surprise toward greater works; in Revelation the world marvels at the beast.

authorNotes.author: Mark
authorNotes.note: Mark notes the wonder of Pilate at Jesus' silence and early death, and Jesus' own amazement at unbelief.

study.translationNote: English versions alternate 'marvel', 'wonder', 'be amazed' and 'be surprised'. The choice matters: 'marvelled' (KJV) sounds admiring, 'were surprised' (NIV, Luke 11:38) can imply disapproval. In 2 Thess 1:10 KJV 'admired' now reads 'marvelled at'; Jude 16 KJV 'having men's persons in admiration' means 'flattering people'.

background.note: Homer uses the verb for the wonder that splendid craftsmanship will arouse.
The Septuagint idiom θαυμάζειν πρόσωπον, 'to regard a person's face', means showing partiality, which God does not do.
Letters open complaints with 'I am surprised that...', showing θαυμάζω as a formula of reproach, like Gal 1:6.
Visitors to the royal tombs at Thebes scratched 'I saw and marvelled' on the walls.

study.exegesisTip: Wonder in the Gospels is a response to revelation but not yet faith; ask whether the marvelling leads to belief, praise, puzzlement or rejection.
study.caution: Whether the crowd's wonder in Luke 4:22 is admiring or already sceptical ('Is this not Joseph's son?') is debated, and affects how the Nazareth scene is read.

study.summary: Animal, especially a wild or dangerous one; used of brutish people and, above all in Revelation, of the monstrous Beast(s) opposed to God.

senses.label: Wild animal
senses.definition: A wild, often dangerous, animal as distinct from domestic animals, birds and reptiles.
senses.note: Jesus 'was with the wild animals' in the wilderness (Mark 1:13).

senses.label: Any animal, creature
senses.definition: An animal of any kind, including a snake.
senses.note: The viper on Paul's hand is called a θηρίον (Acts 28:4).

senses.label: Brutish person
senses.definition: A person who behaves like a savage animal.
senses.note: 'Cretans are always liars, evil beasts' (Titus 1:12), quoting a Cretan poet.

senses.label: The apocalyptic Beast
senses.definition: The monstrous powers in Revelation, from the abyss, the sea and the land, that oppose God, persecute the saints and demand worship.
senses.note: The imagery draws on the four beasts of Daniel 7.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: Nearly all uses are in Revelation, where 'the beast' with its mark and image embodies state power and false worship, finally thrown into the lake of fire.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses the word for animals in Peter's vision and the viper on Malta.

study.translationNote: Most versions keep 'beast' in Revelation, but use 'wild animals' (Mark 1:13) or 'snake' (Acts 28:4, NIV) elsewhere. KJV also uses 'beasts' for the different word ζῷον in Rev 4 ('four beasts'); modern versions write 'living creatures' there, keeping 'beast' for the hostile θηρίον.

background.note: In the Odyssey the word is used of a great stag; it typically means a hunted wild animal.
An official apologises that 'we cannot catch a single animal' of those required.
A prefect rebukes a grave robber: 'you seem to me to have the soul of a beast, not a man', like the insult in Titus 1:12.

study.exegesisTip: In Revelation read 'beast' against Daniel 7, where beasts represent empires opposed to God's people.
study.caution: The identity of the beasts in Revelation (Rome and its emperors, e.g. Nero; a future Antichrist; or recurring anti-God power) is much debated, as is whether the wild animals of Mark 1:13 are a threat or a sign of restored peace.

study.summary: Temple, especially the sanctuary building where the deity dwells; used of the Jerusalem sanctuary, pagan shrines, Jesus' body, believers as God's dwelling, and the heavenly temple.

senses.label: Jerusalem sanctuary
senses.definition: The temple building proper in Jerusalem, containing the Holy Place and Holy of Holies, as distinct from the wider courts (ἱερόν).
senses.note: Only priests entered the ναός; Zechariah burned incense there (Luke 1:9).

senses.label: Pagan temple or shrine
senses.definition: A temple of a pagan god, or a model shrine.
senses.note: Demetrius made 'silver shrines' of Artemis (Acts 19:24).

senses.label: Jesus' body as temple
senses.definition: Jesus' own body, which would be destroyed and raised in three days, as the true dwelling of God.
senses.note: His opponents twisted this saying at his trial.

senses.label: Believers as God's temple
senses.definition: The church, or the individual believer's body, as the dwelling place of God by his Spirit.
senses.note: In 1 Cor 3:16 'you' is plural: the congregation is the temple.

senses.label: Heavenly temple
senses.definition: God's temple in heaven in Revelation's visions; the New Jerusalem has no temple, for God and the Lamb are its temple.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John's Gospel identifies the temple with Jesus' body, and Revelation climaxes with a city whose temple is God and the Lamb.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul applies temple language to the church and the believer's body, with a warning against defiling it.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke opens with priestly service in the sanctuary, yet Stephen and Paul insist that God does not live in hand-made temples.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew features oaths by the temple, Judas casting silver into it, and the tearing of its curtain at Jesus' death.

study.translationNote: Most English versions render both ναός and ἱερόν as 'temple', hiding the distinction between the sanctuary itself and the whole temple complex. Some (e.g. NASB footnotes, NRSV at times) use 'sanctuary' for ναός. This matters where the curtain of the ναός is torn (Matt 27:51) or Judas throws money 'into the sanctuary' (Matt 27:5).

background.note: Tragedy uses ναός, the Doric form, for a god's temple.
The Attic form νεώς appears in 2 Maccabees for the Jerusalem temple.
An inscription on the temple at Priene reads 'King Alexander dedicated the temple to Athena Polias'.
A papyrus uses ναός for the shrine in the inner sanctuary that held the goddess's image.
