study.exegesisTip: When you read 'temple', check whether the Greek is ναός (sanctuary, God's dwelling) or ἱερόν (the whole precinct); Paul's 'you are God's temple' uses ναός, the holy dwelling itself.
study.caution: Whether NT authors always keep ναός and ἱερόν distinct is debated: John 2:20 seems to use ναός of the whole building project, and Matt 27:5 may not mean Judas entered the sanctuary.

study.summary: To crucify: execute by fastening to a cross; in Paul also 'Christ crucified' as the heart of the gospel and, figuratively, putting the flesh or the world to death.

senses.label: Execute by crucifixion
senses.definition: To put someone to death by nailing or binding to a cross, the Roman punishment for slaves and rebels.
senses.note: The crowd's cry 'Crucify him!' (Mark 15:13; Luke 23:21; John 19:6) uses the imperative.

senses.label: Christ crucified, the message
senses.definition: Jesus as 'the crucified one', proclaimed as the centre of the gospel; often a perfect participle stressing the lasting significance.

senses.label: The cross as saving event
senses.definition: Christ's crucifixion as an event done 'for' others, in weakness, by human rulers who failed to recognise him.
senses.note: The apostles' speeches charge 'you crucified' him but 'God raised' him (Acts 2:36; 4:10).

senses.label: Crucify the flesh, the world
senses.definition: Figuratively, to put decisively to death sinful desires, or to be cut off from the world, through union with the crucified Christ.
senses.note: 'Those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh' (Gal 5:24).

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul makes the crucified Christ the content of his preaching and applies crucifixion to the believer's break with the flesh and the world.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew has Jesus predict his own crucifixion and that of the prophets he sends.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John concentrates the uses in the trial before Pilate, where Pilate's authority 'to crucify' is set against the authority given from above.

study.translationNote: The perfect participle ἐσταυρωμένος (1 Cor 1:23; 2:2; Gal 3:1) is rendered 'crucified' or 'him crucified' in most versions; 'the crucified one' or 'as crucified' brings out that Christ remains the one who was crucified. In Gal 3:1 versions differ: 'publicly portrayed as crucified' (ESV) or 'clearly portrayed as crucified' (NIV).

background.note: In Thucydides the verb means to fence with stakes or a palisade, from σταυρός 'stake'.
Hellenistic historians use it for crucifixion.
The Septuagint uses it in Esther for the execution of Haman.

study.exegesisTip: Note the tense: aorists narrate the event, while Paul's perfect participle presents Christ as permanently 'the crucified one'.
study.caution: The verb itself does not specify the shape of the cross; arguments from the earlier meaning 'stake' for a single upright post are disputed, as historical evidence shows Roman crucifixion often used a crossbeam.

study.summary: Deliverance, safety, preservation; in the NT above all God's rescue of his people through the Messiah, received now and completed at Christ's return.

senses.label: Physical safety, survival
senses.definition: Rescue from danger or preservation of life and health in an everyday, physical sense.
senses.note: In ACT 27:34 Paul urges the starving crew to eat 'for your survival'.

senses.label: God's deliverance of Israel
senses.definition: The rescue God promised his people from their enemies, framed in Old Testament language and fulfilled in the Messiah from David's house.
senses.note: 'Horn of salvation' (Luke 1:69) is a Septuagint image for a mighty deliverer.

senses.label: Salvation in Christ, now received
senses.definition: Rescue from sin and its consequences, given through faith in Christ and already enjoyed as a present possession.
senses.note: Often with εἰς: the gospel is power 'for salvation' (Rom 1:16).

senses.label: Final salvation still to come
senses.definition: The full deliverance believers await at Christ's return, the goal toward which present faith looks.
senses.note: 'Our salvation is nearer now than when we first believed' (Rom 13:11).

senses.label: Victory ascribed to God
senses.definition: In heavenly hymns, salvation as God's triumphant saving act, acclaimed as belonging to him and the Lamb.

senses.label: The message or way of salvation
senses.definition: Salvation as the content of the apostolic preaching: the word, gospel or way that brings people to rescue.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke opens with the Jewish hope of national deliverance in the songs of Zechariah and then shows that hope widening to the Gentiles 'to the ends of the earth'.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul holds salvation in tension between present and future: believers are to 'work out' their salvation, which is also 'nearer now' and worn as the helmet of hope.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews presents a 'great salvation' that is eternal, led by Christ its pioneer, inherited by believers and completed at his second appearing.

authorNotes.author: Peter
authorNotes.note: 1 Peter treats salvation as a future inheritance 'ready to be revealed in the last time', searched for by the prophets and grown into by believers.

study.translationNote: Most versions say 'salvation', but where the context is physical rescue they switch: ACT 27:34 is 'for your health' (KJV) or 'survival' (NIV, ESV), ACT 7:25 'deliverance' or 'rescue', and PHP 1:19 'salvation' (KJV) or 'deliverance' (ESV, NIV). The Greek word covers both, so the choice reflects each translator's view of whether spiritual salvation is meant.

background.note: In classical Greek the word means deliverance or preservation, for example of a city or army in danger.
The Septuagint uses it for God's great acts of rescue, such as the deliverance at the Red Sea, which shapes its NT sense.
Private letters regularly ask about or report a person's σωτηρία in the sense of health and well-being.
A fourth-century letter swears 'by your safety', showing how ordinary the word was in daily speech.

study.exegesisTip: Ask whether a passage views salvation as past, present or future, and whether physical rescue or deliverance from sin is in view.
study.caution: In PHP 1:19 scholars debate whether Paul expects release from prison or his ultimate vindication before God, since he echoes Job 13:16.

study.summary: Literally 'pressure'; in biblical Greek, crushing trouble or affliction — hardship, persecution for the faith, inner anguish, and the great distress of the end time.

senses.label: Hardship, trouble in life
senses.definition: Oppressive circumstances such as famine, poverty, bereavement or the burdens of ordinary life.
senses.note: James names the 'distress' of widows and orphans (Jas 1:27).

senses.label: Suffering for the faith
senses.definition: Pressure and hostility that come upon believers because of the gospel, often paired with persecution (διωγμός).
senses.note: 'Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God' (Acts 14:22).

senses.label: Inner distress, anguish
senses.definition: Emotional pressure or anguish of heart, including the pain of childbirth.

senses.label: The end-time tribulation
senses.definition: The unparalleled distress Jesus foretold before the coming of the Son of Man, and the 'great tribulation' of Revelation.

senses.label: Affliction as divine judgment
senses.definition: Distress God brings on evildoers or on those who afflict his people, in just retribution.
senses.note: Paired with στενοχωρία, 'anguish', in Rom 2:9.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul treats affliction as a normal part of Christian and apostolic life that produces endurance, brings comfort to share, is 'light and momentary' beside coming glory, and even fills up 'what is lacking' of Christ's afflictions.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John records Jesus' promise that disciples will have tribulation in the world, and Revelation makes it the shared lot of believers who endure, culminating in 'the great tribulation'.

study.translationNote: English versions spread this one word across 'tribulation', 'affliction', 'trouble', 'suffering' and 'distress'. 'Tribulation' (KJV, ESV) keeps a consistent technical-sounding term, especially in eschatological passages; NIV and others vary the word for natural English. The variation can hide that the same pressure believers face now (Rom 5:3) is named with the same word as the end-time distress (Matt 24:21).

background.note: In secular Greek the word is mostly literal: physical pressure or squeezing, as in Aristotle's scientific writing.
The figurative sense 'affliction, distress' becomes common in the Septuagint, chiefly for Hebrew ṣārāh, as when Jacob recalls God who answered him 'in the day of my distress'.
An inscription already uses the plural for the 'straits' of cities, an early non-biblical metaphorical use.
A Christian letter speaks of someone being 'in great affliction', matching NT usage.

study.exegesisTip: Note what causes the θλῖψις — ordinary hardship, hostility to the gospel, God's judgment, or the end-time crisis — before deciding how it applies.
study.caution: COL 1:24 ('what is lacking in Christ's afflictions') is debated: most see no deficiency in Christ's atoning work but the sufferings the church must still bear in union with him; whether REV 7:14's 'great tribulation' is a future period or the whole church age is also disputed.

study.summary: Small or little — in size, amount, time or distance; of people, small in stature or lowly in status, and in Jesus' teaching 'these little ones', his humble followers.

senses.label: Small in size or stature
senses.definition: Physically small, of objects or of a person's height.
senses.note: Zacchaeus was 'small in stature' (Luke 19:3).

senses.label: Little in amount or degree
senses.definition: A small quantity or degree; neuter μικρόν can mean 'a little' adverbially.
senses.note: 'A little leaven leavens the whole lump' (1 Cor 5:6; Gal 5:9).

senses.label: Lowly, insignificant in status
senses.definition: Small in rank or importance, often in the pair 'small and great' meaning everyone; the comparative means 'least'.
senses.note: 'The least in the kingdom is greater than John' (Luke 7:28).

senses.label: 'Little ones': humble disciples
senses.definition: In Jesus' sayings, the vulnerable and unimportant who belong to him, whom no one must despise or cause to stumble.
senses.note: 'One of these little ones who believe in me' (Matt 18:6).

senses.label: A short time
senses.definition: A little while, a brief interval, often adverbial μικρόν or μετὰ μικρόν.

senses.label: A short distance
senses.definition: Adverbial μικρόν, 'a little farther', of Jesus going on a short way in Gethsemane.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John's main use is temporal: Jesus' repeated 'a little while' in the farewell discourse, the brief time before his departure and return.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew gathers the 'little ones' sayings, making care for insignificant believers a mark of the kingdom.

study.translationNote: In MAR 15:40, 'James the less' (KJV) has become 'James the younger' in ESV and NIV, a different view of whether μικρός refers to height or age. 'Little ones' in Matthew 18 may be read as children or as humble disciples; most modern versions keep 'little ones' to leave both possible.

background.note: Older poetry and Herodotus often use the by-form σμικρός for the same word.
Family letters use ὁ μικρός for 'the little one', a child.
A personal name with μικρός seems to mark age ('junior') rather than height, relevant to 'James the less'.
The phrase κατὰ μικρόν means 'little by little', of money paid in small instalments.

study.exegesisTip: Decide whether size, quantity, time or status is in view; in the Gospels, 'little ones' usually signals Jesus' concern for the weak among his followers.
study.caution: Whether ὁ μικρός in MAR 15:40 means 'short' or 'younger', and whether Matthew's 'little ones' are children or disciples generally, are both debated.

study.summary: Alone, only: of a person by himself, of something as the sole one of its kind, and above all of God as the only true God; neuter μόνον means 'only, merely'.

senses.label: Alone, by oneself
senses.definition: Without company, solitary or left on one's own.
senses.note: Martha complains her sister has left her 'alone' to serve (Luke 10:40).

senses.label: Only, sole, exclusive
senses.definition: The only one(s) of whom something is true, excluding all others.
senses.note: Often reinforced: 'not ... except only' (Matt 12:4).

senses.label: God as the only God
senses.definition: Of God's uniqueness: the only true God, who alone is immortal, holy and to be worshipped.
senses.note: From Deut 6:13, 'him only shall you serve' (Matt 4:10).

senses.label: Adverb: only, merely
senses.definition: Neuter μόνον limits a verb or statement: 'only', 'just'.
senses.note: 'Only believe' (Mark 5:36).

senses.label: 'Not only … but also'
senses.definition: οὐ μόνον … ἀλλὰ καί adds a further, often greater, point to the first.

senses.label: κατὰ μόνας: privately
senses.definition: The idiom κατὰ μόνας means 'in private, by themselves'.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John uses μόνος of the 'only true God' and stresses that Jesus is never 'alone' because the Father is with him.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: In the doxologies of the Pastorals μόνος marks God's incomparable uniqueness: the only God, who alone has immortality.

authorNotes.author: Jude
authorNotes.note: Jude closes with praise 'to the only God our Saviour', and warns against those who deny 'our only Master'.

study.translationNote: English chooses 'alone' or 'only' by context, and the Greek adjective and adverb can be ambiguous. In JAM 2:24 μόνον may go with 'faith' ('not by faith alone') or with the verb ('not only by faith'); versions vary, and the wording affects how James is compared with Paul.

background.note: Homer uses the Ionic form μοῦνος for a warrior 'alone' among many enemies.
A legal document describes 'an old man and alone', i.e. without family to support him.
A letter says 'you are the only one I have as witness', the sense 'sole'.
The idiom 'not only ... but also' is everyday Greek in petitions and letters.

study.exegesisTip: Check what μόνος or μόνον restricts — a person, a thing, or the action of the verb — since its placement often decides the meaning.
study.caution: The force of μόνον in JAM 2:24 and its relation to Paul's teaching on justification by faith remain debated.

study.summary: To bring word, report or announce — especially a messenger reporting back — and, in a more solemn sense, to proclaim or declare God's name and message.

senses.label: Report back to a sender
senses.definition: Of a messenger or servant returning to tell the one who sent him what he found or did.
senses.note: The ἀπο- prefix originally suggested bringing word back from a place.

senses.label: Tell news, inform
senses.definition: To pass on news or information to others, often urgently.

senses.label: Declare openly, confess
senses.definition: To state something publicly before others, as a testimony or admission.
senses.note: The outsider at worship declares 'God is really among you' (1 Cor 14:25).

senses.label: Proclaim God's message
senses.definition: To announce solemnly what God has done or revealed, as the Servant, the Son or the apostles do.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: More than half the NT uses are in Luke–Acts, mostly in narrative reports that move the story along as news passes from one group to another.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: 1 John uses it for the eyewitness proclamation of 'the eternal life' that the apostles saw and heard.

study.translationNote: Versions render it 'tell', 'report', 'bring word', 'show' or 'proclaim/declare'. In narrative it is plain reporting, but in quotations of Scripture (Matt 12:18; Heb 2:12) and in 1 John 1:2–3 most versions choose 'proclaim' or 'declare' to bring out the solemn, public announcement of God's truth.

background.note: From Homer on, it is the regular verb for a messenger bringing tidings.
A letter-writer is distressed by what the bearer of a letter 'reported' about a release, the everyday sense of Mark 6:30.
In court proceedings before an emperor the verb comes close to the legal sense 'appeal'.

study.exegesisTip: Notice who is reporting to whom: in the Gospels and Acts the chain of reports often shows how news of Jesus spread.

study.summary: Second — in order, time or rank; as an adverb, 'a second time, secondly'. It marks the second of two in contrasts such as the second covenant, the second man and the second death.

senses.label: Second in a series
senses.definition: The next after the first in a sequence of persons, things or events.

senses.label: Second in rank or importance
senses.definition: Next in importance after the first, as with the two great commandments or the order of gifts in the church.
senses.note: In 1 Cor 12:28 δεύτερον means 'secondly'.

senses.label: Adverb: a second time, again
senses.definition: Neuter δεύτερον, τὸ δεύτερον or ἐκ δευτέρου, 'a second time', 'again'.
senses.note: ἐκ δευτέρου is a later Greek idiom (cf. 1 Macc 9:1).

senses.label: Second in a first–second contrast
senses.definition: The second of two things set against each other, where the second replaces or surpasses the first.
senses.note: Christ is 'the second man' over against Adam (1 Cor 15:47).

senses.label: The second death
senses.definition: In Revelation, final judgment in the lake of fire, beyond physical death.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews builds its argument on first and second: a second covenant and a second compartment of the tabernacle, and Christ's second appearing for salvation.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: Revelation's 'second death' is the decisive final judgment that cannot harm those who overcome.

study.translationNote: In 2CO 1:15 δευτέραν χάριν is rendered 'a second benefit' (KJV), 'a second experience of grace' (ESV), or 'a double blessing/pleasure' (NIV) — reflecting whether Paul means a second visit or two visits on one journey. In JUD 1:5 τὸ δεύτερον is 'afterward' (KJV, ESV) or 'later' (NIV).

background.note: Already in early poetry it means 'second' in the sense of a further chance: Hesiod warns that 'no second time' will be allowed.
The adverbial phrase ἐκ δευτέρου, 'a second time', appears in later books such as 1 Maccabees.
A letter lists duties 'first ... secondly', the same pattern as 1 Cor 12:28.
Second-century documents use ἐγ δευτέρου for 'a second time', as in Mark 14:72.

study.exegesisTip: When 'second' answers a 'first', ask what the contrast is meant to show — often that the second supersedes the first.

study.summary: To tie or bind — fastening objects, wrapping the dead, binding prisoners — and figuratively being bound by law or the Spirit, Satan's binding power, and 'binding' as declaring forbidden.

senses.label: Tie, fasten things
senses.definition: To tie up an animal or bundle, or fasten something at its corners.

senses.label: Wrap a dead body
senses.definition: To bind a corpse with linen strips for burial.

senses.label: Bind a prisoner
senses.definition: To bind a person with ropes or chains in arrest or imprisonment.
senses.note: Of Paul's chains in Acts 21–28; the word of God, however, 'is not bound' (2 Tim 2:9).

senses.label: Bind spiritual powers
senses.definition: Of Satan binding a sufferer through illness, of binding the 'strong man', and of the binding of angels or the devil.

senses.label: Be bound by obligation
senses.definition: To be held by a legal or moral bond, especially marriage, or constrained by the Spirit.

senses.label: Bind and loose: forbid, declare binding
senses.definition: In the paired 'bind ... loose', to declare something forbidden or binding with heaven's authority.
senses.note: Reflects Jewish usage for forbidding and permitting.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Only Matthew has the 'binding and loosing' sayings, given to Peter and then to the gathered disciples.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Acts traces Paul from binder to bound: he once bound believers, then is himself bound for Jesus' name as Agabus foretold.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses the verb for the marriage bond and for his own imprisonment, while insisting the gospel itself is unbound.

study.translationNote: In ACT 20:22 δεδεμένος τῷ πνεύματι is 'bound in the spirit' (KJV) or 'constrained/compelled by the Spirit' (ESV, NIV): versions differ on whether Paul's own spirit or the Holy Spirit is meant. In MAT 16:19 and MAT 18:18 the future perfect 'shall have been bound' (NASB) stresses that heaven has already decided; most versions simply say 'will be bound'.

background.note: In Homer the verb is used of binding captives' hands.
Curse tablets 'bind' a victim's hands, feet and tongue, illustrating the idea of spiritual binding in Luke 13:16.
A complaint reports that thieves 'bound us along with the guard'.

study.exegesisTip: Ask who binds whom and by what power — human arrest, Satan, law, the Spirit, or authority from heaven.
study.caution: The meaning of binding and loosing in MAT 16:19 and MAT 18:18 is disputed: rabbinic forbidding and permitting, church discipline and forgiveness, or binding evil powers; the future perfect tense adds a further debate.

study.summary: To pursue: to chase or drive out, hence to persecute; and positively, to strive eagerly after a goal such as righteousness, peace or love.

senses.label: Chase, drive from place to place
senses.definition: To pursue someone with hostile intent or drive them away.

senses.label: Persecute
senses.definition: To harass and oppress people, especially for their faith or righteousness.

senses.label: Pursue a goal or virtue
senses.definition: To strive eagerly after something good, seeking it earnestly.
senses.note: Often paired with 'flee' (φεῦγε ... δίωκε, 1 Tim 6:11).

senses.label: Press on toward the goal
senses.definition: Used absolutely, to run hard toward a finish line, of the Christian life.

senses.label: Run after, follow
senses.definition: To go after someone without hostility, following eagerly.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses both meanings: he once 'persecuted' the church in zeal, and now 'presses on' after Christ; he urges believers to pursue love, peace and good.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Acts centres on the risen Jesus' question, 'Saul, why do you persecute me?' — persecuting the church is persecuting Christ.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew's Sermon on the Mount pronounces the persecuted blessed and commands prayer for persecutors.

study.translationNote: One Greek verb lies behind both 'persecute' and 'pursue/press on', so English hides wordplay such as PHP 3:6 and PHP 3:12–14, where the former persecutor now pursues Christ. In ROM 12:13 'pursue hospitality' is softened to 'practice' (NIV) or 'given to' (KJV).

background.note: Sappho uses the verb of love's pursuit: the one who now flees will soon pursue.
Farm letters use it as 'press on with, hurry along' work, close to Phil 3:12–14.
A Christian amulet cries, 'Fly, hateful spirit! Christ pursues thee.'

study.exegesisTip: Look at the object: a person usually means 'persecute', a virtue means 'pursue eagerly', and no object often means 'press on'.

study.summary: Originally to serve or attend; in the NT almost always to heal or cure, especially Jesus' healings of disease and of those afflicted by evil spirits.

senses.label: Serve, wait on
senses.definition: To render service, here of worship offered to God, which he does not need.
senses.note: God is not 'served by human hands' (Acts 17:25).

senses.label: Heal disease and sickness
senses.definition: To restore the sick to health, the usual NT sense, especially in Jesus' ministry.

senses.label: Free from evil spirits
senses.definition: To heal those afflicted by unclean spirits, often linked with or alongside exorcism.

senses.label: Healing ministry entrusted to disciples
senses.definition: The authority Jesus gives the Twelve and the seventy to heal as a sign of the kingdom.

senses.label: Treat, attempt to cure
senses.definition: Medical treatment that may or may not succeed, or the proverbial 'Physician, heal yourself'.
senses.note: The woman with a haemorrhage 'could not be healed by anyone' (Luke 8:43).

senses.label: Heal a wound
senses.definition: Of the beast's mortal wound being healed in Revelation.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew repeatedly summarizes Jesus' ministry as teaching, preaching and 'healing every disease', presenting him as the Servant who bears sicknesses.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke most often uses the word, including Sabbath-healing disputes and healings in Acts.

study.translationNote: Most versions use 'heal', some 'cure' (e.g. 'cure diseases', Luke 9:1), and KJV has 'worshipped' in ACT 17:25 where modern versions say 'served'. Since classical medical usage often meant 'treat', a few commentators suggest 'treat'; in the Gospels the context shows actual cures.

background.note: Homer uses it of being an attendant or doing service.
It is standard for serving or worshipping the gods.
A medical recipe tells the doctor to lay the patient on his back and 'treat him'.
An inscription from the healing sanctuary at Epidaurus reports a boy treated and going away well.

study.exegesisTip: Note what accompanies θεραπεύω — preaching the kingdom, casting out spirits, Sabbath controversy — since healing in the Gospels signals the arrival of God's reign.
study.caution: Ramsay argued that the word strictly means 'treat medically' rather than 'heal'; this holds for some secular texts, but NT contexts usually report completed cures.

study.summary: New — fresh, unused or of a new kind, as opposed to old and worn out; in the NT the newness God brings: new covenant, new creation, new commandment, new heavens and earth.

senses.label: New, unused (things)
senses.definition: Fresh and not yet used, such as new wineskins, a new garment or an unused tomb.
senses.note: A tomb 'in which no one had yet been laid' (John 19:41).

senses.label: Novel, unheard-of
senses.definition: New in kind or unfamiliar, sometimes with a hint of the startling or suspicious.
senses.note: The Athenians loved hearing 'something newer' (Acts 17:21).

senses.label: The new covenant
senses.definition: God's promised covenant (Jer 31:31) established in Jesus' blood, replacing the first.

senses.label: New creation, new humanity
senses.definition: The new existence in Christ, in which God creates a renewed person and one new people.

senses.label: The new commandment
senses.definition: Jesus' command to love one another as he loved, new in its standard and its age.
senses.note: John calls it both old and new (1 John 2:7–8).

senses.label: End-time renewal
senses.definition: The newness of the age to come: new heavens and earth, new Jerusalem, new name, new song.
senses.note: 'Behold, I make all things new' (Rev 21:5).

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John has the most uses: the new commandment in the Gospel and letters, and in Revelation the new song, name, Jerusalem and creation.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul applies καινός to what God has done in Christ: a new creation and a new humanity, served by ministers of a new covenant.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews argues from Jeremiah's word 'new' that the first covenant is made obsolete.

study.translationNote: English has only 'new' for both καινός and νέος, so readers cannot see that MAT 9:17 puts 'new' (νέος, recently made) wine into 'new' (καινός, fresh, unused) wineskins. For EPH 4:24 versions differ between 'new man' (KJV), 'new self' (ESV, NIV) and similar, a choice about the word ἄνθρωπος rather than καινός.

background.note: Herodotus contrasts deeds 'neither new nor old', the basic sense 'new, fresh'.
The Septuagint uses καινός for Hebrew ḥādāš, including the promise of a 'new spirit' within God's people.
An ostracon speaks of οἶνος καινός, showing that in daily usage καινός and νέος overlapped.
A letter-writer goes to town to learn τὰ καινότερον, 'the news', like the Athenians' 'something newer'.

study.exegesisTip: Notice what the 'new' is set against — old garment, first covenant, old self, former things — to see what kind of newness is meant.
study.caution: The traditional distinction (καινός = new in quality, νέος = new in time) is useful but weakened in Koine; Hebrews, for example, can also call the covenant νέα, so the contrast should not be pressed in every passage.

study.summary: To live in a place as a settled resident; to inhabit. Used of people, of God's presence, of demons, and figuratively of Christ, the divine fullness and righteousness making their permanent home somewhere.

senses.label: Inhabit; be a resident of
senses.definition: To live in a town or region as one of its settled inhabitants; the participle often means simply 'the residents' of a place.
senses.note: Often with the accusative of the place ('those inhabiting Jerusalem').

senses.label: Settle; take up residence
senses.definition: To go and make one's home somewhere, or to live there as a settled resident.
senses.note: Also of evil spirits moving in and making a person their home (Matt 12:45; Luke 11:26).

senses.label: God's dwelling place
senses.definition: Of God's presence in a sanctuary, and of the denial that the Most High is housed in buildings made by hands.

senses.label: Divine indwelling (figurative)
senses.definition: Of Christ, the fullness of deity, or righteousness having a permanent home in a person or in the new creation.
senses.note: The verb stresses settled, abiding presence rather than a passing visit.

senses.label: Earth-dwellers
senses.definition: 'Those who dwell on the earth': humanity viewed as settled in this world and, in Revelation, as hostile to God and his people.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Half the NT uses are Luke's, mostly the plain participle for the residents of Jerusalem, Judea, Asia and other regions, which gives Acts its sense of the gospel reaching whole populations.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: Revelation repeatedly uses 'those who dwell on the earth' as a fixed phrase for unbelieving humanity, settled in this world, who persecute the saints and worship the beast.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul's three uses are all theological: Christ dwelling in hearts through faith, and the whole fullness of God dwelling in Christ.

background.note: In classical Greek the verb can mean to settle or colonize a city, as well as simply to inhabit a place.
Papyri use it for where a person lives, e.g. the house in a village where a woman resides.
The Septuagint distinguishes settling (κατοικέω) from sojourning (παροικέω): Jacob 'dwelt' in the land where his father had been a sojourner.
Wisdom of Solomon says wisdom will not 'dwell' in a body enslaved to sin, a close parallel to righteousness dwelling in the new creation.

study.exegesisTip: Contrast κατοικέω (settled residence) with παροικέω (living as a stranger): Hebrews 11:9 says Abraham sojourned in the promised land while 'dwelling' only in tents, and Colossians 1:19 stresses the fullness permanently at home in Christ.
study.caution: In Col 2:9 the fullness of deity dwells in Christ "bodily" (σωματικῶς): most take this of the incarnate Christ, but some read it as "in reality" (as opposed to shadow) or "as an organic whole".

study.summary: Seed: literally the seed of plants or of human procreation; usually, by extension, a person's offspring or descendants, and in Paul both Christ as Abraham's single Seed and believers as Abraham's spiritual offspring.

senses.label: Seed of plants
senses.definition: Seed sown in a field or garden, including the seed of Jesus' parables.
senses.note: In the parable of the weeds the good seed stands for 'the sons of the kingdom' (Matt 13:38).

senses.label: Generative seed; conception
senses.definition: Human procreative seed, and figuratively a life-giving principle implanted by God.
senses.note: In 1 John 3:9 'his seed remains in him' is a metaphor for God's begetting life in the believer.

senses.label: Offspring, descendants
senses.definition: A person's children or posterity, collectively, especially Abraham's and David's line.
senses.note: Usually a collective singular, like English 'offspring'.

senses.label: Christ, the promised Seed
senses.definition: The single descendant of Abraham to whom the promises ultimately point, identified by Paul as Christ.

senses.label: Spiritual offspring
senses.definition: Those counted as Abraham's (or the woman's) children by faith and promise rather than physical descent.
senses.note: Paul distinguishes physical descendants from 'the children of the promise' (Rom 9:7–8).

senses.label: Surviving remnant
senses.definition: A small surviving remainder from which a people can grow again, following Isaiah 1:9.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul turns 'Abraham's seed' into a theological question: the promise belongs to Christ the Seed and to all who belong to him by faith, not to physical descent as such.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John's Gospel records the claim to be 'Abraham's seed' as a boast Jesus does not deny physically but challenges morally; 1 John uses 'his seed' of God's life in the believer.

study.translationNote: Versions render σπέρμα as 'seed', 'offspring', 'descendants' or 'children'. 'Seed' (KJV, ESV in Gal 3:16) keeps the collective singular Paul argues from; 'descendants' is clearer English but plural, which hides the point of Gal 3:16 and the link with the Genesis promises.

background.note: Homer uses the word only metaphorically, of the 'seed of fire' kept alive in embers.
Papyri use it constantly for seed-corn, including loans of seed for the sowing season.
A private letter sends 'some good melon seeds'.
Isaiah's 'unless the Lord had left us a seed' uses the word for a surviving remnant, quoted by Paul in Rom 9:29.

study.exegesisTip: Because σπέρμα is a collective singular, ask whether a passage means one descendant or a whole line; Paul exploits exactly this ambiguity in Gal 3:16 and 3:29.
study.caution: Paul's argument from the singular in Gal 3:16 is debated: some see a rabbinic-style reading of the word, others a corporate sense in which Christ embodies Abraham's people (cf. 3:29). In Heb 11:11, since the phrase normally describes the male role, some read Abraham rather than Sarah as the subject.

study.summary: Literally 'speak well of': to praise God, to say a blessing over food, to invoke God's favour on someone, or (with God as subject) to bestow favour; the participle means 'blessed'.

senses.label: Praise God
senses.definition: To speak well of God in thanksgiving and worship.
senses.note: In 1 Cor 14:16 'blessing' parallels 'thanksgiving'.

senses.label: Say a blessing over food
senses.definition: To pronounce the customary blessing at a meal, praising God for the food and setting it apart for use.
senses.note: With an object (Mark 8:7; Luke 9:16) the food itself is said to be blessed; 1 Cor 10:16 speaks of 'the cup of blessing which we bless'.

senses.label: Invoke blessing on someone
senses.definition: To call down God's favour on a person, as a parent, priest or Jesus himself does.
senses.note: Hebrews argues that 'the lesser is blessed by the greater' (7:7).

senses.label: Bless those who curse
senses.definition: To answer insult and persecution by wishing and seeking good for the offender.

senses.label: God bestows blessing
senses.definition: With God as subject: to prosper, favour and enrich people with good gifts.
senses.note: God's 'blessing' is active benefit, not merely a kind word.

senses.label: Blessed (participle)
senses.definition: εὐλογημένος: one who is under God's favour, or the one acclaimed as coming with God's authority.
senses.note: 'Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord' quotes Psalm 118:26.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke frames his Gospel with blessing: Zechariah and Simeon bless God at the start, and at the end the risen Jesus blesses the disciples as he parts from them, and they continually bless God in the temple.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews uses blessing as a sign of rank and covenant succession: Melchizedek blesses Abraham, and the patriarchs pass on the blessing by faith.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul links blessing to the Abrahamic promise fulfilled in Christ and to the Lord's Supper, and makes blessing persecutors a mark of apostolic conduct.

study.translationNote: English 'bless' covers several Greek ideas. Versions vary at the feeding miracles and the Last Supper between 'blessed' (KJV, ESV), 'gave thanks' and 'spoke a blessing' (MSB). English 'blessed' also translates two other words: μακάριος ('blessed/happy', as in the Beatitudes) and εὐλογητός (used of God, 'Blessed be God', Eph 1:3).

background.note: In classical Greek the verb simply means to praise or speak well of, e.g. a city.
The Septuagint gives it the Hebrew sense of bārak, 'to bless', as when Rebekah's family blesses her before she leaves.
An inscription records a Jew named Ptolemaios who 'blesses God'.
The usage was not confined to Jews: a pagan inscription 'blesses' the god Pan.

study.exegesisTip: Ask who blesses whom: people bless God (praise), people bless people (invoke God's favour), God blesses people (bestows favour), and over a meal the blessing is thanksgiving to God.
study.caution: At the feedings and the Last Supper it is debated whether Jesus 'blessed' the bread itself or, following Jewish custom, blessed God for it; the texts that give the food as object (Mark 8:7; Luke 9:16) suggest the line between the two is thin.

study.summary: A part: a share or portion (and so one's lot), a part of a whole, a district or region, a party or line of business, and, in phrases, 'in part', 'in turn' or 'in this respect'.

senses.label: Share, portion; lot
senses.definition: What is allotted to someone: a share in a person or blessing, and so one's destiny or fate.
senses.note: 'Have a part with me' (John 13:8) means fellowship and participation, not a mere piece.

senses.label: Part of a whole
senses.definition: A piece or portion as distinct from the whole, or a side of something.
senses.note: Also of the body's parts working together (Eph 4:16).

senses.label: Region, district
senses.definition: In the plural, the districts or territory belonging to a province or city.

senses.label: Party; branch of business
senses.definition: A group within a larger body, or a line of trade.
senses.note: Acts 19:27: 'this trade of ours' of the silversmiths.

senses.label: Adverbial: in part, in turn
senses.definition: In set phrases: ἀπὸ μέρους or ἐκ μέρους 'partly, in part'; κατὰ or ἀνὰ μέρος 'one by one, in detail'.
senses.note: ἐκ μέρους can also mean 'individually' (1 Cor 12:27).

senses.label: Matter, respect
senses.definition: With ἐν: in respect of a matter, 'in this regard'.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses 'in part' theologically: present knowledge and prophecy are partial and will give way to the complete, and Israel's hardening is partial.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: In Revelation μέρος is a person's share in the destiny God assigns: a part in the first resurrection, in the tree of life, or in the lake of fire.

study.translationNote: Phrases with μέρος are rendered differently. Rom 11:25 ἀπὸ μέρους is 'in part' (KJV, ESV) or 'partial hardening' (NASB); 1 Cor 12:27 ἐκ μέρους is 'members in particular' (KJV) or 'individually members' (ESV); 2 Cor 2:5 ἀπὸ μέρους is 'to some extent' or 'in part'.

background.note: Classical Greek uses μέρος for one's lot or destiny, e.g. a share in a tomb.
Papyri use it of each 'party' to a contract, like the Pharisees' party in Acts 23.
A petition asks for an inquiry 'into the matter', the sense found in 2 Cor 3:10.
ἀπὸ μέρους means 'partly': doors were found 'partly burnt down'.

study.exegesisTip: When μέρος appears in a phrase (ἀπὸ μέρους, ἐκ μέρους, ἐν μέρει), translate the phrase as a unit; the meaning comes from the idiom, not from 'part' alone.
study.caution: In Eph 4:9 'the lower parts of the earth' may mean the earth itself as lower than heaven (Christ's incarnation), or the regions below the earth (a descent to the realm of the dead); both views have strong support.

study.summary: To sin: to do what is wrong in God's sight, whether against God or against another person; in John and Hebrews the present tense often stresses ongoing, habitual sinning.

senses.label: Sin against God
senses.definition: To break God's will and so incur guilt before him; often used absolutely, 'to sin'.
senses.note: The classical image of 'missing the mark' is not in view in NT usage.

senses.label: Wrong another person
senses.definition: With εἰς ('against') or ἐνώπιον ('before'): to offend or injure someone, which is also sin before God.
senses.note: Sinning against fellow believers is sinning against Christ (1 Cor 8:12); sexual sin is 'against one's own body' (1 Cor 6:18).

senses.label: Go on sinning
senses.definition: In the present tense: to continue in sin as a settled pattern of life.
senses.note: Contrast the aorist in 1 John 2:1, 'if anyone does sin'.

senses.label: Act wrongly in a matter
senses.definition: Of whether a particular course of action is wrong, as when Paul says marrying is not sin.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses the aorist for the universal fact of sin, whether with or without the law, tracing it to Adam's one act.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John rejects both the claim to be sinless and the idea that one born of God can live in sin, and distinguishes sin that leads to death.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke shows sin's confession and forgiveness between people: the prodigal's 'I have sinned' and the call to forgive a brother who sins and repents.

study.translationNote: In 1 John 3:6–9 the KJV has 'does not sin' / 'cannot sin', while the NIV and ESV render the present tense as 'keep on sinning' or 'make a practice of sinning', to avoid contradiction with 1 John 1:8–10.

background.note: Homer uses the verb for failing to obtain or losing something, as when the Cyclops recalls he would lose his sight.
The Septuagint uses it chiefly for Hebrew ḥāṭāʾ, including the cognate phrase 'you have sinned a great sin'.
A son's letter to his mother says 'I know that I have sinned', strikingly like the prodigal's words.
A private letter protests, 'I have done you no wrong'.

study.exegesisTip: Watch the tense and the preposition: an aorist marks an act of sin, a present can mark habitual sin, and εἰς names the person wronged.
study.caution: In Rom 5:12 'because all sinned' may refer to everyone's own sins or to humanity sinning in Adam; and 1 John 5:16's 'sin leading to death' is variously explained as apostasy, a sin punished by physical death, or a persistent rejection of Christ.

study.summary: Resurrection: the rising of the dead to life — above all Jesus' own resurrection and the general resurrection at the last day; once, in Luke 2:34, a 'rising' in the sense of being raised up.

senses.label: Rising up
senses.definition: A raising up or restoration (not from death), the opposite of a fall.
senses.note: 'The fall and rising of many in Israel'.

senses.label: Jesus' resurrection
senses.definition: Jesus' rising bodily from the dead, the centre of the apostles' witness.
senses.note: Also baptism saves 'through the resurrection of Jesus Christ' (1 Pet 3:21).

senses.label: Resurrection of the dead
senses.definition: The future raising of the dead at the last day, denied by the Sadducees and affirmed by Pharisees and Christians.
senses.note: A basic article of faith in Heb 6:2.

senses.label: Resurrection to life or judgment
senses.definition: The resurrection seen in terms of its outcome: to life for the righteous, to judgment for evildoers.

senses.label: Return to earthly life
senses.definition: Restoration of the dead to this life, as in the Old Testament stories.
senses.note: Hebrews contrasts it with 'a better resurrection' in the same verse.

senses.label: Christ as the resurrection
senses.definition: By extension, Jesus himself as the one who brings resurrection life.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses the word most (17×): in Acts resurrection is the core of apostolic preaching, the point of dispute with the Sadducees, and the topic that provokes mockery in Athens.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul argues that denying the resurrection of the dead denies Christ's, and warns against teaching that the resurrection has already happened.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John holds the future resurrection 'at the last day' together with Jesus' claim to be the resurrection now.

background.note: Aeschylus has Apollo say that once the dust drinks a man's blood there is no rising again, typical of Greek denial of bodily resurrection.
Classical Greek more often used it for removal or displacement, e.g. of suppliants from a temple.
Inscriptions and papyri use it for the erection of a monument or statue.
2 Maccabees speaks of a 'resurrection to life' that the wicked will not share.

study.exegesisTip: Note the genitive: 'resurrection of the dead' (the general event), 'resurrection from the dead' (rising out from among the dead), and 'his resurrection' (Christ's).
study.caution: In Acts 17:18 many think the Athenians took 'Anastasis' as a goddess alongside Jesus. 'The first resurrection' in Rev 20:5–6 is read as a bodily resurrection before a millennium or as a spiritual sharing in Christ's life.

study.summary: A generation: a step in a family line, the people living at one time (especially Jesus' unbelieving contemporaries), people of a certain kind, or by extension an age or period.

senses.label: Generation in a genealogy
senses.definition: One step of descent in a family line.

senses.label: Contemporaries; people of one time
senses.definition: All the people living in a given period.
senses.note: David 'served his own generation' (Acts 13:36).

senses.label: 'This generation': Jesus' contemporaries
senses.definition: The people of Jesus' own day, especially viewed in their unbelief and liable to judgment.
senses.note: Usually with negative adjectives: 'wicked and adulterous', 'unbelieving'.

senses.label: People of a certain kind
senses.definition: A group marked by a shared moral character, 'a crooked and perverse generation'.
senses.note: Echoes Deuteronomy 32:5.

senses.label: Age, period of time
senses.definition: In the plural, successive generations as ages of history; doubled, 'to all generations' means forever.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew concentrates 'this generation' sayings that pronounce judgment on Jesus' contemporaries for refusing him, climaxing in the woes and the discourse on the end.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses the plural for past ages in which the mystery of Christ was hidden, now revealed.

study.translationNote: Most versions keep 'generation', but Luke 16:8 is rendered 'in their generation' (KJV, ESV) or 'in dealing with their own kind' (NIV), and in Matt 24:34 some older commentators preferred 'race' (the Jewish people), a sense the word has in classical Greek but rarely if ever in the NT.

background.note: In Homer the word means race or family, 'of this race and blood'.
A will uses it of a man's issue or descendants.
The sense 'one step of descent' appears in a priest exempted 'of the fourth generation'.
The Septuagint chiefly renders Hebrew dôr, but can also use it for kindred, as when Jacob is told to return to his 'kindred'.

study.exegesisTip: In the Gospels 'this generation' is almost always a moral as well as a time term: it names Jesus' contemporaries as a body that rejects him.
study.caution: Matt 24:34 (Mark 13:30; Luke 21:32) is debated: 'this generation' may be Jesus' contemporaries (with 'all these things' fulfilled by AD 70), the generation that sees the end-time signs, or, less likely lexically, the Jewish race or 'this kind' of unbelieving people.

study.summary: To go through: to pass through a place, cross over to somewhere, travel about (often preaching), pierce through, or spread abroad like a report.

senses.label: Pass through a place
senses.definition: To go through a town, region or space on the way elsewhere.
senses.note: Hebrews 4:14: Jesus 'has passed through the heavens'.

senses.label: Go over, cross to
senses.definition: To go across to a destination: the other side of the lake, Bethlehem, a nearby town.

senses.label: Travel about, go around
senses.definition: To go from place to place through a region, often preaching or doing good.

senses.label: Pierce; pass through
senses.definition: Of things passing through something narrow or penetrating it.
senses.note: Simeon's 'a sword will pierce your soul' (Luke 2:35).

senses.label: Spread abroad
senses.definition: Of a report, or of death, spreading through a population.
senses.note: Death 'spread to all people' (Rom 5:12).

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Three-quarters of the uses are Luke's; in Acts the verb regularly describes the missionaries' journeys through regions as the word spreads.

study.translationNote: Renderings vary with context: 'passed through', 'went about', 'traveled', 'crossed over'. At Heb 4:14 the KJV has 'passed into the heavens', while modern versions have 'passed through the heavens', which better reflects the verb and Hebrews' picture of the high priest passing through to God's presence.

background.note: Homer uses it of a weapon passing right through.
A decree regulates billeting of officials 'passing through' a district.
Very common of time that has passed, 'in the past fourth year'.

study.exegesisTip: The prefix δια- usually signals movement through or across a space; in Acts the verb often summarises a missionary circuit rather than a single journey.
study.caution: W. M. Ramsay argued that in Acts the verb is almost a technical term for missionary travel; others think this presses ordinary language too far, since the verb is used of any journey (e.g. Luke 2:15).

study.summary: To loose: untie or release what is bound, set free, break up or destroy, annul a law, and (in Jesus' sayings on binding and loosing) declare permitted or release.

senses.label: Untie, loosen
senses.definition: To undo something tied: sandal straps, a tethered animal, and the seals of a scroll.
senses.note: Also 'to break the seals' of the scroll (Rev 5:2).

senses.label: Set free, release
senses.definition: To free a person or being from bonds, illness, death's grip, or a marriage tie.
senses.note: Some manuscripts of Rev 1:5 read 'freed (λύσαντι) us from our sins'.

senses.label: Destroy, break up, dissolve
senses.definition: To break something into pieces or bring it to an end: a temple, a ship, a dividing wall, the elements, the devil's works.
senses.note: Of dismissing an assembly (Acts 13:43).

senses.label: Annul, break a law
senses.definition: To set aside or treat as not binding a commandment, the law, the Sabbath, or Scripture.

senses.label: Loose (binding and loosing)
senses.definition: In Jesus' commission: to declare not binding or to release, with heaven's backing.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John uses the verb for the authority of Scripture and law ('cannot be broken'), for Jesus' temple saying, and for the Son's mission to destroy the devil's works.

authorNotes.author: Peter
authorNotes.note: 2 Peter uses it three times of the final dissolution of heaven and the elements by fire.

study.translationNote: At Rev 1:5 the KJV follows manuscripts reading λούσαντι, 'washed us from our sins', while modern versions follow λύσαντι, 'freed us from our sins'. At Matt 5:19 versions vary between 'break', 'relax' (ESV) and 'annul' for setting aside a commandment.

background.note: In Homer the verb is used of releasing a captive, as when Agamemnon refuses to release Chryseis.
Papyri use it for opening a will, a parallel to 'breaking the seals' in Rev 5:2.
It is used of the discharge of a marriage contract.
An inscription threatens a curse on anyone who 'breaks' its regulations, as in Matt 5:19.

study.exegesisTip: Identify what is being 'loosed': a bond (release), a structure (destroy), or a law (annul); the object determines the sense.
study.caution: The 'binding and loosing' of Matt 16:19 and 18:18 is explained as rabbinic language for forbidding and permitting conduct, as granting or withholding forgiveness, or as authority over evil powers; the future perfects ('will have been loosed') are also debated.

study.summary: To experience what is done to one; almost always to suffer — of Christ's passion, of believers' suffering for him, and of illness or misfortune.

senses.label: Christ's suffering and death
senses.definition: Jesus' passion, foretold in Scripture and necessary for the Messiah.
senses.note: Often 'suffer many things' with 'be rejected'; sometimes 'suffer' sums up the death itself (Heb 9:26).

senses.label: Suffering for Christ
senses.definition: Believers' suffering on account of their faith, righteousness, or the kingdom.
senses.note: Acts 9:16: 'how much he must suffer for my name'.

senses.label: Illness, harm, misfortune
senses.definition: To undergo pain, injury, or distress of any kind.

senses.label: Experience (neutral)
senses.definition: To undergo or experience something, good or bad, without the idea of pain.
senses.note: Possible, not certain, at Gal 3:4.

authorNotes.author: Peter
authorNotes.note: 1 Peter uses the verb more than any NT book: Christ suffered as an example, and believers who suffer unjustly for doing good share his path and receive God's favour.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke stresses the scriptural necessity of the Messiah's suffering, especially in the risen Jesus' teaching and the apostles' preaching.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews links Jesus' suffering with his priestly sympathy and obedience: he suffered when tempted and learned obedience from what he suffered.

study.translationNote: At Gal 3:4 the KJV, ESV and NASB have 'suffered so many things', while the NIV and NRSV have 'experienced so much'; the Galatians are not elsewhere said to have been persecuted, and the context speaks of receiving the Spirit and miracles, so a neutral 'experience' is possible.

background.note: Wills use the euphemism 'if anything happens to me' (literally 'if I suffer anything') for death.
A petitioner complains that he is 'constantly suffering violence' from a neighbour.
A Christian letter promises help 'in whatever you may suffer, God helping you'.
Amos condemns those who feel nothing over the ruin of Joseph.

study.exegesisTip: Hebrews 5:8 plays on the proverbial pair ἔμαθεν ἀφ᾽ ὧν ἔπαθεν, 'he learned from what he suffered'; the sound-play highlights that suffering was the school of the Son's obedience.
study.caution: 1 Pet 4:1 ('whoever has suffered in the flesh has ceased from sin') is debated: it may refer to Christ, to the believer who suffers persecution and so breaks with sin, or to the believer's union with Christ's death.

study.summary: To make one's voice heard: cry out aloud, crow (of a rooster), call or summon someone, invite a guest, or address a person by a name or title.

senses.label: Cry out, speak aloud
senses.definition: Without an object: to raise the voice, call out loudly, often with 'a loud voice' (φωνῇ μεγάλῃ).
senses.note: Used of Jesus' final loud cry from the cross (LUK 23:46).

senses.label: Crow (of a rooster)
senses.definition: Of an animal's cry: the crowing of the cock in Jesus' prediction of Peter's denial and its fulfilment.

senses.label: Call, summon someone
senses.definition: With a person as object: to call someone to come, have them called, or send for them.
senses.note: 'He is calling Elijah' (MAT 27:47; MAR 15:35) means calling on him for help.

senses.label: Invite as a guest
senses.definition: To call someone to a meal or banquet, i.e. to invite.
senses.note: The same verb that summons can carry the social sense of hospitality.

senses.label: Address by name or title
senses.definition: To call a person by name, or to address someone with a title.
senses.note: 'You call me Teacher and Lord' (JOH 13:13): the title stands in the nominative as a form of address.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John uses the verb for Jesus' personal call: the shepherd calls his own sheep by name, Mary is told 'the Teacher is calling you', and Lazarus is called out of the tomb.

authorNotes.author: Mark
authorNotes.note: In the Bartimaeus scene Mark repeats the verb three times in one verse, turning the summons into a moment of hope: 'Take courage! He is calling you.'

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke often pairs the verb with 'a loud voice' for solemn or urgent cries, from Jesus' last words to Paul's shout to the jailer.

background.note: Homer uses it (in the aorist) of speaking aloud, as in the formula 'so speaking, he departed'.
Council minutes record what the senators 'cried out' together, an acclamation formula.
An inscription forbids anyone to 'utter a word' during a ritual, showing the plain sense 'speak, utter'.

study.exegesisTip: Look at what follows the verb: no object means a loud cry, a rooster means crowing, and a personal object means summoning or inviting.

study.summary: Of matching weight or value: worth as much as, fitting or in keeping with, worthy of something good, or deserving of punishment.

senses.label: Equal in value, comparable
senses.definition: Weighing as much as, worth comparing with something else.
senses.note: Present sufferings are 'not worth comparing' with the coming glory.

senses.label: Fitting, in keeping with
senses.definition: Corresponding to or befitting something, appropriate.
senses.note: 'Fruit worthy of repentance' is fruit that matches repentance, not fruit that earns it.

senses.label: Worthy, deserving (good)
senses.definition: Of persons or things that merit or are fit for something good: wages, welcome, honour, acceptance.
senses.note: 'Worthy of all acceptance' (1TI 1:15; 1TI 4:9) is a Pastoral formula for a reliable saying.

senses.label: Fit to belong to Christ
senses.definition: Suited to share in the kingdom or to follow Jesus, often with the negative 'not worthy of me'.
senses.note: In MAT 22:8 those invited proved unworthy by refusing the invitation, not by lacking merit.

senses.label: Not worthy (humble confession)
senses.definition: With a negative, a confession of unfitness before someone greater.

senses.label: Deserving punishment
senses.definition: Meriting a penalty such as blows, death or judgment.
senses.note: Absolute in REV 16:6: 'they deserve it'.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: Revelation's heavenly hymns acclaim God and the Lamb as 'worthy' to receive glory and to open the scroll, after a search finds no one else worthy.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: In the mission and parable material Matthew uses 'worthy' for those fit to receive the messengers and the kingdom, and 'not worthy of me' for divided loyalty.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: The Pastoral Letters use the word for sayings 'worthy of full acceptance' and for what is due to workers, elders and masters.

study.translationNote: In MAT 3:8 and LUK 3:8 older versions have 'fruits worthy of repentance' (KJV) or 'meet for repentance', while NIV and others say 'in keeping with repentance'. The Greek means fruit that corresponds to repentance; 'worthy' can wrongly suggest earning it.

background.note: The root idea is weighing as much: in Homer a prize is 'worth an ox', and the Greeks are 'not worth one Hector'.
A complaint about robbers lists a stolen tunic 'worth six drachmas', the plain commercial sense of value.
A letter asks a favour because 'the man is worthy of it', the absolute use seen in MAT 10:11, 13.

study.exegesisTip: Ask what the genitive measures: value (Rom 8:18), fittingness (Matt 3:8), deserved good (Luke 10:7) or deserved penalty (Rom 1:32).

study.summary: To reckon: count or number among, credit to someone's account, regard as, think about carefully, judge or conclude, and occasionally plan; Paul's key word for righteousness credited to faith.

senses.label: Count, number among
senses.definition: Literally to count or class someone with a group.
senses.note: Quoting Isa 53:12: 'he was numbered with the transgressors'.

senses.label: Credit to someone's account
senses.definition: A bookkeeping term: to put something down to a person's account, whether wages, sin or righteousness.
senses.note: Love 'keeps no record of wrongs' (1CO 13:5) uses this ledger sense.

senses.label: Reckon as, regard as
senses.definition: With εἰς, to treat or count something as something else.
senses.note: The construction reflects Hebrew ḥāšab lĕ in Gen 15:6.

senses.label: Think over, consider
senses.definition: To reason out, weigh or ponder something.
senses.note: 'Think about these things' (PHP 4:8) means deliberate, sustained reflection.

senses.label: Judge, conclude, consider
senses.definition: To reach or hold a settled judgment or opinion about something.
senses.note: In ROM 6:11 believers are to regard themselves as what God has made them: dead to sin, alive to God.

senses.label: Intend, plan
senses.definition: To reckon on doing something, to purpose.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul accounts for most uses. In Romans 4 he expounds Gen 15:6 with the accounting image: righteousness is credited as a gift, not paid as wages, and sin is not counted against the forgiven.

authorNotes.author: James
authorNotes.note: James quotes the same Gen 15:6 text but links it to Abraham's faith being completed in action.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke has Jesus apply Isa 53:12 to himself: he is 'counted among' the lawless.

study.translationNote: Versions vary in Romans 4 between 'counted' (KJV, ESV), 'credited' (NIV, MSB), 'reckoned' (RV, NRSV) and 'imputed' (KJV in ROM 4:6, 8). All render one accounting verb; 'imputed' carries later theological associations, while 'credited' best keeps the bookkeeping picture.

background.note: In Herodotus it is a plain verb of arithmetic: to count, calculate.
Business documents use it for entering sums to someone's account, the sense Paul uses in Romans 4.
A camel return reports a foal 'now counted among the full-grown', a parallel to 'numbered with the transgressors'.
A petition asks who is so lacking 'in reasoning' (ἐν τῷ λογίζεσθαι), showing the wider sense 'think, reason, judge'.

study.exegesisTip: Check the construction: a dative with εἰς ('credited to him as') signals the accounting sense; ὅτι or an infinitive signals a judgment or opinion.
study.caution: Whether Paul's 'credited as righteousness' means God counts faith itself as righteousness, or credits the righteousness of another (Christ) to the believer, is a long-standing debate between theological traditions.

study.summary: A memorial: in the NT almost always a tomb or grave, especially a rock-cut tomb, including the tomb of Lazarus and the empty tomb of Jesus; occasionally a monument built in someone's honour.

senses.label: Memorial monument
senses.definition: A monument built or decorated to honour the dead, especially prophets and the righteous.
senses.note: Jesus turns the building of prophets' tombs into evidence of complicity with those who killed them.

senses.label: Tomb, burial place
senses.definition: A grave or rock-hewn tomb where a body is laid.

senses.label: Tombs as unclean places
senses.definition: Burial sites as haunts of the demon-possessed and as sources of ritual defilement.
senses.note: Unmarked graves (LUK 11:44) defiled those who walked over them unawares.

senses.label: The empty tomb of Jesus
senses.definition: The tomb visited by the women and disciples on the first day of the week and found empty.

senses.label: Graves opened at resurrection
senses.definition: The graves as the dwelling of the dead, from which they will be called out.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John uses the word most, binding the raising of Lazarus from his tomb to the empty tomb of Jesus and to the promise that all in the graves will hear his voice.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew alone reports tombs opening at Jesus' death, and sharpens the charge against those who adorn the tombs of the righteous.

study.translationNote: Older versions often say 'sepulchre', modern ones 'tomb', and some 'grave' (JOH 5:28; LUK 11:44). The Greek word, from μνήμη 'memory', means a memorial; NT authors also use μνῆμα and τάφος with little difference.

background.note: Classical writers use it for any memorial or lasting record, such as 'memorials of good and evil' left by Athens.
The Septuagint uses it for Hebrew qeber, as in Abraham's request for a burial place among the Hittites.
A papyrus mentions 'the tombs' of a village; the word is less common in the papyri than one might expect.
Herodes Atticus calls a monument to his wife a μνημεῖον while stating that it is not a grave, showing the memorial sense.

study.exegesisTip: Remember the root idea of remembrance: a tomb was a visible memorial, which gives force to Jesus' charge of honouring prophets with monuments (Luke 11:47).

study.summary: To place beside or present (offer, provide, prove), or, in intransitive forms, to stand by, be present, attend on, appear before, help, or be at hand.

senses.label: Stand by, be present
senses.definition: To stand near or beside someone; the participle means 'bystander'.

senses.label: Attend, appear before
senses.definition: To stand before a superior, whether as a servant in attendance or as one summoned before a ruler or judge.
senses.note: Gabriel 'stands before God' as an attendant (LUK 1:19); all will 'stand before' God's judgment seat (ROM 14:10).

senses.label: Stand by to help
senses.definition: To come to someone's side to support or defend them.

senses.label: Present, offer, put at disposal
senses.definition: To place something or someone at another's disposal; to offer as a sacrifice or dedicate.
senses.note: ROM 12:1 uses the term in its sacrificial sense: offer your bodies as a living sacrifice.

senses.label: Present before God or Christ
senses.definition: To bring people into God's or Christ's presence in a certain state, often at the final day.

senses.label: Prove, demonstrate
senses.definition: To set before the mind by argument, i.e. to prove a charge.

senses.label: Be at hand, have come
senses.definition: Of a time or event: to have arrived; of rulers, to take their stand.
senses.note: MAR 4:29 'the harvest has come' or 'is ready'.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses the verb for self-offering and presentation: yielding the body's members to God, offering bodies as a sacrifice, and Christ presenting his people holy and blameless.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke mostly uses the intransitive forms for standing by or appearing: angels standing beside the disciples or Paul, and attendants in courts.

study.translationNote: Renderings vary with context: ROM 12:1 'present' (KJV, ESV) or 'offer' (NIV), the latter making the sacrificial sense explicit. In 1CO 8:8 KJV has 'meat commendeth us not to God', while ESV and NIV have 'food will not bring us near to God'; the verb literally means 'present us' to God.

background.note: Polybius uses it in the basic transitive sense 'place beside', of stationing cavalry on each wing.
Guild officers guarantee to 'produce' accused members before the court, the legal sense of presenting someone.
An inscription speaks of 'presenting' customary sacrifices to the city's gods, the sense behind ROM 12:1.
A letter says the sesame crop 'is ready', supporting the sense 'the harvest is ready' in MAR 4:29.

study.exegesisTip: Check the form: present, future and first aorist are usually transitive ('present, place'), while perfect and second aorist are intransitive ('stand by, be present').
study.caution: The force of 1CO 8:8 is debated: whether food does not 'commend' us to God, does not 'bring us near', or will not determine how we are 'presented' at the judgment.

study.summary: A sheep; often an image of people as vulnerable, needing a shepherd, and especially of those who belong to Jesus the Good Shepherd.

senses.label: Sheep (the animal)
senses.definition: A literal sheep, as livestock, sacrificial animal or illustration in a parable.

senses.label: Defenceless victim
senses.definition: A sheep led to slaughter or sent among wolves: an image of helplessness and innocence.
senses.note: 'Wolves in sheep's clothing' (MAT 7:15) exploits the same image.

senses.label: Leaderless people of God
senses.definition: Israel or the disciples as a flock without a shepherd, scattered or lost.
senses.note: MAT 26:31 quotes Zech 13:7: strike the shepherd and the sheep will be scattered.

senses.label: Christ's own flock
senses.definition: Those who belong to Jesus, know his voice and follow him as their shepherd.

senses.label: Sheep versus goats
senses.definition: The righteous separated from the wicked at the final judgment, as a shepherd separates sheep from goats.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: Over half the NT uses are in John 10 and 21: Jesus is the gate and the good shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep, and Peter is commissioned to tend them.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew stresses Jesus' mission to 'the lost sheep of the house of Israel' and pictures the final judgment as separating sheep from goats.

authorNotes.author: Peter
authorNotes.note: 1 Peter describes readers as sheep that went astray but have returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of their souls.

background.note: In Homer and Herodotus the word covers flocks and four-footed livestock generally, not only sheep.
A census of livestock counts '38 sheep, of which eight are rams, 13 lambs', the ordinary Koine sense.
A letter gives orders 'that the sheep may be folded there', the everyday shepherding behind John 10.

study.exegesisTip: Read the shepherd–sheep sayings against Old Testament texts such as Ezekiel 34, Psalm 23 and Zechariah 13:7, which Jesus and the evangelists draw on.

study.summary: End: the close or termination of something, the final End of the age, the outcome or destiny of a course, the goal or aim, and also a tax or toll.

senses.label: End, termination
senses.definition: The point at which something stops or is finished.
senses.note: Christ as 'the Beginning and the End' (REV 21:6; REV 22:13).

senses.label: The End of the age
senses.definition: The final consummation of history in God's plan.

senses.label: To the end; fully
senses.definition: In set phrases (εἰς τέλος, ἕως/μέχρι τέλους): to the very end, continually, or completely.
senses.note: Context decides between 'to the end' (time) and 'to the uttermost' (degree).

senses.label: Outcome, result, destiny
senses.definition: Where something leads or how it turns out.
senses.note: 'The outcome of the Lord' (JAM 5:11) is how the Lord brought Job's case to its conclusion.

senses.label: Goal, purpose
senses.definition: The aim toward which something is directed.

senses.label: Tax, toll
senses.definition: A tax or customs duty paid to the authorities.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul often speaks of the 'end' of a way of life as its outcome (death or eternal life), and calls Christ the τέλος of the law.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews repeatedly urges holding fast confidence and hope 'to the end'.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: In Matthew 'the end' is the close of the age, and salvation belongs to the one who endures 'to the end'.

authorNotes.author: Peter
authorNotes.note: 1 Peter uses it for the approaching end of all things, the outcome of faith, the fate of the disobedient, and 'finally' (τὸ δὲ τέλος).

study.translationNote: In ROM 10:4 most versions say Christ is 'the end of the law' (KJV, ESV), while the NIV 2011 has 'the culmination of the law' and others suggest 'goal'; the word can mean termination, goal or both. In JOH 13:1 εἰς τέλος is 'to the end' or 'to the uttermost'; in 1TH 2:16 versions vary between 'at last', 'to the uttermost' and 'fully'.

background.note: Homer uses τέλος for the fulfilment or coming to pass of a wish or curse, the root idea of accomplishment.
A legal phrase 'as if the judgment had τέλος' means it was concluded and in force, illuminating 'has its fulfilment' in LUK 22:37.
εἰς τέλος appears meaning 'completely': an enterprise 'utterly ruined', relevant to 1TH 2:16.
An ostracon receipt records payment of the 'alien tax', the fiscal sense in ROM 13:7.

study.exegesisTip: Ask whether τέλος marks a stopping point, a result, or a purpose, and note the genitive: 'the end of what?' often decides it.
study.caution: ROM 10:4 is much debated: Christ as the termination of the law as a way to righteousness, as its goal and fulfilment, or both. The sense of εἰς τέλος in 1TH 2:16 ('at last', 'fully', 'until the end') is also disputed.

study.summary: The number four, used for ordinary counts and in compound numbers, and in apocalyptic texts for the four directions of the world and the four living creatures around God's throne.

senses.label: Four (simple count)
senses.definition: The cardinal number four in ordinary narrative detail.
senses.note: Lazarus' 'four days' in the tomb (JOH 11:17) stresses that death was beyond doubt.

senses.label: In compound numbers
senses.definition: As part of larger numbers such as 24, 84 or 144,000.

senses.label: Four winds, four corners
senses.definition: The four directions as an image of the whole earth.

senses.label: Four living creatures
senses.definition: The four heavenly beings around God's throne in Revelation, leading creation's worship.
senses.note: Their imagery draws on Ezekiel 1 and Isaiah 6.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: Most uses are in Revelation, where four marks the created world (four corners, four winds, four angels) and the four living creatures, alongside the twenty-four elders.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Acts uses the number in vivid narrative detail: the sheet's four corners, four squads of soldiers, Philip's four daughters, and four anchors in the storm.

background.note: Thucydides already has the dative τέσσαρσι, the form also found in Acts.
The poetic dative τέτρασι occurs in later prose including the Septuagint.

study.exegesisTip: In Revelation, four often points to the whole created order (four corners, four winds), while in narrative it is simply a count.
study.caution: How far numbers in Revelation carry symbolic meaning, and what each signifies, is debated; avoid building doctrine on number symbolism alone.

study.summary: Value set on something: a price paid, and above all honour, esteem and respect, given to people, conferred by God, or ascribed to God in worship.

senses.label: Price, sum paid
senses.definition: The amount of money paid or received for something.
senses.note: 'The price of blood' (MAT 27:6).

senses.label: Bought at a price
senses.definition: The cost of redemption: believers belong to God because they were purchased.

senses.label: Honour, respect to people
senses.definition: Esteem and respect shown to others in the community and society.
senses.note: Concretely, 'honours' as gifts or tokens of respect (ACT 28:10).

senses.label: Honour conferred, dignity
senses.definition: Honour as a status or office, especially honour bestowed by God.
senses.note: Often paired with 'glory' (δόξα) as the reward of the faithful (ROM 2:10; 1PE 1:7).

senses.label: Honour ascribed to God
senses.definition: Honour given to God and the Lamb in doxology and worship.

senses.label: Honourable use
senses.definition: In the phrase εἰς τιμήν: for noble or honourable purposes, as opposed to common use.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses the potter's image of vessels for honourable or common use, and calls believers to outdo one another in showing honour.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: In Revelation honour is part of the heavenly acclamations to God and the Lamb, regularly joined with glory and power.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews applies Psalm 8's 'crowned with glory and honour' to Jesus and insists that no one takes the honour of priesthood on himself.

authorNotes.author: Peter
authorNotes.note: 1 Peter promises honour at Christ's revelation to tested faith and to believers, and calls husbands to honour their wives.

study.translationNote: In 1PE 2:7 the KJV has 'unto you therefore which believe he is precious', while ESV and NASB have 'the honor is for you who believe'; τιμή can mean preciousness or honour. In 1TI 5:17 'double honour' (most versions) may include payment, as the following verse about wages suggests.

background.note: In Homer τιμή is the honour and standing due to a hero or god, a central value of the epic world.
A senator visiting Egypt is described as 'of high rank and honour'.
An inscription speaks of paying 'honour' to the emperor Augustus, background for doxologies giving honour to God alone.
A royal official complains that oil is sold at a higher 'price' than fixed by decree.

study.exegesisTip: Decide whether money value or personal regard is meant; in passages like 1 Tim 5:17 both may be in view.
study.caution: Some passages are disputed: whether 'double honour' (1TI 5:17) includes financial support, whether 1PE 2:7 speaks of Christ's preciousness or believers' honour, and the obscure phrase in COL 2:23 ('of no value' or 'not in any honour').

study.summary: To give thanks, especially to God: in prayer, before meals, at the Last Supper, and in Paul's thanksgivings for his churches; occasionally thanks to people.

senses.label: Give thanks to God
senses.definition: To express gratitude to God in prayer or worship.
senses.note: The Pharisee's 'I thank you that I am not like other men' (LUK 18:11) shows the form emptied of humility.

senses.label: Say grace at a meal
senses.definition: To give thanks to God over food before eating.
senses.note: Giving thanks over food sanctifies it for the eater (1CO 10:30).

senses.label: Thanksgiving at the Last Supper
senses.definition: Jesus' thanks over the bread and cup at the final meal with his disciples.
senses.note: The later term 'Eucharist' comes from this verb and its noun.

senses.label: Thanks for fellow believers
senses.definition: Thanksgiving to God for the faith and growth of others, typical of Paul's letter openings.
senses.note: Passive in 2CO 1:11: thanks may be given by many on our behalf.

senses.label: Thank a person
senses.definition: To express gratitude to a human benefactor, or to Jesus.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul opens most letters with thanksgiving for his readers, names ingratitude as a root of human rebellion, and calls for thanks in all circumstances.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
