authorNotes.note: Luke contrasts the healed Samaritan's thanks with the Pharisee's self-congratulation, and shows Paul giving thanks over bread before all on the ship.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John notes Jesus' thanks at the feeding of the five thousand, recalling it as the place 'where the Lord had given thanks', and his thanks before raising Lazarus.

background.note: The verb is rare in the Septuagint and appears only in later books, e.g. Judith's call to give thanks to the Lord who tests his people.
Early papyri use it in its older sense 'to oblige, do a favour': 'you will oblige me'.
A letter writer 'gave thanks to the gods' on hearing of a relative's health, using the ἐπί construction found in 1 Cor 1:4.
A soldier writes 'I thank the lord Serapis' for rescue at sea, showing the thanksgiving formula at the start of ordinary letters.

study.exegesisTip: In Paul's letters, read the opening thanksgiving closely: it usually previews the main themes and concerns of the letter.
study.caution: Whether Paul's thanksgiving over bread on the ship (ACT 27:35) is meant to echo the Lord's Supper is debated; most see an ordinary meal described with deliberate overtones.

study.summary: To weep aloud: the audible crying and lamenting of grief, especially over the dead, but also tears of remorse, compassion, and the distress that God promises to turn into joy.

senses.label: Mourning and lament for the dead
senses.definition: Loud, public weeping in grief, typically at a death, often paired with wailing or beating the breast; with a direct object, to weep for or bewail someone.
senses.note: Often joined with πενθέω 'mourn', θρηνέω 'wail' or ἀλαλάζω 'shriek' (Mark 5:38; John 16:20).

senses.label: Tears of remorse and repentance
senses.definition: Weeping that springs from awareness of one's own sin or failure, as in Peter's bitter weeping after his denial or the sinful woman's tears at Jesus' feet.
senses.note: James 4:9 calls for weeping as part of humbling oneself before God.

senses.label: Weeping in compassion for others
senses.definition: Grief felt for the plight or sin of others, or sharing in their sorrow.
senses.note: Jesus weeps over Jerusalem's coming judgment (Luke 19:41); Paul weeps over 'enemies of the cross' (Phil 3:18).

senses.label: Present sorrow reversed by God
senses.definition: The weeping of God's people in this age, contrasted with the laughter or joy that God will give, or held loosely in view of the passing world.
senses.note: In Luke 6:25 the reversal also runs the other way: those who laugh now will weep.

senses.label: Wailing at divine judgment
senses.definition: The anguished lament of the proud and wealthy when judgment falls on them.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke frames weeping within God's reversal of fortunes (beatitude and woe), and shows Jesus responding to weepers with compassion and weeping himself over Jerusalem.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John uses the word at the grave of Lazarus and the empty tomb, where Jesus' question 'Woman, why are you weeping?' leads into resurrection joy; in Revelation the seer weeps until the Lamb is found worthy, and the merchants weep over Babylon.

background.note: From Homer on, the verb is used of loud lament for the dead, as when Achilles tells Priam he may weep for his son Hector later.
A second-century letter of consolation says, 'I wept over the blessed one as I wept over Didymas.'
A husband tells his wife who has left him that since she went he has been 'weeping by night and mourning by day'.

study.exegesisTip: κλαίω is audible, often public weeping rather than quiet tears (for which δακρύω is used), so notice who weeps, over what, and how Jesus or the author responds.

study.summary: To hate: active hostility toward people or abhorrence of things; in Semitic idiom also to love less or set aside one thing in favour of another.

senses.label: Personal hostility toward people
senses.definition: Ill will and enmity toward another person, the opposite of love; those who 'hate' someone are their enemies.
senses.note: Jesus' command to love enemies and do good to those who hate you reverses the popular maxim of Matt 5:43.

senses.label: The world's hatred of disciples
senses.definition: The hostility and persecution that Jesus and his followers suffer from unbelieving people because of his name and their witness.

senses.label: Abhorrence of evil or of things
senses.definition: Strong aversion or rejection directed at actions, practices or things rather than persons.
senses.note: Morally good when aimed at wickedness (Heb 1:9; Rev 2:6); in John 3:20 the evildoer hates the light.

senses.label: Love less, set aside (comparative)
senses.definition: A Semitic idiom in which 'hate' means to give something lower priority or to disregard it in comparison with a stronger loyalty, not emotional loathing.
senses.note: Compare Gen 29:30–31, where Leah is 'hated' in the sense of being loved less than Rachel.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: Half the NT uses are Johannine. John sets love against hate in stark dualism: the world hates Jesus and his disciples, evildoers hate the light, and anyone who hates a brother remains in darkness and is a murderer.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke states the demand of discipleship in its starkest form, 'hate' one's own family and life, using the comparative idiom.

study.translationNote: Most versions keep 'hate' even in comparative passages such as Luke 14:26 and Rom 9:13, preserving the shock of the idiom; some paraphrases render it 'love less' or 'by comparison', which clarifies the Semitic sense but loses the sharpness of the demand.

background.note: Homer has the verb once: Zeus 'hated' (would not allow) that Patroclus' body should become a prey for dogs, showing the sense of refusing or rejecting.
The Septuagint renders Hebrew śānēʾ, which can mean relative disregard; Malachi's 'Esau I hated' is the text Paul quotes.
A fifth-century petition says that 'the laws hate those who commit injustice'.

study.exegesisTip: When 'hate' stands opposite 'love' in a choice between two loyalties (God or money, Christ or family), read it as a statement of priority rather than of emotion.
study.caution: Romans 9:13 ('Jacob I loved, Esau I hated') is debated: some read it of God's choice of nations and their historical roles, others of the election of individuals; interpreters also differ on how far the comparative 'love less' sense softens the word there.

study.summary: To lead astray or deceive; in the passive, to wander, go astray, or be mistaken. Used of lost sheep, false teachers and messiahs, Satan's deception, and self-deception.

senses.label: Wander, go astray (literal)
senses.definition: In the passive, to stray from the right path, used of sheep and of wanderers without a home.
senses.note: 1 Pet 2:25 echoes Isa 53:6, 'all we like sheep have gone astray'.

senses.label: Lead astray, deceive
senses.definition: To cause others to believe what is false, especially by false prophets and false messiahs claiming Jesus' authority.
senses.note: Jesus himself was accused of 'leading the people astray' (John 7:12).

senses.label: Satanic and end-time deception
senses.definition: The deception of the nations by Satan, the beast and false prophets, and by Babylon's sorcery.
senses.note: Also of the false prophetess 'Jezebel' leading Christ's servants astray (Rev 2:20).

senses.label: Be mistaken, err in understanding
senses.definition: In the passive, to be wrong in one's thinking about God or Scripture.

senses.label: Stray morally; self-deception
senses.definition: To wander from the truth into sin, or to deceive oneself about one's condition before God.
senses.note: The warning formula 'Do not be deceived' introduces a sober moral truth (1 Cor 6:9; Gal 6:7; Jas 1:16).

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses 'Do not be deceived' (μὴ πλανᾶσθε) to introduce a moral warning that readers might talk themselves out of, as Stoic teachers also did.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: In 1 John the danger is deception about sin and about Christ; Revelation portrays Satan as 'the one who deceives the whole world' until he is bound and judged.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew repeats the warning against deception throughout the end-time discourse, even to the point of the elect being deceived 'if possible'.

study.translationNote: English uses different words for the same Greek: 'deceive' or 'lead astray' for the active, but 'go astray', 'wander', 'err' or 'be mistaken' for the passive (Mark 12:24 KJV 'do ye not therefore err', modern versions 'you are mistaken'). 'Do not be deceived' may also be read as middle, 'do not deceive yourselves'.

background.note: In classical prose the verb means to make someone wander, as of Io driven over the earth.
The Septuagint uses the word chiefly for Hebrew tāʿâ 'wander, go astray', as in Isaiah's picture of straying sheep.
A second-century complaint speaks of someone 'injuring me much and ending by deceiving me'.
The Stoic Epictetus uses the same exhortation as Paul, 'Do not be deceived, men'.

study.exegesisTip: Check the voice: active (someone deceives others), passive (someone is led astray or simply errs), and whether a deceiver is named or the error is self-inflicted.

study.summary: A strengthened form of πᾶς: 'all, the whole, everyone, everything', often with a note of completeness ('all together', 'every bit'); a favourite of Luke.

senses.label: Everyone, all together
senses.definition: All the persons in view, without exception, often with a sense of a united group.
senses.note: James 3:2: 'we all stumble in many ways' includes the teacher himself.

senses.label: Everything, all things
senses.definition: The neuter used as a noun for the totality of things in view.
senses.note: Mark 8:25: the healed man 'saw everything (or everyone) clearly'.

senses.label: The whole, the entire
senses.definition: Used with a noun to stress the entirety of a group or thing.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: About four-fifths of the NT uses are in Luke–Acts, part of Luke's more literary style; he uses it for the united believing community ('all together', 'everything in common').

background.note: Homer describes a bowl as ἅπας silver, that is, solid silver throughout, showing the force 'wholly, entirely'.
A complaint of 89 BC says the attacker struck the writer with many blows 'on every part of my body'.

study.exegesisTip: Read ἅπας as 'all' like πᾶς; any extra emphasis ('all together, every one') must be judged from context rather than assumed from the form.
study.caution: Scholars differ on how much ἅπας strengthens πᾶς in Koine: older grammars stress emphasis, while papyrus evidence suggests the choice was often stylistic or for sound (ἅπας tends to follow a consonant). Manuscripts also frequently vary between the two words.

study.summary: A door or gate: the literal entrance of a house, room, prison, temple or tomb, and figuratively a way of access, an opportunity, or a sign that something is near.

senses.label: Door of a house or room
senses.definition: The ordinary door of a home or room, opened, shut or knocked at.
senses.note: Mark 2:2: 'not even the space by the door' was free.

senses.label: Entrance of temple, prison or tomb
senses.definition: The gate or doorway of a larger structure, including the temple gate, prison doors, and the entrance of a rock tomb closed by a stone.

senses.label: The shut door of the kingdom
senses.definition: In parables, the door into the feast or the kingdom, which can be entered now but will one day be shut.

senses.label: Christ the door; access to God
senses.definition: The way of entrance into salvation and fellowship: Jesus as the door of the sheep, Christ knocking at the door, and a door opened into heaven.

senses.label: Opportunity, opening for mission
senses.definition: An opening God provides, especially for preaching the gospel or for faith.
senses.note: Paul pairs a 'great door' with 'many adversaries' (1 Cor 16:9).

senses.label: At the doors: imminence
senses.definition: Standing 'at the door(s)' pictures something or someone very near, especially the coming of the Son of Man or the Judge.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John develops the door as a Christological image: Jesus is the door of the sheep, through whom one enters and is saved; in Revelation Christ stands at the door and knocks, and sets an open door before the church.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses the word only figuratively, for an opportunity for gospel work opened by God.

study.translationNote: Versions differ between 'door' and 'gate'. In John 10 some render 'door' (KJV, ESV) and others 'gate' (NIV), since the entrance to a sheepfold is more like a gate; the temple entrance in Acts 3:2 is usually called the 'gate Beautiful'.

background.note: From Homer on the word often appears in the plural for double or folding doors.
A man reports being attacked while 'sleeping at the door of the house which I inhabit'.
Leases often require the tenant to return the premises with 'the doors and keys' received, since doors were valuable and detachable.

study.exegesisTip: When the door is figurative, ask who opens or shuts it and what lies beyond it: salvation (John 10), mission (Col 4:3), revelation (Rev 4:1), or judgment (Jas 5:9).

study.summary: To build: literally to construct houses, towers or temples; figuratively God or Christ building his people, and believers 'building up' one another in faith and love.

senses.label: Construct a building
senses.definition: To build houses, towers, barns or a town, often in Jesus' parables about foundations and counting the cost.
senses.note: 'The builders' (οἱ οἰκοδομοῦντες) who rejected the stone come from Ps 118:22 (Matt 21:42; 1 Pet 2:7).

senses.label: Build or restore sacred structures
senses.definition: To build temples, synagogues or tombs, including Herod's temple, Solomon's house for God, and the prophets' tombs.

senses.label: Christ building his people
senses.definition: Figuratively, Christ building his community or a temple 'not made with hands', and believers being built as living stones into a spiritual house.

senses.label: Build up, edify
senses.definition: To strengthen others (or a church) in faith, understanding and love, so that the community grows.
senses.note: God's word of grace is 'able to build you up' (Acts 20:32).

senses.label: Embolden (ironic)
senses.definition: To 'build up' someone in a harmful direction, encouraging a weak conscience to act against itself.
senses.note: KJV 'emboldened'; Paul plays on the word used positively in 1 Cor 8:1.

senses.label: Lay foundations; re-establish a system
senses.definition: To build on a foundation in missionary work, or to rebuild a way of life one has torn down.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul makes 'building up' the test of conduct and of spiritual gifts in church life: love builds up, and what is done in worship should build up others rather than oneself.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses the word mostly literally, especially in parables of building and in Stephen's speech on the temple, but also of the church being built up.

study.translationNote: The KJV's 'edify' and modern versions' 'build up' translate the same verb used for building houses; 'build up' keeps the architectural picture Paul intends. In 1 Cor 8:10 the KJV 'emboldened' and modern 'encouraged' hide Paul's ironic use of the same word.

background.note: Xenophon already uses the verb metaphorically: 'build other works of friendship'.
The Septuagint renders Hebrew bānâ, including God's promise to 'build up' his people rather than tear them down.
A third-century BC papyrus speaks of digging a foundation 'so as to build'.
An early saying of Jesus on papyrus speaks of 'a city built on the top of a high hill' that cannot fall or be hidden.

study.exegesisTip: Behind Paul's 'building up' stands the picture of the church as God's building or temple, so ask how a given action strengthens the whole community, not just the individual.
study.caution: Matt 16:18 ('on this rock I will build my church') is a classic point of debate: the rock is variously taken as Peter himself, Peter's confession of Jesus as the Christ, or Christ.

study.summary: To try or test: to attempt something, to put someone to the proof, to try to trap someone, to tempt someone to sin, or to provoke God by distrust.

senses.label: Attempt, try to do
senses.definition: With an infinitive, to make an effort to do something.

senses.label: Test, prove (neutral or good)
senses.definition: To put someone to the test to discover or demonstrate what they are, including God's testing of his people and self-examination.
senses.note: Heb 11:17: Abraham was 'tested' when he offered Isaac.

senses.label: Undergo trial and suffering
senses.definition: To be tried by hardship and pressure, as Christ was and as believers are, under God's faithful limits.

senses.label: Test with hostile intent; trap
senses.definition: To question Jesus in order to catch him out or discredit him.

senses.label: Tempt, entice to sin
senses.definition: To try to draw someone into sin, above all as the work of Satan, 'the tempter'.
senses.note: James 1:14: each person is tempted when drawn away by their own desire.

senses.label: Put God to the test
senses.definition: To challenge or provoke God through unbelief, demanding proof instead of trusting him.
senses.note: Echoes Israel's testing of God in the wilderness.

authorNotes.author: James
authorNotes.note: James insists that God tempts no one to evil; temptation arises from a person's own desire, even though trials can test and refine faith.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews stresses that Jesus was tested in every way as we are, yet without sin, so he can help those being tested; it also warns against testing God as Israel did.

authorNotes.author: Mark
authorNotes.note: Mark repeatedly portrays the religious leaders 'testing' Jesus with loaded questions, after Satan tested him in the wilderness.

study.translationNote: The one Greek verb covers both 'test' and 'tempt', and English must choose. Where the aim is to prove or refine (God testing Abraham) versions say 'test'; where the aim is to cause sin (Satan) they say 'tempt'; for the wilderness story some modern versions prefer 'tested' to show it was a trial of Jesus' sonship as well as an enticement.

background.note: In Homer the verb means to make trial of someone, to sound them out.
The Septuagint uses it for Hebrew nāsâ, of God testing Abraham.
It is also used of Israel testing the LORD at Massah through unbelief.
Plutarch reports a Spartan's view that the man of many friends is proved (πειράζεται) by misfortune, showing the word's link with probation.

study.exegesisTip: Ask who is doing the testing and for what purpose (God to refine, Satan to make fall, opponents to trap, people to provoke God); that, not the verb alone, decides between 'test' and 'tempt'.
study.caution: Interpreters differ on how to reconcile God testing people (Gen 22:1; Heb 11:17) with James 1:13, 'God tempts no one': many distinguish testing for proof from enticing to sin, while others see one experience viewed from God's purpose and from the tempter's. Whether Jesus' being tempted (Heb 4:15) implies he could have sinned is also debated.

study.summary: To be more than enough: to be left over, to abound or overflow, to excel or exceed; transitively, to make something abound. A favourite word of Paul for overflowing grace and growth.

senses.label: Be left over
senses.definition: Of food or goods, to remain over and above what was used.

senses.label: Have plenty, surplus wealth
senses.definition: To have more than one needs, or the surplus itself, often contrasted with lack.
senses.note: Luke 12:15: life does not consist in the abundance of possessions.

senses.label: Abound, overflow (of blessings)
senses.definition: Of grace, comfort, thanksgiving or faith, to be present in great and increasing measure.

senses.label: Abound in, excel (of persons)
senses.definition: Of people, to be rich in or grow more and more in a quality or work.
senses.note: Rom 15:13: 'abound in hope by the power of the Holy Spirit'.

senses.label: Exceed, be better off
senses.definition: To surpass a standard or another person, or to gain an advantage.
senses.note: 1 Cor 8:8: eating does not make us 'better off'.

senses.label: Cause to abound (transitive)
senses.definition: To make something overflow, especially God lavishing grace, or to give someone more.
senses.note: A later Greek development; earlier the verb was intransitive.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Two-thirds of the uses are Paul's. He uses the word for the superabundance of God's grace in Christ and for believers' growth in love, hope, thanksgiving and good works.

study.translationNote: English varies widely ('abound', 'overflow', 'excel', 'increase', 'be left over', 'do so more and more'), so readers of a translation may miss that one verb lies behind them. Where the verb is transitive (2 Cor 9:8; 1 Thess 3:12) versions use 'make abound' or 'make increase'.

background.note: Xenophon uses it of an enemy that 'will go beyond us', outflanking a line.
Ecclesiastes asks what advantage a human has over a beast.
A second-century BC Delphic inscription provides for any surplus remaining from the interest.

study.exegesisTip: Note whether the verb is intransitive (something abounds) or transitive (God makes it abound), and look for Paul's typical source of the overflow: God's grace producing believers' abundance.

study.summary: Slanderous; as a noun, a slanderer or false accuser, and above all 'the devil', the chief adversary of God and humanity who tempts, deceives, accuses and is finally defeated.

senses.label: Slanderer, malicious gossip
senses.definition: Of human beings, a person who spreads damaging talk or false accusations.
senses.note: Only in the Pastoral Letters, in lists of vices or qualifications.

senses.label: The devil as tempter and adversary
senses.definition: Satan as the one who tempts, snatches away the word, prompts betrayal and seeks to devour believers, whom they must resist.
senses.note: Believers are told to give him no foothold and to resist him (Eph 4:27; Jas 4:7).

senses.label: The devil's power and defeat
senses.definition: The devil as holder of the power of death and oppressor of people, whose works Christ came to destroy and who is destined for eternal fire.

senses.label: Devil's offspring or agent
senses.definition: People who share the devil's character or serve his purposes, called a 'devil' or his 'children'.
senses.note: Used of Judas in John 6:70.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John stresses the devil's character: a murderer and liar from the beginning, sinning from the start; people show whose children they are by their deeds. Revelation identifies him with the ancient serpent and Satan.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: In Ephesians and the Pastorals the devil schemes and sets snares, while in the Pastorals the word also describes human slanderers.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke presents Jesus' ministry as liberation of those oppressed by the devil, after the devil's departure 'until an opportune time'.

study.translationNote: Most versions translate the noun with the article as 'the devil', while the adjective-like use in the Pastorals is rendered 'slanderers', 'malicious talkers' (NIV), or 'false accusers' (KJV, 2 Tim 3:3). The underlying meaning 'accuser' is lost in the English 'devil'.

background.note: In classical Greek the word is an adjective, 'slanderous'; Aristophanes uses the superlative of a scheming slave.
The Septuagint renders Hebrew śāṭān 'adversary, accuser' with διάβολος, as in the heavenly court scene of Job.
In Esther it is used of a human enemy.

study.exegesisTip: Keep in mind that διάβολος means 'slanderer, accuser', the Greek counterpart of Satan ('adversary'); Revelation brings the names together in REV 12:9.
study.caution: In 1 Tim 3:6–7 it is debated whether 'the judgment of the devil' means the condemnation the devil himself incurred (through pride) or a judgment brought about by him, and whether 'the snare of the devil' refers to Satan or to human slanderers.

study.summary: To declare or show to be in the right: to vindicate, to acquit or pronounce righteous (above all God's verdict on believers in Paul), to claim to be righteous, and to set free from.

senses.label: Declare righteous before God
senses.definition: God's verdict of acquittal, pronouncing the ungodly righteous through faith in Christ and by grace, apart from works of the law.
senses.note: Rom 4:5: God 'justifies the ungodly'; Rom 8:33 sets it opposite condemnation.

senses.label: Pronounced righteous at judgment
senses.definition: To be recognized as righteous in God's judgment on the basis of conduct, words, or a repentant heart.
senses.note: James 2:24: 'a person is justified by works and not by faith alone'.

senses.label: Vindicate, show to be right
senses.definition: To demonstrate that someone or something is in the right, as wisdom by its results or God in his words.
senses.note: 1 Tim 3:16: Christ 'vindicated by the Spirit'.

senses.label: Claim or acknowledge as right
senses.definition: Human verdicts: to justify oneself before others, or to acknowledge that God is just.

senses.label: Set free from
senses.definition: With ἀπό, to release from sin or from that from which the law could not free.
senses.note: Rom 6:7: 'one who has died has been freed (justified) from sin'.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Most uses are Paul's. He sets justification 'by faith' against 'by works of the law', grounds it in God's grace and Christ's death, and presents God as both just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus.

authorNotes.author: James
authorNotes.note: James argues that Abraham and Rahab were justified 'by works', insisting that genuine faith is shown in deeds.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke contrasts self-justification with God's verdict on the humble: the tax collector goes home justified, and Paul's preaching in Acts announces justification through Jesus.

study.translationNote: Most versions use 'justify'; some prefer 'declare righteous' or 'acquit' to bring out the courtroom verdict, and a few 'make righteous' or 'put right'. Where the sense is demonstration rather than verdict, versions use 'vindicate' (Matt 11:19; 1 Tim 3:16) or 'acknowledged God's justice' (Luke 7:29); Rom 6:7 is usually 'freed' or 'set free'.

background.note: Classical writers use the verb for 'deem right' or 'claim as a right'.
In the Septuagint it describes judges acquitting the innocent and condemning the guilty, the background for the NT's forensic sense.
God declares, 'I will not acquit the wicked', which sharpens Paul's claim that God justifies the ungodly.
A first-century court record uses the verb for a judge's verdict that a sum be repaid.

study.exegesisTip: Identify the setting and the judge: God's courtroom verdict (Paul), demonstration of being in the right (wisdom, God, Christ), or a human claim of rightness (Luke 10:29).
study.caution: Two debates surround this verb. First, Paul (justified by faith apart from works, Rom 3:28) and James (justified by works, not by faith alone, Jas 2:24): many see them addressing different questions, with James using the verb of demonstrating righteousness, while others see a real difference of emphasis. Second, whether Paul's 'justify' is purely a declaration of status, also includes moral transformation, or chiefly concerns membership in God's covenant people.

study.summary: To boast, take pride in, or exult over something: self-congratulation over one's own standing or achievements, or (positively) joyful confidence in God, in Christ, in hope, and even in weakness.

senses.label: Boasting in human standing
senses.definition: To pride oneself on one's own privileges, achievements or appearance, as if they gave a claim before God or others.
senses.note: The flaw is not speaking well of something but trusting in what one has received as if it were one's own (1 Cor 4:7).

senses.label: Arrogant boasting
senses.definition: Proud, self-assured talk that leaves God out of account, condemned as evil.

senses.label: Glorying in God and Christ
senses.definition: Confident, grateful exultation in God, the Lord or Christ Jesus as the true ground of one's standing.
senses.note: 'Let him who boasts boast in the Lord' echoes Jeremiah 9. In Rom 2:17 Paul grants that the Jew rightly glories in God, then exposes the inconsistency.

senses.label: Rejoicing in hope and trials
senses.definition: Joyful exultation over God's future glory and, paradoxically, over present afflictions and humble status.
senses.note: Here 'rejoice' or 'exult' is often a better English equivalent than 'boast'.

senses.label: Speaking proudly of others
senses.definition: To speak with pride and confidence about other people, especially a church's faith or generosity.

senses.label: Paul's apostolic 'boasting'
senses.definition: Paul's reluctant, ironic self-commendation in defence of his ministry, kept within God-given limits and centred on his weaknesses.
senses.note: He calls it speaking 'as a fool' (2 Cor 11:16) and turns it upside down by boasting of what shows his weakness.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Almost every NT use is Paul's, and nearly half fall in 2 Corinthians 10–12, where he answers rivals' boasting with a 'fool's boast' about weakness. Elsewhere boasting is excluded by grace but redirected to God, Christ and the cross.

authorNotes.author: James
authorNotes.note: James contrasts a right exultation — the lowly brother in his exaltation — with the evil boasting of those who plan their future without God.

study.translationNote: Most modern versions use 'boast', but the KJV often has 'glory' (e.g. 1 Cor 1:31; Gal 6:14), and in Rom 5:2–3 versions vary between 'rejoice' (KJV, ESV, NIV), 'exult' (NASB) and 'boast' (NRSV). 'Boast' keeps the link with Paul's argument about human pride; 'rejoice' or 'exult' conveys the positive, joyful confidence the same verb can express.

background.note: In early poetry the verb can mean simply to talk loudly or out of turn, then to boast or vaunt oneself.
A letter-writer protests that he does not boast about the money he has sent, showing the everyday sense of bragging.
A later papyrus speaks of boasting in vain hopes.

study.exegesisTip: Look at the object after ἐν, ἐπί or ὑπέρ: what a person boasts in reveals where his confidence lies, and decides whether the verb is condemned or commended.
study.caution: In the love chapter (1 Corinthians 13, on giving up the body) the manuscripts divide between 'that I may boast' (καυχήσωμαι, preferred in many modern editions) and 'to be burned' (καυθήσομαι, followed by the KJV); both readings have serious defenders.

study.summary: The numeral 'five', used for ordinary counts in narrative, most memorably the five loaves, and in parables and visions; it does not decline.

senses.label: Counted quantity in narrative
senses.definition: A plain count of people, things or days in historical narrative.

senses.label: The five loaves
senses.definition: The five loaves of the feeding of the five thousand, recalled later as a sign the disciples failed to understand.
senses.note: Recorded in all four Gospels; John alone says they were barley loaves.

senses.label: In parables and sayings
senses.definition: A figure within Jesus' parables and teaching, often set against other numbers to build a contrast.
senses.note: Five wise and five foolish; five talents against two and one; five sparrows for two pennies.

senses.label: A small number contrasted
senses.definition: Five as a deliberately small amount set against a huge one.
senses.note: Five intelligible words outweigh ten thousand in a tongue (1 Cor 14:19).

senses.label: In larger numbers
senses.definition: Combined with words for thousands or ten-thousands to express large totals.
senses.note: ACT 19:19: 'fifty thousand' (five myriads) pieces of silver.

senses.label: In apocalyptic vision
senses.definition: A set period or count within Revelation's visions.
senses.note: The five months of the locusts and the five kings who 'have fallen'.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew's parable of the talents repeats 'five' to describe the servant who received most and doubled it.

background.note: The ordinary Greek word for 'five' from Homer onward, indeclinable as in the NT.
Used in land records, e.g. a holding of five arourae.

study.exegesisTip: Treat the number as a plain count unless the text itself signals symbolism; the narrative point usually lies in the contrast (five loaves for thousands, five words against ten thousand).
study.caution: Some interpreters read the Samaritan woman's five husbands (John 4:18) as an allusion to the five peoples and their gods settled in Samaria (2 Kings 17), or the five porticoes of John 5:2 as the five books of Moses; such symbolic readings are disputed.

study.summary: To do or practise: to carry out deeds, especially as a pattern of conduct (often evil); also to collect money owed, to attend to one's affairs, and to fare.

senses.label: Practise as a way of life
senses.definition: To do certain things habitually, so that they characterise a person; mostly of sinful conduct.
senses.note: 'Those who practise such things' is a recurring formula in Paul's vice lists.

senses.label: Do deeds that will be judged
senses.definition: To perform actions, good or bad, viewed as accountable before God.

senses.label: Commit a crime or wrong
senses.definition: To commit an act, especially one that would merit punishment or death.

senses.label: Act against one's will
senses.definition: Of the divided self in Rom 7: to carry out what one does not intend.
senses.note: Paul alternates πράσσω with ποιέω here without a clear difference.

senses.label: Attend to, be engaged in
senses.definition: To be occupied with a task or affairs, or to act in a certain way.
senses.note: 1 Thess 4:11: 'to mind your own business'.

senses.label: Collect or exact payment
senses.definition: To exact money owed, as of tax collection or interest.

senses.label: Fare, be in a condition
senses.definition: Intransitively, to get on or be doing (well or otherwise).

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses the verb in legal settings to stress that Jesus and Paul had 'done nothing' deserving death, and that Jerusalem acted in ignorance.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses it for the conduct God judges ('those who practise such things') and for actions done 'through the body'.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John sets 'practising evil' against 'doing the truth' and 'doing good' (with ποιέω), sharpening the moral contrast.

study.translationNote: In Acts 15:29 εὖ πράξετε is rendered 'you will do well' (KJV, ESV, NIV) or 'it will go well with you'; the phrase can mean 'act rightly' or 'fare well', and a letter-closing formula of this kind may carry both senses. Elsewhere versions vary between 'do', 'practise' and 'commit' according to context.

background.note: Used of being in employment or on duty.
Used of exacting payment from sureties, as in Luke 3:13.
εὖ πράσσειν serves as a letter greeting, 'to prosper'.
εὖ πράττειν could mean both 'prosper' and 'act rightly'.

study.exegesisTip: Ask whether the verb describes a settled pattern (often present participle: 'those who practise') or a single deed under judgment, and whether a nearby ποιέω is a stylistic variant or a real contrast.
study.caution: The older claim that πράσσω denotes habitual action while ποιέω denotes a single act is too rigid; the two often overlap (e.g. Rom 7:15–19), and any contrast must be shown from context.

study.summary: A ruler or leader: political rulers, magistrates, Jewish leaders and synagogue heads; Christ as ruler of earth's kings; and Satan as 'ruler' of demons and of this world.

senses.label: Rulers of nations
senses.definition: Kings, governors and political authorities who hold power over peoples.
senses.note: In REV 1:5 the risen Christ is 'ruler of the kings of the earth'.

senses.label: Magistrates and judges
senses.definition: Local officials with judicial authority.

senses.label: Jewish leaders
senses.definition: Members of the ruling council in Jerusalem or prominent leaders of the people.
senses.note: Nicodemus is 'a ruler of the Jews' (JOH 3:1).

senses.label: Synagogue leader
senses.definition: The head or presiding official of a local synagogue.
senses.note: Jairus (LUK 8:41).

senses.label: Ruler of demons; of this world
senses.definition: Satan, as the chief of demonic powers and the one who holds sway over the world opposed to God.
senses.note: John speaks of 'the ruler of this world' who is 'cast out' and 'judged'.

senses.label: Rulers of this age
senses.definition: The powers of the present age who did not understand God's wisdom and crucified the Lord of glory.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John alone uses 'the ruler of this world' for Satan, whose defeat comes through the cross; he also notes rulers who believed in Jesus but feared to confess him.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke repeatedly names 'the rulers' with the chief priests as responsible for Jesus' death, while also saying they acted in ignorance.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul speaks of rulers as God's servants for order (ROM 13:3), but also of 'rulers of this age' and 'the ruler of the authority of the air'.

study.translationNote: The KJV's 'prince' ('prince of the devils', 'prince of this world') sounds royal in modern English; modern versions prefer 'ruler'. Jairus and the man in Luke 18:18 are 'ruler' in older versions but 'synagogue leader' or 'leader' in many modern ones, which clarifies the office but can blur the shared word.

background.note: From the participle of ἄρχω, 'ruling', used of a commander or ruler.
At Athens the archons were the chief magistrates, one of whom gave his name to the year.

study.exegesisTip: Identify which realm the ἄρχων governs — a nation, a court, the Sanhedrin, a synagogue, or the demonic world — since the same word spans all of them.
study.caution: Whether 'the rulers of this age' in 1 Cor 2:6–8 are the human authorities who crucified Jesus, spiritual powers behind them, or both, is debated.

study.summary: To serve: to wait on people at table, to care for someone's needs, to render service in Christ's pattern, to serve as a deacon, and to administer or convey something entrusted.

senses.label: Wait at table
senses.definition: To serve food and attend to guests at a meal.
senses.note: In LUK 12:37 the master astonishingly waits on his servants.

senses.label: Care for, attend to
senses.definition: To look after someone's needs, provide for or assist them, whether with food, money or personal help.
senses.note: Used of angels and of the women who supported Jesus from their means.

senses.label: Service as Christ's pattern
senses.definition: The self-giving service that marks Jesus' mission and true greatness among his followers.
senses.note: 'Not to be served but to serve' (MAR 10:45).

senses.label: Serving the needy and saints
senses.definition: Practical aid to fellow believers, including the collection for Jerusalem.

senses.label: Serve as deacon
senses.definition: To hold and carry out the recognised office of deacon in a church.

senses.label: Administer, convey
senses.definition: To administer a gift or deliver a message on another's behalf.
senses.note: The Corinthians are a letter 'delivered' or 'ministered' by Paul (2 Cor 3:3).

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke develops the table-service image: the Master who waits on his servants, Jesus 'among you as one who serves', and the dispute over serving tables in Acts 6.

authorNotes.author: Peter
authorNotes.note: 1 Peter uses the verb for administering God's grace through gifts and for prophets who served later believers by their message.

study.translationNote: Versions choose between 'serve', 'minister to', 'wait on' and 'provide for' (e.g. Luke 8:3). 'Minister' can sound like an ecclesiastical role, 'serve' can sound generic, while 1 Tim 3:10 is rendered 'serve as deacons' or (KJV) 'use the office of a deacon', because there the verb refers to the office.

background.note: Used absolutely in classical Greek for performing a service.
An apprenticeship contract binds a boy to serve and do everything commanded him.
An inscription uses the passive of drinking cups 'used in service' at a cult.

study.exegesisTip: Ask who is served and with what — food, money, personal help, a gift or a message — to decide whether the verb is domestic, practical, official or a model of discipleship.
study.caution: Some recent scholarship (notably J. N. Collins) argues that the διακον- words denote acting as a commissioned agent or go-between rather than humble menial service; others maintain the sense of lowly service, especially at table. The popular derivation from 'through the dust' is not accepted.

study.summary: Testimony or witness: evidence given in court, the testimony borne to Jesus by God and by others, eyewitness report, a person's reputation, and in Revelation the faithful witness of believers.

senses.label: Legal testimony, evidence
senses.definition: Evidence given by witnesses in a trial, which must agree to be valid.
senses.note: JOH 8:17 recalls the law's requirement of two witnesses.

senses.label: Witness borne to Jesus
senses.definition: Testimony given about who Jesus is — by John the Baptist, by Jesus' works, by the Father, and by Jesus himself.
senses.note: Jesus' self-testimony is contested in JOH 5:31 and JOH 8:13–14.

senses.label: God's testimony about his Son
senses.definition: The witness God himself has given concerning Jesus, which is greater than human testimony and contains eternal life.

senses.label: Eyewitness report
senses.definition: The reliable account of someone who saw events, especially of the Gospel's witness or Paul's testimony about Christ.

senses.label: Reputation, good report
senses.definition: What others attest about a person's character; also a statement judged true.

senses.label: The testimony of Jesus
senses.definition: In Revelation, the witness to Jesus that believers hold and maintain, often at the cost of their lives.
senses.note: Faithful witness and martyrdom are closely linked (REV 6:9; REV 20:4).

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: Most uses are Johannine. The Gospel and letters frame Jesus' identity as a trial with many witnesses; Revelation speaks of 'the testimony of Jesus' held by the faithful.

authorNotes.author: Mark
authorNotes.note: Mark uses the word only in the trial of Jesus, where false testimonies fail to agree.

study.translationNote: Most versions have 'testimony' or 'witness', but the KJV uses 'record' (e.g. John 1:19; 1 John 5:10–11) and 'report' (1 Tim 3:7). 'Witness' can mean either the person or the evidence in English, whereas μαρτυρία is always the evidence given.

background.note: Already in Homer for testimony or evidence.
A technical legal term: to serve someone with a subpoena to give evidence.
Common in legal documents, e.g. 'to give evidence' or registering a petition 'as evidence'.
An inscription honours an athlete with a record of his victories, showing the sense 'commendation'.

study.exegesisTip: Note whose testimony it is and about whom; John builds a courtroom case for Jesus' identity with a chain of witnesses.
study.caution: In Revelation 'the testimony of Jesus' (e.g. REV 19:10) may mean the testimony Jesus himself gave (subjective genitive) or believers' testimony about Jesus (objective genitive); interpreters divide, and some see both.

study.summary: The ear: the physical organ, hearing or 'someone's hearing', and above all the capacity to understand and respond, as in 'he who has ears, let him hear'.

senses.label: The physical ear
senses.definition: The bodily organ of hearing.
senses.note: Stephen's hearers 'stopped their ears' to avoid hearing (ACT 7:57).

senses.label: Hearing, reaching someone's notice
senses.definition: In idioms, what comes to or is spoken into someone's hearing, whether privately whispered or reaching them as news.
senses.note: 'Into the ear' means privately, as opposed to proclaiming from housetops.

senses.label: Ears to hear: responsive hearing
senses.definition: The ear as the faculty of spiritual understanding, calling hearers to grasp and obey what is said.

senses.label: Dull or closed ears
senses.definition: Hearing without understanding, as an image of spiritual insensitivity and judicial hardening.
senses.note: Drawing on Isa 6:9–10; Stephen speaks of ears 'uncircumcised'.

senses.label: Blessed and attentive ears
senses.definition: Ears that truly receive God's revelation, or that are told to let words sink in.
senses.note: 1 Cor 2:9: what no ear has heard, God has revealed by his Spirit.

senses.label: The Lord's ears
senses.definition: Figurative of God's attentive hearing of the prayers and cries of his people.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: In Revelation every letter to the seven churches ends 'He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches', echoing Jesus' Gospel saying.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke frames Israel's response in terms of ears: Stephen's 'uncircumcised ears', ears covered against his words, and Isaiah's word on dull hearing at the close of Acts.

study.translationNote: Idioms are often rendered by sense: Luke 4:21 'in your hearing' (ESV, NIV) for 'in your ears' (KJV); Matt 10:27 'whispered in your ear' for 'hear in the ear'; Luke 9:44 'let these words sink into your ears' or 'listen carefully'.

background.note: A petitioner says he 'turned a deaf ear' to someone, comparable to Acts 7:57.
A magic spell asks a deity to 'open my ears' to receive an oracle.

study.exegesisTip: When ears are mentioned with hearing or not hearing, the issue is usually understanding and obedience, not the physical sense.

study.summary: To come, arrive or appear: reaching a place or a person, coming on the scene publicly, arriving for official business, and once 'coming to stand by' someone.

senses.label: Arrive at a place
senses.definition: To come to or reach a town, building or region.

senses.label: Come to a person
senses.definition: To come up to someone, often to make a request, deliver a message or report.

senses.label: Appear publicly on the scene
senses.definition: Of a significant figure's coming forward in public ministry or redemptive role.
senses.note: Christ 'came' (appeared) as high priest of the good things to come (HEB 9:11).

senses.label: Arrive on official business
senses.definition: To arrive for a hearing, an inspection or an official visit.

senses.label: Come to someone's support
senses.definition: With the dative of the person, to come alongside someone in need.
senses.note: 'At my first defence no one came to stand by me.'

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Most NT uses are Luke's; it serves as his favourite literary synonym for 'come', especially in participles that open a scene ('when he arrived …').

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew uses it to introduce the public arrival of the Magi, of John the Baptist and of Jesus at the Jordan.

study.translationNote: In 2 Tim 4:16 the KJV and ESV have 'stood with me' or 'came to stand by me' and the NIV 'came to my support'; the verb itself means 'came', and the idea of support comes from the dative 'to me'. Versions also vary between 'came', 'arrived' and 'appeared' (Matt 3:1; Heb 9:11).

background.note: A common everyday word for coming or arriving, as in an urgent summons.
A letter-writer adds 'if you come, God willing', a pious formula with this verb.
Used of a court that 'comes round' on a six-monthly circuit.

study.exegesisTip: Treat the word as an ordinary 'come/arrive' unless context (a public figure's appearance, an official hearing, or a dative of support) adds more.

study.summary: Prayer: speaking to God in worship and petition, both the practice and particular prayers; also a 'place of prayer', especially a Jewish meeting place.

senses.label: Prayer as a devoted practice
senses.definition: Communion with God sustained as a habit to which believers devote themselves.
senses.note: Often paired with προσκαρτερέω, 'persist, be devoted to'.

senses.label: Particular prayers offered
senses.definition: Specific prayers, often plural, made for oneself or others and heard by God.
senses.note: Paul's formula 'remembering you in my prayers' (also PHM 1:4).

senses.label: Prayer among other requests
senses.definition: The general word for prayer set beside petition (δέησις), intercession and thanksgiving.

senses.label: Believing, powerful prayer
senses.definition: Prayer with faith that accomplishes what God promises.
senses.note: JAM 5:17 'prayed with prayer' is a Hebrew-style idiom for earnest prayer.

senses.label: House or hour of prayer
senses.definition: The temple as the house of prayer and the set times of prayer there.
senses.note: Quoting Isa 56:7.

senses.label: Place of prayer
senses.definition: A Jewish meeting place for prayer, a synagogue or an open-air site.
senses.note: At Philippi, by a river outside the gate.

senses.label: Prayers of the saints as incense
senses.definition: In Revelation, believers' prayers presented before God's throne like incense.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke shows Jesus spending the night in prayer and the early church constantly 'devoted to prayer'; prayer marks turning points.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul repeatedly assures churches of his prayers and asks for theirs.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: Revelation pictures the saints' prayers as incense rising before God and shaping events.

study.translationNote: In Acts 16:13 the KJV has 'where prayer was wont to be made', while modern versions have 'a place of prayer', following the attested use of προσευχή for a Jewish prayer-house. In Jas 5:17 the Hebraic 'prayed with prayer' becomes 'prayed earnestly' or 'prayed fervently'.

background.note: The Septuagint calls the temple 'a house of prayer', the text Jesus quotes.
A pagan father congratulates his son on his marriage 'in accordance with our common prayers', showing the word was not exclusively Jewish.
As early as 217 BC a petition mentions a garment deposited in 'the place of prayer of the Jews'.
An inscription grants a Jewish place of prayer the right of asylum.

study.exegesisTip: Check whether the word names the activity of prayer, a specific prayer, or a place; in Acts 16:13–16 it is a location.
study.caution: Matt 17:21 is absent from many early manuscripts, and 'and fasting' in Mark 9:29 is also textually uncertain; whether the 'place of prayer' at Philippi was a building or an open-air site is debated.

study.summary: To touch or take hold of: Jesus' healing touch and the touch of those seeking healing, ritual and ascetic 'touching', sexual relations, harming someone, and holding on to someone.

senses.label: Jesus' healing touch
senses.definition: Jesus' touching the sick, the dead or the fearful to heal, restore or reassure.
senses.note: Touching a leper (MAT 8:3) breaks a purity barrier; the cleansing flows the other way.

senses.label: Touching Jesus for healing
senses.definition: People touching Jesus or his garment in faith to receive healing power.
senses.note: Power goes out from him at the touch (LUK 6:19; MAR 5:30).

senses.label: Touch in blessing
senses.definition: Laying hands on children to bless them.

senses.label: Handle in ritual terms
senses.definition: Touching or handling what is regarded as unclean or forbidden.
senses.note: In COL 2:21 Paul quotes ascetic rules he rejects.

senses.label: Have sexual relations
senses.definition: A euphemism: to touch a woman, i.e. to have sexual intercourse.

senses.label: Harm
senses.definition: To lay hold of someone in order to injure.
senses.note: 'The evil one does not touch him.'

senses.label: Hold on to, cling
senses.definition: To keep hold of a person.

authorNotes.author: Mark
authorNotes.note: Mark repeatedly portrays touch as the channel of healing power, in both directions — Jesus touching and crowds pressing to touch him.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul's uses concern abstaining: from sexual relations, from the unclean, and (rejected) ascetic regulations.

study.translationNote: In John 20:17 the KJV 'Touch me not' suggests Mary may not touch Jesus at all, while modern versions ('Do not cling to me', 'Stop holding on to me') reflect the present imperative with μή, which forbids continuing an action already under way. In 1 Cor 7:1 'not to touch a woman' (KJV, ESV) is rendered by its meaning in the NIV ('not to have sexual relations with a woman').

background.note: Healing by touch is reported at the shrine of Asclepius at Epidaurus.
A Delphic inscription uses the verb for laying hold of a person in order to enslave.
A royal letter uses it of someone pressing his view: he 'kept urging it upon us'.

study.exegesisTip: Notice who touches whom and what boundary is crossed — purity, sexuality, or the power of the evil one — since 'touch' in the NT is rarely just physical contact.
study.caution: The reason for 'Do not cling to me' in John 20:17 ('for I have not yet ascended') is much debated: Mary must let go because a new relationship awaits after the ascension, or because Jesus must still go to the Father. Whether 1 Cor 7:1 states Paul's own view or quotes a Corinthian slogan is also disputed.
